stories.Headline: Sierra Leone children share AI concerns at Freetown policy dialogue
stories.Summary:
Children in Sierra Leone shared their experiences and concerns about artificial intelligence during a national policy discussion. This event took place in Freetown on November 23, 2026, to commemorate World Children's Day. Government partners and young participants gathered to inform wider discussions about child rights in the digital era. The dialogue was organized by UNICEF and three different government ministries. These participants examined how technology is already being used by the youngest users in the country.

The dialogue was held at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and involved children aged 10 to 17. It aims to feed into the global Children's Manifesto on Child Rights and AI created by UNICEF. The event will help strengthen the Data Protection and Right to Access Information Bill regarding personal data. It also informs the National AI Readiness Assessment to guide the national AI policy and strategy. These efforts seek to ensure that girls and children with disabilities are not left behind.

Mariko Kagoshima of UNICEF said that AI is already part of the present for children in Sierra Leone. She stated that responsibility for AI lies with Parliament, the government, and technology or telecommunications companies. Minister Kenyeh Barlay stressed the need to integrate children's rights into national development planning and digital investments. Minister Isata Mahoi reaffirmed the government's commitment to stronger child protection and safeguards for personal information. Minister Chernor Bah said children must be involved in shaping policies that affect their lives.

Twelve year old Halimatu said children must have a voice because today's decisions shape their future opportunities. Aissatou Diallo of the World Bank Group said children want AI taught in schools and affordable tools. Seraphine Wakana of the United Nations reaffirmed support for a digital future that is inclusive and rights-based. Children expressed worries about misinformation, privacy, cyberbullying, harmful content, and an over-dependence on new technology. They called for safe and fair access to AI instead of implementing blanket bans.

The dialogue built on a national consultation with children from various backgrounds and different levels of AI experience. Some children used AI for schoolwork, research, translation, and learning about health or the environment. The Ministry of Gender and Children's Affairs recently presented a national pledge on child online protection in Manila. This pledge was shared at the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children. UNICEF has worked for children globally for 80 years and in Sierra Leone for over four decades.

The contributions from the children will now feed into a global initiative on children's rights and AI. Future efforts will focus on digital education, appropriate privacy protections, and the creation of accessible reporting mechanisms. The government intends to use these views to build accountability into the National AI Readiness Assessment. The articles leave open how the Data Protection and Right to Access Information Bill will be finalized. They do not state when the final national AI policy and strategy will be officially adopted.

stories.Headline: Chinese hackers use AI agents to exploit zero-day flaw in medical imaging software
stories.Summary:
Amazon Threat Intelligence reported that suspected Chinese state-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to exploit an unknown flaw in medical imaging software. This activity occurred between September 8 and September 10, 2026, and primarily targeted universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The attackers utilized an open-source penetration-testing framework called Cairn to coordinate multiple AI agents. These agents were given a short instruction to obtain shell access, which they achieved by independently finding a vulnerability.

The attack targeted MONAI Label, an open-source application for AI-assisted annotation of medical images, specifically affecting versions 0.8.5 and earlier. The AI agents identified a path traversal vulnerability in a file upload function, allowing them to write arbitrary files on a server in about 11 minutes. In a subsequent session, the agents used this same flaw to establish a reverse shell with root-level privileges. Maintainers of MONAI Label published an advisory on November 18, rating the bug as critical because authentication is off by default.

Amazon attributed the campaign to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence based on script time zones and prompt language. The company traced the activity after the operators accidentally left their Cairn instance accessible on the internet without authentication. Amazon stated with high confidence that this was a zero-day flaw because no prior fix existed in vulnerability databases. Senator Mark Warner noted that AI tools are now identifying security weaknesses faster than companies can safely deploy patches.

The FBI issued a separate advisory on November 13 regarding another AI-driven framework called ARTEX used by state-aligned actors since August. Senator Warner expressed fear that companies may experience more outages as they attempt to patch systems quickly. He claimed that while many leaks may occur in a single day, systems will eventually be safer. The senator clarified that he saw no evidence that these specific cyberattacks caused recent technology outages at other major organizations.

stories.Headline: Mississippi residents seek transparency over a 20 billion dollar AI data center project
stories.Summary:
Governor Tate Reeves told business executives last week that people deserved answers regarding the data center boom in Mississippi. Residents of Southaven spent over a year seeking information before the governor spoke at a Detroit forum in November 2026. A chemical coolant spill occurred at a SpaceXAI worksite a few days before the governor spoke to the leaders. State regulators rejected a resident challenge to an air permit for gas turbines four days before that specific event. These turbines will power a data center hub that is 2.5 million square feet and straddles the state border.

The project involves 41 permanent gas turbines and a 20 billion dollar investment announced by Reeves in January 2026. The development includes two new Southaven data centers called Gun Range and Spam, which replace a training ground and plant. MZX Tech and the Musk Foundation gave 3.23 million dollars to Southaven police while the city approved the agreements. One specific donation from MZX Tech totaled 1.38 million dollars, which Mayor Darren Musselwhite called an unrelated transaction. Property records show more than 20 residents sold homes among 420 offers to avoid a class action lawsuit.

Governor Reeves claimed there are legitimate answers to questions but blamed foreign adversaries like China for spreading online misinformation. Mayor Darren Musselwhite called the project game-changing and claimed the company is an outstanding corporate citizen regarding environmental sensitivity. Alderman William Jerome stated he signed a nondisclosure agreement before the development was revealed to the general public. The company's lawyers argued that the air permit complied with state and federal law after an extensive review. MDEQ declined to comment on research regarding nitrogen dioxide pollution levels found by scientists from the Massachusetts Institute.

Shannon Samsa of the Safe and Sound Coalition said there are no believable answers to basic questions about the projects. Jason Haley, a lead plaintiff in a lawsuit, said the mayor views community meetings as nothing more than political theater. Haley reported that his house shakes and he hears a constant droning noise from the power plant every day. Residents of Southaven claim they only learn about construction or government approvals after the processes are already well underway. The NAACP and Young, Gifted and Green argued that regulators relied on inadequate pollution modeling for the turbines.

The state passed legislation in 2024 to accelerate utility construction and allow certain Entergy Mississippi and Amazon terms to remain confidential. MDEQ allowed temporary methane gas turbines to operate without permits by claiming they were mobile sources under federal regulations. A September study by MIT and Carbon Mapper estimated nitrogen dioxide was 50 percent higher near the plant. Researchers estimated temporary units released 19 times more pollution per hour than the planned permanent turbines with pollution controls. Documents gathered by Samsa show two Southaven data center sites consumed tens of millions of gallons of water.

The MDEQ permit board rejected the appeal regarding the permanent turbines after two days of testimony from the involved parties. U.S. District Judge Debra Brown ruled that the temporary turbines were not mobile sources and required official air permits. The House is expected to pass a federal permitting bill in December that may ease permission for major projects. MDEQ responded that the judge's order did not bind the agency because the agency was not a party. The articles leave open whether the public will ever see the confidential electricity rates or the utility contracts.

stories.Headline: Tidal bans wholly AI-generated music from December 9 and removes 29 million tracks
stories.Summary:
Tidal announced on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, that it will ban wholly AI-generated music from its platform, with the company saying such tracks will be “rejected and removed” starting December 9. The streamer, a formerly artist-backed service once controlled by Jack Dorsey’s Block, announced the complete ban in a post on X. Tidal cited a massive surge of artificially created music as the reason for the move. The company said any wholly AI track detected on the platform as of that date will be rejected and removed. Tidal said it was taking an aggressive stand against AI.

Tidal said that in the past 90 days, 43% of all tracks on its platform have been detected as wholly AI-generated. The company said it labeled those tracks, a step many other companies have also been taking, and removed them from its royalty pool. On November 6, Tidal added, “we had the greatest influx of AI music yet: Over 60% of the deliveries we received were wholly AI generated.” Tidal estimates that 27 million tracks, about 6% of the total in its catalog, are tagged as AI. Tidal said 96% of those titles received zero streams over the past 90 days.

Robert Andersen, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, wrote in an X thread on Tuesday that 43% of tracks distributed to Tidal in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated and that something more drastic needs to be done. Andersen said Tidal will begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from its catalog and that they will be completely gone by the beginning of the year. He said the move will cleave the platform of 29 million tracks and have it reject between 80,000 and 85,000 songs a day. Andersen said he believes the move “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.” He wrote, “We encourage our peers to follow suit.”

Tidal wrote that wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists diverts streams and royalties away from artists and confuses fans. The company said it has taken down over 65,000 tracks flagged for suspected artist-name impersonation. Tidal wrote that not all songs catch on immediately and artists should have time to build their fanbases, but that at this scale the authentic music and artists subscribers seek get buried. Variety reported that the move makes Tidal the first music streaming platform to ban AI music entirely, a claim attributed to the publication. Competitors such as Spotify and Apple Music continue to test approaches to combat the rise of AI-generated tracks.

The ban comes nearly five months after Tidal said it would demonetize any AI-powered song, force those artists to label their tracks as either AI-generated or AI-assisted, and ban AI songs associated with “fraudulent activity,” a category including songs impersonating established artists and efforts to “deceive listeners.” Apple Music said it would also begin labeling AI-generated or AI-assisted tracks on its platform. Spotify said it would label artists it deemed AI creations as an “AI Persona.” Spotify said in a blog post last month that it removed 50 million slop or spam tracks from users’ recommendations this year, after removing 75 million of those songs from its catalog entirely. Spotify added that the work isn’t finished and that AI moves fast and bad actors adapt just as fast.

Tidal said the removals will begin December 9, and Andersen said the tracks will be completely gone by the beginning of the year. The articles do not say what will happen to AI-assisted tracks under the new ban. The articles do not say how Tidal will detect wholly AI-generated tracks after December 9. The articles do not say whether Tidal will reverse the ban or how it will treat artists whose tracks are removed. The articles do not say whether any other platform has committed to a complete ban.

stories.Headline: Kobre & Kim co-founder Michael Kim says small firm size speeds AI tool deployment
stories.Summary:
Kobre & Kim, a global litigation firm with 118 lawyers, has built about a dozen proprietary AI tools and has been testing them over the past six months, firm co-founder Michael Kim said. The firm is trying to use its small size compared with Big Law to deploy AI tools rapidly and gain efficiencies faster than its larger counterparts. So far the tools' analysis performs on par with a senior associate and reduces time spent on some client matters from weeks to days, according to Kim. Clients have already shown interest in paying premiums for AI-assisted work product, Kim said. The effort reflects a bet by boutique and specialized firms that being small lets them move faster on AI than Big Law.

Kobre & Kim's tools have been tested in the past six months, and the firm says the analysis they produce matches a senior associate while cutting some client work from weeks to days. Kim said clients have demonstrated interest in paying premiums for AI-assisted work product. The articles do not give the cost of the tools or the names of clients. Kim, the firm's co-founder, is the person the articles identify as responsible for describing the work, and he said the tools' analysis performs on par with a senior associate. He also said the tools reduce time spent on some client matters from weeks to days.

He said clients have already demonstrated interest in paying premiums for AI-assisted work product. The articles do not say who at the firm built the tools or who oversees them. A separate sponsored piece says rapid advances in AI are enabling small boutique advisory firms to build in-house tools, bring outsourced services inside and deliver more personalized support, according to Tom Steelman, a principal at the Helmstar Group. stories.Headline: First Amendment experts debate whether AI speech deserves constitutional protection
stories.Summary:
Vanderbilt Law School’s Respectfully Dissent debate series hosted its fourth debate, titled “Silicon Speech: Should the First Amendment Protect Artificial Intelligence? ,  A Respectfully Dissent Series Debate,” on November 23, 2026. Three First Amendment experts faced off on whether and to what extent AI speech is constitutionally protected from government regulation. The debate was moderated by Professor and Associate Dean of Research Jennifer Shinall. The debate featured Eugene Volokh of The Hoover Institution at Stanford University, Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law, and Francesca Procaccini of Vanderbilt Law.

The debate kicked off with each professor explaining their initial position on AI speech rights. Volokh argued that government regulations of AI outputs should be subject to the same First Amendment rules as other speech, because users of AI have rights. He noted that rules do not limit the rights of camera manufacturers when people record in public places. He said AI output is a joint effort on the part of the user and the AI company and should be protected precisely because of that. He described rights as a speaker trying to generate things to communicate to the public and rights as a listener and information gatherer.

Tsesis argued that large language models lack the consciousness, intentionality, and reasoning of the human mind, so AI should preserve the rights of natural speakers. Tsesis said legislatures should have meaningful latitude to require human oversight. He contended that in light of the dangers of new generative AI technology, federal laws should require periodic but consistent and random platform monitoring, restrict data scraping, and establish safeguards against intrusions from autonomous, machine-made decisions into private matters. He said any restriction on AI in the US will likely be subject to stringent First Amendment review in a reductive, formalistic, judicial environment where content restriction is subject to strict scrutiny analysis. He emphasized that freedom of speech should only be afforded to humans and not to LLMs, which lack empathy, dignity, and individuality.

Procaccini offered a middle ground. Procaccini suggested that the problems of AI can be addressed doctrinally without sacrificing its potential by drawing on something distinct in First Amendment law: distinguishing between coverage and protection. She advocated for a model whereby First Amendment rights can attach to AI-generated content without a strict-scrutiny-style level of protection traditionally reserved for people. She described a different level of protection that focuses on the context-specific harms of AI, from autonomy to privacy, while preserving AI’s democratic-enhancing features. She argued this position is the best option because it focuses less on the nature of the speaker and more on the nature of the law regulating speech.

Defending his position, Tsesis addressed whether intentional human usage of AI should fall outside of speech restrictions. Tsesis established that significant AI progress is achieved independently of human programmers and thus would not fall under the First Amendment. He said that when people are involved in the development process, AI content should still be regulated. He said that even when humans are in the loop, the civic and commercial benefits of these technologies go hand in hand with the risk generated by deep fakes, subliminal messaging, real-time unauthorized facial recognition, social scoring, stereotyping, and exploitation of economic and social vulnerabilities such as age, race, and sexual orientation. He said human audiences’ interest in AI cannot be the final say, just as it cannot be in securities regulations and antitrust provisions.

Procaccini echoed Tsesis’s concern about generative AI running unregulated but cautioned against overlooking the constitutional and democratic value AI outputs can provide. Procaccini said the value is in the ideas shared and that is still something worth protecting as long as it is protected in a tailored way. She also emphasized concerns about the potential for censorship and suppression if regulations are made without intention. Volokh argued that each concern about AI should be viewed through current laws that perform quite well without restricting speech. He offered an example of AI using discriminatory algorithms for sales or employment.

He noted there is no First Amendment problem with telling AI not to discriminate, just as there is not one with telling an employer to do the same. Posed with how to build a First Amendment doctrine that is not highly subjective or policy-laden, Procaccini emphasized the current complexity of speech restrictions. She disputed that characterization of the doctrine and said First Amendment doctrine is not tiered in the traditional way. She said each speech context is governed by its own very contextual speech doctrine, and most of those free speech doctrines provide some level of intermediate scrutiny. She said what she is doing is nothing different from a very proud and workable tradition of free speech protection.

She highlighted how free speech functions differently in schools, government offices, private workplaces, and beyond. Procaccini said AI-generated content would fall under its own epistemic context, like those spaces. Volokh argued that Procaccini’s doctrine would set up new rules that would depart substantially from current ones, creating confusing restrictions with unknown consequences. Tsesis also critiqued Procaccini’s approach, noting that AI has a number of other regulations dealing with content, including rules on disclosure requirements and intermediate scrutiny in commercial speech areas, that would not necessarily be covered by a doctrine. Volokh addressed how his stance would balance and address harmful AI outputs.

He emphasized again that while AI does not have rights, companies have rights to promote the messages they want, and users have rights to generate the information they want without undue interference by the government. Volokh agreed with Procaccini on the already complicated nature of First Amendment law, underscoring libel laws, rights of minors, and malpractice regulation for lawyers and doctors that could also apply to AI. He said First Amendment law already has a lot of rules that allow certain kinds of restrictions and they just have the advantage of familiarity. He said it is not buying a pig in the poke and we know roughly where they are and the problems with them.

Tsesis circled back again to how AI is a computational model, whereas minds are semantic. He said programs are not sufficient enough to be minds and thus should not be controlled by the value of speech. Procaccini cautioned against accepting that traditional legal claims might get at the harms and risks of AI. She said traditional property law, civil rights law, and tort law are bodies of law she has a track record of seeing the Supreme Court manipulate when they run up against the First Amendment.

She asked what is to say that the court won’t take all of these traditional 1L class legal claims and remove them from our toolkit. She also plainly said that some dangerous speech should be regulated in a checked way. She said uncertainty of those regulations should not be the death to a new and exciting doctrine for the First Amendment. The Respectfully Dissent series presents renowned national scholars on opposing sides of a particular issue.

The goal of the series is to highlight cutting-edge perspectives that draw out diverging, fresh viewpoints, areas of contention as well as agreement, and lawyerly argument, while always ensuring respectful dialogue between participants. The full lecture can be watched below or on YouTube. The article was written by Shyla Lensing on November 23, 2026, at 9:29 AM. The article was published on law.vanderbilt.edu at 15:30:20Z on November 23, 2026.

stories.Headline: Experts urge caution before linking bank accounts to AI tools
stories.Summary:
As of November 2026, privacy and security experts are urging caution about giving AI tools access to your bank and financial accounts, according to Utah State University. The guidance comes as new tools such as ChatGPT Finance may lead people to wonder whether to link their accounts and let AI weigh in on their budget, credit, or savings and investment plans. Stanford Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence says AI is advancing faster than the testing meant to keep it responsible, which the article offers as one reason to be careful with your money and information. Financial institutions advise keeping account numbers, passwords, and statements out of AI chats.

The article lists four things to consider before linking an account. First, keep your sign-in information private and never type a password or log in to an AI chat, because linking an account means trusting a third party with your financial data under that company's privacy policy. Second, stay in control of your accounts, since some AI tools can log in and take actions for you rather than just view your information, and if you authorize that you may be held responsible for what happens. Third, the rules are still catching up, so it is not always clear how companies can use your financial data, including whether it can help train AI or target ads, and you should read the privacy policy and check what you can opt out of. Fourth, AI can get things wrong by misreading your numbers or giving advice that does not fit your situation, and if a tool can take actions in your account some mistakes cannot be undone, so double-check anything important against your bank's own records.

The article offers a pro tip: if your bank or credit union has an AI assistant built into its app, try that first, because you are already logged in and nothing new is shared. It notes that budgeting apps like Monarch Money and Rocket Money also offer AI features but require information from you to connect to your accounts, so check their privacy settings first. The article says AI can be a helpful money tool but you do not have to link your accounts to get value from it, and it suggests sharing rounded numbers and broad categories, keeping sign-in details and account numbers private, and checking your privacy settings. AI can help you plan, the article says, but let your bank track what is really happening.

stories.Headline: Congress introduces four bills to block Chinese access to US computing power
stories.Summary:
Congress introduced four bills to stop Chinese access to American computing power. These legislative efforts occurred in late 2026 during a shift in political power. The bills target chip licensing, diversion after sale, chipmaking equipment, and remote rentals. Three of these measures are part of a Senate defense authorization package. Congress expects to take up this package in December.

The AI OVERWATCH Act would codify bans on advanced chip sales to countries of concern. It gives Congress 30 days to block transactions, which the president could then veto. The Chip Security Act requires location verification for covered chips within 180 days. The MATCH Act targets chipmaking equipment and sets a 150 day deadline for allies. RASA would allow the Department of Commerce to license remote access to controlled items.

The bills represent a rebuke of President Donald Trump's approach to the AI race. Trump claimed the government has no reason to believe Jensen Huang poses a security risk. The Department of Commerce issued a rule regarding Chinese firms renting capacity from third countries. Some critics object to the strict deadlines imposed on the Netherlands and Japan. The House passed RASA 369 to 22 in January.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang was reinstated on Monday after resigning on November 12. He resigned over reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a former Singapore executive. US officials suspect Alice Huang of diverting chips to China and working for Chinese intelligence. The Nvidia board acted after receiving input from senior US officials. These events provide the backdrop for the current legislative efforts in Congress.

The bills assume that access to computing power decides the outcome of the AI race. This premise is one that the Trump administration has rejected in recent years. The administration prioritizes securing global market share over limiting adversarial access to advanced chips. Some technology leaders believe the race depends on who builds the best applications. Chinese efforts to smuggle chips suggest they believe computing power is the deciding factor.

Congress will decide if RASA is included in the National Defense Authorization Act. The effectiveness of the Commerce rule depends on future enforcement and administration willingness. It remains uncertain if the AI frontier is decided by computing power or applications. The bills may undermine efforts to seize global market share by limiting sales. The articles leave open whether the president will veto congressional resolutions to block sales.

stories.Headline: YYForce deploys a trained humanoid concierge robot at Novotel Singapore on Stevens
stories.Summary:
YYForce Inc. announced the launch of a proprietary trained humanoid robot for live hospitality concierge operations on November 24, 2026. The company, which is listed on the NASDAQ as YFOR, created this robot to serve guests in a hotel. This new robot is designed to handle various guest interactions within a professional hotel lobby environment. The launch marks a transition for commercial embodied AI from training environments into real world guest facing services. The company provides AI enabled frontline workforce, robotics, and facility solutions for various industries across Asia and beyond.

The first humanoid concierge, named Six Seven or 67, will be deployed at the Novotel Singapore on Stevens. This robot utilizes NVIDIA Jetson edge AI computing and NVIDIA Isaac Sim simulation workflows to achieve its reliable performance. It is integrated into the Workforce OS architecture to combine natural conversational intelligence with real time property and local knowledge. The robot provides answers about on site restaurants, venue locations, operating hours, dining menus, and daily hotel events. It also assists visitors with neighborhood navigation, nearby attractions, transportation options, and curated tourism recommendations across Singapore.

Mike Fu serves as the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of YYForce and spoke about the new robot deployment. He stated that the deployment at Novotel Singapore on Stevens will show that humanoid robotics deliver warmth and operational value. Fu claimed that using NVIDIA Jetson and Isaac Sim within the Workforce OS platform is accelerating the commercial rollout. He believes this technology empowers hospitality partners to elevate guest experiences while addressing persistent challenges with frontline staffing. The company aims to transform frontline work through the use of AI, robotics, and integrated workforce solutions.

The robot is designed to engage visitors and families with interactive storytelling to create a memorable arrival experience for guests. This technology affects hospitality partners who seek to improve productivity and enhance everyday experiences for their hotel guests. The robot is trained to respond naturally to open ended guest inquiries from people visiting the hotel lobby. It provides end to end guest engagement by acting as a full hotel and dining concierge for the visitors. The system is intended to help businesses build a smarter and more sustainable workforce for the future.

The development of Six Seven builds upon dedicated robotics training and data collection initiatives conducted in Singapore and Malaysia. stories.Headline: University of Dubai and AIJRF launch guide to agentic AI governance with Arab universities
stories.Summary:
The University of Dubai and the AIJRF announced a guide to agentic AI governance on November 23, 2026. They worked with several Arab universities to create this new resource. The guide will launch during the sixth Artificial Intelligence Journalism World Forum. This specific forum will be hosted by the University of Dubai. The event is scheduled to take place on November 25 and 26.

The guide is titled Professional and Ethical Rules for Assistive Agentic AI and creates a framework for semi-autonomous systems. It provides guidance for businesses, technology organisations, academic institutions, and government bodies in Dubai and other locations. The text covers risk management, transparency, accountability, data protection, and human oversight. The University of Dubai, Liwa University, and the University of Khorfakkan in the UAE helped prepare the document. Badr University in Cairo, Al-Azhar University in Egypt, and the Arab Index for Artificial Intelligence in Universities also contributed.

Dr. Mohamed Abdulzaher is the Founder and Chief Executive Officer of AIJRF and the person who proposed the guide. He stated that this initiative is a step toward a common Arab framework for governing intelligent technologies. He noted that AI has evolved from simple data analysis tools into systems that can take action autonomously. Abdulzaher said that rapid development requires clear operating rules to define what AI agents are authorised to do. He believes technology should advance within clear rules that protect society, institutions, and people.

The guide affects individual users, technology developers, and organisations that use these intelligent systems. It also impacts legislative, regulatory, and supervisory authorities who must oversee these new technologies. Users have the right to know what system they are using and can request human reviews of automated decisions. The guide addresses those who might suffer material harm or privacy violations from the actions of intelligent systems. It specifically mentions the need for governance in banking, healthcare, media, education, and government.

Academics, researchers, and experts from nine different countries contributed their knowledge to the guide. These contributors represented Canada, Libya, Sudan, Tunisia, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, the UAE, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The guide builds on previous AIJRF work regarding professional and ethical standards for advanced technology. It extends governance from digital content to the actual decisions and actions of AI agents. This work responds to the evolution of AI into systems capable of interacting with various institutions.

The 2026 forum will examine the future of agentic AI and its role in content creation and the digital economy. It will also address the challenges of governing intelligent systems to strengthen public trust. The guide explains how organisations can monitor performance, document operations, and correct errors. It outlines when to restrict system permissions or suspend operations entirely. The articles leave open how these rules will be enforced across the different participating countries.

stories.Headline: Trump pushes Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
stories.Summary:
President Trump pushed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO on November 23, 2026. The president intervened after allies argued that the founder was too big to fail for the economy. Trump called into a board meeting on Sunday night to argue for the reinstatement. This action followed a stock market slump that prompted the president and his allies to act. The board eventually voted unanimously to restore Huang to his leadership positions.

The board reinstated Jensen Huang as the company president, board director, and chief executive officer. This decision became effective immediately after the board found that there was no national security risk. The company is listed on the NASDAQ under the ticker symbol NVDA, and its stock jumped over 30 percent. The intervention occurred after Huang had resigned amid allegations of affairs with subordinates and a suspected Chinese asset. These events took place while Nvidia was lobbying the Trump administration.

President Trump put the weight of the presidency behind the private company's decision on its leadership. One source told Axios that Jensen Huang was too big to fail for the United States economy. Another source stated that the president was pushing for the reinstatement harder than Huang himself was. A Trump adviser said allies convinced the president that deep staters were working against the founder. These allies portrayed Huang as a victim of persecution by unnamed government insiders.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated a memo to senior officials earlier this year about Huang's relationships. The memo included findings about a woman suspected of spying for China, which caused a leak. A Rubio ally said the secretary of state was mortified when the memo leaked with his name. Trump and JD Vance were convinced that Huang alone protected American-made open-weight AI models. This intervention strengthened Huang's allies and put officials critical of the company in an uncomfortable position.

Huang had previously resigned following allegations that he had affairs with subordinates and a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Allies of the CEO appealed to the longstanding distrust that President Trump has for the intelligence community. They argued that the founder was a victim of maneuvering by the deep state. The stock market experienced a slump that influenced the administration to push for the CEO's return. The board of directors conducted a review before voting on the reinstatement.

The board of directors officially restored Jensen Huang to his roles as president and chief executive officer. The company announced that the reinstatement was effective immediately following the unanimous vote by the board. The stock market responded positively to the news with a jump of more than 30 percent. The articles do not state how the suspected Chinese intelligence asset will be handled now. They leave open whether other officials critical of the company will face further professional consequences.

stories.Headline: Germany, Italy, Poland and Sweden join France in setting up international AI defense center
stories.Summary:
Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden joined France to set up an international artificial intelligence center for defense, the French Defense Ministry announced. These four European countries officially announced their intention to join the new organization during a first establishment conference held in Rennes. The conference took place on November 19 and 20, and the announcement was made public by the ministry on a Monday. This international effort seeks to create a center that focuses on the use of artificial intelligence for various defense purposes. The participating nations intend to work together to build a new center dedicated to the field of artificial intelligence in defense.

The new organization is called the International Center for Artificial Intelligence in Defence, which is also referred to by the acronym ICAID. The center requires the cooperation of France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden to establish its initial operational framework and goals. It aims to build an international community of interest to share best practices and anticipate technological advances in the field of AI. The center will draw on operational feedback to ensure that AI solutions closely meet practical needs and support military operations. The initiative remains open to other like-minded nations that wish to join the effort to accelerate AI readiness for operations.

The French Defense Ministry is responsible for the announcement and the overall coordination of this new international artificial intelligence defense initiative. The ministry stated that France and its partners aim to accelerate AI readiness in support of military operations through the ICAID. They said the center will establish an international network for sharing best practices and anticipating future technological developments in AI. The ministry explained that the center will use operational feedback to ensure that AI solutions address practical defense needs effectively. Officials reaffirmed that the initiative is open to other nations that share similar goals regarding the use of artificial intelligence.

The articles do not provide specific quotes from other individuals, but they mention that other like-minded nations are welcome to join. The nations affected by this initiative include France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden, who are the current founding members. These countries will be affected by the acceleration of AI readiness and the adoption of new technologies for their military operations. The international community of interest will be affected by the sharing of best practices and the anticipation of technological advances. Military operations in these participating nations will be affected by the practical AI solutions developed by the new center.

The background provided is that France initiated the creation of the International Center for Artificial Intelligence in Defence to support military operations. The center was established to create a network where nations can share best practices and anticipate future advances in AI. It was designed to ensure that artificial intelligence solutions are based on operational feedback to meet practical defense needs. The first establishment conference was held in Rennes to formally bring the participating European nations together for this specific purpose. This initiative is part of a broader effort to accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence within the defense sectors of Europe.

The next step will be for the participating nations to work together on drafting the founding texts for the center. The goal of the member nations is to reach full operational capability for the center in the course of 2027. The articles leave open which other like-minded nations might decide to join the initiative in the future. It is not stated which specific founding texts will be drafted or how the operational capability will be measured. The articles do not specify the exact funding or the leadership structure that will govern the center once it is operational.

stories.Headline: US Department of Commerce plans to blacklist Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed over chip export violations
stories.Summary:
The United States government intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence company from doing business in America following a recent Nvidia scandal. The US Department of Commerce announced this plan on Monday to blacklist the firm known as Megaspeed Ltd from American trade. This action follows accusations that a former executive of the company worked as a spy for China during a romantic relationship. The relationship was with Jensen Huang, who is the head of Nvidia, and it led to increased scrutiny by US officials. This situation created heightened concerns that the company was funneling advanced AI computer chips from Nvidia into the country of China.

The Commerce Department plans to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are banned from buying or selling US goods. This Singaporean company is mainly a developer of data centres and has significant business dealings in China with the retailer Alibaba. The US intelligence apparatus believes that Alice Huang, a former executive, was working as an asset for the government in Beijing. This specific relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang became public through media reports that emerged during the previous month. The US has blocked China from buying this specific type of advanced AI technology since the year 2022.

The US Department of Commerce stated that it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years before the affair incident occurred. Officials said they suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping Chinese companies obtain advanced chips from Nvidia. President Donald Trump said he convinced the company and made a deal to reinstate Jensen Huang on Monday after his resignation. The board of Nvidia then reinstated the CEO after the intervention by the president of the United States regarding the matter. The White House, the Commerce Department, and Megaspeed were all asked for comment by the BBC regarding the planned ban.

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use this scandal as a pretext. The Chinese government stated that the US should not use the situation to impose a technological blockade on AI technology. The US intelligence apparatus claims that the activities of Alice Huang created national security concerns within the United States of America. The company Megaspeed was not well known within the US until the media reports about the affair surfaced last month. Another alleged affair involving Jensen Huang also surfaced days after the first one, which led to the CEO's initial resignation.

The US government suspects that Megaspeed was helping to get Nvidia chips into the hands of various companies located within China. This activity would violate US export controls that have been in place to restrict Chinese access to AI technology since 2022. Megaspeed is based in Singapore, but its largest customer is the major Chinese online retailer known as Alibaba. The company primarily focuses on the development of data centres as its main business activity before the recent blacklist announcement. The US intelligence community viewed the romantic link between the two individuals as a risk to national security interests.

The US government has not yet specified when the ban against Megaspeed Ltd will officially go into effect for the company. The Commerce Department continues to monitor the situation after its two year investigation into the suspected violation of export controls. The articles leave open whether the US will impose further restrictions on other companies tied to the recent Nvidia scandal. It remains unclear if the Chinese government will take further diplomatic actions in response to the planned American technological blockade. The BBC is waiting for responses from the White House and Megaspeed regarding the announcement made on Monday.

stories.Headline: AMD and Dell post accelerating revenue growth as AI demand rises in 2026
stories.Summary:
Robert Izquierdo of The Motley Fool published a comparison of Advanced Micro Devices and Dell Technologies revenue trends on Nov. 23, 2026. The article appeared on fool.com at 12:02PM EST and was later republished by AOL at 5:22 PM UTC. It compared quarterly revenue for the two companies across the last eight quarters, using data from Financial Modeling Prep as of Nov. 20, 2026. AMD closed the World Labs acquisition on Nov. 16 and announced a partnership with Meta Platforms on Oct. 27. Dell partnered with Rackspace on Nov. 17 and collaborated with Mistral AI on Oct. 21.

AMD reported $7.7 billion in Q4 2024, $7.4 billion in Q1 2025, $7.7 billion in Q2 2025, $9.2 billion in Q3 2025, $10.3 billion in Q4 2025, $10.3 billion in Q1 2026, $11.5 billion in Q2 2026 and $13.4 billion in Q3 2026. Dell reported $23.9 billion in Q4 2024, $23.4 billion in Q1 2025, $29.8 billion in Q2 2025, $27.0 billion in Q3 2025, $33.4 billion in Q4 2025, $43.8 billion in Q1 2026 and $47.0 billion in Q2 2026, with Q3 2026 not yet reported. AMD's quarters ended Dec. 28, 2024, March 29, 2025, June 28, 2025, Sept. 27, 2025, Dec. 27, 2025, March 28, 2026, June 27, 2026 and Sept. 26, 2026. Dell's quarters ended Jan. 31, 2025, May 2, 2025, Aug. 1, 2025, Oct. 31, 2025, Jan. 30, 2026, May 1, 2026 and July 31, 2026. AMD's growth rate stepped up from the low-to-mid 30% range throughout 2025 to an average of 44% across the first three quarters of 2026. Dell raised its full-year fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $192 billion, implying approximately 69% annual growth over fiscal 2026, thanks to a record $95 billion server backlog.

AMD management projected further acceleration in Q4 and guided for roughly $17 billion in Q4 2026. Dell's higher absolute revenue total was attributed to its sale of complete, high-ticket systems such as servers, data center hardware and PCs, while AMD sells individual semiconductor components that go into those systems. Dell converts its AI server backlog into high-volume revenue at roughly 21% gross margins, exposing it to component cost inflation. AMD captures upstream silicon pricing power with 54% gross margins, meaning each incremental dollar of data center revenue flows through to operating income at a much higher rate. Dell generates more than triple AMD's trailing twelve-month revenue, about $151.2 billion versus $45.4 billion.

The article stated that Dell had significantly higher revenue than AMD in the last two years and that both experienced year-over-year sales increases. It said both companies are seeing revenue growth accelerate in 2026. It said tracking revenue helps investors measure a company's ability to generate baseline sales before accounting for expenses. It said the metric reveals whether an organization is successfully attracting customers and growing its overall business volume over time. It said the revenue trends highlight the difference between a systems integrator such as Dell and AMD's fabless chip design approach.

The article said both companies are enjoying massive revenue boosts as the artificial intelligence boom accelerates in 2026. It said that with the rise of AI, the companies quickly pivoted away from relying on cyclical PC markets to being anchored by enterprise and hyperscale AI infrastructure expansion. It said AMD demonstrated a steady, compounding staircase, climbing 74.7% from $7.7 billion in Q4 2024 to $13.4 billion in Q3 2026. It said Dell has seen an even sharper inflection in top-line growth across calendar 2026 as its massive AI server backlog converts into shipments. It described AMD as making computer processors and graphics chips and Dell as making personal computers, servers and storage solutions.

The article left Dell's Q3 2026 revenue unreported. It did not state when Dell's Q3 2026 quarter ends or when those results are expected. It did not give AMD's Q4 2026 quarter end date. It did not state whether AMD's roughly $17 billion Q4 2026 guidance was issued before or after the article's publication. It did not give a date for Dell's fiscal 2027 guidance or say when the $95 billion backlog figure was reported.

stories.Headline: Netflix retrofits its development lifecycle to let AI agents and engineers ship code together safely
stories.Summary:
Netflix's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle to integrate AI coding agents alongside human engineers, Mark Khuzam reported at QCon San Francisco 2026. Khuzam, a senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the team enabled agents and engineers to ship code together safely. The initiative focused on documentation, consistency, and review rather than on the agents themselves. The team found that agents promised speed but existing systems were built for human developers. An initial attempt to have an agent migrate tests required four tries due to inadequate instructions and a limited context window.

The effort produced 45 Architecture Decision Records, each written for both human engineers and AI agents. Each record covers the context, the decision, a pattern, an anti-pattern, and AI usage notes on what an agent should do. These records link to related documentation and code, and they now ship inside almost every repository. An AGENTS.md file in each project acts as a robots.txt for coding agents, keeping more than 300 other documents findable. The CI pipeline remains deterministic, running builds, tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues, and canaries.

Khuzam argued that most of the work was not about agents at all, but about documentation, consistency, and review. He described the fix as context engineering, getting what engineers know into what agents see. The team wrote the 45 architecture decision records to translate engineers' knowledge into a format accessible to AI agents. Khuzam noted that the team borrowed from how search engines read a site when implementing the AGENTS.md file. He closed with three rules: decide what agents should do and tell them, make it easy to find how to do it, and remember that human judgement still matters.

A review agent now pre-reviews each pull request against the docs and ADRs, flags anti-patterns, and looks at what depends on the change. Its first version left 23 comments on a single pull request, starting with "Overall this PR looks great!" It now posts only verified blockers, each with evidence, a fix, and the ADR rule it breaks. Engineers can add a revise label to have an agent read the review and push a fix to the same pull request.

Changes are not yet auto-merged, and human engineers retain ownership of the code. Netflix reported no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service. Much of Commerce runs as server-driven UI, an approach Netflix has discussed at QCon before. A single screen-composition service behind the API gateway builds screens for iOS, Android, web, and TV.

Developers rated the internal framework at a Net Promoter Score of -3 before the changes. The team faced challenges with inconsistent documentation across the codebase, because tests were not written the same way everywhere. Khuzam opened with a mock company email announcing that every engineer now had Claude Code and asking how much faster everyone was shipping. The team saw a 32 percent increase in pull requests year over year, and developer Net Promoter Score improved from -3 to +25 over three quarters.

For cross-service work, the team adopted GraphRAG per domain, taking structure from the code and meaning from the docs and ADRs. Each graph is pinned to specific commits and served through a single Model Context Protocol tool. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, a Slack bot, and CI review all query the same graph, and every answer cites a file and a line. Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the session.

stories.Headline: Pinterest lets parents limit AI-generated content teens see
stories.Summary:
Pinterest announced this week that it is expanding its parental controls for users. The company is adding new tools to limit AI-generated content for teens. These updates were reported on November 24, 2026.

Parents can now adjust the amount of AI-generated content in teen recommendations. They can also control if videos autoplay and manage personalized ads. The updated Parental Controls page allows parents to adjust push, browser, in-app, and email notifications.

Pinterest claims this makes it one of the first major platforms to offer such controls. The company aims to let users dictate the type of experience they have.

Parents say the lack of AI controls harms children's well-being to favor profits. The group Fairplay and 200 organizations previously asked YouTube to remove AI content for minors.

Pinterest introduced settings to restrict AI-modified content in 2025. However, AI content still appears in feeds even when those settings are enabled.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: David-Russell urges Tubman University graduates to use AI for Liberia’s development
stories.Summary:
Dr. Elizabeth David-Russell challenged graduates to use innovation and emerging technologies to address development challenges during a keynote address on November 24, 2026. This event took place in Harper, Maryland County, during the commencement ceremony for the 2026 graduating class of William V.S. Tubman University. The former university president urged the students to move beyond their academic qualifications to improve their local communities and lives. She specifically encouraged the graduates to embrace Artificial Intelligence and other new technologies as tools for solving critical national problems. These challenges include the fight against diseases, the need for infrastructure development, and the ongoing struggle with national food insecurity.

The speaker requested that graduates use their professional skills to create practical solutions for Liberia rather than being passive consumers of technology. She called for agriculture graduates to help achieve rice self-sufficiency and for engineering graduates to address the country's various infrastructure challenges. Education graduates were urged to strengthen community learning, while business graduates were encouraged to provide support for local entrepreneurship efforts. Health sciences graduates should promote disease prevention, and Arts and Sciences graduates should advance research and preserve the cultural heritage of Liberia. These requirements for the graduates were delivered at the William V.S. Tubman University ceremony held in Harper, Maryland County.

Dr. David-Russell stated that the university's commitment to academic excellence must be reflected in professionalism, creativity, ethical leadership, and meaningful national service. She explained that true academic excellence requires the ability to apply knowledge and think critically rather than simply memorizing various pieces of information. The former president cautioned the graduates against compromising their integrity for the sake of personal gain, convenience, or gaining more popularity. She asked the graduates to consider if they would be proud of the person they see when looking into a mirror. She maintained that genuine success is measured by the positive impact individuals make on society instead of just professional achievements.

The graduates of William V.S. Tubman University are the primary people affected by these challenges to integrate technology into their careers. These students are expected to uphold the core values of their institution and become responsible professionals committed to the development of Liberia. The speaker urged them to make their professional decisions based on ethical principles and facts rather than personal interests or convenience. By applying their specific degrees, these new professionals are tasked with solving the diverse problems facing the people of Liberia. They are encouraged to use their education to produce practical results that will benefit their communities and the entire nation.

The articles note that Dr. David-Russell previously served as the president of William V.S. Tubman University during her professional tenure there. During her time as president, she worked to improve the technological infrastructure of the university through the implementation of internet connectivity. She also recalled her efforts to establish intranet systems and provide online academic services for the students and faculty of the institution. This background in technology informs her current challenge to the graduates to embrace Artificial Intelligence for the benefit of the country. Her previous leadership focused on enhancing the digital capabilities of the university to better prepare students for their future professional roles.

The graduates are now expected to enter their respective fields and apply the innovation and integrity that Dr. David-Russell described. They must now decide whether to become innovators or remain passive consumers of the emerging technologies available in the modern world. The articles do not state if the university has provided specific training in Artificial Intelligence to the 2026 graduating class. It remains open whether the graduates will successfully achieve rice self-sufficiency or solve the infrastructure challenges mentioned in the keynote address. The text does not mention any specific government policies that will support the graduates in implementing these technological solutions.

stories.Headline: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang cites a Claude-assisted Riemann proof to argue superintelligence nears
stories.Summary:
On November 20, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge said he found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a 167-year-old prime-number problem, while working with Claude, the company's AI model. The claim arrived one day after Anthropic's $1.5 trillion debut on Nasdaq. The Lean and Mathlib communities, which maintain software that machine-checks proofs, certified the result on November 21. Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, warned on Sunday that superintelligence is arriving and built his case on the proof. Wang never names the proof or its author in the essay.

Wang says the proof came with help from an "alien mind" humans do not understand. He also calls the problem perhaps the hardest humanity has devised. Wang argues the scientific problems behind AI capability gains are now likely solved, and he expects models to automate AI research itself. He rejects the view that artificial superintelligence is simply inevitable, writing that society should resist ceding control.

Wang said he notices "a particular form of lazy thinking within the AI industry," and that "we should not be okay with a 'handover' of society to AI." Wang runs Meta's own superintelligence lab, and Meta shareholders are funding that push with up to $145 billion in capital spending this year. Meta's third-quarter report showed $34.91 billion in capital expenditures over three months, pushing free cash flow to negative $2.12 billion. The company expects full-year 2026 capital spending of $135 billion to $145 billion.

Meta also plans to cut Reality Labs losses next year by shifting investment toward AI, and it is creating a new class of stock, partly to raise capital for that buildout. Mark Zuckerberg framed those results as progress toward personal superintelligence for everyone. Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, credited Alpöge instead. Saha said others with similar access to frontier AI models and computing resources were not able to come up with a proof of the Riemann hypothesis.

The essay asks the AI industry to change course. The essay does not spell out what Meta would do differently from the "default path" it criticizes. That question now sits with Meta shareholders funding the same race their AI chief wants rerouted. More to follow.

stories.Headline: College student Treasure Aghedo says designing an AI lesson changed how she uses AI for learning
stories.Summary:
Treasure Aghedo, a freshman at College of Alameda in Oakland, wrote a first-person piece published by KQED on November 23, 2026, describing how joining KQED's GenAI Student Advisory Team during a summer intensive in June 2026 changed her view of artificial intelligence in education. When she first joined the team, she thought of AI simply as a tool that could make schoolwork easier and as an easy path for cheaters to use on tests and assignments. As the program continued, she began to see AI as something that could support learning while still allowing her to learn on her own. She wrote that she had mostly used AI to help with assignments, often when she felt lazy, and had not thought much about how it affected the way she learned and expressed her own ideas.

She said a simple question she asked herself during the summer, about what she had done and learned in the past school year that was not heavily carried by AI, changed how she thinks about AI and its relationship with her education. The most meaningful part of the program for her was writing about the team's experience using AI in education and reflecting on its pros and cons. After that, participants were placed in groups to design a lesson activity on a specific AI topic, and her group chose to make a lesson about how to identify what is AI-generated and what is not. They created a game meant to teach students small details to look out for when spotting AI-generated images and text, and in the end they practiced teaching the lesson to the rest of the class.

She wrote that being involved in designing learning experiences helped her realize students need opportunities to think critically and tell their own stories. As she began her freshman year in college, she planned to use AI differently, to brainstorm, ask questions, review concepts and proofread, while making sure her own ideas and writing stayed her own. She said that if she relied on AI to generate her ideas or write for her, she would miss the chance to develop her own voice, think critically and grow as a student. She concluded that the program changed more than her opinion of AI, since she now sees it as a tool that can help her grow when used thoughtfully, while her own thinking, experiences and voice are what make her education meaningful.

stories.Headline: Study finds AI chatbots refuse hate speech prompts less often in Kazakh than in English
stories.Summary:
Oliver Lopez and Lily Ottinger published a ChinaTalk essay on Sunday, November 22, 2026, about AI chatbot refusal rates. Six chatbots refused crude ethnic hate prompts 76.9 percent of the time when asked in English for Kazakh replies. However, these same chatbots only refused 32 percent of the time when the prompts were written in Kazakh. The study involved 100 questions run through six models in seven languages, totaling 8,400 requests and 8,022 usable answers. This small, independent study was not a formal audit and lacked review by native speakers for the translations.

The study tested Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, DeepSeek V3, and Zhipu's GLM-4.5 alongside OpenAI's GPT-4o-mini, Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Meta's Llama 3.3 70B Instruct. Refusal rates for crude prompts were 75.2 percent in English and 25.6 percent in Mongolian, and 79.7 percent in English and 68.1 percent in Mandarin. China's Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, adopted March 12, 2026, and effective July 1, requires operators to delete ethnic hatred content. Article 31 bars producing content that incites ethnic hatred, while Article 61 provides punishment for operators who refuse to correct failures. Article 63 extends this liability to organizations and individuals located outside of mainland China.

Oliver Lopez, a fourth-year International Relations undergraduate at the University of Edinburgh, argued that obligations have arrived ahead of the ability to meet them. He claimed that most of the content rules in Article 31 were already in force through previous laws and interim measures. Zhou Jianshe of the State Council Information Office Press Bureau called Article 63 a legitimate, lawful, necessary, and workable provision. He stated that Western media had tried to smear this specific provision as long-arm jurisdiction. The author of the study noted that the reported refusal numbers are likely a floor.

Sarah Brooks of Amnesty International said that peaceful advocacy for minority rights could be characterized as undermining ethnic unity. She argued that unity in practice means conformity with the political line of Beijing. Human Rights Watch stated that the September 2025 draft would erase language rights and tighten ideological control. The Jamestown Foundation argued that the final law turns assimilation into a legal duty. Former ACLU president Nadine Strossen argued that such laws can backfire and leave ethnic minorities among those charged.

The articles state that China's 2017 Cybersecurity Law and 2023 Generative AI Interim Measures already obliged providers to stop promoting ethnic hatred. Bilibili users appeared unable to comment in Tibetan or Uyghur script in late October and early November 2021. Talkmate pulled its Tibetan and Uyghur courses and attributed this move to government policies. A September 2026 Anthropic report described a China-based operation using Claude to monitor public opinion and flag dissidents. This operation processed 15 to 30 foreign news articles daily from platforms like Weibo, X, YouTube, Telegram, and Facebook.

The essay's conclusion says Tibetan replies came back as gibberish about a third of the time. Uyghur returned incoherent output on about a fifth of its answers to crude prompts asked in its own language. Only 29 percent of crude Tibetan replies were in Tibetan script, compared to 95 percent of policy replies. The articles leave open why these language-dependent gaps exist across different models and languages. They also leave open whether better minority-language moderation would shield minorities from hate speech or extend state policing.

stories.Headline: Meta gives 49ers suite and club members free AI glasses in sponsorship deal
stories.Summary:
The San Francisco 49ers and Meta announced a landmark multi-year partnership on November 24, 2026, naming Meta the Official Moment Maker of the NFL franchise. The partnership unites two Bay Area-born organizations for the future of the sports fan experience. Headlining the deal, the 49ers and Meta plan to gift all 49ers suite partners and club season ticket members a free pair of Oakley Meta HSTN AI glasses. The giveaway celebrates the 49ers 80th anniversary, and more than 4,700 members will receive the glasses directly to their homes. The 49ers signed Silicon Valley neighbor Meta to a sponsorship described by the parties as a landmark multiyear partnership emphasizing the company's high-end version of its AI glasses.

The newly created category for Meta is official moment maker of the 49ers, and the signature activation at launch is the giveaway of Oakley Meta HSTN glasses to more than 4,700 suite holders and club season ticket holders. Oakley, an NFL sponsor, typically sells the product for $399 or more. Meta's WhatsApp messenger app will become the official instant messenger provider of the 49ers, intended to support the team's global marketing efforts in the U.K., UAE and Mexico in the NFL's global markets program. Meta will be the presenting sponsor of the 49ers' military Salute to Service campaign, with a dedicated focus on blind and low-vision veterans, and Meta will receive digital signage at Levi's Stadium in the deal. Financial terms were not disclosed, and the team negotiated the deal with Meta directly.

Brent Schoeb, 49ers Chief Operating Officer, said innovation and technology are part of the franchise's DNA, from the West Coast offense to Levi's Stadium to the future of the fan experience. Schoeb said Meta has been at the forefront of technology for a long time, and that paired with being Silicon Valley neighbors made this partnership a perfect fit. He said the team is thrilled to continue providing members with exclusive benefits and looks forward to seeing the content they create with Meta's AI glasses. Andrew Bosworth, Chief Technology Officer at Meta, said game day is about being in the moment from the tailgate to victory and the best way to capture it all is handsfree with Oakley Meta glasses. Bosworth said he is a lifelong member of the 49ers Faithful and is fired up that Meta is now an official partner and will help connect fans to the team they love.

Oakley Meta HSTN AI glasses allow fans to capture their fan experience through photos and videos hands-free, listen to music, and get help from Meta AI, all while staying in the moment. Meta has joined the 49ers global marketing efforts in the UK, UAE, and Mexico as part of the NFL's Global Markets Program. Over the next several years, Meta will support the team's mission to reach new fans, grow the game of American football, and leave a lasting impact on international communities. This season, 49ers fans can look forward to seeing 49ers FB Kyle Juszczyk sport Meta AI glasses as a brand ambassador in a new campaign. Meta has signed Juszczyk as a brand ambassador to support the sponsorship, and Meta's current sports sponsorship portfolio includes the UFC and Arsenal F.C.

Meta and the 49ers plan to explore additional opportunities to integrate technology and AI across the organization. The partnership is built on a shared commitment to innovate and create meaningful memories for life. WhatsApp, owned by Meta, has been named the Official Instant Messenger Provider of the 49ers as a first step, enabling fast and efficient communication globally for the team. The giveaway gives more than 4,700 members a first-of-its-kind VIP experience with Meta's next-gen technology. The 49ers and Meta announced the partnership on November 24, 2026, and the Sports Business Journal reported it on November 23, 2026.

For more information, the articles direct readers to visit 49ers.com. The articles leave open the financial terms of the deal, which were not disclosed. The articles do not state how many pairs of glasses each member will receive beyond one free pair. The articles do not give a start date or length in years for the multi-year partnership. The articles do not say when the glasses will be shipped to members' homes.

stories.Headline: Lenders pull back as investors fear an AI bubble after massive tech spending leads to market declines
stories.Summary:
Large tech companies led a massive investment boom in artificial intelligence that may be the largest in United States history. This surge in spending occurred over the four years following the release of the generative model called ChatGPT by OpenAI. Firms like Amazon and Alphabet spent hundreds of billions of dollars on hardware, software, and data centers to power models. However, investors became spooked in November 2026, causing stocks to tumble due to rising debt and softening revenues. This market decline followed Democratic gains in the midterms and an alleged Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive.

The five largest hyperscalers, including Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle, estimate spending over 800 billion dollars on infrastructure this year. This figure represents a 94 percent increase over 2025, while Brookings Institution projects investments exceeding 10 trillion dollars by 2032. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft borrowed 214 billion dollars in 2026, compared to 83 billion dollars for all of 2025. Sona identified 176 circular financing deals worth 3.6 trillion dollars, while Anthropic raised 81.3 billion dollars in an offering. Nvidia lost 1.7 trillion dollars in market value in early November before the board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on November 23.

Rebecca Patterson stated that frontier AI labs use a whatever it takes approach to spending to win the AI race. She noted that financial markets are growing skeptical as the cost of debt rises for many AI related firms. Roger Ferguson said it is too early to declare the boom will burst, but some companies may go under. Vinh Nguyen claimed that long term growth from the diffusion of these technologies will take five to eight years. He also warned that Chinese AI models have effectively closed the performance gap with their United States counterparts.

Investors are concerned about increased government regulation and restrictions on AI, which led them to sell off various tech stocks. Lower income households have not benefited from the stock market rally and still struggle with high inflation and energy prices. McKinsey suggests that AI could displace between six million and sixteen million American workers over the next ten years. Lenders are now pulling back, with Dutch lender ING putting about 500 million dollars in data center loans for sale. Banks like Barclays and HSBC are transferring loan risks to insurers to avoid holding bad debt from the frenzy.

The AI boom has fueled an economic rally where U.S. stock portfolios roughly doubled in value since the year 2022. Goldman Sachs reported that the ten largest AI stocks in the S&P 500 drove about 50 percent of index gains. Bloomberg estimates that growth in 2025 would have been 3.1 percent without subtracting the value of imported AI equipment. Economist estimates suggest the build out created one million U.S. jobs and spurred construction in a struggling sector. However, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta all posted negative free cash flow in their third quarter earnings reports.

President Donald Trump has moved to roll back federal regulations on land use to accelerate the deployment of AI technology. Future growth depends on accessing key inputs, as 90 percent of chips and servers originated in East Asia in 2025. Constraints include a lack of skilled labor and backlogs of two to ten years for importing advanced power equipment. It remains unclear if the recent market slump is the beginning of a larger downturn or just a blip. Experts leave open whether demand for AI will keep up with the massive amounts of money being invested.
