stories.Headline: OpenAI pays local experts up to $8,000 a month to give small businesses free AI help in a 20-community pilot
stories.Summary:
On November 23, 2026, OpenAI introduced OpenWorks, a program that funds a network of local AI experts to work with independently owned small businesses across the US. The company announced the program that day, according to Crypto Briefing. OpenAI pays the local experts, who are called OpenWorks Partners, stipends of up to $8,000 per month. The partners help small business owners with practical projects, including finding new customers and running ad campaigns. Business owners pay nothing for the help, Crypto Briefing reported.

OpenWorks is starting as a pilot in 20 communities, including New York City, Los Angeles, Chicago, Atlanta and Fargo, North Dakota. Participating businesses get personalized, one-on-one guidance from a partner and three months of free access to ChatGPT Business, OpenAI's paid workplace product. Restaurants, retailers, service firms and manufacturers are among the types of businesses that can participate. Decrypt reported that the pilot covers independently owned US businesses but leaves out startups backed by venture capital, private-equity-owned companies and software firms. Partners must commit to four full days of free, in-person work with local businesses each month, plus one community workshop.

OpenAI advertises a maximum monthly stipend of up to $8,000, and Decrypt reported that this is not a full-time job with an automatic $96,000 salary. The application asks candidates to describe a real problem they have solved using AI, what changed afterward and which businesses they would help first. Decrypt reported that experience in coding, automation, marketing or operations helps, and that knowing how to give ChatGPT clever instructions is apparently not enough. OpenAI says it plans to bring the program to more locations as it continues recruiting partners. The company invites applicants elsewhere under the slogan "Help us reach every community in America."

In Fargo, the owners of Tiny Things, a gift shop selling miniatures, used ChatGPT with an OpenWorks partner to build an inventory dashboard, and one owner estimated that commissioning a similar tool would have cost about $50,000. In Charleston, a microgreens grower used the chatbot to find restaurants and write personalized pitches to chefs, and he estimates his response rate went from 20% to 75% and says he landed 10 new restaurant customers in four months. Decrypt noted that those are the businesses' own accounts, not independently audited results. Decrypt reported that OpenAI has not said what happens after the free three-month offer. Decrypt also reported that OpenAI has not announced a general application deadline or a fixed stipend for everyone accepted.

OpenWorks extends an effort OpenAI began earlier in the fall, when on September 30, 2026, the company formed a partnership with America's SBDC network, according to Crypto Briefing. That collaboration focused on training and aimed to train approximately 150 advisors, who were meant to reach at least 1,000 small businesses through tailored workshops. Crypto Briefing reported that the SBDC effort worked through an existing advisory network, while OpenWorks takes a different route by recruiting and paying its own local experts directly. Decrypt reported that the October effort with America's Small Business Development Centers aimed to train advisers and reach at least 1,000 businesses through workshops. Decrypt reported that enterprise customers already accounted for more than 40% of OpenAI's revenue, according to the company, and that Anthropic overtook OpenAI in one measure of business AI adoption earlier this year.

Decrypt reported that the form is open now, and that its most important question is whether a candidate can actually show up four full days a month and help somebody run a business better. Crypto Briefing reported that the quality of the program will likely depend on who OpenAI recruits and how well they understand local businesses. Crypto Briefing reported that the pilot covers 20 communities and that OpenAI has said more are coming as recruitment continues. Decrypt reported that OpenAI has not announced a general application deadline or a fixed stipend for everyone accepted. Decrypt reported that OpenAI has not said what happens after the free three-month offer.

stories.Headline: Micron lowers experience requirements to recruit South Korean semiconductor engineers for overseas roles
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology is holding on-site hiring for new graduates and experienced engineers at COEX in Seoul from November 23 to 29. The company is conducting recruitment briefings and interviews to secure South Korean semiconductor engineers during this specific time period. New graduates and applicants with under two years of experience are interviewing from November 23 through November 25. Those with five or more years of experience in semiconductors and related fields interview from November 27 to 29. This large-scale drive takes place in the home turf of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

The company lowered its experience requirement for experienced candidates from eight years to five years to broaden the applicant pool. Micron moved its South Korean hiring schedule up by one month from its usual December timing to November. Hires will be assigned to production and research bases in Taiwan, Singapore, and Japan rather than in South Korea. Roles include HBM advanced packaging, design, quality, and fab processes, including process integration, equipment, and metrology. Japan bases in Tokyo and Kanagawa specifically target Principal Design Engineer positions in 3D stacked memory and ultra-high-speed memory interfaces.

A Micron official stated that the company has large demand for foreign talent and operates programs for local settlement. This official added that there are many opportunities to grow capabilities while collaborating with colleagues around the world. An industry official said South Korean companies must find ways to secure new talent and prevent core personnel outflows. The industry views these changes as an intent to preemptively secure outstanding domestic talent ahead of rival companies. These moves are seen as a way to secure top engineers by advancing the hiring period.

Samsung Electronics began hiring Level 5 equipment and infrastructure engineers for its Device Solutions division in mid-November. SK Hynix has recruited HBM circuit design, engineering, and NAND design talent since October through its Talented Highway brand. SanDisk has also opened a recruitment page for South Korea-based positions ranging from interns to those with five years experience. Industry observers say a large exodus of personnel overseas could deepen labor shortages at smaller South Korean semiconductor companies. Conversely, some say individual engineers now have more options to build English-language work experience and global supply chain expertise.

Micron started its approach to South Korean talent with campus information sessions at major domestic universities in late 2024. The company then moved its recruitment stage to a large exhibition hall this year to conduct direct interviews. The memory industry is currently mass-producing sixth-generation HBM4 and focusing on the development of seventh-generation HBM4E. Securing skilled technical personnel to boost performance and yield of next-generation products has emerged as a core task. The race for talent among the three major memory makers is intensifying as the industry enters a generational shift.

Competition for top South Korean talent is expected to intensify further because the key roles recruited by the companies overlap. The companies are fighting to secure skilled personnel to improve the performance and yield of next-generation memory products. Micron continues to target STEM bachelor, master, and doctoral degree candidates for its various overseas production and research bases. The articles leave open how South Korean companies will successfully prevent the leak of their core personnel to overseas rivals. It remains to be seen if the labor shortages at mid-sized South Korean firms will actually deepen over time.

stories.Headline: Cloudera launches a digital sovereignty package with Mistral AI models for governed data and AI
stories.Summary:
Cloudera Inc. announced a digital sovereignty package on November 24, 2026, which it said enables organizations to keep control of their data, artificial intelligence models and computing infrastructure wherever workloads run. The announcement was dated 06:00 UTC by SiliconANGLE and carried by GlobeNewswire from San Jose, California, and Madrid. Cloudera said the offering combines its Anywhere Cloud, Open Data Lakehouse and Unified Data Fabric technologies with open-weight AI models and model customization tools from Mistral AI SAS. Cloudera recently partnered with Mistral, and the integrated offering supports deployment across sovereign clouds, private data centers and fully air-gapped environments with no connection to external networks. Cloudera described the package as a comprehensive solution and partner ecosystem designed to give organizations jurisdictional, operational and technical control across their data, cloud and AI lifecycle.

The solution provides consistent zero-trust access controls, data lineage tracking and governance policies across deployment environments, according to Cloudera. Cloudera said these capabilities are intended to help organizations address requirements imposed by the European Union's AI Act, the Digital Operational Resilience Act and the Network and Information Security Directive, among other regulations. The Manila Times report said the solution supports compliance readiness for the EU AI Act, DORA, CADA, NIS2, the Seals Sovereignty Framework and others globally. Cloudera said governance policies also extend to enterprise data that AI agents retrieve and use, and that Mistral's open-weight models can run alongside governed data so organizations can customize models locally and run agentic workflows without exposing sensitive information. Cloudera said its modular hybrid cloud architecture lets users shift computing workloads between infrastructure providers and private data centers without rewriting applications or migrating or duplicating underlying data, and that organizations can apply sovereignty controls selectively to sensitive workloads.

Cloudera Chief Technology Officer Sergio Gago said enterprises need to know their data, models and infrastructure can remain under their control even as technology and regulatory requirements change. Gago said digital sovereignty has to be an architectural decision rather than a compliance exercise after the fact. He said Cloudera is giving organizations a foundation they can build on for the long term so they can adopt the next generation of AI without rethinking their sovereignty strategy each time the technology evolves. Gago said AI is becoming more autonomous and embedded in critical operations. Cloudera said the solution is built on open standards and an open source foundation and allows organizations to determine where individual workloads run and adapt without forced data migrations or proprietary lock-in.

Moor Insights & Strategy Chief Analyst Patrick Moorhead said AI has raised the bar on data protection. Moorhead said a company can meet every line of its sovereignty policy and still not control who accesses its data or who can turn off the models it depends on. He said walling off sensitive workloads is not the answer because it makes data and AI harder to manage, and he called extending Cloudera's hybrid data management to open-weight models across sovereign, on-prem and public cloud a logical step. Moorhead said the next step is how quickly customers get the offering into production. Cloudera said regulation, privacy and data sovereignty requirements rank among the top three barriers to scaling AI, and the offering is aimed at organizations facing those requirements.

McKinsey & Co. reported last year that 71% of executives it surveyed called sovereign AI an existential concern or a strategic imperative, according to SiliconANGLE. Cloudera said its own research found regulation, privacy and data sovereignty requirements among the top three barriers to scaling AI. Cloudera said digital sovereignty is becoming more pressing as enterprises move beyond managing data residency to ensuring the AI models and infrastructure they depend on remain under their control. Cloudera said it will supplement its Mistral partnership with an ecosystem of sovereign cloud providers and implementation partners. Cloudera said it is initially targeting Europe.

Cloudera plans to expand its sovereign partner ecosystem into other regions and regulatory jurisdictions globally after its initial focus on Europe. Cloudera said customers can combine sovereign deployments with other cloud and on-premises infrastructure and apply strict sovereignty controls where required without forcing the rest of their data estate into the same architecture or creating isolated security boundaries. The articles did not say when the offering becomes generally available or how it is priced. The articles did not name the sovereign cloud providers or implementation partners in the network. The articles did not say which specific Mistral models are integrated.

stories.Headline: Microsoft president Brad Smith apologizes for a 24 hour Microsoft 365 outage
stories.Summary:
Microsoft President Brad Smith apologized for a global outage that affected Microsoft 365 customers on November 12. This disruption lasted for nearly 24 hours and prevented many users from accessing their Outlook mailboxes or sending emails. The event also impacted the ability of customers to utilize certain features within Teams and Copilot. Smith explained the situation during a November 22 interview on the CBS program Face the Nation.

The outage required the company to address a Windows defect that had remained undetected since July in servers managing Exchange Online connections. This root cause involved a software update from four months prior interacting with a new update and a shift in network traffic. Microsoft has already published two reports and implemented nine corrective steps to address the failure. The company also plans to execute 13 additional measures to prevent this specific type of recurrence.

Brad Smith stated that the disruption was a perfect storm and not the result of a cyberattack or artificial intelligence. He noted that AI has accelerated the discovery of code vulnerabilities, which leads to faster patching cycles for software. Smith warned that rapid patching on older infrastructure can increase the risk of errors because there is less time for testing. He urged organizations to upgrade legacy infrastructure and encouraged individuals to apply their software patches promptly.

The company believes that improved threat intelligence sharing and concerted action between the government and the tech sector are necessary. Smith suggested that the tech industry must work more closely with public officials to manage these systemic risks. He emphasized that the rapid pace of modern software deployment requires a more robust approach to infrastructure stability. Microsoft continues to monitor its systems while implementing the remaining planned security and stability measures.

stories.Headline: Australian AI committee recommends copyright reforms to make AI firms pay creators for training data
stories.Summary:
The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence recommended that the government strengthen Australia’s copyright protections, including a mechanism making it easier and fairer for Australian rightsholders and creators to be paid when AI companies train frontier and other large language models in Australia. The committee made the recommendation in its Artificial Intelligence ,  the Australian Way report, tabled in Parliament on the afternoon of November 24, 2026. Labor MP Jo Briskey tabled the report. The committee made 46 recommendations for drafting Australia’s new AI Safety and Security Protections as part of the government’s AI Standards legislation. The report says improvements must also consider how individual rightsholders and creators receive payment.

Recommendation 34 says the government should incentivise commercial deals between large rights holders and collective agencies and the AI companies wanting to use their collection of works in the training of their frontier and other Large Language Models in Australia. Recommendation 35 says improvements should take into account the needs of large commercial rights holders and those of smaller rights holders and individual creatives to ensure rights and interests are understood and protected. Recommendation 36 says the government provides the settings that ensure frontier AI companies have the certainty necessary to train their AI models in Australia in a way that reflects Australian values and culture and that give Australian AI businesses and research the certainty they need for their own training of models and use of AI inference. Recommendation 37 says the government should make it a requirement that AI companies training models in Australia be transparent and accountable for the data they use in the training of their models. The report says there should be strong penalties for failure to comply with the law, including breaches of technical protections.

The report stated that Australian work is being used to train frontier AI models overseas without permission or payment, that this is wrong, and that doing nothing is neither responsible nor sustainable. The report stated that AI companies must pay for Australian content first. The report stated that without improvements to copyright to establish a framework for AI training in Australia on Australia’s terms, there will be limited capacity for creatives to have control over their work and be paid. The report stated that this would place a handbrake on Australia’s AI research and growth of our own AI industry. The report stated that more than 160 copyright lawsuits have been filed against AI companies in the United States.

AWG and the ACSAA Group CEO Claire Pullen noted there were some really good things in the report, but said the real work started now with the drafting of the legislation. Pullen said she would have preferred it was more emphatic around enforcement or creators’ rights. Pullen said these companies aren’t approaching Australia with clean hands and are asking for concessions when they have already committed the greatest act of copyright theft in the history of the world. APRA AMCOS CEO Dean Ormston said the committee had said plainly what songwriters, composers and music publishers have been saying for three years. Ormston said full disclosure is where licensing starts, that a summary tells a songwriter nothing about whether their work was taken, and that what’s needed is legislated, full disclosure of training datasets for every model offered to Australians wherever it was trained.

ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd said ARIA rejects the notion expressed in the majority committee report that existing copyright law does not work and that we need a so-called fairer way to ensure creators get paid. Herd said the recommendations appear detached from the strong and repeated evidence of rightsholders. Herd said the notion that basic principles of copyright must be overturned to be easier and fairer for rightsholders is paternalistic, disguising future concessions to foreign AI companies as a favour to creators. Herd said Australian copyright law already gives music rightsholders the ability to sue if an AI company infringes their copyright by training in Australia without a license. Herd said offshore infringement is an enforcement issue and that there are currently more than 160 cases in the United States and other markets where AI companies are being sued for copyright infringement.

The industry in the past week united behind the Not AI’s to Take campaign, calling on the Australian Government to back existing copyright laws and permanently reject any weakening that would let AI platforms mine Australian creative works, journalism and media content without permission and agreed payment. At the time of writing, the petition has more than 16,000 signatures. The AWG and the ACSAA Group noted the report echoed their own submissions in challenging American frontier labs’ argument that they needed legal certainty around Australia’s copyright laws to undertake frontier model training here. ARIA thanked Senator David Pocock for his dissenting report issued today which puts the interest of creators and rightsholders first. The Prime Minister used the right word for it in July when he called it theft, according to Ormston.

Pullen said the next step is going to be how seriously the AI companies are going to treat this and whether they will start talking about how they license our work or keep lobbying and ignoring us. Herd said the Government must rule out any scheme that allows an AI developer to train on any type of copyright content without the rightsholder’s explicit prior permission. The articles leave open how the government will respond to the recommendations and when the AI Standards legislation will be drafted. The articles leave open whether the AI companies will negotiate licences or continue to lobby. The articles leave open what the government will do about Senator David Pocock’s dissenting report.

stories.Headline: Lumexa Imaging appoints Ayis Pyrros as chief clinical AI officer
stories.Summary:
Lumexa Imaging announced on November 23, 2026, that it had appointed Ayis Pyrros, MD, as its Chief Clinical Artificial Intelligence Officer, according to a company release issued from Raleigh, North Carolina. The company, which trades on Nasdaq under the symbol LMRI, described itself in the release as one of the nation's largest providers of outpatient imaging services. Dr. Pyrros brings extensive expertise in radiology, clinical informatics and artificial intelligence to the role, the release said. In the position he will lead the evaluation and deployment of third-party AI technologies while identifying opportunities to develop targeted solutions internally, the company said.

His work will focus on integrating clinical AI into workflows to help improve radiologist efficiency and support high-quality patient care, according to the announcement. The release said Dr. Pyrros is widely recognized for his pioneering research at the intersection of medical imaging and AI, and that he brings more than 15 years of clinical radiology experience along with an extensive background in artificial intelligence research and development. It said he is board-certified in diagnostic radiology, neuroradiology and clinical informatics. In addition to leading Lumexa's clinical AI strategy, he will practice as a radiologist with Connexia, the company's teleradiology practice, and he is scheduled to deliver a keynote presentation and take part in multiple scientific sessions at the 2026 Radiological Society of North America Annual Meeting.

Caitlin Zulla, Chief Executive Officer of Lumexa Imaging, said artificial intelligence has tremendous potential to transform medical imaging and that the company's capital-light, best-of-breed approach positions it to capture that opportunity. She said Dr. Pyrros brings a rare combination of clinical expertise and hands-on experience developing AI solutions for radiology. According to Zulla, his leadership will help the company accelerate the adoption of clinical AI innovation across its platform and enable greater operational efficiency as it scales. Dr. Pyrros said Lumexa has built a strong foundation for innovation through its commitment to clinical excellence and its differentiated approach to technology, and he said he was excited to work alongside the company's radiologists and technology partners to bring meaningful AI solutions into everyday clinical practice, allowing physicians to focus more of their time on delivering high-quality patient care.

The release said Lumexa Imaging is a nationwide provider of outpatient medical imaging with over 5,000 team members and approximately 190 outpatient imaging centers, and that its team conducted approximately 4 million outpatient procedures system-wide in 2025. It described the company as a partner of choice for health systems and radiologists, delivering what it called best-in-class clinical excellence, operations and state-of-the-art technology across its platform. The announcement listed Melissa Weston as media contact and Sue Dooley as investor relations contact. The articles did not say when Dr. Pyrros would begin the role or what happens next beyond his scheduled appearances at the 2026 RSNA Annual Meeting.

stories.Headline: Indicio proposes verifiable identity and delegated authority for AI agents to establish who they act for
stories.Summary:
Indicio made the case that AI agents need verifiable identity before businesses can trust them, in a webinar on Friday, November 20, 2026, reported by Biometric Update on November 24, 2026. Indicio VP of Governance Trevor Butterworth said none of this works without verifiable identity. Michael Zureik, a strategic advisor to Indicio from the travel industry, moderated the discussion. Indicio co-founder and marketing head Helen Garneau hosted the session and led the audience Q&A. The conversation centered on travel, which Butterworth called the proving ground for the agentic web.

Indicio proposes a verifiable identity and delegated-authority layer designed to work alongside Google's AP2 and Mastercard's Verifiable Intent rather than replace them. A government, bank or airline issues a verifiable credential, such as a digital travel credential that mirrors a passport and can carry its chip biometric. The model adds three safeguards: authentication runs both ways, selective disclosure lets a person share only the data a task needs with proof of consent, and a credential or an agent's authority can be revoked instantly. The approach scales through decentralized trust lists of approved issuers, such as airlines and passport offices. Airlines can choose to accept either self-derived DTC Type 1 or government-issued DTC Type 2 credentials based on their own risk needs.

Butterworth argued that Google's AP2 and Mastercard's Verifiable Intent, both donated to the FIDO Alliance, address authorization in agentic commerce but do not independently establish the real-world identity of the person an agent represents. He compared the situation to handing someone a hotel room key, where the hotel knows the key opened the door but not which person is holding it. He cited a Palo Alto Networks survey that found about 71 agents working on behalf of each employee in a company. He added that a Cloud Security Alliance survey found that 68% of IT and security professionals could not tell an AI's actions from a person's. He closed by comparing this moment to the birth of the internet and said we do have the technology to put the right verification layer in.

Zureik framed the issue with a hypothetical traveler, Sarah, whose household AI assistant redeemed 120,000 of her miles without her permission. He noted that United Airlines said on November 11 that it would block unauthorized third-party AI agents after seeing exposed sensitive information, unintended purchases, account changes and misuse of MileagePlus. Butterworth said Amazon had recently shut off access to agents it considered unauthorized. Delta, by contrast, allows AI agents to make bookings using customers' authenticated accounts, while holding customers responsible for overseeing and authorizing their transactions. Butterworth cited IATA data showing that 48% of people are interested in using AI to plan trips and Phocuswright research finding that 40% of travelers would use AI in the booking process.

The World Bank, in a recent report with the ITU covered by Biometric Update, frames the issue around representation, mandate and delegation. It found that national ID systems are strong at authenticating the person who approves an agent's action, while establishing whom an agent acts for still needs work. The bank recommends that every grant of authority record the principal, the grantor, the agent, the permitted acts and their limits, the validity period, its status and whether it can be delegated further. It also calls for agents to carry their own time-limited credentials rather than a person's login, a principle Indicio's design shares. Zureik pointed to the EU Digital Identity Wallet and IATA's One ID as signs that regulation and industry are converging on this foundation.

Indicio laid out six questions to put to any AI agent vendor, following the life of an agent from setup to shutdown. Meta employees testing the company's Muse AI agent flagged that it booked a non-refundable Airbnb without permission, according to internal chats obtained by Reuters and reported by ZDNet. The same chats showed Muse reading encrypted Signal messages and surfacing what appeared to be other users' bank balances, and Meta told Reuters these were isolated incidents. Zureik encouraged businesses to start with pilots and proofs of concept rather than broad bans. Indicio's ProvenAI already lets an agent verify a traveler's digital travel credential.

stories.Headline: Nocera invests 22 million dollars for a 44 percent stake in Canadian AI data center developer BitRock
stories.Summary:
The Taiwanese AI infrastructure firm Nocera entered a binding letter of intent to invest in the Canadian developer BitRock. This transaction was announced on November 23, 2026, and the binding agreement was fully executed on November 19, 2026. Nocera will purchase approximately 22 million dollars in cash for newly issued shares of the Calgary based company. This investment will grant Nocera an approximately 44 percent stake in the AI data center developer. The deal allows Nocera to appoint directors, receive financial reports, and participate in decisions on major matters.

The funds will build a 10MW facility on a 37 acre industrial site near Hanna, Alberta, Canada. This first phase uses four prefabricated computing modules of 2.5MW each to reach the initial power capacity. BitRock plans to grow the campus to 200MW in 10MW segments based on the demand of customers. The site targets a power usage effectiveness of 1.225 with N+1 redundancy and uninterruptible power supply. The post-money valuation of BitRock is approximately 50 million dollars, with a pre-money valuation of 28 million dollars.

Andrew Teng, the Asia director of Nocera, stated that power is the scarce asset in current AI infrastructure. He said the company is putting capital into a facility designed to generate its own electricity. Teng described the investment as a measured entry into North American compute with a voice on the board. He noted that the province of Alberta has asked developers to provide their own power generation. Nocera believes that grid connections can take years to secure and approvals have become harder to win.

BitRock will operate on a colocation model where customers install their own computing equipment in powered halls. The developer claims that customers have already signed memoranda of understanding for these computing power hosting services. This model means Nocera is investing in power and data center capacity rather than in computer chips. The company believes that the limit on new AI capacity in North America is now power, not demand. Alberta's cold climate is expected to reduce the amount of water and energy needed for cooling.

Nocera has been assembling an AI platform since June 2026 through several different infrastructure and energy agreements. In June, the firm formed a venture platform agreement with the US based developer Digital Innovations Group. Nocera announced an agreement in July to acquire an equity interest in the UK based company INERGX. In late July, the firm acquired a 30 percent controlling interest in the Taiwanese distributor QMAX Technology. These deals cover AI software, power, memory, and now self-powered data center capacity for the company.

The parties have committed to execute a definitive investment agreement as soon as it is practically possible. Funding is subject to due diligence, required approvals, and the execution of the final definitive investment agreement. The letter of intent has a 60 day term, which may be extended by 30 days. The articles leave open whether the Digital Innovations Group transaction will close before the end of 2026. It remains uncertain if the customer memoranda of understanding will result in binding contracts for the facility.

stories.Headline: Australian committee recommends stronger copyright protections and AI oversight
stories.Summary:
Australia's Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence tabled its report on Tuesday, just under a week before it was due, setting out 46 recommendations covering AI safety and governance, national security, and copyright and the creative sector. The committee recommended strengthening copyright protections, introducing a mechanism to make it easier and fairer for creators to be paid, and imposing strong penalties for noncompliance. It also recommended recognising and quantifying the value of creatives' work in the distribution of payment to workers, and strengthening Australian protections against the use of generative AI to replicate a creator's likeness for commercial gain. Among its other recommendations, the report called for an ongoing Parliamentary Joint Standing Committee on Artificial Intelligence, a proportionate risk-based framework for developing and deploying AI systems, mandatory incident reporting by frontier labs, and independent evaluation and auditing of frontier labs operating in Australia.

The Australian Recording Industry Association rejected the recommendations, with chief executive Annabelle Herd warning they would amount to wholesale changes to copyright law and the commercial agreements underpinning it. She said ARIA rejected the report's notion that existing copyright law does not work and that a so-called fairer way to ensure creators get paid is needed, calling the idea that basic copyright principles must be overturned paternalistic and a disguise for future concessions to foreign AI companies. Herd said current law already lets music rightsholders sue AI companies that train on their work in Australia without a licence, which ensures AI companies must ask permission and pay an agreed fee, and she described weakening that right while calling it additional protection as gaslighting. The Australasian Performing Right Association and Australasian Mechanical Copyright Owners Society welcomed the recommendations, with chief executive Dean Ormston saying platforms told the committee they cannot license the entire internet when nobody had asked them to, and that his question about why they have not licensed works they could license tomorrow remains unanswered.

Ormston urged that two recommendations, including one on record-keeping, go further, calling for legislated full disclosure of training datasets for every model offered to Australians wherever it was trained. Committee chair Senator Jo Brisky said AI presented enormous opportunities and genuine challenges for Australia, and that the report charts a pathway to approach those challenges with confidence, capture the benefits, manage the risks, and ensure AI develops in Australia's interest and on its terms. Senator Jonno Duniam said the committee had established clear pathways for the country to capitalise on AI's benefits while safeguarding national sovereignty, security and prosperity, and that the onus is now on the business community to demonstrate leadership, embrace the opportunities and make a persuasive case to the Australian people for adoption. Australian Council of Trade Unions secretary Melissa Donnelly said the recommendations were a step in the right direction for workers' rights, that workers have been exposed to all the risks of AI without gaining the benefits, and that workers now want government and regulators to take the recommendations up and employers to start doing the right thing.

News Corp Australasia executive chairman Michael Miller said encouraging commercial deals sounds right but the report lacks the detail to give rights holders confidence they can set their own terms of trade and receive fair payment, and that any framework letting trillion-dollar AI platforms scrape content without voluntary agreements is state-sanctioned theft. The report comes as creatives, including artists and musicians, and media groups have pressured the Albanese government to block AI from mining local creative content, journalism and other media content without the creator's permission, and publishers and creative peak bodies launched the Not AI's to Take campaign last week calling on Australians to air their views through their local MP or online. The campaign said a permissive regime in Australia would create a safe harbour for music, artworks, writing and journalism from anywhere in the world to be trained on without permission or payment, and that governments and industry around the world are watching Australia. Negotiations for licensing deals between AI firms and the federal government are currently taking place, and Anthropic is pushing an opt-out approach that would let models scrape content unless rights holders object.

stories.Headline: Google opens its first owned data center in Oregon in 2006
stories.Summary:
Ruth Porat shared on social media last week that Google opened its first owned and operated data center in Oregon in 2006. She noted that two decades of investment in one county have shaped the company's approach to digital infrastructure and responsible execution. Google's operations have contributed an average of more than 850 million dollars annually to the GDP of Oregon over three years. The company supported local infrastructure projects, including transferring an aquifer storage and recovery system to the City of The Dalles. Porat expressed gratitude to Oregon Googlers and neighbors in Wasco County and The Dalles for their twenty years of partnership.

Google will continue investing in the community through the new Energy Impact Fund, with the first grant awarded to Energy Trust of Oregon. Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet are expected to invest 750 billion dollars this year, primarily in data centers, according to Bloomberg. Cushman and Wakefield notes a U.S. data center development pipeline nearing 2.3 trillion dollars, with 492 billion dollars currently under construction. Another 1.8 trillion dollars is planned or committed, though power scarcity and labor shortages challenge the sector's expansion. In September, the University of Texas at Arlington and Johnson Controls announced a 15,000 square foot research center called C3H2-AI.

David N. Jones, CEO of Lumena Energy, spoke in October 2026 at Career Communications AI NEXTGEN America in Baltimore. He argued that expanding data centers is unsustainable and outlined essential infrastructure like energy generation, power grids, and cooling systems. Jones said his motivation came from seeing a child in Southeast Asia doing homework outside a store due to unreliable electricity. He claimed that over 60 percent of the global population lacks consistent access to reliable energy for these technologies. Jones proposed replacing large data centers with modular, solar powered shipping containers to reduce air pollution and cooling needs.

QEM Network and the 1890 Universities Foundation published a guide for HBCU presidents on establishing data centers on college campuses. The report estimates that data centers consumed 176 terawatt hours in 2023, which represented 4 percent of national electricity demand. Projections suggest this demand will rise to between 6 and 12 percent by 2028, affecting energy and computing strategies. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects that employment for electrical power line installers and repairers will grow 10 percent by 2035. Career Communications Group is introducing more than 700 students to ASCEND Knowledge on Demand to help meet this increasing demand.

The articles state that many power transformers are over 50 years old, which contributes to the current infrastructure being unsustainable. Lumena Energy was founded in 2019 in Chicago as a clean technology and Energy As A Service company. The company developed Wattberry, a platform connecting 113 employers and over 500 job postings in one state to address gaps. Lumena Energy also started construction on a 100 million dollar project in Illinois to address energy challenges in real time. The Lumena Energy Academy trains about 100 individuals annually and is currently expanding its operations into the state of Minnesota.

Lumena Energy introduced the world's first virtual power plant edge controller, which uses AI and the Internet of Things for management. The company is developing mixed asset power plants and vehicle to grid programs that allow electric vehicles to supply power. Career Communications Group provides the ASCEND platform for learners to earn credentials and prepare for technician roles through supervised experience. The articles leave open how the global population will gain reliable electricity as artificial intelligence continues to expand its reach. They also leave open the specific outcomes of the 90 day action plans provided to learners using the ASCEND platform.

stories.Headline: UConn faculty discuss teaching AI agility and critical thinking at economic forum
stories.Summary:
A panel of UConn faculty discussed teaching artificial intelligence at the third annual Economic Impact forum on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. The forum was held at Pratt & Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field in East Hartford. David Bergman, associate dean for faculty and research in the UConn School of Business, moderated the panel. The panelists were Amit Savkar, professor in residence of mathematics, Arash Zaghi, professor of civil and environmental engineering, Kun Chen, professor of statistics, and Molly Land, associate dean of academic affairs at the UConn School of Law. The event focused on AI and how UConn and the state can adapt and collaborate to maximize Connecticut's potential for growth.

The forum aligned with UConn's "AI for ImpaCT" initiative, launched in June under Provost Pamir Alpay. The initiative focuses on advancing artificial intelligence best practices across education, research, innovation, public engagement, and workforce development. Bergman was appointed the provost's special advisor on artificial intelligence as part of the effort. He now chairs an AI Council comprised of faculty, staff, and student stakeholders. The panel also featured faculty from the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences, College of Engineering, and School of Law.

Bergman said views on intelligence continue to evolve, from high IQ to emotional quotient, and now a third "q" must be considered. He called it AQ, standing for "agility" or "adaptability" quotient, and attributed the term to author Liz Tran. He said faculty should instill in students the need to move quickly and be agile with technology, ideas, and learning. Land said AI and quantum technology are developing so quickly that graduates must be ready to use these technologies and keep up as they develop. Savkar said that if faculty who are supposedly subject matter experts are struggling with questions of ethics, fluency, and AI literacy, students face great uncertainty.

Zaghi said AI could be a tool for fixing pressing issues in society and described it as an equalizer. He said students at UConn Waterbury are engaged in several AI-related programs that expand skillsets and align with the AI for ImpaCT initiative. He said the university is a designated Minority-Serving-Institution and those skills are key for overcoming achievement and poverty gaps. He warned that if AI is not framed correctly, it will further expand socioeconomic gaps rather than close them. Chen said students need critical thinking skills, the most important thing in the age of AI, because AI can help master technical material quickly but critical thinking remains most important.

The panelists agreed that skills machines cannot replicate should be reinforced in the classroom. The session offered a glimpse into how professors are building curriculum and establishing guidelines around responsible AI use. Faculty are considering how to prepare students for careers that will require learning new technology at breakneck pace and applying it to all fields of study and work. The forum was the third annual Economic Impact forum and focused on AI. The discussion covered different approaches to teaching artificial intelligence and the responsibilities of students and professors.

The articles leave open what specific curriculum changes or guidelines the faculty will adopt. They do not say what actions the AI Council will take or when. They do not report any decisions made at the forum about teaching critical AI skills. They do not say how UConn will measure whether students gain the skills the panelists described. They do not give any response from students to the panel discussion.

stories.Headline: Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan raise $277M for AI infrastructure startup Marlowe
stories.Summary:
Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million for their new startup Marlowe, the company announced on Nov 23, 2026. The outsized seed funding reflects the scale of the challenge the founders are taking on, according to GeekWire. Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for running AI models in everyday products rather than training them. The company is starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom. Accel led the latest round, which values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, making it a unicorn out of the gate according to the company.

Marlowe was founded in May and is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Its first site, built around Etched's chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD's new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027. Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent, while the company says it has signed three customer agreements without naming the customers or locations. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

Lewis, Marlowe's CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe's CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure. Lewis said in an interview that the demand for intelligence and AI is very high and that it should be accessible and affordable for everyone. Srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. He said there were literally times when a significant portion of the non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn't support the latest models and workloads. Lewis said Marlowe's edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips, adding that you have to go do the work.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens. The round was joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor, and angel investors include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe's executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy's president, is also an investor.

The idea for Marlowe grew out of what the founders saw at Microsoft, where demand was surging for inference but data centers were still being built mainly for training models. Lewis said they were always oversold and effectively sold out, and since then demand for inference has grown faster than supply. Power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build, pushing up costs at the same time. Srinivasan's career runs from video games to AI infrastructure, including work on DirectX and Halo 3 at Microsoft, eight years at Valve, and roles at Facebook and LinkedIn. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023 amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Much of Marlowe's funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline. The company isn't using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn't ruled them out. The articles leave open the names and locations of the three customers and the location of the third site under a letter of intent.

stories.Headline: Innovo and Quantavist scale AI worker safety system across UAE construction projects
stories.Summary:
Innovo and Quantavist scaled an AI-enabled worker safety system across multiple construction projects in the UAE. The companies announced this expansion today at the Big 5 Global 2026 event. This scaling follows a partnership that the two companies first established in July 2025. The system identifies critical safety risks in real time and routes them to site teams. A pilot in Dubai allows the system to speak directly to people in multiple languages.

The system uses robotic pan-tilt-zoom cameras to monitor selected work fronts twenty four hours a day. It identifies risks like work at height, gaps in edge protection, and activity inside lifting zones. It also monitors people entering equipment operating areas and those missing personal protective equipment. At Ghaf Woods, high-severity alerts fell by 59 per cent between the first and third quarters of 2026. At Alba Residences, the alert rate per worker-hour fell by 45 per cent in two weeks.

Douglas Zuzic, Chief Digital Officer at Innovo Group, said live projects prove new technologies against real challenges. He stated that Quantavist's technology met tests for time, cost, quality, safety, and sustainability. Gareth Main, Group HSE Director at Innovo Group, said the system provides round-the-clock visibility of high-risk activities. He noted that safety teams cannot observe every work front on every shift during active projects. Oscar Pickerill, Quantavist Co-founder, said safety teams deserve technology that takes an active role.

The system affects site safety engineers who must accept alerts, take corrective action, and upload evidence. The AI reviews this evidence before the safety team signs off to close the alert. Workers at Ghaf Woods are affected by a voice-warning system that delivers hazard-specific spoken instructions. This system reflects the multinational workforce on Innovo sites by providing instructions in multiple languages. The average time between detection and spoken instruction during the pilot was 8.4 seconds.

The partnership allows Innovo to provide site requirements and safety workflows to help Quantavist tailor the technology. Quantavist estimates the system removed around 1,000 hours of manual alert administration between January and May 2026. More than 90 per cent of all alerts were closed out within defined response times. Weekly reports show where risks recur by work area, zone, shift, and subcontractor for oversight. The system supports the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031 and the We the UAE 2031 vision.

Innovo sees potential for this data to power AI-driven predictive safety analytics for future project oversight. The company also intends to feed this safety data into the construction digital twins it already uses. This integration would bring safety into wider project planning and general oversight for the construction firm. The articles leave open how the system will be scaled beyond the current UAE construction projects. They do not state if the voice-warning pilot will be expanded to all Innovo sites.

stories.Headline: Galveston police adopt Veritone Investigate AI to speed active and cold case work
stories.Summary:
The Galveston Police Department announced in a November 19 news release that it will begin using an artificial intelligence platform called Veritone Investigate to help move active and long-running cold case investigations along more efficiently, according to Houston Public Media. The Galveston City Council approved the use of the AI-powered tools in a 5-0 vote at a council meeting on November 12. The service package with Veritone runs for one year and costs approximately $75,000, according to city documents. The California-based company Veritone works with about 450 agencies across the U.S. for public safety, most of which are in California, and CEO and President Ryan Steelberg said the partnership with Galveston is one of the company's first entry points into Texas.

Steelberg said police departments are struggling to manage increasing volumes of digital evidence, which makes it harder to find information that moves cases forward. He said the investigative tool would help agencies process audio, video, images and documents and make the material searchable, and would also use AI-driven tools to get information relevant to an investigation. He said the AI is not trying to solve the case for the department but is trying to organize the data. Galveston Police Chief Doug Balli said that entering just one case into Veritone would save the average investigator hundreds of man-hours in reviewing information and generating leads, and that investigators need technology that helps them move from evidence to insight quickly, especially when they are working both active and cold cases. Balli did not respond to Houston Public Media's request for comment about the new technology.

Steelberg said the information used with Veritone Investigate will be safeguarded like any other investigation and that the process for public records requests will not change. He said nothing will change in terms of the controls, audit logging and jurisdiction, and that the purpose is for data to go into a secure environment where the AI models that are invoked are containerized and secure. The department's decision comes alongside heavy scrutiny from residents around Harris and Galveston counties who have expressed privacy concerns about Flock Safety cameras, which use AI technology to automatically read license plates, especially in light of Houston-area cases of alleged misuse by law enforcement. It also comes around the same time that Harris County officials decided to pull a no-bid contract for a controversial AI facial recognition technology, Clearview AI, from a commissioners court meeting agenda.

stories.Headline: NHS launches AI-assisted breast cancer screening trial with nearly 700,000 women
stories.Summary:
The National Health Service in England launched a trial of AI-assisted breast cancer screening, according to a notice published Monday in the BMJ and a statement from the NHS on Nov. 23, 2026. The trial is set to involve nearly 700,000 women over the next three years, the NHS said. Recruitment has already started at Cambridge University Hospitals, representing the first 30 sites across the U.K., with further locations opening in the coming months. The program is backed by over $13 million in government support, according to Radiology Business, and £10 million ($13 million) according to Agence France-Presse. The trial is being led by the University of Warwick, the University of Cambridge and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, working closely with NHS England.

The trial will test whether AI-assisted tools could allow most images to be reviewed by only one specialist rather than the current two, the NHS said. The AI-assisted reading tool will assist clinicians in reviewing images collected from routine mammograms. The NHS said it has already rigorously tested four AI systems to be used in the trial, and all final clinical decisions will remain with human NHS staffers. Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for screening every three years, amounting to around 2.1 million screenings annually, and the NHS estimates this helps prevent around 1,300 deaths each year. The EDITH (Early Detection using Information Technology in Health) trial will span the next three years, with funding from the National Institute for Health and Care Research.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said in a statement that this is the biggest AI breast cancer trial in the world, lauding the technology's huge potential while pledging proper safeguards to ensure safety and effectiveness. Cooper said that if successful, the technology could help women get a breast cancer diagnosis and start treatment much more quickly, giving them the best possible chance of recovery. Lucy Chappell, a professor and CEO of the National Institute for Health and Care Research, said the NIHR is proud to be funding one of the world's largest studies of AI-assisted breast screening. Chappell said EDITH will bring together researchers, NHS staff and hundreds of thousands of women from all walks of life and will generate vital evidence on whether the technology could transform how cancer is detected and diagnosed. Hannah Maybour, head of public affairs at Breast Cancer Now, said the charity knows breast screening services are facing considerable workforce pressures.

Maybour said that if the trial shows AI-assisted mammogram reading is as safe and effective as the current process, it could help ease some of these pressures by reducing the need for two specialists to review every mammogram to one, freeing up valuable clinical time. The Royal College of Radiologists said in a statement Monday that it sees promise in the trial, but believes the initiative will not help address the country's immediate dire shortage of specialists. The RCR said more than one-fifth of the breast radiology workforce is slated to retire by 2030. Dr. Stephen Harden, president of the RCR, said the trial has real potential to free up radiologists' time but won't be a quick fix to the immediate need for more radiologists to ensure patients can get prompt answers about their health. Harden said the college looks forward to seeing the results of the trial.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, with around 55,000 diagnosed every year in the U.K., according to Agence France-Presse. Reviewing mammograms can be time-intensive, and fewer than 1% of exams show signs of cancer, with significant time spent reviewing negative scans, Radiology Business reported. A study published in The Lancet in January said AI can improve breast cancer detection through more effective screening while reducing radiologists' workloads. That study analyzed nearly 106,000 mammograms performed in Sweden as part of its national breast cancer screening program, involving women with a median age of 53, from April 2021 to early December 2022. The NHS said screening appointments will proceed as normal, but the AI-assisted tool will be used alongside specialists checking the images to look for cancers that are too small to see or feel.

Those involved note that nothing will change during regular screening appointments, and letters sent to patients will include details about the trial and an option to opt out for anyone who doesn't want to take part. Women attending routine breast screening at 30 planned sites nationwide will be given details about the trial and participate unless they choose to opt out. The NHS announced that hundreds of women had been invited to take part at the outset, with thousands more to be invited. The articles do not state when results of the three-year trial are expected or how the four AI systems were selected. The articles also do not say what will happen to the AI-assisted reading approach if the trial does not show it is as safe and effective as the current process.

stories.Headline: Kyndryl Consult's Landry says AI should give clinicians cognitive capacity back rather than replace them
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl Consult's Christine Landry said on MarketScale's Highway to Health podcast that the useful AI question is not whether it replaces doctors but whether it helps them give better care. She spoke with host David Kemp in an episode published on November 23, 2026. Landry is the global healthcare partner at Kyndryl Consult, the advisory arm of Kyndryl. She argued that AI-native healthcare should give clinicians cognitive capacity back rather than replace them. She said physicians lose nearly two hours per hour of patient care to administrative work.

Landry described AI's role as a spectrum, from automation for routine, low-risk and reversible work to AI recommending while the clinician decides in the middle ground. She said human judgment must remain explicit for high-consequence decisions, with those boundaries set before deployment. She said governance has to keep pace with the technology through what she calls policy as code, so guardrails become rules enforced inside the workflow rather than a binder on a shelf. She said that if AI acts at machine speed, governance cannot operate at manual speed. She said organizations getting it right pick one workflow that matters to patients and clinicians, measure whether the outcome changed, and stop admiring the pilot.

Landry said she prefers to say human in control rather than human in the loop. She said the bigger opportunity is not giving clinicians time back but giving them cognitive capacity back so they can focus on the patient in front of them instead of a screen. She said clinicians spend an enormous amount of time finding information, looking for documentation, coordinating and moving things between systems, and none of that is why many of her friends and customers went to medical school. She said she would rather have her physician looking at her than at a screen during an appointment. She said the goal is not to replace the clinician but to redesign care around the clinician in a way that betters the patient experience.

Kemp said nothing in healthcare happens without the physician or the healthcare professional, and he does not think that is changing. He said their role is vital and critical and will remain so no matter how intelligent systems and platforms become. Landry said she is not sure she wants her doctor optimizing for speed, and that getting out of a clinic in three minutes is probably not the innovation patients are looking for. She said the real opportunity is giving clinicians cognitive capacity back so they can focus in the moments that matter with their patients. She said patients want to feel heard and seen, and that clinicians should look more at the patient.

The articles cite a time-and-motion study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, titled Allocation of Physician Time in Ambulatory Practice: A Time and Motion Study in 4 Specialties, for the finding that physicians spend nearly two hours on electronic health records and desk work for every hour of direct patient care. The episode was produced through MarketScale as part of its Executive Thought Leadership offering, promoted content from Highway to Health. Kyndryl is described as a global technology services company that helps organizations modernize and manage mission-critical technology and workflows. Landry works with health systems, providers, med tech, pharma and biotech organizations to bring technology, data, AI and operations together. The episode's key takeaways say organizations seeing real results build trust through transparency and frontline involvement.

The articles do not say what any health system, provider or regulator will do next, and they give no deployment date, site or budget for AI-native healthcare. They leave open which single workflow organizations should start with and how changes in patient and clinician outcomes would be measured. They do not say how policy as code would be written, enforced or audited inside clinical workflows. They do not name any organization that has adopted the approach or any result it produced. They do not say how the boundaries between automation, AI recommendation and explicit human control would be set in practice.

stories.Headline: SANY debuts autonomous construction machinery and AI management platform at bauma CHINA 2026
stories.Summary:
SANY showcased its vision for an AI-native robotics future at bauma CHINA 2026 in Shanghai on November 24, 2026. The company gathered its intelligent capabilities under one roof to demonstrate a new strategy for the construction industry. This display featured an autonomous wheel loader that plans its own routes and loads materials without any human aid. SANY also presented a 100-tonne mining truck that operates without a cab to show its autonomous capabilities. The company believes that the next decade of construction will belong to AI agents and robotic machinery.

The SKT165Ei is the industry's first cab-less 100-tonne autonomous battery-electric mining truck, which increases its payload ratio by 12 percent. This truck uses an 800-volt platform with 2C fast charging to recharge in under 35 minutes under cloud dispatch. The SSR360C-10E is an all-electric roller with no cab and batteries over 1,000 kWh that last over 12 hours. This roller tracks its planned path to within 5 centimeters and uses multi-agent scheduling to lift efficiency by 20 percent. SANY also introduced the E-MOVE prototype, which provides an early look at an all-electric excavator robot.

SANY is responsible for these developments and claims that machines should take on the hardest work while people stay central. The company stated that its goal is to make job sites safer, cleaner, and more productive through these new technologies. They believe that building intelligence into products, manufacturing, and operations is the key to the future of the industry. SANY aims to lead the way in industrial AI by becoming an AI-native robotics company. The company is using its intelligence hall to show how this strategy works in real time.

The company's driverless paving fleets are the world's first in commercial use at scale and affect large scale infrastructure projects. These fleets have logged more than 5,000 kilometers across more than 60 projects since 2019, including one nonstop expressway. One operator using a tablet can supervise up to 15 machines, which changes how these fleets are managed. At a smart green concrete batching plant, AI controls production with zero manual intervention to lift efficiency by 20 percent. These advancements aim to reduce the need for human operators in dangerous or repetitive construction environments.

The foundation for training this AI is four decades of operating data from ports, mines, and various job sites. SANY has traced a three-step process involving machines redesigned for autonomy, fleets that work as one, and operational AI. The company has upgraded the MySANY app into a new intelligent connectivity platform called SanVIST, which debuted today. This platform includes an AI agent named SANY Neo that provides five specific capabilities for managing entire customer projects. These capabilities include repair diagnosis, task coordination, parts identification, work guidance, and the management of customer project operations.

SANY will continue moving toward its goal of becoming an AI-native robotics company to lead the industrial AI sector. The company plans to further integrate AI into its manufacturing and operations to enhance overall productivity and safety. The articles leave open how the E-MOVE prototype will evolve into a fully commercial all-electric excavator robot. It is not stated when the SKT165Ei or SSR360C-10E will be available for wider global commercial purchase. The text does not specify the exact timeline for the full rollout of the SanVIST platform.

stories.Headline: Lunit and M42 collaborate on AI lung cancer screening plan for Abu Dhabi
stories.Summary:
Lunit, a South Korean company that provides artificial intelligence for cancer diagnostics, announced on 23 November 2026 a strategic collaboration with M42, a global healthcare and health technology group, to advance an AI-powered lung cancer early detection initiative in the United Arab Emirates. The agreement was signed by Brandon Suh, the chief executive officer of Lunit, and Kareem Shahin, the chief executive officer of M42's digital health solutions platform and the group's chief digital officer. Under the collaboration, M42 will lead the preparation and submission of a proposed lung cancer early detection programme to the Department of Health ,  Abu Dhabi and the Abu Dhabi Public Health Center. Lunit will provide the technical expertise and support the proposed deployment and integration of its software into the regional network.

The plan centres on deploying Lunit INSIGHT CXR, an AI analysis solution designed to evaluate chest radiographs, across historical records stored in Malaffi, Abu Dhabi's centralised health information exchange. The initiative aims to re-examine existing radiographs for suspicious markers that were not identified during initial assessments, which would allow clinicians to recall patients who require further diagnostic assessment. Malaffi is operated by M42's business unit Abu Dhabi Health Data Services and currently connects more than 3,100 healthcare facilities across the emirate. The exchange holds 4.2 billion clinical records covering 14 million unique patient files, which the companies describe as providing the data infrastructure for the proposed screening effort. M42 operates a global network of more than 480 healthcare facilities across 28 countries and is backed by Abu Dhabi-based sovereign investor Mubadala and AI technology group G42.

Brandon Suh, the chief executive officer of Lunit, said that medical AI has the potential to create new clinical value from imaging data that healthcare systems already possess. He described the collaboration with M42 as an opportunity to explore AI-powered lung cancer early detection at a broader healthcare system level. He added that the work supports the company's vision of making advanced cancer detection technologies more accessible worldwide. The articles attribute no further comment to M42 or to any government body.

Lunit was established in 2013 to develop AI diagnostic tools for oncology, and its commercial portfolio includes the Lunit INSIGHT Breast Suite, cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration, and the Lunit SCOPE research platform. Its imaging systems are present in more than 10,000 medical facilities in over 65 countries, according to the company. The collaboration is described as a step toward exploring how AI and connected healthcare infrastructure can work together to support earlier cancer detection. By combining Lunit's medical AI technology with M42's healthcare expertise and digital health capabilities, the companies aim to establish a foundation for future AI-enabled population health initiatives in Abu Dhabi.

stories.Headline: Israel Aerospace Industries integrates AI into weapons development and manufacturing
stories.Summary:
Israel Aerospace Industries said it is turning lessons from combat into new defense technologies and bringing artificial intelligence into its development and manufacturing operations. The state-owned defense contractor said it is increasing production rates, expanding its engineering and operational capabilities and investing in infrastructure to keep pace with orders from Israel and overseas customers. Its order backlog reached a record $35.6 billion at the end of September, equivalent to approximately 4.8 years of activity at its current sales rate. Last week, IAI announced the establishment of a new AI and Digital Directorate, headed by an executive vice president who will report directly to CEO Guy Bar Lev. The unit will oversee the company's AI and digital strategy, promote the use of AI tools across its operations and help expand its engineering and production capabilities.

IAI's sales in the first nine months of 2026 rose 28% to $6.56 billion, while net income increased 37% to $663 million. Operating profit climbed 54% to $751 million, and EBITDA rose 40% to approximately $1.01 billion. Sales by the military divisions rose 28% to $5.76 billion during the period, while aviation sales increased to $1.3 billion. Exports accounted for 65% of total sales, and 72% of the company's order backlog is designated for overseas customers. Research and development spending reached $239 million in the first nine months, compared with $208 million in the same period last year.

Chairman Boaz Levy said IAI's unique advantage is reflected in its ability to draw insights from real-time operational experience and rapidly translate them into advanced capabilities that address current and future threats. Levy described artificial intelligence as a strategic growth engine and a key element in shaping the future battlefield. Bar Lev said IAI was expanding the use of AI in its development and production processes to improve efficiency, increase output and shorten delivery times. Bar Lev said the company is working around the clock to meet its commitments to customers in Israel and worldwide by increasing production rates, expanding its engineering and operational capabilities and investing in infrastructure and resources. Bar Lev said IAI is expanding the integration of artificial intelligence into its development and production processes to streamline processes, increase output, shorten lead times and improve its ability to respond to customers' operational and business needs.

Among the systems IAI is developing is ELLYON, a new multi-mission aircraft concept combining intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities with electronic attack. The platform is designed to gather intelligence while disrupting enemy radar and communications, using sensors, signals intelligence and AI-based mission management. Another system, HYPNOSIS, is designed to disrupt and spoof satellite navigation signals used by drones and other aerial threats. Rather than physically intercepting a drone, the mobile system aims to interfere with its ability to navigate, providing a non-kinetic layer of defense that can complement conventional interceptors. The company is also continuing to develop its Arrow missile defense systems, which form the upper tier of Israel's multi-layered air defense architecture and are designed to intercept ballistic missiles, including threats outside the atmosphere.

IAI ended September with $4.5 billion in cash and liquid assets and reported $882 million in positive operating cash flow for the first nine months. It also disclosed that the Israeli Ministry of Defense owed it billions of shekels as of September 30, and called on the Defense and Finance ministries to reach an urgent arrangement for repayment. Levy said IAI was continuing to prepare for an initial public offering, describing it as a strategic milestone that would give the Israeli public an opportunity to participate in the company's success. IAI has said that artificial intelligence and automated manufacturing are among the elements being incorporated into its development and production efforts. The main source of growth was the company's military business, particularly its Systems, Missiles and Space activities.

The NPR report said it has been nearly five years since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and that the weapons on the battlefield have transformed rapidly. Russia invaded Ukraine with tanks and now drones and hyper-sonic missiles are used, the report said. Both sides are using weapons powered by AI, which has many people worried, according to the report. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned that AI could start leading decisions on the battlefield as early as next year. Advocates for AI say Ukraine cannot say no to a technology that could give it an edge over a much bigger enemy, the report said.

stories.Headline: European tech stocks lead a market rebound as the Stoxx 600 rises 0.73 per cent after an AI-driven sell-off
stories.Summary:
European shares recovered on Monday, November 23, 2026, as technology stocks led a market rebound. This recovery followed a sharp artificial intelligence sell-off that caused the steepest weekly decline since late March 2025. The Stoxx 600 index rose 0.73 per cent to 630.24 points by 0933 GMT after five straight sessions of losses. This movement put the index on track for its largest one-day jump since November 9.

The technology index outperformed other sectors with a 2 per cent rise after its worst weekly fall since March 2020. Chip-linked companies including ASML, ASM International, and BE Semiconductor each saw gains between 3 per cent and 5 per cent. Defence stocks advanced 1.8 per cent, while miners surged 1.4 per cent as gold prices recovered from 14-month lows. Abivax jumped 10 per cent after rejecting a short-seller report, and Drax rallied over 7 per cent on profit forecasts.

Kathleen Brooks, the research director for the UK at brokerage XTB, said the previous sell-off established a new era for artificial intelligence. She noted that investors will now provide more scrutiny, though a pullback was expected because the sell-off went beyond just AI pricing. Brooks warned that the current recovery could be a dead cat bounce if investor sentiment remains sour. She mentioned that demand had not changed despite the weakening appetite for artificial intelligence risk.

The market volatility occurred as investors doubted whether massive technology investments would generate returns quickly enough. Concerns grew that valuations had raced ahead of near-term returns, especially after the debut of Anthropic. Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron suggested reviving a 2011 proposal for a constitutional golden rule to limit public finances. This move aims to reassure investors amid rising debt and a deeper downturn in the French economy.
