stories.Headline: Woman sues Los Angeles police under California reproductive privacy law over stillbirth interrogation
stories.Summary:
A woman is suing the city of Los Angeles and detectives within the Los Angeles Police Department for allegedly unlawful interrogation and investigation following a stillbirth she had in 2024. The complaint was filed late last week by If/When/How alongside law firm BraunHagey & Borden LLP, according to one article, and this month according to another. The plaintiff was granted anonymity Thursday and is referred to in the complaint as Jane Doe. This is the first known lawsuit under California’s Reproductive Privacy Act, which was amended in 2022. The law prohibits the state from taking punitive action based on pregnancy decisions and outcomes.

The plaintiff alleges that in November 2024 she was unhoused, living in a city shelter and menstruating irregularly due to her epilepsy medication. An emergency visit for stomach pains revealed she was pregnant, but the fetus did not have a heartbeat. According to the complaint, Doe was initially informed she was still in the first trimester and could miscarry at home but subsequently learned she was around 29 weeks pregnant. She passed significant blood clots in the shelter toilet, left without flushing and was taken by ambulance to the hospital and treated for significant blood loss. The complaint says Doe did not realize she had passed the stillbirth.

According to the complaint, police showed up at the hospital, shackled her to a bed and interrogated her for hours, telling her a fetus had been found outside the shelter. The complaint said this was the first time Doe learned she had passed into the toilet and the first time she heard someone had reportedly moved the fetus to an alley outside the shelter. The complaint alleges police continued to pursue a homicide investigation for about a year despite being told by a medical examiner that fetal demise had occurred in utero. The Los Angeles Police Department declined to comment citing the pending litigation. Sara Ainsworth, chief legal and policy director at If/When/How, said all the different things they did to Ms. Doe are a violation of the Reproductive Privacy Act.

Ainsworth said it is very important to show the state actors in California that they must abide by the law, which prohibits criminalizing somebody. She said California’s strong right-to-sue protections could become a legal roadmap for other states. At least 13 states and the District of Columbia have in recent years enacted measures to ensure protections for people’s pregnancy decisions and outcomes, including California, Colorado, Hawaii, Illinois, Michigan, Missouri, Montana, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia and Washington. Among the few other places that explicitly allow damages suits, including D.C., Colorado and Illinois, California is the only state to eliminate common legal immunities for law enforcement, Ainsworth said. In California, Doe alleges she had to leave the shelter after police told reporters they suspected a homicide and headlines circulated about a newborn baby dropped from a fourth-floor window.

In February 2025, Doe contacted a legal helpline run by If/When/How and started working with litigation counsel Shantal McNeil, who helped Doe navigate the investigation and petitioned the city attorney not to bring charges. McNeil said reputational damage and other harms often outlast these types of arrests and investigations, even when charges are dropped or never filed. She said police often investigate vulnerable women like the California plaintiff, who according to her attorneys is a young woman. McNeil said people mistakenly think every pregnancy ends in a healthy baby, and if you don’t act the way police think you should, it is suddenly suspicious or criminal behavior. She said the hospital told Doe to go home because she was having a miscarriage, and the fact that any of this happened after that is quite mind boggling.

Ainsworth noted that in other states it can be harder to determine who is accountable, saying it is typically hard to hold government officials accountable for wrongful criminalization because of legal barriers. She said the Reproductive Privacy Act in California explicitly allows a private right of action and eliminates some of those immunities, allowing government actors who normally are shielded to be held accountable. Women in other states have sued for facing criminal charges after a pregnancy loss, including Brittany Watts in Ohio, who last year sued the city of Warren, city policy officers and a hospital after she was arrested and charged with abuse of a corpse following a miscarriage in her home. In the first three years after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, more than 900 women faced criminal charges for conduct related to their pregnancies. The vast majority of the charges were for child abuse, neglect or endangerment, most related to substance use during pregnancy, but some involved allegations related to failing to obtain prenatal care or other actions taken or not taken during pregnancy or after pregnancy loss.

stories.Headline: Bill Ackman says AI fears hit only a small slice of S&P Global as ratings drive real risk
stories.Summary:
Bill Ackman said AI fears hit a single-digit slice of S&P Global, and the rest of the company drives its earnings, according to remarks relayed on the We Study Billionaires podcast. The comments were reported by TIKR.com in an article last updated on Nov 23, 2026, written by Roxanna Maglangit and reviewed by Michael Douglass. S&P Global lost about $40 billion of market value in about 10 days this year, as AI-agent fears also hit FactSet and MSCI. In the first week of February, Anthropic released a set of plugins for its Claude assistant, and the market reaction was to sell every company that makes money selling information to professionals. S&P Global's 2026 guidance then came in light, and Bill Ackman's Pershing Square had disclosed a new stake in S&P Global over the summer.

Capital IQ clients pay by the seat, and an AI agent that does the clicking and the reading could make the seat unnecessary. Daniel Mahncke estimates that Capital IQ subscriptions bring in something like 6% of company revenue and even less of profit, roughly $900 million against fiscal 2025's $15.3 billion of total revenue. The Market Intelligence division that includes Capital IQ still grew revenue 7% in the third quarter, and FactSet grew its organic annual subscription value 7.0% in the fiscal year ended Aug. 31. S&P Dow Jones Indices grew revenue 20% to $554 million in the third quarter, driven mainly by asset-linked fees on higher assets under management. MSCI's Index segment revenue rose 18.1% in the third quarter, and consensus has normalized EPS rising from $17.95 this year to $22.77 in fiscal 2028, or about 13% a year.

Ackman argues investors fixated on threats to a single-digit slice of the company and lost sight of the fact that future earnings growth will be driven almost entirely by the benchmark business. O'Malley relayed that case on the show and said he thinks Ackman is mostly right. O'Malley was blunt about the ratings risk, saying that if it becomes clear AI was a bubble and it has popped, there will be a drought in debt issuance. Mahncke noted that the hyperscalers issued something like $240 billion of debt in the first nine months of this year, which is more than S&P had assumed for the entire year. The article's author wrote that Ackman has the AI story right and that the risk worth pricing in is a down cycle in ratings once AI borrowing slows.

S&P Global's ratings revenue grew 11% over those nine months, to $3.91 billion, and Moody's investment-grade ratings revenue jumped 18% in the third quarter on tech borrowers, including AI-related and hyperscaler financing. Moody's total ratings revenue slipped 1%, and the article says the ratings business is riding a wave of AI debt. TIKR tracks 23 analysts on S&P Global, and more than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. FactSet was called almost entirely an interface by Mahncke, and the article says it is far more exposed than S&P Global. The article says that if the company most exposed to this threat is still growing, a 6% slice won't sink S&P Global.

Even after a rebound from its June low, S&P Global trades at 23x forward earnings, well below its five-year average of 28x. It bottomed at 20x in late June, the cheapest it has been in five years. The article says the discount, at five turns below its average multiple, more than covers the ratings cycle risk. The article states that the market is pricing the wrong fear and that Ackman has the AI story right. The article says the real AI exposure is in ratings, where S&P Global gets paid when companies borrow, and right now the biggest borrowers are building data centers.

The next test comes in early February with fourth-quarter results and 2027 guidance. Guidance that keeps EPS on track for the $20.16 consensus would back Ackman's case, while a ratings outlook that leans even harder on hyperscaler deals would mean the cycle risk is growing. The article leaves open what S&P Global stock is actually worth, offering a TIKR valuation model that starts from Wall Street consensus estimates or adjusted inputs. The article's disclaimer states that its content is not intended as investment or financial advice and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any stocks. The disclaimer adds that the analysis might not include recent company news or important updates and that TIKR has no position in any of the stocks mentioned.

stories.Headline: TensorWave signs six-year deal to supply OpenAI with 457 MW of AMD-powered AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
TensorWave signed a multi-year partnership with OpenAI to provide 457 megawatts of AI infrastructure powered by AMD hardware, the company announced on November 17, 2026. TensorWave is the infrastructure provider supplying the capacity, OpenAI is the recipient, and AMD is the silicon supplier whose hardware powers the deployment. The announcement appeared under TensorWave's dedicated TensorWave & OpenAI partnership coverage and was reported by Ashish Joshi. The 457-megawatt figure is the total scale of the deployment covered by the partnership rather than a partial tranche. The multi-year structure indicates sustained provision of infrastructure over the life of the agreement rather than a one-time transaction.

Futurum reported on November 19, 2026 that the agreement is a six-year, 457 MW infrastructure deal to deliver dedicated AMD Instinct MI455X GPU capacity across multiple U.S. data center sites. The deployment will use AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs in infrastructure purpose-built for AMD Helios rack-scale systems, with dedicated single-tenant capacity connected through high-performance Ethernet networking. TensorWave expects to bring the first capacity online in the first half of 2027 and complete the full deployment by early 2028. The deal makes TensorWave the first publicly announced neocloud provider supporting the OpenAI-AMD strategic collaboration, which targets 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct GPU deployments beginning with 1 gigawatt in 2026. The agreement is TensorWave's largest to date.

AMD SVP of AI Vamsi Boppana stated that the three-way combination is building the foundation to deliver AI compute at extraordinary scale and advance the broader AI ecosystem. TensorWave President Piotr Tomasik said the ability to deliver hundreds of megawatts of advanced compute reliably and at speed will separate the companies that can support frontier AI from those that cannot. TensorWave was the first public cloud to deploy AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs and has continued expanding across successive generations including MI325X and MI355X. That track record as an AMD Helios launch partner gave OpenAI confidence in TensorWave's ability to operate purpose-built Helios rack-scale systems at extreme scale. TensorWave has more than 2 gigawatts of long-term data center capacity already secured.

In January 2026, Cerebras secured a strategic multi-year $10 billion compute agreement with OpenAI, validating its hardware for the most demanding frontier AI applications. In late February 2026, Meta announced a multi-year agreement to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of AMD-based infrastructure, including the co-design of custom Instinct MI450-based GPUs. OpenAI is deliberately distributing compute commitments across multiple vendors and infrastructure models, which reduces single-source dependency and ensures redundancy for large and complex AI model training and inference workloads. Hyperscalers bring their own software, operations teams, and increasingly their own silicon, whereas neoclouds, enterprises, telcos, and sovereign AI factories need the GPU vendor to supply much of the operating stack. For AMD-centric workloads, that distinction makes a dedicated neocloud like TensorWave a more natural fit than a hyperscaler optimized around its own silicon.

The agreement illustrates how frontier AI compute demand has grown to a scale where purpose-built, long-term neocloud capacity contracts are becoming the preferred procurement model for leading AI labs. At 457 MW committed over six years, this single neocloud deal illustrates how large individual infrastructure tranches within the 6 GW program will be. Multi-year, multi-hundred-megawatt, single-tenant capacity contracts with specialized neocloud providers are displacing the on-demand hyperscaler model for the most demanding workloads. The procurement logic is built around guaranteed capacity, hardware specificity, and operational control rather than flexibility and shared tenancy. As frontier model complexity continues to grow, this template is likely to become the norm rather than the exception for labs operating at OpenAI's scale.

What to watch includes whether TensorWave brings initial AMD Helios systems online on schedule in 1H 2027 and which additional neocloud providers announce roles within the 6 GW OpenAI-AMD program in Q1-Q2 2027. Also to watch is how NVIDIA-aligned neocloud providers respond with comparable long-term capacity offerings to retain frontier AI customers. Further items are whether Meta's up to 6 GW AMD infrastructure commitment advances to named neocloud or operator announcements in early 2027 and whether additional multi-year, dedicated-capacity agreements with new vendors are announced as the broader 6 GW AMD program scales through 2027. The articles leave open which additional neocloud providers will join the program and how NVIDIA-aligned providers will respond.

stories.Headline: Governors propose principles for state role in AI regulation
stories.Summary:
The National Governors Association (NGA) announced a set of principles on Sunday, November 22, 2026, to ensure states have a role in regulating artificial intelligence. The bipartisan council released the framework as the new Congress prepares to take office in January. The council is led by Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, the NGA chair, and Indiana Gov. Mike Braun, the NGA vice chair. North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein and Utah Gov. Spencer Cox joined Moore and Braun in calling for Congress to include governors in AI regulation discussions.

The principles call for federal and state governments to both play a role in AI regulation, with Washington overseeing national and international risks. States would retain authority to govern AI use within their existing responsibilities, including protecting workers, consumers and children. The framework urges independent evaluations or audits of frontier AI models and reporting of serious safety incidents to federal authorities and affected states. It also calls for federal standards for AI threats to critical infrastructure, including financial systems, and for international cooperation on AI standards, trade and security. The council recommends safeguards when automated systems affect housing, employment, lending, insurance or access to essential services.

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said governors agree that AI poses both opportunities and risks and that humans must stay in control. He said governors will focus on creating jobs and making sure workers have a voice in deployment of new technology. Indiana Gov. Mike Braun said artificial intelligence has great potential to generate economic growth, create high-quality jobs, increase wages and make government services more efficient. Utah Gov. Spencer Cox said, "We don't have to choose between innovation and safety." NGA CEO Brandon Tatum said no federal AI policy will be effective without governors' input and that governors intend to work with Congress, the White House and industry leaders.

The NGA document cautions against federal overreach when it comes to interfering with state laws. It warns that governors will judge any effort to preempt state law against the association's standing Principles of Federalism. The council urged Congress to approach any preemption cautiously and consult a representative cross-section of states. The governors called for clear technical definitions, safeguards proportionate to demonstrated risks and regular reviews as AI capabilities change. They said rules should avoid creating unnecessary barriers for smaller companies entering the market.

States are already stepping up their efforts to regulate AI. New York Attorney General Letitia James last week created a dedicated enforcement unit called the AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement, and Transparency (ASSET) Unit to police model developers and chatbot operators. The ASSET Unit will lead enforcement of New York's frontier AI safety law, the RAISE Act, when it goes into effect January 1. California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI last week, alleging the company knowingly developed and tested advanced AI models without required safeguards. The suit focuses on a July incident in which agents running on OpenAI's AI models attacked fellow tech company Hugging Face. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit singles the company out over "a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab."

Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte, who chairs the House Republican Policy Committee, said Sunday he believes Congress can pass a bipartisan measure before the year ends. The bill is titled the Great American AI Act and is built on a discussion draft he released in June with Rep. Lori Trahan. The draft would create a federal framework for AI governance and allow federal preemption of state AI laws for three years. The draft would bar states from laws targeting AI model development while leaving states free to regulate the technology's use. The Trump administration urged lawmakers in March to enact legislation preempting state AI rules, and in December the president said he would withhold federal broadband funding from states whose AI laws his administration judged to be holding back American dominance.

stories.Headline: European Commission confirms AI-assisted cyberattack on its Brussels headquarters
stories.Summary:
The European Commission detected a cyberattack on October 22 and confirmed the incident on October 26 after an initial investigation. This event marked the first time the 27-member bloc reported a cyberattack that utilized an artificial intelligence tool. The attack targeted the headquarters of the executive branch of the European Union located in the city of Brussels. A spokesperson for the Commission spoke to the press about the event on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Investigators have been dealing with this AI-generated attack for almost a month since it was first detected.

The Commission temporarily took several applications offline, and most of these digital tools have since been restored by the authorities. Politico reported the attack lasted ten days and affected reimbursement tools, translation tools, and databases for timesheets and salaries. The EU agency CERT-EU oversees digital security for institutions that employ about 40,000 people just in the city of Brussels. The European Commission informed the departments concerned and remains in contact with the European Data Protection Supervisor and CERT-EU. No similar incidents were reported by the European Parliament or the European Council, the other two main EU institutions.

Thomas Regnier, a spokesperson for the European Commission, stated that AI-assisted tools can be misused to detect vulnerabilities in digital systems. He confirmed that AI tools were used in this case and noted that no one is immune to global cyberattacks. Regnier said that investigators found no evidence of a data breach affecting the Commission staff as a whole. He declined to identify the specific AI tool used or say who was behind the campaign against the bloc. The spokesperson also stated that he was unaware of any ransom demand and that many campaign elements were contained.

Politico first reported the incidents, though Thomas Regnier declined to confirm the specific reports regarding the affected databases and tools. The attack affected the executive body of the 27-nation EU, but other main institutions did not report similar cyber incidents. Staff members of the European Commission were the primary group mentioned in the context of potential data breach investigations. Cybersecurity experts have been working to manage the fallout and restore the digital tools that were taken offline. The reports indicate that the attack targeted key systems used for administrative tasks like salaries and reimbursement.

The EU agency CERT-EU posted a blog on November 4 warning about threats from a specific AI tool called ARTEX. This tool was designed to use artificial intelligence to identify vulnerabilities in digital systems across various global networks. The agency assessed that the public availability of ARTEX would likely accelerate adoption by threat actors for automated attacks. Such attacks are expected to be more frequent, faster, and more scalable with a higher success rate for attackers. This background explains the nature of the AI tools that can be misused to target institutions like the EU.

The European Commission continues its investigation into the attack, but Regnier declined to confirm if the campaign has fully ended. He also declined to assess the total scale of the attack while the official investigation remains ongoing at this time. The articles leave open the identity of the attackers and the specific AI tool used in the October cyberattack. It remains unclear which specific applications are still offline or when all digital tools will be fully restored to service. No final conclusion has been reached regarding the total impact of the breach on the European Union executive branch.

stories.Headline: Trump orders federal contractors to notify the White House before sharing information with Congress
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump on Friday issued Executive Order 14438, which was posted on the White House website late on Nov. 20, 2026. The order requires every company with a federal contract to alert the White House before sharing information with Congress. It also requires contractors to withhold material the administration says is protected by executive privilege, or risk losing government business. The order is titled "Protecting the Executive's Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting." Reuters, in a report published by CNBC, said the order expands Trump's efforts to limit congressional oversight.

Section 2 of the order says all federal contractors must immediately notify the White House and the contracting agencies of any pending or future congressional request respecting the contractors' communications or work with the executive branch. Contractors must abide by instructions from the White House and contracting agency related to withholding communications the White House or agency has determined are protected by executive privilege. Agencies are directed to coordinate with the White House and contractors on responses to congressional requests, including the assertion of privileges. The requirements also apply to subcontractors, and prime contractors are made responsible for ensuring subcontractor compliance. Each agency must promptly inform its contractors and subcontractors of the new obligations and require compliance.

The Office of Management and Budget is to write guidance on how agencies check that contractors are complying, and the order directs immediate compliance with no deadline specified for that guidance. If a contractor or subcontractor fails to comply, contracting agencies shall consider all appropriate actions consistent with applicable law, including potential termination or cancellation of contracts and potential debarment or suspension of contractors. The order cites the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act and the common law as its legal basis. It argues Congress cannot seek information from agencies, employees or contractors without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core Executive functions. It says certain congressional leaders have threatened to intrude on executive prerogatives by harassing private companies that contract with the Federal Government.

The White House defended the order as necessary to protect sensitive government communications, including on national security, and said contractors answering congressional requests on their own could expose privileged information and force costly legal disputes, according to the Reuters report. The order itself frames the rule as an efficiency measure, saying separate litigation strategies by contractors and the government over the same requests waste taxpayer money. The order states it creates no right or benefit enforceable at law against the United States and must be implemented consistent with applicable law. It does not mention existing federal whistleblower protections for contractor employees. The order does not specify how contractors should handle conflicting directives from Congress and the executive branch.

The order follows a directive this week from White House Counsel Will Scharf requiring federal agencies to obtain White House approval before employees agree to testify before Congress. Democrats won both chambers in this month's midterm elections and take control of Congress in January. Democrats have vowed to investigate the administration, the Trump family's business dealings and its relationships with private companies. Representative Robert Garcia of California, who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee, this week asked 12 of Trump's allies, former aides and family members to preserve documents related to alleged Trump family corruption and government misconduct. The offices of Garcia, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Elizabeth Warren did not respond to requests for comment on Friday night, Reuters reported.

The restrictions could face legal challenges, particularly if contractors are told to withhold information sought through congressional subpoenas, according to the Reuters report. Executive privilege lets presidents protect certain confidential communications, but courts can step in when Congress and the White House dispute access to information. Trump's Justice Department has also argued that privilege can extend to communications between the president and outside advisers who do not work for the government. For industry, the immediate consideration is how companies receive, escalate and respond to congressional inquiries, including those received by subcontractors. The order leaves open how contractors should handle conflicting directives from Congress and the executive branch.

stories.Headline: Charlotte restaurant bans AI-made flyers for band bookings
stories.Summary:
Diamond Restaurant in Plaza Midwood, Charlotte, North Carolina, said in a social media post that it would no longer accept AI-generated flyers as a valid form of advertisement for band bookings. The restaurant announced the policy in an Instagram post that went viral, and staff members said responses to the post have been mixed. The post stated the new rule that to play music at the restaurant or book an event, your flyer must be made by a person, not a computer. The policy took effect on Sunday, November 22, 2026, according to Queen City News, while WBTV reported the restaurant said it was effective Sunday. Staff member Ryan Armstrong, a musician and one of the staff members at the Diamond Restaurant, said he was proud when his boss took the stand to ban AI flyers on their social media.

The policy applies to bands promoting shows at the restaurant and covers flyers for band bookings and events at the venue. Queen City News reported the policy starts on Sunday, November 22, and WBTV reported the restaurant said it was effective Sunday. The announcement was shared hundreds of times online, and the Instagram post went viral. The restaurant is located in Plaza Midwood in Charlotte, North Carolina. The articles give no other numbers, dates or places for the policy itself.

Armstrong said the restaurant's owners are not telling people what to think about AI but want to use their platform to support local artists, musicians and designers who create the work themselves. He said everybody came to the conclusion that they wanted to support local artists and that most of these communities do not want these data centers and the great proliferation and exponential rate of expansion of their construction using our resources. He said that as an artist himself he understands that new tools develop all the time, and that in the case of AI we are seeing its development abuse artists and intellectual property of many different contributors. He said they thought real artists should be prioritized over this particular function of AI. Armstrong, who is part of a band named Sand Dollar Starship, also said the decision is a way to take a stance against data center projects as Charlotte continues to debate their construction.

Armstrong said he thinks it is akin to what the kids would say is cringe, but he thinks it is just a little cheap and a little soulless. He said that when AI scrapes all of the data from the internet, from prior work, the contributions of authors, historians, visual artists and musicians, just to replicate it in a way that is without human engagement, it just feels hollow and empty. He said there is a certain class of people that may want to replace human talent, and that we are seeing a lot more AI-generated music and a lot more AI-generated art out there. He said he thinks it is dangerous when we start replacing human heart and soul and skilled labor with something that is soulless. He said there are a lot of people just cranking out awesome art who are happy to get a couple free tickets to a show, and that art will generate so many more people in the room at that show.

Armstrong said the policy will also help promote people working in other areas of the creative industry, and he described it as a symbiotic sort of situation for many artists as long as they are willing to work with others in their community of various talents and skills. He said the AI conversation is going to be here and is not going anywhere, and that AI is probably not going anywhere either. He said he just thinks it matters how we use it and that we do it with intention, and that we move forward together instead of in some sort of isolationist every man for themselves kind of situation. Charlotte City Council member Dimple Ajmera said during the October meeting that in the next 11 months we will have an opportunity to put guardrails in place to protect our residents, to protect our neighborhoods and to protect water and the electricity grid. The articles say the policy prompted a necessary conversation, particularly about data centers and AI's role in creative industries.

The articles say the policy comes as Charlotte leaders continue a moratorium on new data center development through next October, giving the city more time to study their impact on neighborhoods, natural resources and infrastructure. WBTV reported that the Charlotte City Council extended the pause on data center construction until October 2027. Queen City News reported that as communities across the country wrestle with the rise of AI, one Charlotte restaurant is taking a stand, saying human creativity should come first. The articles say that as the use of artificial intelligence becomes more popular, many people are turning to it to help promote businesses and events, and that for some, including one local restaurant in Plaza Midwood, the growing use of AI is taking work away from local artists. The articles give no further background on the restaurant or the policy.

The articles do not say what the restaurant will do if a band submits an AI-generated flyer, or whether any bookings have been refused under the policy. They do not say how the restaurant will check whether a flyer was made by a person or a computer. They do not say whether other venues have adopted similar policies. The articles leave open how the mixed responses to the post will develop. They also leave open what the city's study of data centers will find before the moratorium ends.

stories.Summary:
The Times published an article on 22 November 2026 asking what school children hope and fear about artificial intelligence, and the piece was framed around how to protect under-16s from new technology while also helping them to use it. The article says an NSPCC campaign hopes to address this issue, and the writer Alice Thomson saw how students react to it. The piece lists cheating and deepfakes among the concerns it raises about the technology. The article carries no further detail in the text available about what happened, who did it or when beyond that publication.

The article presents the question of protecting under-16s from new technology alongside helping them to use it, and it names the NSPCC campaign as the effort that hopes to address this issue. It gives no numbers, dates or names about the campaign itself beyond the organisation and the writer who observed the students. The only date the article gives is its own publication date of 22 November 2026. It gives no further figures about the technology, the children or the campaign.

The article attributes the campaign to the NSPCC and reports that Alice Thomson saw how students react to it, without quoting any student, parent or official by name in the text available. It does not say what the NSPCC said about the campaign or what any school or government body said about the issue. The concerns it lists, cheating and deepfakes, are given as part of the question the article poses rather than as statements from a named person. No responsible official is named beyond the organisation and the writer.

The context the article gives is the debate over how to protect under-16s from new technology while also helping them to use it, and it places the NSPCC campaign within that debate. It does not say what happens next, what the campaign will do, or what any school, government or regulator plans to change. The article offers no timeline beyond its publication on 22 November 2026. stories.Headline: Law firm argues that legal advice still needs a human as AI tools risk invented provisions
stories.Summary:
Michael Kyprianou & Co. LLC published an article on 20 November 2026 arguing that legal advice still needs a human even as generative AI tools draft contracts in seconds. The article says chatbots like ChatGPT can produce polished contracts fast, cheaply and at any time. It warns that relying on chatbots without professional oversight exposes businesses to hidden risks, from hallucinated legal provisions to unenforceable clauses. The piece says such flaws only reveal themselves when disputes arise, for example when a payment is late or a partner walks away. The article appeared on Legal 500 and was written by the firm Michael Kyprianou & Co. LLC.

The article says ChatGPT launched in November 2022 and that generative AI has since become part of everyday legal work. It cites Wolter Kluwer's "Future Ready Lawyer 2024" report finding that 76% of in-house lawyers use generative AI at least once a week, for document analysis, first drafts, translation and case law searches. It cites a 2024 Stanford study finding popular language models hallucinating in 69 to 88% of legal queries, testing older models so today's results may differ. It cites a 2025 Stanford RegLab and Yale study finding specialised legal tools built to search trusted sources gave inaccurate answers in 17 to 33% of cases. The article says language models predict likely words rather than understanding law, and when they lack information they still produce convincing invented statutes, rulings and sources, known as hallucinations.

The article places full responsibility for the content and consequences of documents on the lawyer, regardless of whether a digital tool was used. It says no rule prohibits lawyers from using AI, but professional bodies such as the National Chamber of Legal Advisers in Poland already issue guidance. It says that when an AI-written contract fails, nobody answers for it and the loss is the client's. It says sharing personal data with a provider makes a company a data controller and requires a data processing agreement, otherwise the company risks trouble with the data protection authority. It says law firms using AI responsibly rely on Enterprise or API versions with security certifications, anonymise data and uphold procedures against informal use of AI.

The article says a lawyer asks about the business, what the client cannot afford to lose and what the other side might do, while a chatbot answers only what was typed. It says problems hide in a vague deadline, a missing liability cap or a termination clause that would not hold up in court. It says a lawyer reads the other side's drafts as an adversary would and knows the client's bargaining position and what to walk away from. It says generic text can quietly breach mandatory provisions or ignore recent changes in local law.

It says the quality of an answer depends on the quality of the question, and asking the correct question requires knowing what the right answer looks like. The article says AI looks cheaper because the cost of a mistake is invisible when choosing. It says a wrong answer may lead to a dispute over a clause that does not say what was intended, a payment that cannot be enforced or a missed deadline. It says these costs usually exceed a consultation and occur when options are limited.

It says a good law firm uses AI for faster drafts, research and document analysis, then verifies every source and spends the saved time on advice. It says AI can help prepare by explaining a term, summarising a text or listing questions for a meeting. The article says AI should not decide when someone is about to sign something involving a significant sum of money or a relationship at stake, or when in dispute with the other party, or when a deadline is approaching. It says AI is a real tool that raises the quality of legal services but does not replace judgement, accountability or someone working to solve the problem.

It advises using AI to prepare and relying on a lawyer when the decision matters. It says the content is intended as a general guide and specialist advice should be sought for specific circumstances. The article leaves open how the cited hallucination rates may differ with today's models. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Van Hollen pledges AI safety laws and a joint committee in bid to lead Senate Democrats
stories.Summary:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, and AI regulation has become a major flashpoint in that race, The Washington Sun reported on November 24, 2026. Senators meet Dec. 1 to vote on new leaders for the 120th Congress. Van Hollen is leveraging attention from technology outages, voter anger at AI companies and the costs of their data centers, and the spy scandal surrounding Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. Congress has long discussed AI and the need for guardrails but has not acted in any significant way. Many see the technology posing an alarming threat to the nation and world.

Van Hollen's audience includes more than 30 Democrats who have not yet pledged their support to either candidate. In a letter responding to Sen. John Hickenlooper over the weekend, Van Hollen pledged to create a joint committee on AI, reform Senate rules and pass basic safety laws in his first 100 days as leader. The rules overhaul he backs comes from Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Steve Daines of Montana, and would need a two-thirds vote to pass, similar to the House's suspension calendar. Van Hollen pointed to a 2022 bipartisan tech antitrust bill that he said got stuck on the calendar after Schumer did not bring it to a floor vote that year.

Van Hollen said his joint committee would not usurp the lawmaking powers of the committees of jurisdiction and that the Democratic leader should not sit on it. Van Hollen told The Sun that tackling AI safety is an urgent matter and that it is an important part of why new leadership is needed for the future. Allison Biasotti, a spokeswoman for Schumer, said Schumer has been working with incoming Democratic committee chairs to develop an ambitious AI agenda before Democrats take over in January. Biasotti said Senate Democrats will make AI a top priority of the new Democratic majority and are working to deliver comprehensive legislation addressing risks to national security, workers and consumers while keeping America at the forefront of innovation. Schumer has emphasized the need to regulate the growing industry with a Democratic majority but has not backed a specific plan.

Schumer declared last week that Democrats will investigate the recent outages themselves if the Trump administration won't. Hickenlooper sent a letter to Schumer and Van Hollen last week asking for their day one AI plans, and told The Sun he wants a clear pledge on what the two would do. Hickenlooper said AI touches everything and that a select committee is essential so it can get the priority it needs. Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, slated to lead the Senate Finance Committee, has said he needs to see more specifics on what an AI committee would do. Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, set to lead the Senate Budget committee, told The Sun he is still in listening mode, though he has a sense of urgency ahead of the leadership elections.

Kaine said the right level of anxiety is somewhere between people saying the sky is falling and Donald Trump saying to relax. Some incoming Democratic committee chairs are unlikely to want to give up their jurisdiction. Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico, Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Hickenlooper have said a select committee is essential. Van Hollen said in his letter that as Democratic leader he would support mandatory independent testing of leading AI models and hold companies liable for risks from models they never release.

Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, expected to chair the Commerce Committee, has proposed a six-point framework giving the government a role in setting AI safety standards. Sens. Andy Kim of New Jersey, Brian Schatz of Hawaii and Mark Warner of Virginia, the prospective Senate Intelligence Committee chair, have proposed an AI safety board and enforceable testing standards. As majority leader in the previous Congress, Schumer convened a series of closed-door insight forums in 2023 with tech executives, including Huang. The forums resulted in a bipartisan framework calling for spending at least $32 billion per year on AI research.

A joint committee as proposed by Van Hollen would include members from the House, where a bipartisan group of over two dozen members launched an AI Safety and Innovation Caucus last week. Rep. Nathaniel Moran of Texas, one of its co-chairs, backed the idea regardless of who leads the Committee, saying a bicameral, bipartisan joint committee puts the right structures and processes in place. The progressive wing of the caucus has called for restricting AI until a federal agency can be formed to oversee it. The articles do not say what happens after the Dec. 1 vote or which candidate will win.

They do not say whether the Merkley and Daines rules proposal will come to a vote. They do not say what the six-point framework or the proposed AI safety board would contain. They do not say when the promised comprehensive legislation or the basic safety laws would be introduced. They do not say what the bipartisan framework's $32 billion figure would fund.

stories.Headline: Congressional Research Service urges Congress to evaluate defense against agentic AI cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
A new report from the Congressional Research Service warns that agentic artificial intelligence could automate complex cyberattacks that usually require entire teams of hackers. The document highlights a mid-September 2025 operation that Anthropic attributed to a Chinese state-sponsored group known as GTG-1002. This specific group allegedly automated between 80 percent and 90 percent of a campaign that targeted approximately 30 different organizations. Some researchers have since questioned whether this particular attack was actually as autonomous or successful as the initial reports claimed.

The report suggests that Congress should evaluate if the Department of Defense is appropriately postured to detect and respond to these autonomous threats. It notes that the Cybersecurity and Information Systems Information Analysis Center has found no official government policies specifically addressing agentic AI yet. Under Section 1535 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, which became Public Law 119-60 on December 18, 2025, the Secretary of Defense must establish an AI Futures Steering Committee by April 1. Additionally, the report questions if voluntary partnerships with the Department of Commerce Center for AI Standards and Innovation should be made mandatory.

The Congressional Research Service describes agentic AI as systems that can pursue specific goals while requiring very limited human supervision. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency claims that its AI Cyber Challenge showed AI agents can fix open-source vulnerabilities faster than human teams. This capability could potentially support a strategy of AI-on-AI defense to counter the speed and scale of autonomous attacks. The AI Futures Steering Committee is expected to deliver its official findings to congressional defense committees by January 31, 2027.

Congress may use these upcoming findings to determine the necessary authorizations, appropriations, and general oversight for Department of Defense agentic AI programs. Lawmakers are also considering the reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, which was part of Public Law 114-113. This specific information-sharing law is currently set to expire on December 11 under an amendment found in Section 2011 of Public Law 119-103. These legislative steps aim to address the evolving capabilities of militaries exploring autonomous decision-making and operations.

stories.Headline: Landlord's AI grants tenant a rent extension then landlord evicts her
stories.Summary:
Laura Mack, a tenant in North Carolina, says her landlord evicted her even though she had received an email from the leasing office granting her an extension to pay $4,000 in overdue rent, according to WRAL News. The message turned out to have been written by the landlord's AI assistant, which the landlord claims acted without their knowledge. Mack has now gone to court to try to reverse the eviction, saying she feels deceived because nothing at the time made clear she was talking to an AI. The emails from Colony Townhome Apartments, which WRAL viewed, sounded human to her, and she says she had no reason to doubt them.

The AI asked Mack what date would work best for her to pay and then approved her request, saying that paying on November 30, the last day of the month, worked. Days later she received an abrupt eviction notice, and when she confronted the leasing office, the leasing agent allegedly said it was the AI agent, Olivia, that had been emailing her and had mistakenly granted the extension. The complex had told residents back in December 2025 that the new AI agent could handle their rent and maintenance questions, and Olivia's messages are normally supposed to be marked as coming from an AI, but the ones Mack received showed no such disclosure. The AI even mentioned the hole in her downstairs bathroom ceiling and said it was sorry she was dealing with that, which led Mack to believe she was writing to someone from the office.

State senator Jim Burgin told WRAL that the situation is ridiculous and that notification is one thing while liability is another. He said that before someone evicted that lady, they should have reviewed their documents. Burgin has proposed a "Bot Bill" that would require users to be informed whenever they are communicating with an AI, but in the past three years he has tried to introduce it, it has not advanced in the legislature, according to WRAL. Mack is now living out of a hotel until she finds a permanent place to stay or wins her battle in court, and she said that if she was told till the 30th, she would get out by the 30th, but that the other side should at least honor that.

stories.Headline: Senate passes bill to speed permits for energy projects and data centers
stories.Summary:
The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, S.5653, on Nov. 19, 2026, by a 62-33 vote, with 14 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent joining most Republicans. Thirty Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent voted against the bill. The bill's sponsors are Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Republican Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance vouched for the legislation in a Nov. 20 news conference. The bill must win approval in the House to advance, and the House could amend it, which would require the Senate to approve the new text. The bill would limit the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act. The Natural Resources Defense Council's analysis concluded that under the bill a court "can never invalidate a permit" based on a violation of the National Environmental Policy Act or the National Historic Preservation Act. The bill would cut the time to build a major new transmission line from 10-plus years to five or six.

About 2,000 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are waiting to connect to the grid, and 85 percent of that capacity is solar, wind, or storage. The bill requires data centers to pay for their impact on electricity supply rather than shifting those costs to ratepayers. Juniper Katz, a University of Massachusetts-Amherst assistant professor of public policy, said there are priorities both sides want and the bill "is not perfect." Geoffrey Henderson, a University of Michigan assistant professor of environmental policy and planning, said it is reasonable to be concerned that development of each kind of project Ruffalo mentioned could be facilitated by the bill. Henderson also said the bill's impacts are highly uncertain, depending on political, market, geopolitical and legal outcomes.

The NRDC analysis said that if the Trump administration issued a blanket grant of all permits for oil and gas infrastructure without any environmental review, the bill provides no clear mechanism for a future administration to revoke those permits. Ruffalo's representative did not respond to an inquiry for the article. Mark Ruffalo said in a Nov. 18 video viewed 22 million times that the bill would fast-track AI data centers, pipelines, mines, power plants and ICE camps while sacrificing clean water, tribal rights, public lands and endangered species. Groups supporting the bill include the Solar Energy Industries Association, the AFL-CIO, the American Petroleum Institute and the Edison Electric Institute.

Groups opposing it include the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Climate Justice Alliance, a range of tribal organizations, the NAACP and the American Civil Liberties Union. Opponents say their concerns about ICE facilities stem from the use of the National Environmental Policy Act to oppose ICE facilities in court in Maryland, Arizona and Florida. Ezra Klein, a New York Times columnist considered left of center, said he was "unnerved" by conflicting interpretations of certain provisions but still supported the bill. The bill grew out of concerns from both fossil fuel backers and renewable energy supporters that opponents could stymie projects for years in the courts.

Supporters said growing energy demand and rising electricity prices meant a failure to build new infrastructure would consign the United States to a spiral of insufficient energy supplies and higher costs. Critics say the bill effectively guts tools to prevent local governments, citizens, Native American tribes and other local interests from blocking harms caused by such projects. Critics also say the Trump administration, which refuses to acknowledge the possibility of emissions-driven climate change, could wield the law to advance fossil fuel projects over renewable energy infrastructure. The NRDC analysis devotes almost 1,000 words to describing what it considers the bill's positive features, including improving electric capacity by increasing how much power existing transmission lines can carry and enabling construction of new lines.

The bill's fate in the House is uncertain, and the potential for updated language and the difficulty of predicting how courts would interpret its provisions make it difficult to know whether Ruffalo's scenario will come to pass. The bill could also boost non-energy projects that have faced long-running challenges in the courts, including rail and transit, affordable housing and broadband access, Klein wrote. The bill does not directly address ICE detention facilities. The articles leave open whether the House will amend the bill and whether the Senate would then approve new text.

stories.Headline: Dutch hospitals must inventory and classify AI systems in 2026 to meet EU AI Act duties
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Global Advisory Experts on November 24, 2026, is a guide for Dutch hospitals and clinics on the EU AI Act, and it states that the Regulation attaches binding duties to Dutch care providers as its requirements phase in. The guide says 2026 is the year for hospitals to get organised, and it addresses hospital boards, compliance officers, chief information officers, chief medical information officers and quality and safety managers. It states that the AI Act, the Medical Device Regulation, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation, the General Data Protection Regulation and Dutch healthcare law each place their own demands on the same tool. The article says the guide explains what applies, when it applies, and how it sits alongside existing medical device and data protection rules. It states that generic policies will not cover that, and it presents itself as a jurisdiction-specific roadmap.

The article states that the AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and applies directly in every EU Member State, including the Netherlands, without national transposition. It says Dutch hospitals are caught as deployers of AI systems and, in some cases, as providers where they build or substantially modify tools in-house. It states that AI that is, or is a safety component of, a medical device under the MDR or IVDR is generally classed as high-risk, which brings the strictest obligations. It says the Regulation entered into force on 1 August 2024, that prohibitions on unacceptable-risk practices and the general provisions applied from early 2025, and that obligations for general-purpose AI models followed later in 2025. The article states that high-risk systems that are, or are safety components of, products covered by EU harmonisation legislation such as the MDR and IVDR have the longest transitional period, running to around mid-2027.

The article states that the AI Act forms part of the European Commission's wider European approach to artificial intelligence, and that Member States must still designate national competent authorities to supervise and enforce it. It says a hospital is usually a deployer of systems bought from vendors, and that if it develops a tool internally, puts a system on the market under its own name, or substantially modifies a third-party system, it may become a provider. It states that providers of high-risk AI carry the full weight of conformity assessment, technical documentation and post-market monitoring, while deployers have a narrower but still significant set of duties covering human oversight, monitoring of operation and use in line with the instructions. It says the five priority actions for 2026 are to inventory every AI system in use, classify each against the high-risk criteria, assign governance responsibilities, align supplier contracts with AI Act duties, and put human oversight and post-market monitoring procedures in place. The article states that transitional arrangements are detailed and system-specific, so the dates for each tool should be checked against the current text of the Regulation.

The article states that the MDR is Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and the IVDR is Regulation (EU) 2017/746, and that the AI Act adds AI-specific obligations on top, including data governance, transparency, human oversight and post-market monitoring of AI performance. It says the Regulation tries to avoid duplicated burdens by allowing AI Act requirements to be built into the existing medical device conformity assessment where possible, so one process can address both. It states that almost all clinical AI processes health data, which the GDPR treats as a special category of personal data with enhanced protection, and that hospitals need a valid legal basis for processing, data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing, and a clear approach to the rules on automated decision-making where AI outputs materially affect patients. It says the Dutch Data Protection Authority enforces the GDPR and issues guidance on AI and health data, and that the AI Act's data governance rules and the GDPR are distinct but reinforce each other. The article states that Dutch sector law sits over the EU regimes and names the Wet kwal, Wkkgz and WGBO.

The article states that the difficulty is that several regimes apply at once, and that the AI Act does not replace the MDR, IVDR or GDPR but sits on top of them. It says governance is not optional, and that human oversight, risk management, technical documentation and post-market monitoring all need named owners, standard operating procedures and board-level reporting. It states that the first route to high-risk status captures most clinical AI, and that if a tool is software qualifying as a medical device under the MDR or a diagnostic device under the IVDR, and that device needs notified-body involvement, the associated AI is treated as high-risk. It says the European Commission's medical devices portal and Medical Device Coordination Group guidance help establish when software is a medical device at all, and that the European Data Protection Board gives guidance on how the GDPR intersects with AI. The article states that Dutch government guidance on AI policy gives national context for how the EU obligations fit the domestic landscape.

The article states that for planning purposes 2026 should be treated as the year to complete internal readiness, so that systems, documentation and oversight processes already work when the high-risk obligations apply in full. It says procurement and IT roadmaps will need AI Act milestones next to existing MDR compliance schedules, and that classifying systems, rewriting contracts and building governance takes real time. It states that each system must be assessed on its own intended purpose and device class, and that borderline cases should go to qualified regulatory advisors. It says the determination should be recorded for every system and that it must be able to be defended. The article states that the window during 2026 is finite, and it leaves open the detailed transitional dates for each tool, which it says must be checked against the current text of the Regulation.

stories.Headline: Tidal bans fully AI-generated tracks and will remove over 29 million songs starting December 9
stories.Summary:
The music streaming service Tidal announced on Tuesday that it will ban and remove millions of songs created entirely by artificial intelligence. This decision follows a massive surge in submissions where over 43 percent of tracks uploaded in the last 90 days were AI generated. The company intends to stop the flood of low quality content that is currently inundating its digital platform. This aggressive move aims to protect the visibility of human musicians against a tide of automated audio.

The removal process will begin on December 9 and is expected to delete more than 29 million songs by the end of the year. Under these new rules, the platform will reject between 80,000 and 85,000 tracks every single day. Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering tracks that are 100 percent AI generated based on their metadata. While fully automated songs are banned, the service will still accept music that was created with AI assistance.

Robert Anderson, who leads Tidal Music, stated on X that previous efforts to demonetize AI tracks in June were not enough of a deterrent. He explained that the sheer scale of these uploads means authentic artists are getting buried under a mountain of synthetic content. The company noted that 27 million tracks, or 6.3 percent of its library, are fully AI generated. They further observed that 96 percent of those specific automated tracks have received no streams at all.

Tidal claims to be one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music in such an outright manner. Other services like Deezer are introducing filters, while Spotify and YouTube Music have chosen to label the content instead of removing it. The company believes that drastic action is necessary to maintain the authenticity of the music discovery experience for its subscribers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming

stories.Headline: UK financial watchdog warns AI firms that transaction tools may require authorization
stories.Summary:
Britain’s financial watchdog warned technology companies on Tuesday that artificial intelligence tools able to handle financial transactions could bring their businesses under regulatory oversight, according to Reuters. The Financial Conduct Authority said companies developing autonomous AI products should work out whether their operations need regulatory authorization and should consult the authorities when appropriate. The guidance arrives as AI developers move beyond ordinary chatbots toward digital assistants that can carry out transactions and manage consumers’ financial affairs. The announcement coincided with Meta Platforms’ launch of its Muse AI assistant in Britain, an application Reuters reported has more than 10 million downloads since its US debut in September.

The FCA said a company’s regulatory obligations depend on the activities it performs rather than on its classification as a technology business, and services involving payments, financial recommendations and the marketing of financial products could fall within its jurisdiction. According to Meta, the Muse platform can help users renew auto insurance policies, obtain refunds and complete digital purchases. The FCA did not single out Meta or any other technology company in its guidance. Meta said in an emailed statement to Reuters that it had engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and would continue to do so.

The FCA said consumers should examine the safeguards available when delegating financial tasks to digital assistants and should consider the risks of sharing personal data. The regulator also acknowledged the potential economic benefits of AI adoption, including greater competition, improved productivity and broader access to financial services. However, the FCA said it was prepared to intervene against businesses conducting regulated activities without the necessary authorization. The growing autonomy of AI systems is raising questions about accountability, financial liability and the protection of sensitive personal information.

Articles.Title: UK Warns Tech Giants AI Agents May Fall Under Financial Regulation

stories.headline_source: UK Warns Tech Giants AI Agents May Fall Under Financial Regulation

stories.Headline: Corgi applies for a national bank charter to offer deposits and loans
stories.Summary:
Corgi, a two-year-old artificial intelligence-powered insurance startup, applied last week for a national bank charter with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, according to Banking Dive. The company currently serves roughly 300,000 insurance customers, mostly small-business owners, and has since diversified into exchange-traded funds. If approved, Corgi's banking subsidiary would be based in Salt Lake City, with loan production offices planned for San Francisco and New York. Corgi has also applied for deposit insurance with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., according to a LinkedIn description from one of the proposed bank's executives.

The charter Corgi applied for would force the insurer to become a bank holding company subject to Federal Reserve supervision, a structure the article describes as somewhat unique. Corgi plans to offer checking and savings accounts, treasury services, credit cards, loans and lines of credit. Corgi plans to commit at least $75 million in initial capital to build its bank, CEO Nicolas Laqua said. The company had a private valuation of $4 billion as of June, according to CB Insights, while Bloomberg put Corgi's value at roughly $7 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Corgi raised about $450 million in its latest funding round, according to the company's website. Corgi has tapped Jason Wessling, who until August served as CEO of Oregon-based Pacific West Bank, to serve as the banking subsidiary's president and CEO. Eric Vigil, who served until September as chief compliance officer at Austin, Texas-based American Bank, will be Corgi Bank's compliance chief, according to his LinkedIn profile. Rudolph Garcia, a veteran chief credit officer at San Francisco-area lenders Altos Bank and Beacon Business Bank, is slated to serve as Corgi Bank's credit chief.

Laqua told Bloomberg that AI lets the firm remove a lot of paperwork that wasn't possible before, which lets it make banking, as well as insurance, a lot more affordable. Victoria Baptiste, principal at consulting firm FS Vector, told American Banker that the oversight is the kind nonbank financial firms, including insurers, left banking to avoid, and she called Corgi's proposed offerings pretty traditional. Roman Goldstein, a senior director at financial services advisory firm Klaros Group, told American Banker that Corgi's use of AI to drive down consumer costs will be an advantage in the review process, but that regulators will probe how the firm uses AI and whether it is well-controlled. The article notes that roughly 45 insurance companies applied to become thrifts between 1997 and 2000, according to research from the University of North Carolina, and that many insurance firms left the banking space when the Dodd-Frank Act placed thrifts under the Fed's purview.

Articles.Title: AI-forward insurance startup Corgi applies for bank charter

stories.Headline: South Korea deploys 8,000 metal detectors and seeks 10-year exam bans to curb AI cheating
stories.Summary:
South Korea’s Education Ministry unveiled a set of measures on Nov 24 to tighten exam security, ahead of high school final exams, as AI-assisted cheating spread from national exams into classrooms. The ministry said it will deploy nearly 8,000 metal detectors for use in high schools and seek penalties ranging from expulsion to decade-long bans on the university entrance exam. The move came after three cases of cheating involving smart glasses were detected in high school exams in 2026. Some schools had already acted, including Baehwa Girls’ High School in Seoul, which issued an emergency notice on Nov 22, a day before its senior students’ final exams, and extended the measures on Nov 23 to first- and second-year students. The crackdown also follows last week’s Suneung, during which five test-takers were caught with smart glasses, miniature cameras or wireless earphones, and all five were referred for criminal investigation.

The government plans to distribute 7,989 metal detectors to the country’s 2,387 high schools, allocating three per school, with students screened before or after exams and checked again after restroom visits. Bags must be stored at least 50m from examination rooms, proctors will inspect glasses and clothing for concealed devices, and schools will disable campus Wi-Fi and monitor wireless signals. Students caught cheating with smart devices could receive zeros for all subjects examined that day, while schools will be encouraged to introduce disciplinary measures ranging from suspension to expulsion. The ministry is pursuing amendments to the Higher Education Act to extend bans on entrance exam participation for serious cheating from one year to up to 10 years, and other proposals include legal grounds for metal detector inspections, whistleblower rewards and prison sentences of up to five years for serious violations. The stakes are high because more than 80% of university places for the 2027 academic year will be allocated through early admissions, in which school records play a major role.

The ministry said it plans to obtain prior consent from students and parents to address potential human rights concerns over searches without an explicit legal basis. It also plans to establish a legal basis for metal detector inspections at high schools and to develop technological countermeasures in cooperation with the Science Ministry. Similar security measures will apply to university-administered entrance exams, including essay tests and interviews. Suspicious activity could trigger metal detector screening of an entire examination room.

Articles.Title: Metal detectors, expulsion, 10-year ban: Tougher measures in South Korea to combat AI exam cheating - The Straits Times

stories.Headline: Korea plans 10-year exam cheating ban and five-year prison terms for AI-assisted cheating
stories.Summary:
Korea's Ministry of Employment and Labor announced on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, that it plans to extend the ban on retaking national technical qualification exams from three years to 10 years for people caught cheating, and to raise the maximum prison sentence to five years, which is more than double the current limit. The measures respond to concerns about AI-assisted cheating using smart glasses, miniature cameras and modified calculators. The first case of cheating with smart glasses in a national qualification exam was detected in May, and miniature cameras and modified calculators have since been used in connection with the tax accountant licensing exam. The ministry will also publish the scores of the top two candidates, along with average scores and score distributions by subject, to restore public trust in exam results.

The government has already begun tightening supervision, with stricter electronic device checks, additional proctors and Bluetooth-detection applications, and these measures were first applied to the security instructor licensing exam on Saturday, where six violations were detected among 11,554 candidates, including possession of tablets and smartwatches and failure to switch off mobile phones. Under the tightened rules, proctors will check that all electronic devices are switched off before collecting them, make random calls to test takers' phones before each session, and wear nonwoven fabric coverings to block hidden cameras. Authorities plan to introduce radio-frequency detectors, devices that can identify electronics even when switched off, mobile surveillance cameras and proctors' body cameras by the first half of 2027, and will conduct a comprehensive review of national qualification exams administered this year. The government also plans rewards for reporting cheating, seeks to standardize penalties across professional licensing exams including new criminal sanctions, and intends to expand practical and interview-based assessments.

Separately, the Ministry of Education announced that high school students caught using smart devices to cheat will receive zero scores in every subject tested that day, rather than only the subject in which they were caught, and schools will be advised that disciplinary penalties may include expulsion. Starting with this year's high school final exams, students will be encouraged to wear buttonless clothing or cover buttons with stickers, proctors will check glasses and clothing before each session, schools will collect electronic devices, store bags away from exam rooms and use metal detectors, and Wi-Fi will be shut down during exams while proctors monitor Wi-Fi and Bluetooth signals. The new guidelines apply starting this semester, and middle schools are also encouraged to tighten supervision. The education ministry acknowledged that screening all students with metal detectors would be difficult to implement immediately.

Articles.Title: Korea to raise ban for AI cheaters on licensing exams to 10 years, prison term to 5 years - The Korea Times

stories.Headline: Tidal bans wholly AI-generated tracks and rejects new AI deliveries from December 9
stories.Summary:
Tidal said on Tuesday that it would ban tracks it believes are completely AI-generated, starting next month, according to Variety. The service will remove the AI tracks starting Dec. 9, Variety reported. Tidal is the first music streaming platform to ban AI music entirely, the service said, a claim Variety reported as Tidal's. The announcement came nearly five months after Tidal said it would demonetize any AI-powered song, force those artists to label their tracks as either AI-generated or AI-assisted and ban AI songs associated with fraudulent activity, a category that includes songs impersonating established artists and efforts to deceive listeners. Robert Andersen, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, wrote about the move in an X thread on Tuesday.

Tidal said it would remove all tracks it determines are 100% AI generated, according to The Hollywood Reporter. Tidal said it is also banning distributors from delivering these tracks to it and will reject deliveries if their metadata says they were generated solely using AI tools. Tracks made with assistance from AI will still be allowed, and the new ban goes into effect December 9. Tidal said that in the past 90 days about 43 percent of tracks distributed on the platform were identified as wholly AI-generated, and that on Nov. 6 alone 60 percent of newly uploaded songs were AI tracks. Tidal said 96 percent of those tracks have generated zero streams.

Andersen wrote that 43% of tracks distributed to Tidal in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated, and that something more drastic needs to be done. Andersen wrote that Tidal will begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from its catalog, and they will be completely gone by the beginning of the year. Andersen said 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays. Andersen said the move will cleave the platform of 29 million tracks and have it reject between 80,000 to 85,000 songs a day. Andersen wrote that Tidal encourages its peers to follow suit.

Tidal said in a social media post on Tuesday that AI music diverts streams and royalties away from the artists and confuses fans. Tidal said that to ensure it remains the best place for artists to share their work and for listeners to enjoy it, it is removing all tracks it determines are 100% AI generated. Tidal said wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale. Tidal said that at this scale the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried. The Hollywood Reporter said Tidal now has the most stringent anti-AI policies among the music streaming services, and is one of the few notable platforms beyond Bandcamp, the music distribution service popular among indie artists, to have outright banned AI music.

The Hollywood Reporter said Spotify and Apple Music, the two largest DSPs, have taken steps to either label AI tracks and artists or remove them from recommendations, but still allow fully-generated songs to get uploaded to their respective platforms. Variety reported that Apple Music said it would also begin labeling AI-generated or AI-assisted tracks on its platform, while Spotify said it would label artists it deemed AI creations as an AI Persona. Spotify said in a blog post last month that it also removed 50 million slop or spam tracks from users' recommendations this year, which came after it removed 75 million of those songs from its catalog entirely. The Hollywood Reporter said fans and the music industry alike have voiced their frustration about AI music flooding streaming platforms. The Hollywood Reporter said Universal Music Group CEO Lucian Grainge, on an earnings call in October, advocated for streaming services to pay out AI-generated tracks less than music from human artists.

Tidal said it has seen an influx of AI-generated tracks on its platform over the past several months, according to The Hollywood Reporter. Tidal said that not all songs catch on immediately and artists should have time to build their fanbases, but that this situation is different. Spotify said this work isn't finished, that AI moves fast and bad actors adapt just as fast, and that as AI makes music more abundant it believes listeners will value human artistry even more. Spotify said its job is to make Spotify the place they find it. The articles leave open which tracks Tidal will determine are wholly AI-generated and how it will make that determination.
