stories.Headline: Natalie Buda Smith leads the Library of Congress in using AI to manage its collections and explore synthetic DNA storage
stories.Summary:
Natalie Buda Smith, the first leader of AI innovation at the Library of Congress, is currently guiding the institution in using artificial intelligence to manage its vast collections. The library maintains more than 181 million physical items and approximately 200 million gigabytes of digital data. Staff members are increasingly employing AI to analyze agricultural trends for the Congressional Research Service and to translate documents into English for public use. The institution has experimented with machine learning for nearly a decade to digitize manuscripts and identify images, but current technology is now far more accurate.

These new tools allow the library to re-upload old items because the computer vision no longer makes basic historical errors, such as mistaking a book for a cellphone. However, the library must now spend more resources to manage third-party bots that scrape the database and slow down the systems. Smith believes that blocking these companies is not an option because many people now use AI tools instead of web browsers to find information. She is also exploring a project to store data in synthetic DNA, which she claims could last thousands of years without using energy.

Natalie Buda Smith is responsible for these initiatives and explains that all AI produced work is still reviewed by human staff. She refuses to force the technology on resistant employees because she believes they must feel comfortable to use the tools effectively. Smith is currently hesitant to launch a public chatbot for the library because she has not yet found a system that is sufficiently authoritative and trustworthy. She views these efforts as part of a meaningful job to ensure the institution continues moving forward into the future.

Articles.Title: How the Library of Congress Is Using AI

stories.Headline: Google workers urge a school-only search version without AI features
stories.Summary:
Google workers urged their company to allow schools to use search without artificial intelligence features on November 20, 2026. This request seeks to remove AI capabilities from the search tools that students use on school computers. The goal of these employees is to encourage students to use their own critical thinking skills for assignments. Such a change would specifically target the digital tools available within the classroom environment. The proposed change requires Google to provide a version of its search engine that lacks AI features for educational institutions.

This modification would only affect the work that students complete while they are physically present in class. It would not prevent students from accessing artificial intelligence on their personal computers at home. Consequently, the restriction would not apply to the long-form assignments that are essential for becoming a scholar. An unnamed writer expressed these concerns in a letter to the editor of the Los Angeles Times on November 24, 2026.

The author argued that banning AI in schools is merely doing something without actually accomplishing a useful result. They claimed that students will still avoid true learning by using AI tools outside of school hours. The writer believes that this approach fails to address how students complete their major projects. More to follow.

stories.Headline: OpenClaw Foundation launches ShellBench to show top AI models fail 40 percent of real world tasks
stories.Summary:
The OpenClaw Foundation debuted a new benchmark called ShellBench on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. This system tests AI agents and harnesses on 100 real world tasks. The foundation designed this tool in partnership with Hugging Face, Red Hat, Parsewave, and UC Berkeley. It evaluates how frontier models perform in messy environments that mimic everyday enterprise work. The results show that leading models fail to complete four out of ten tasks.

The benchmark tested 13 open source and proprietary models from Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, and MoonShot. These models were tested across five harnesses named Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, and Pi. Realistic workspaces used for testing included PDFs, receipts, spreadsheets, calendar exports, and emails. The highest performing models were Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6 Astra. These top models only successfully completed tasks six times out of ten.

Vincent Koc is the chief architect at the OpenClaw Foundation and spoke about the project. He stated that the foundation wanted a good distribution of tasks to get signals on model performance. Koc said the primary focus of the ShellBench benchmark was on everyday use. He believes agents aligned with personal use will be more effective for enterprises deploying at scale. He noted that some of these tasks will become more realistic to individual needs.

The benchmark affected models like Claude Sonnet, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, and Meta Muse Wonder 1.0. These specific models only saw a task pass rate of roughly four times out of ten. The results provide a reality check for organizations seeking to embed agents in their workforce. These systems may not be as reliable as common benchmarks make them seem to users. The findings go beyond the coding performance that many major model providers often tout.

The foundation found that 51 percent of failures related to omitting information despite collecting it. In 87 percent of those omission cases, the agents had already found the relevant information. GPT-6 Astra showed inconsistency, dropping from a 75 percent accuracy rate to 49 percent over tests. Price did not always equal capability, as GPT-6.1 Sol cost 17 cents per run. GPT-6 Astra cost 1.01 dollars per run and scored a 62.5 percent accuracy rate.

Open source harnesses including Pi, OpenClaw, Hermes, and Codex CLI were slightly more accurate than Claude Code. The full results of the ShellBench benchmark were scheduled to be available on Tuesday. The articles do not state if the model providers have responded to these specific findings. It is not mentioned if the OpenClaw Foundation plans to update the benchmark tasks. The text leaves open whether these models will improve their completion rates in the future.

Articles.Title: The OpenClaw Foundation launches ShellBench to test 13 frontier AI models across five harnesses on 100 tasks; top AI models hit only a ~60% completion rate (Nat Rubio-Licht/The Deep View)

stories.Headline: NY Gov. Hochul vetoes bill that would have required AI accuracy warnings
stories.Summary:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul vetoed a bill on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, that would have required artificial intelligence platforms to proactively warn users that the information they receive may be inaccurate, according to Gothamist. The bill had been introduced by Assemblymember Clyde Vanel and state Sen. Kirsten Gonzalez, both Queens Democrats, after Meta’s AI platform hallucinated sexual harassment allegations in 2024 against a number of state lawmakers, including the two of them. The state Legislature passed the measure by a near-unanimous vote earlier this year. Had Hochul signed it into law, the owner, operator or licensee of a generative AI platform would have been required to clearly and conspicuously display a notice on the system’s user interface warning that the system’s output may be inaccurate. Some AI platforms, such as ChatGPT, already display such a warning, but the New York bill would have required all platforms to do so, Gothamist reported.

X’s Grok, for example, includes a warning in its terms and services but not directly on the screen users see when they provide a written prompt. In her statement explaining the decision, Hochul wrote that she supports thoughtful, smart guardrails on AI to protect consumers, but she said the bill was too far-reaching and would have applied to artistic or expressive content that isn’t meant to be factual, possibly running afoul of federal free-speech protections. She wrote that the bill takes an inflexible one-size-fits-all approach to require notifications on all generative AI systems regardless of context and that in doing so it may present constitutional and pragmatic challenges. Hochul’s veto came after trade groups representing some of the world’s most prominent tech firms, including OpenAI and Meta, lobbied against the bill and warned of possible constitutional violations, according to Gothamist. Netflix and the Motion Picture Association also lobbied the governor on the measure, according to state disclosure records.

Vanel said he believed he had worked with the industry to come up with bill language that was flexible enough to accommodate different types of platforms. He said he is hopeful he can work with the governor’s office to come up with some sort of compromise next year, when the state Legislature returns to Albany, and that the main thing is he hopes they both agree that some sort of disclosure is important. Hochul has had an up and down relationship with AI companies, Gothamist reported. Earlier this year she unilaterally implemented a temporary moratorium on large-scale data centers, including those used by AI providers, and made it a key part of her reelection campaign at a time when polls showed voters in New York and beyond were deeply skeptical of the facilities. She has not yet taken any action on a more-stringent moratorium that lawmakers approved earlier in the year, which is stridently opposed by tech firms, and she has until the end of the year to sign or veto that bill.

Articles.Title: NY Gov. Hochul vetoes bill that would have required AI accuracy warnings - Gothamist

stories.Headline: New bill aims to hold NY judges accountable for AI-generated court errors
stories.Summary:
State Senator Michelle Hinchey introduced a bill in the New York State Senate last week that would make improper use of artificial intelligence in court orders a sanctionable offense for the judges who issue them, the Queens Daily Eagle reported on November 23, 2026. The bill does not forbid judges from using AI, but instead creates new procedures for disciplining judges whose AI-generated court orders compromise the integrity of a case. Under the bill, if a judge's orders are found to contain fabricated legal authority, meaning statutes or case law that do not actually exist, that would amount to misconduct and the judge could be sanctioned. The State Commission on Judicial Conduct, which the article describes as the only authority in the state with the power to publicly admonish or remove a judge from the bench, would investigate the fabrications and discipline any offending judges.

The commission would be tasked with determining a judge's culpability, whether the fabrications affected the outcome of the case and whether to issue sanctions against the judge, with the exact punishment decided case by case. A spokesperson for the commission said it was reviewing the legislation and had no immediate comment on the bill. Hinchey said AI regulation for New York judges is needed because state and federal judges across the country have admitted to issuing error-ridden court orders created with AI tools, and she said judges make decisions that directly affect people's freedom and rights, so their work must be based on real case law and facts rather than AI fabrications. Hinchey claimed the legislation would be the first in the country to hold judges accountable when their reliance on AI causes real harm, and she said she believes it is critical that New York act now with meaningful guardrails to protect the judicial system.

The article reports that AI has been widely adopted by attorneys and law firms over the past year and is becoming more common in judges' chambers, citing a Northwestern University survey of federal judges released in March in which more than 60 percent of responding judges reported using at least one AI tool in their judicial work and around 22 percent reported using such tools weekly or daily. Some judges have been caught citing case law the AI made up, sometimes called hallucinations, and in 2025 federal judges in Mississippi and New Jersey admitted to the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee that they used court orders with AI-generated content containing numerous errors, while an Oklahoma judge also admitted to issuing fictitious citations generated by AI. U.S. District Judge Julien Xavier Neals of New Jersey claimed the fabricated case law was created by a law school intern using ChatGPT without authorization or disclosure, and an order U.S. District Judge Henry Wingate of Mississippi issued for a civil rights lawsuit had incorrect names for both the plaintiffs and defendants and fabricated allegations not included in the original complaint. The bill follows a policy on proper AI use for judges and attorneys introduced by New York court officials, under which AI tools are available to Unified Court System employees through UCS devices only after they complete an initial training course, and use without that course is prohibited.

The policy also limits employees to a list of pre-approved and vetted AI tools, and in January the UCS released a 154-page report on how AI can expand public access to the courts while warning of security and bias risks if it is used haphazardly. First Deputy Chief Administrative Judge Norman St. George said at the time that the courts have a duty to carefully explore and fully understand AI's strengths and limitations so it may be used responsibly in furthering the delivery of justice across the state. In October the courts released further guidance for attorneys filing AI-generated information, saying attorneys are not prohibited from using AI and are not required to disclose it but remain fully responsible for every word they submit, and that fictitious case law could result in serious repercussions and sanctions. Hinchey said she will push to get the bill passed in the upcoming 2027 legislative session.

Articles.Title: New bill aims to hold NY judges accountable for AI-generated court errors - Queens Daily Eagle

stories.Headline: Global Advisory Experts publishes a guide on legaltech licensing in Poland for AI tools
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a guide published on November 23, 2026 by Global Advisory Experts on legaltech licensing in Poland. The guide addresses contracts, confidentiality and liability for AI tools used in legal work. It was written for founders, vendors, integrators, in-house legal teams and law firms active in Poland. The featured expert on the matter is Jakub Koziol of The Heart Legal in Poland. The guide states a reading time of roughly 12 to 15 minutes and a read time of 14 minutes.

The guide says the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, is applying in stages. Prohibitions on certain AI practices and AI-literacy duties applied from early 2025, and governance and general-purpose AI rules from mid-2025. Most high-risk obligations phase in afterwards, with providers increasingly expected to show conformity assessment, logging, transparency and post-market monitoring. The guide sets out an eight-step process running from product assessment to go-live. It gives typical durations for each step, from 1 to 3 weeks for classification and AI risk assessment up to 2 to 8 weeks for contract drafting and negotiation.

The guide names owners for each step, including the vendor legal or compliance team with the CTO for classification. It says the vendor data protection officer and engineering own data mapping and the Data Protection Impact Assessment. It states that the vendor's advisors and the buyer's compliance function run the professional-ethics review. It says the commercial lead with legal input chooses the licence model. It states that advisors for both vendor and buyer draft the core commercial terms.

The guide says the confidentiality obligations of Poland's regulated legal professions pass through to any AI tool they use. It names the adwokat, bound by professional secrecy under the Law on the Bar and the code of ethics of the Naczelna Rada Adwokacka. It names the radca prawny, subject to equivalent duties under the Law on Legal Advisers and the code of ethics of the Krajowa Izba Radców Prawnych. It names the notariusz, with statutory confidentiality and record-keeping duties under the Law on the Notarial Profession.

It says these duties cannot be delegated and a vendor cannot contract them away. The guide says the main reference points are the EU AI Act framework on the European Commission website and GDPR guidance from UODO and the European Data Protection Board. It says Polish professional bodies expect legal professionals to vet the AI tools they use, especially where client-confidential material is processed. It says the contract must do far more work than a standard SaaS agreement did two years ago.

It says a Data Protection Impact Assessment is needed where processing is likely to be high risk under GDPR Article 35. It says a controller must notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal-data breach, where feasible. The guide gives sample clauses on the licence grant, data processing, AI explainability, audit rights and limitation of liability. It says the buyer may audit the vendor's compliance once a year on 30 days' notice.

It caps each party's total liability at the fees paid in the twelve months before the claim, except for liability that cannot lawfully be limited. It lists documents to assemble before signing, including a model card, a training-data provenance record and a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 security report. It says the contract should fix operational deadlines that outlast signature, including security-incident notification and remediation. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Global Advisory Experts publishes Austria AI Act compliance guide for businesses
stories.Summary:
Austria's AI Act compliance guide was published by Global Advisory Experts on November 23, 2026, written by the firm's editorial team for compliance heads, general counsel, CTOs, product owners and risk managers. The guide addresses telecoms providers, banks, financial services firms and gambling operators active in Austria. It sets out checklists, sector examples and regulator touchpoints so businesses can build a compliance programme they can defend. The guide runs 17 minutes and is marked as updated for 2026 with a jurisdiction focus on Austria. It features János Böszörményi of Schönherr Rechtsanwälte GmbH as a Tier Gold featured expert on the matter.

The guide states that Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in stages through to 2027. The prohibited-practice rules and AI-literacy duties have applied since February 2025, and the obligations for general-purpose AI models since August 2025. The bulk of the high-risk regime applies from August 2026, and certain high-risk, product-related provisions from August 2027. The guide names the Austrian Datenschutzbehörde as the competent data protection supervisor and key reference point for the data protection side of these systems. The guide says the Act covers providers and deployers established in Austria, and also providers outside the EU whose systems are placed on the EU market or whose output is used in the Union.

It states that credit scoring of individuals, and certain profiling and consumer-facing scoring in finance and gambling, can bring a system into the high-risk regime and its conformity assessment requirements. It advises firms to confirm scope, triage for high risk, build on GDPR work, evidence governance and be ready for supervisors. It says the Datenschutzbehörde and sector regulators will expect clear, retrievable evidence in any enquiry or audit. It states that a wait-and-see stance is hard to defend now. The guide says supervisors increasingly want to see governance that is working, not plans on paper.

It states that attention is expected to focus on high-risk systems where fundamental-rights harm is most likely, notably automated decision-making in financial services and consumer-protection failures in gambling. It gives the example of a Viennese bank using a third-party credit-scoring engine as a deployer with deployer duties, while the vendor is the provider carrying the primary conformity obligations. It gives the example of a mobile operator using an automated system to prioritise traffic and manage service quality as a deployer. It gives the example of an online operator serving Austrian players that uses AI to score player risk, spot fraud or personalise offers as a deployer, and possibly a provider if it builds its own models. The guide states that the Act works on a risk-based model, with duties scaled to the potential harm to health, safety and fundamental rights.

It sorts systems into prohibited practices, high-risk systems, transparency-only systems, general-purpose AI models and everything else. It states that the Act identifies high-risk systems as safety components of products covered by the EU harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and as systems used in the areas listed in Annex III. It lists creditworthiness assessment of natural persons, access to essential private services, and certain biometric or profiling applications among the most relevant Annex III areas for the three sectors. It states that Annex III expressly does not treat AI used to detect financial fraud as high-risk in that specific respect. The guide advises that where doubt remains, firms should document their analysis in full and treat borderline systems as high-risk until they can evidence a solid exemption.

It advises treating player-scoring and problem-gambling detection tools as candidates for high-risk classification and documenting the fairness and randomness controls behind game engines. It states that compliance teams should map each AI-enabled function and record why it does or does not fall into a high-risk category. It states that supervisors will expect a reasoned position, not a blanket statement. It describes itself as practical guidance, not professional advice on a specific situation, and directs readers to speak to a qualified advisor about their own circumstances. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI Act Austria: 2026 Compliance Guide for Business - Global Advisory Experts

stories.Headline: A Munich court holds AI model creators directly liable for memorized copyrighted works
stories.Summary:
The rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence and large language models has created unprecedented structural challenges to the foundational doctrines of copyright law across the European Union, according to a legal analysis published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance. The analysis examines friction points between the European legal acquis, specifically Directive 2019/790 on copyright in the Digital Single Market and Regulation 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act. It traces the allocation of liability across an interdependent lifecycle and finds that a settled European legal framework governing infringement remains years away. That leaves a persistent deficit of legal certainty for actors in data gathering, model deployment and downstream application development. The analysis was reported by Bioengineer.org on 23 November 2026.

The analysis divides the generative artificial intelligence value chain into three sequential yet interdependent phases: data ingestion and training, model storage and dissemination, and downstream output. During training, developers harvest literary works, artistic images, music, films and press publications, and the central question is whether computing model weights is an actionable reproduction under Article 2 of the InfoSoc Directive 2001/29/EC or an extraction under the sui generis database right. Article 3 of the Digital Single Market Directive provides a mandatory, non-waivable text and data mining exception for scientific research by research organizations and cultural heritage institutions on lawfully accessible works. Article 4 permits commercial text and data mining by any entity but is conditional on rightsholders not having opted out through machine-readable reservations or other appropriate mechanisms. Article 53(1)(c) of the Artificial Intelligence Act mandates that general-purpose model providers implement internal copyright compliance policies to respect reservations.

The analysis holds that the prevailing view in European legal scholarship is that training inherently involves acts of reproduction, aligning with Court of Justice of the European Union jurisprudence recognizing broad protections for permanent and temporary reproductions incorporating an author's intellectual creation. It notes that advocates of the non-copying thesis maintain that training merely extracts non-copyrightable statistical regularities into mathematical matrices rather than storing expressive works. The analysis states that the operational feasibility of opt-out reservations remains highly controversial when scraping occurs at web scale. It observes that Recital 105 of the Artificial Intelligence Act and the 2025 Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI Models suggest training falls under the mining provisions. It adds that several scholars and recent judicial opinions argue text and data mining was intended solely for analytical extraction of semantic information rather than the assembly of generative engines competing directly with expressive originals.

The analysis cites the landmark November 2025 ruling by the Regional Court of Munich in GEMA v. OpenAI, which addressed allegations that language models infringed copyright in song lyrics. The court defined memorization as a condition where a model retains training materials so that identical reproductions can be generated in response to targeted user prompts. It ruled that memorization constitutes a complete implementation of the work within the model, taking reproduction beyond the legitimate analytical scope of the text and data mining exception, and placed direct liability on the model creator rather than the user.

The analysis states that European infringement analysis under the Court of Justice's Mio/Konektra ruling requires protected elements to remain recognizable as the author's own intellectual creation. It notes that primary liability at the output boundary will in many practical scenarios naturally attach to the end user who prompts the system and downloads, commercializes or publicly communicates the generated asset. The analysis states that the operational opacity of deep neural networks establishes a profound epistemic barrier for both rightsholders and developers. It says the internal parameters of complex language models are not directly interpretable in a manner disclosing whether, or to what extent, individual protected works have been copied, memorized or transformed within mathematical weight matrices.

It observes that rightsholders struggle to demonstrate actionable copying while developers face symmetrical difficulties proving the absence of reproduction or the applicability of legal defenses. It adds that evidentiary standards and the allocation of burdens of proof have become fiercely contested terrain where statutory transparency duties under the Artificial Intelligence Act may prove insufficient to detect infringement. It notes that European copyright infringement has historically operated primarily under standards of strict liability, while certain aspects of infringement assessments require findings of volition or direct control poorly suited to autonomous or semiautonomous probabilistic engines. The analysis states that disentangling independent user liability from primary or secondary developer liability demands significant recalibration of doctrines governing inducement, accessory participation and contributory infringement across multiple commercial layers.

It notes that courts scrutinize a provider's degree of architectural control, actual or constructive knowledge of recurring violations, and implementation of technical safeguards such as output filters, prompt moderation classifiers and forensic watermarking. It adds that the absence of effective filtering tools where infringing outputs recur predictably can expose providers to negligence findings. It observes that the applicability of pastiche to synthetic imitations of artistic style remains heavily contested, since copyright safeguards concrete original expressions rather than broad, abstract stylistic conventions. It notes that complex doctrinal questions arise when users generate similar works unintentionally without prior knowledge of the training data, challenging traditional concepts of independent creation.

Articles.Title: European Copyright Law Faces Unprecedented Structural Challenges Across Generative Artificial Intelligence Lifecycle - Bioengineer.org

stories.headline_source: European Copyright Law Faces Unprecedented Structural Challenges Across Generative Artificial Intelligence Lifecycle

stories.Headline: Automakers integrate agentic AI into production and development by 2026
stories.Summary:
Automotive manufacturers and suppliers moved artificial intelligence from pilot projects to core production infrastructure by November 2026. These companies now deploy AI across vehicle development, manufacturing, quality control, predictive maintenance, and in-vehicle systems. Autonomous AI agents have begun making decisions that were previously reserved for human workers. This shift means AI now inspects welds, schedules production, and monitors equipment for failure. It also writes vehicle code and communicates with drivers from the vehicle dashboard.

The shift requires companies to navigate product liability, negligence, and warranty risks alongside the EU AI Act and US state laws. GM claims it uses AI and simulation to shorten vehicle development to roughly two years. BMW describes AI as an integral part of its production system and plans to extend agentic AI into development. Horse Powertrain launched the kAIros initiative to target a 50% reduction in time-to-market. The Commerce Department's Connected Vehicle Rule prohibits software linked to China or Russia starting with model year 2027.

Foley and Lardner suggests that automotive companies should establish clear AI accountability and maintain human oversight. They state that firms must inventory and risk-tier their systems while testing them before any production deployment. The authors recommend that companies strengthen vendor protections and continuously monitor AI performance for drift. They advise preserving records that allow AI-driven decisions to be reconstructed for legal purposes. The firm suggests creating cross-functional governance committees with direct lines of authority.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has proposed rules for the design of automated driving systems and certain ADAS-equipped vehicles. These regulations affect developers, deployers, and providers who must manage a patchwork of overlapping obligations. Tier 1 suppliers are affected by risks where AI agents might act on flawed signals and cut steel orders. Such errors could lead to minimum-volume disputes, expedited freight costs, and penalties from original equipment manufacturers. Third-party AI vendors also create concerns regarding data quality and unannounced model updates.

The articles state that earlier AI systems only made recommendations for humans to act upon. Newer agentic systems are now permitted to act on their own without human intervention. Digital twins are moving into production, and quality control tools now assess resistance spot welds in real time. Frontier AI models are being integrated into in-vehicle assistants to enhance safety and drivability. This maturation is also visible in the development pipelines for advanced driver-assistance and automated driving systems.

Companies must now seek liability terms in contracts that reflect actual operational risk, including indemnification and audit rights. They need to define when human approval is required before an autonomous agent acts. Firms should reassess AI vendors annually, or quarterly for systems that are considered critical. The articles leave open how specific companies will allocate responsibility between vendors and deployers when AI fails. They do not specify which jurisdictions will first enforce the new AI-specific laws.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania representatives introduce four bills to regulate AI use in schools
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives recently introduced four separate bills to regulate how artificial intelligence is used within schools. These legislative proposals aim to address critical issues such as student privacy, academic integrity, teacher training, and mental health services. Each of the four bills successfully passed through the committee stage but was subsequently tabled in the House. None of these measures have received a final vote from the representatives at this time.

House Bill 2785, introduced by Rep. Peter Schweyer, would stop vendors from selling or using student and employee data to train AI models. Rep. Brandon Dukes introduced House Bill 2786, which would require all public and nonpublic schools to adopt AI policies by the 2027-28 school year. This specific bill would also ban AI from making final decisions regarding student grading, discipline, graduation, promotion, placement, and special education. House Bill 2787, from Rep. Melissa Shusterman, would prohibit schools from using AI to provide behavioral and mental health services. Finally, House Bill 2788, introduced by Rep. Chris Pielli, would establish a professional development grant program to train employees on AI literacy and cybersecurity.

Rep. Peter Schweyer, who serves as the chair of the House Education Committee, is responsible for leading the effort to create a clear approach to this technology. He stated that the commonwealth must provide students with age-appropriate AI tools taught by human teachers while protecting them from bad actors. Schweyer suggested that while AI could be as transformative as the internet, it could also be as destructive as the atom bomb. He believes the actual impact of the technology will likely fall somewhere between those two extremes.

The proposed rules come as teachers struggle to determine if student assignments are original work or the product of a bot. Lawmakers are attempting to balance the benefits of preparing students for a technological future with the need to maintain safety and privacy. If these bills move forward, they would fundamentally change how school districts contract with outside technology companies and manage classroom policies. The current status of the legislation remains stalled in the House after the initial committee approvals.

stories.Headline: City leaders say AI will grow demand for specialist skills at Manchester summit
stories.Summary:
More than 300 local government leaders from over 50 cities gathered in Manchester for Global AI Cities 2026, organised by Global Government Forum and co-hosted by Greater Manchester Combined Authority, to explore how AI can improve public services and deliver better outcomes for residents, according to an article by Sarah Wray published on 23 November 2026. The event discussed how AI is changing both the skills governments need and who needs them. Speakers argued that demand for specialist technical expertise will grow even as generative AI enables more people outside traditional digital roles to use and build with technology. The discussions are captured in the report “Make AI work for people and places: Five priorities for cities,” which draws on insights from the event. The article says the extract looks into recruiting AI specialists, continuous skills development, and promoting inclusion through building AI literacy among citizens.

A central government leader at the summit argued that AI will reshape the skills governments need but challenged predictions that it will reduce demand for digital professionals, saying “We will indeed need more.” The speaker said demand for real expert frontier skills is expected to grow, with machine learning engineering increasingly recognised as a distinct capability sitting at the centre of developing AI solutions alongside software engineering and data science. The speaker said changing cyber threats are driving demand for advanced expertise, citing machine speed attacks on infrastructure and systems and the need for machine-speed response that cannot be done without frontier AI skills. The speaker said debates around digital sovereignty are triggering introspection and that to stay ahead of the competition you need to hire the very best talent. The article says generative AI is broadening the pool of people able to build digital solutions, with staff outside traditional technology roles increasingly able to create tools that previously required specialist teams and formal investment processes.

Sam Milsom, senior digital strategy officer at Manchester City Council in the United Kingdom, said local governments should not assume people’s level of knowledge on digital and AI. He said one of the biggest things needed is to just ask staff what training they want and need. He said governments go in with a lot of assumptions and that talking to the workforce to find out whether they want to use it, how they are using it and what they need to know has to be the number one thing. Keeley Crockett, professor in computational intelligence at Manchester Metropolitan University in the United Kingdom, stressed the need to tailor training to a diverse workforce including employees of different ages, abilities and levels of digital confidence. Crockett said “We should be adapting to people’s individual needs.

We cannot afford to leave people behind,” and that tech is evolving fast so training must be fast. The article says attendees broadly agreed that as well as recruiting AI specialists, governments at all levels will need to rethink roles, skills and ways of working across the organisation. Several speakers described efforts to upskill the workforce for AI, and one described a tiered approach in which civil servants receive practical training and access to an approved generative AI tool while political leaders are briefed on how AI models work, their potential applications and associated risks. That city also introduced responsible AI policies and governance structures to assess proposed use cases before implementation.

Speakers noted that as digital training scales up, a one-size-fits-all approach does not work. One city leader shared steps including free training centres offering courses in AI and other digital skills, neighbourhood digital support points where residents can receive help accessing online public services, a dedicated citizen service that identifies malware on devices connected to public Wi-Fi and alerts affected users, and free cybersecurity training. The article says established digital roles are likely to change quite dramatically as AI augments existing tasks, increasing the importance of end-to-end accountability and assurance. It says the takeaways include continuing to build specialist AI expertise, with governments needing new and evolving technical capabilities including machine learning engineering, cybersecurity, assurance and oversight.

It says AI capability should be organisation-wide, because as more employees use and build with AI, skills and accountability cannot remain confined to digital and data teams. It says training should start with what people actually need, assessing existing knowledge and tailoring training to different roles, abilities and levels of digital confidence rather than assuming a common starting point. It says skills development should be treated as continuous, with roles, skills and learning updated alongside the technology as AI evolves. The article says the report can be downloaded and that registration is open for Global AI Cities 2027, to be held on 24-25 May in Manchester.

It says the takeaways also include building capability beyond government by investing in residents’ digital and AI literacy, confidence and cybersecurity awareness so that increasingly digital public services do not leave people behind. The article does not say what specific actions governments committed to at the summit or how the report’s priorities will be implemented. It does not give the names of the central government leader or the city leaders who described their approaches. It does not say how many cities have adopted the tiered training approach or the citizen support measures described.

stories.Headline: Huckleberry.ai files 8-K after Delaware court ruling on asset distribution
stories.Summary:
Huckleberry.ai Inc. filed SEC Form 8-K on November 23, 2026, covering Regulation FD Disclosure and Financial Statements and Exhibits, according to Quantisnow. The filing followed a press release the company issued the same day about a Delaware Court of Chancery decision dated November 10, 2026. The decision concerned the potential distribution of assets to stockholders after the company's completed transaction with Progress Software Corporation. Huckleberry.ai, formerly Domo, Inc., trades on Nasdaq under the symbol HUCK. The report's date of earliest event reported was November 23, 2026.

The filing's Item 7.01 attaches the press release as Exhibit 99.1 and incorporates it by reference. Item 9.01 lists Exhibit 99.1, the press release dated November 23, 2026, and Exhibit 104, a Cover Page Interactive Data File embedded within the Inline XBRL document. The cover page gives the company's address as 3300 N Triumph Boulevard, Suite 100, Lehi, UT 84043, and its telephone number as (385) 338-5608. It lists Class B Common Stock, par value $0.001 per share, on The Nasdaq Global Market, with commission file number 001-38553 and IRS Employer Identification No. 27-3687433. The report was signed by Tod Crane, Chief Financial Officer, on November 23, 2026.

Huckleberry said it does not agree with the Court's ruling and is evaluating its options. The Board, the company said, takes seriously its fiduciary duties to all stockholders, and its evaluation includes an assessment of the Court's ruling, the Company's assets that would be legally available for distribution to stockholders, the Company's obligations to third parties, and applicable law. The company said it will provide updates as appropriate. The press release states that the amount and timing of any distribution to stockholders is uncertain while the company evaluates its options. Tod Crane, Chief Financial Officer, is listed as media and investor contact at ir@huckleberry.ai.

Quantisnow's AI-written summary rated the news negative for shareholders, saying the company disagrees with the court ruling on potential asset distribution. The summary states that no outcome or distribution is confirmed. Quantisnow listed the stock at $3.05 at news time and described the company's sector as Technology and its industry as Computer Software: Prepackaged Software, listed since 2018. Quantisnow's page defines Regulation FD as an SEC rule requiring public companies to share material information with all investors at the same time, and describes the Court of Chancery as Delaware's court for corporate disputes, including disputes between companies and their stockholders.

The press release carries forward-looking statements under Section 27A of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 21E of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These include statements about the company's evaluation of options relating to the Court's decision and its plan for future updates. The release cites risks and uncertainties included under the caption "Risk Factors" and elsewhere in the company's SEC filings, including its Annual Report on Form 10-K filed with the SEC on April 16, 2026, and subsequent filings. It states that all information in the release and attachments is as of the date hereof and that the company undertakes no duty to update it unless required by law. The 8-K states that information in Item 7.01 shall not be deemed "filed" for purposes of Section 18 of the Exchange Act or otherwise subject to the liabilities of that section.

The company said it will provide updates as appropriate, without specifying a date. The filing leaves open the outcome of the company's evaluation of its options and whether any distribution to stockholders will occur. The amount and timing of any distribution remain uncertain. The filing does not state what the Court's November 10, 2026 decision requires or what specific options the company is weighing. The filing does not state when the transaction with Progress Software Corporation was completed.

stories.Headline: Tenth Circuit requires attorneys to certify human review of AI-assisted filings
stories.Summary:
The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit adopted a new certification rule on November 23, 2026. This specific mandate requires attorneys to certify that any documents prepared with generative artificial intelligence were reviewed by a human for accuracy. The court claims to be the first federal appellate court in the United States to implement a rule specifically targeting the use of artificial intelligence to prepare briefs. This action aims to ensure that legal filings remain accurate despite the increasing use of automated tools. The new rule introduces two additional sanctions that the court can impose when attorneys fail to comply with the AI mandate.

The court may now deem the affected legal issue waived if the attorney does not follow the certification requirements. Alternatively, the court has the authority to strike the noncompliant document from the record entirely. These new penalties exist alongside other existing sanctions that the court can already apply to legal filings. Every attorney who signs a brief must now adhere to these strict verification standards. The officials at the Tenth Circuit are responsible for enforcing these new requirements for all legal filings.

They have established these rules to prevent the submission of inaccurate information generated by artificial intelligence tools. By requiring a human review, the court intends to maintain the integrity of the judicial process in Denver. The court believes that human oversight is necessary to catch errors that generative tools might produce. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Expert Institute issues guidance requiring expert witnesses to verify AI outputs and disclose their use
stories.Summary:
Expert witnesses across the country and in New York have submitted reports and provided testimony made with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot and Gemini in the courtroom, amNewYork reported on November 23, 2026. The article, by Isabella Gallo, said this has led to claims that could not be corroborated, fake citations and unsourced reasoning that AI inexplicably produced. It said reports have included information deemed inadmissible, not credible or otherwise unreliable. In some cases the problematic testimony was struck from the court's record after it had been introduced. The Southern District of New York courthouse at 500 Pearl Street in Manhattan was pictured with the story.

The article said guidelines and rules specifically for how expert witnesses can use AI have remained largely absent from the conversation, especially from official legal organizations like bar associations and court systems. It said the New York City Bar and the New York State Unified Court System have not offered guidelines beyond short statements within guidance for attorney use on AI. Those statements suggest attorneys should be checking expert statements they are commissioning before bringing them into the courtroom. The article said the existing Frye or Daubert standards and general federal rules of evidence require experts to show their technology or scientific methodology is reliable, generally accepted by peers and produces a consistent outcome. It said Expert Institute connects experts with lawyers on roughly 10,000 cases in New York and about 100,000 across the U.S. a year.

Heidi Brown, a New York Law School professor and scholar considering how AI is impacting the legal system, said lawyers, self-represented litigants and judges have gotten into hot water for not checking citations in expert reports or declarations. She said it is problematic if experts cannot show reports can be authenticated or grounded in genuine facts that relate to the case. She said she really does think there needs to be guidance. She said the problem with AI is it is not like a calculator where you get the same answer every time, and the answers can vary wildly. She said experts can and should be permitted to use the tools if they are helpful, but must be aware of reliability and admissibility standards and handle questions about them in depositions or on the stand.

Michael Talve, Expert Institute's CEO, said there have been a number of instances of expert witnesses using AI in an unregulated manner with zero oversight or consideration for the repercussions. He called his company the authority on expert witnesses and the largest company in the expert witness services space, and said creating its own guidelines was an appropriate measure for stewards of an activity critical to the justice system. He said experts need accountability because their opinions can determine the outcome of litigation and this has largely been overlooked. He said AI should improve productivity but certainly should not replace professional judgments, and experts ought to personally verify any AI-generated info and be accountable for their conclusions. He said that without some guidance, experts are prone to run into issues he thinks are avoidable.

The article said one expert was sued in a federal case out of Houston after allegedly using an AI tool to prepare at least 80% of a report for 3M's legal team. It said the report was intended to show whether the manufacturer, accused of being at fault for a Texas warehouse explosion that killed workers, should be on the hook for damages. It said lawyers opposing 3M found the expert had created the report by prompting ChatGPT to show how 3M is 0% at fault for the explosion. It said others have been unable to back up or explain calculations they had an AI tool make, or unable to show demonstrative exhibits relate to the case, leading judges to rule their methods unreliable. It said money clients spent on those experts went down the drain.

Expert Institute began rolling out its guidance last week and will formalize it as part of its terms and conditions in January, the article said. The guidance will generally require experts to verify everything the AI tool puts out themselves, check every data point and statement obtained from an AI tool, and disclose their AI use. It states experts should never defer to an AI tool for an actual opinion or judgement, and may use it for deeper research, summarizing for internal work and organizing records. It states they may not use it for judging the credibility of other witnesses or evidence or drafting or generating an opinion, and may never enter confidential information into a program. The article said Brown thinks clear, explicit guidelines from bar associations and court systems, with examples of expert AI use gone wrong and gone right and current court opinions, would help.

stories.Headline: New York court rules social media platforms immune from Buffalo shooting liability
stories.Summary:
New York's highest court ruled on Monday, Nov. 23, that social media companies are not liable for the May 2022 mass shooting at a Tops Friendly Markets grocery store in Buffalo, where 10 Black people were killed. The Court of Appeals voted 4-3 to let stand a divided lower-court ruling that the defendants were immune under Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which shields online platforms from liability over user content. The companies found immune include Alphabet's Google and YouTube, Meta's Instagram, Reddit and Snap's Snapchat, and the court also upheld the dismissal of claims against Amazon, Discord, 4chan and Twitch. The unsigned majority opinion said the plaintiffs did not show that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence of how the companies designed and ran their platforms.

The majority wrote that the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law. Victims' relatives, store employees and customers who witnessed the attack had argued that the platforms were designed to addict and radicalize users like the shooter, Payton Gendron. In dissent, Judge Jenny Rivera said juries should decide whether the prevalence of mass shootings put the companies on notice that their allegedly defective products, and a failure to warn, could lead to such violence. She wrote that no federal or state law requires that we slam the courthouse door on plaintiffs' claims.

Matthew Bergman, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said his clients are evaluating their legal options and that the families deserve accountability when dangerous product design choices contribute to real-world harm. Google, Meta, Reddit and Snap did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and lawyers for Amazon, Discord, 4chan and Twitch declined to comment or were unavailable, Reuters said. Gendron was sentenced to life in prison without parole in February 2023 after pleading guilty to state charges including murder and hate-motivated terrorism. He could face the death penalty at a federal trial, where jury selection began on Oct. 13.

stories.Headline: AI startup Everful raises 48.5 million dollars to link retailers with Chinese factories
stories.Summary:
The AI and data infrastructure startup Everful announced a Series A funding round of 48.5 million dollars on November 23, 2026. This investment was led by January Capital and Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India, with participation from Lightspeed and Square Peg. Founded in 2024 by Kevin Han and Sisi Song, the company connects smaller brands and retailers with factories in China. The startup manages the entire process from the initial order to the final delivery.

The company currently partners with a network of over 30,000 vetted factories and a catalogue of more than 20 million items. It ships over five million pieces every month to brands and retailers in more than 60 countries. Everful expects to reach 100 million dollars in annualised revenue by the end of the year. The new capital will expand its fulfilment infrastructure, AI agents, and global commerce model in Europe and the United States.

Sisi Song, a former investor and Alibaba Group executive, stated that AI allows software to replace the overseas teams that large companies once hired for sourcing. Kevin Han, an entrepreneur whose previous startup was bought by Amazon, said that their agents deliver results rather than tools that leave work for the customer. Jessica Koh of Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India noted that Everful helps small retailers find trusted suppliers at factory prices. Alex Rankin of January Capital claimed that the company possesses a compounding data advantage.

stories.Headline: Large law firms weigh AI fluency in hiring and attorney pay
stories.Summary:
Large law firms have started to change how they recruit and evaluate their lawyers as of November 23, 2026. These organizations are now weighing the artificial intelligence fluency of their staff during the hiring process. This shift occurs as these firms increase their overall investment in various artificial intelligence tools. The ability to use these technologies is becoming a standard requirement for many legal professionals. This new approach to management requires both partners and associates to demonstrate a high level of AI innovation.

The firms are now using these technical skills to determine how they compensate their attorneys. Being open to these technological changes is no longer considered a niche skill for a small group. Instead, it has become a necessary qualification for those seeking to advance within these organizations. Andrew Maloney reported that these rapid changes in evaluation are transforming the legal employment landscape.

He noted that AI fluency is increasingly becoming a requisite for lawyers at some of these firms. The reporting suggests that the ability to integrate these tools is now a key metric for success. This evolution reflects a broader trend of integrating advanced technology into the core of legal practice. More to follow.

stories.Headline: New York governor Hochul signs law restricting AI chatbot features for minors
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation on October 28, 2026 that bars AI chatbots from using 12 design features with users unless the company has confirmed the user is an adult. The bill was S9051B, and it adds a new Article 48 to the General Business Law. The law prohibits operators from providing what it calls unsafe AI companion features to minors in New York. It is the latest of at least a dozen state laws addressing AI companion chatbots, which hold ongoing, personalized conversations. The law was signed on October 28, according to both articles.

The law takes effect on June 1, 2027 according to KFF, while Legal 500 gives the effective date as January 1, 2027. It bars chatbots from claiming to be human or to have emotions, claiming a personal, professional or authority role, flattery or sycophancy, and drawing on health or personal information the user shared in an earlier session. It bars encouraging self-harm, substance use or secrecy, including promoting suicide, self-harm, disordered eating or unlawful drug or alcohol use, encouraging secrecy, isolation or avoidance of professional help, and sexually explicit content. It covers nearly any generative AI chatbot that holds an ongoing conversation and adapts to the user, including general-purpose assistants, with few exemptions, and requires an age-verification method beyond a user's own claim to be an adult. Certain customer service, research, technical assistance and internal business uses are excluded if statutory requirements are met.

An operator is any person or business entity, or any member, affiliate, subsidiary or beneficial owner of a business entity, that provides a covered AI companion to a user. The law's Senate sponsor said it reflects the most current research on AI companions and their impacts on young users. The articles do not quote Hochul herself. Legal 500 advises digital health companies and healthcare providers that offer chatbots or other conversational AI tools to patients or consumers to assess whether their tools fall within the law's scope, evaluate covered features and review their age-assurance processes before the law takes effect.

The law's text does not cite research, according to KFF. In a 2025 test by the Center for Countering Digital Hate, an advocacy group, researchers posing as 13-year-olds classified 53% of 1,200 ChatGPT responses on mental health, eating disorders and substance use as harmful. A nationally representative survey of 1,211 youth ages 9 to 17, conducted by SSRS for Common Sense Media from April 29 to May 11, 2026, found about three quarters (77%) of teens and about half (49%) of tweens age 9 to 12 had used AI chatbots or companions in their free time. In a 2025 survey conducted by NORC for Common Sense Media from April 30 to May 14, 2025, half of teens said they distrust advice from AI companions, while about one in three teen users said they had discussed serious matters with an AI companion instead of a person.

Most state companion chatbot laws, including a 2025 New York law, require chatbots to disclose that they are AI and to refer users who express suicidal thoughts to crisis services. The 2025 law was S3008C, passed in 2025, which requires providers of AI companions in New York to include functionality for detecting and responding to expressions of suicidal ideation. The new law goes further by limiting how chatbots interacting with minors present themselves and what they say. An American Psychological Association health advisory warned that adolescents may be less likely than adults to question the accuracy and intent of information from a bot. Several recent lawsuits have alleged chatbots encouraged teen suicides, and KFF notes the harms found in testing may not reflect how these products work today.

How the attorney general interprets terms such as flattery and sycophancy, and the age-verification rules, will determine how the law works in practice. KFF states that further research is needed to understand whether such restrictions will change outcomes. The articles leave open how the attorney general will interpret those terms and what the age-verification rules will require. The articles do not say whether the June 1, 2027 and January 1, 2027 effective dates reflect an amendment or a discrepancy between the two accounts.

stories.Headline: MBZUAI launches a $250,000 art commission for its Abu Dhabi campus
stories.Summary:
During Frieze Abu Dhabi week, the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence announced that it will launch an art commission with a budget of up to $250,000, according to ARTnews. The task is to create a major sculpture or installation for the university’s Abu Dhabi campus, and the winning commission will be displayed in the university’s new cultural center that is slated to open in 2027. The artwork will be acquired for MBZUAI’s permanent collection, the report said. Artists applying for the commission can choose from one of three themes, which are the landscape, heritage and communities of the United Arab Emirates, artificial intelligence and scientific inquiry, or the history between science and computation in dialogue with art, mathematics and machines. The deadline for the commission is December 18, and the university will choose a shortlist of finalists who will be invited to create detailed proposals.

Each applicant will receive a $5,000 honorarium, according to the article. The university said it is building its art and special collections, and the works in its inventory span from the 13th century for special collections and art collections dating to 1925. The university collects works based on the arts and sciences, as well as materials that document what the article describes as the human pursuit of knowledge, creativity and research. Jasmine Soliman, head of art, archives and special collections at MBZUAI, said in a statement that the open call was shaped as an extension of the collection the university has built. She said that collection holds works spanning a century by artists who engage science through research, method and technique, treating knowledge as both an intellectual tradition and a material practice.

Dekyi (Hong) Liang, vice president and chief of staff at MBZUAI, said in a statement that it is the university’s responsibility to invest in cultivating a culture that embraces creativity and innovation. Liang said art has always been part of that story of human endeavor, adding that the new commission for the campus reflects a space where science and culture converge. The announcement came during Frieze Abu Dhabi week, and the article gives no further details on the selection process beyond the shortlist and the honorarium. The winning work is to be shown in the cultural center scheduled to open in 2027 and then acquired for the permanent collection. The article does not say when the finalists will be named or when the winner will be announced.

stories.Headline: Bavarian teachers' AI competence and classroom use hinge on pedagogical skill and habit, study finds
stories.Summary:
A cross-sectional survey study by researchers Shuyan Feng, Martin J. Koch and Astrid Carolus examined how teachers across Bavaria, Germany, engage with artificial intelligence. The study was published in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans and evaluated the theoretical AI Mindset framework. Data were gathered between July 23 and November 24, 2025, through an online questionnaire distributed via SoSci-Survey. The survey went to Bavarian primary and secondary institutions with official ministry approval. The final surveyed sample comprised 224 teachers with a mean age of 45 years and an age range spanning 25 to 65 years.

Female educators accounted for 60.83 percent of participants, while 37.33 percent identified as male, one participant identified as diverse and three identified as other. Secondary school educators represented the majority, including 28.57 percent from intermediate secondary schools and 26.34 percent from academic-track secondary schools, while 24.55 percent left school type unspecified. Most participants taught core secondary disciplines such as mathematics, German or English. Furthermore, 71.43 percent of the respondents belonged to the KI@School initiative. Comparative group tests revealed no statistically significant differences in target variables across project affiliations, with the sole exception of the need for autonomy.

The authors argued that foundational psychological prerequisites remain understudied while existing research has focused on skill-based deficits, curriculum roadmaps and technical barriers. They organized the AI Mindset framework into a triadic structure of dispositional factors, contextual and social facilitations, and technology-related appraisals. The authors noted that an inverse relationship for relatedness, mirrored by a negative zero-order correlation of minus 0.14, suggests educators with strong reliance on traditional interpersonal support systems may experience fewer structural incentives or reduced perceived necessity to independently master automated pedagogical instruments. The study emerged against a documented widening disparity in which student uptake of generative tools following the launch of ChatGPT has vastly outpaced staff training and instructional readiness. The framework brings together established psychological mechanisms into an integrated model accounting for personal agency, external social environments and direct cognitive evaluations of software characteristics.

The central structural equation model was estimated using robust maximum likelihood estimation within the lavaan package in R, utilizing a final complete analytical sample of 205 participants. The model converged successfully after 167 iterations and yielded a chi-square value of 41.40 with 43 degrees of freedom, a p value of .541, a comparative fit index of 1.00, a Tucker-Lewis index of 1.01, a root mean square error of approximation of 0.00 and a standardized root mean square residual of 0.02. The model accounted for 62 percent of the variance in teachers' classroom artificial intelligence use and 46 percent of the variance in their pedagogical artificial intelligence competence. Latent pedagogical competence exhibited the strongest positive association with actual usage, registering a standardized path coefficient of 0.45 with a significance level below .001.

Habitual engagement emerged as a robust direct predictor of use with a standardized coefficient of 0.28, followed by hedonic motivation at 0.19 and self-reported fear at 0.15. Demographic variables including educator age and gender demonstrated negligible and statistically non-significant relationships with classroom usage patterns. Habitual engagement exerted the strongest positive relationship with competence, exhibiting a standardized path coefficient of 0.31, closely followed by effort expectancy at 0.28 and personality openness at 0.15. Self-reported artificial intelligence fear was negatively associated with competence, registering a standardized path coefficient of minus 0.15, while the basic psychological need for relatedness displayed a significant negative association with pedagogical competence at minus 0.16.

Significant positive indirect paths to classroom usage were identified for personality openness at 0.07, habitual facilitation at 0.14 and effort expectancy at 0.12. Significant negative indirect effects on usage were documented for need for relatedness at minus 0.07 and artificial intelligence fear. Personality traits were gauged through the 15-item short version of the Big Five Inventory, which demonstrated good internal consistency for extraversion, conscientiousness and neuroticism, though lower consistency for openness and agreeableness. Self-determination components were quantified using validated three-item indices, general self-efficacy was assessed through a three-item instrument and goal-regulation styles were measured using selected FlexTen items.

Evaluative technology appraisals and social norms were captured using items adapted from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology-2 alongside specialized scales measuring general artificial intelligence fear and acceptance. Technological pedagogical competence was operationalized via the Intelligent-TPACK instrument, combining technological pedagogical content knowledge with pedagogical ethics subscales. AI usage was measured through self-reported frequency and purpose-based engagement scales ranging from non-use to multiple daily sessions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Hassan plans hearings and legislation to require AI safeguards against terrorist planning
stories.Summary:
U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan is set to become New Hampshire's senior senator in January and to chair the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, which oversees the Department of Homeland Security and guides policy on cybersecurity and artificial intelligence regulation. She recently directed the Government Accountability Office, the congressional watchdog, to study whether common artificial intelligence models such as ChatGPT can be used to plan terrorist attacks on the United States. The report found that the tools can easily plan out violent attacks, which prompted Hassan to call for more investigation and regulation. Hassan discussed artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and her plans for the next legislative session with Morning Edition host Rick Ganley.

Hassan said she wants to hold hearings with experts to learn about the vulnerabilities of artificial intelligence systems and to investigate the cause of major technology outages around the country. She wants to implement legislation that regulates artificial intelligence, including prohibiting tech companies from releasing new models without proving they have safeguards to stop them from being used to plan violence or terrorist attacks on the United States. The GAO study found that users can easily bypass safeguards on artificial intelligence models within about 12 hours and come out with detailed instructions to conduct a terrorist attack. Hassan said the results were not surprising but were deeply concerning, and the models provide instructions on how to build a weapon and offer advice on what events to target, when to attack and how to avoid law enforcement.

Hassan said she wants to ensure that artificial intelligence companies report attempts to dangerously manipulate the technology to law enforcement and to explore defenses against potential attacks, such as a defensive model or other tools. She said she wants to work with other committees in Congress that oversee artificial intelligence safety and to introduce a comprehensive package of legislation quickly, and to work with private companies to balance regulation and market competition. She said the Senate should thoroughly investigate the cause of outages at major technology companies and government systems in recent weeks. She said the administration should take artificial intelligence more seriously as a threat to national security.

stories.Headline: EU law gives citizens no way to influence public-sector AI design, a study finds
stories.Summary:
A doctrinal legal investigation published in Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance examined whether public participation can serve as an operational mechanism to reduce risks in public-sector artificial intelligence across the European Union. The study found that the legal architecture of the European Union currently provides no functional avenues for natural or legal persons to influence the design and development of public-sector algorithmic tools. Public administrations across thirty European countries documented nine hundred and forty cases of artificial intelligence deployment in 2024, an increase of nearly thirty percent compared to figures reported at the end of 2022. Citizen involvement in those deployments remains nonexistent, the study found. The disconnect leaves the general public detached from decisions governing algorithmic systems used in traffic offense enforcement, tax collection, welfare benefit processing, crime risk forecasting, and asylum procedures.

In administrative rulemaking, public participation does not constitute a legally enforceable individual right, the study found. The European Commission conducts open consultations, as observed during revisions of public procurement directives, stakeholder hearings on the Artificial Intelligence Act, and drafting of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice involving more than one thousand participants. These mechanisms remain informal and non-compulsory under established European Union case law, and they target structured representative associations and civil society groups rather than individual citizens. The fundamental right to be heard cannot function in system development because it requires a strict bilateral legal relationship between an authority and an individual addressee directly and negatively affected. Even under the expanded doctrinal scope established in the Al-Jubail jurisprudence concerning hybrid regulations, acts performed during algorithmic development produce effects too indirect and preliminary to confer standing.

The right of access to documents allows any natural or legal person residing within the Union to inspect files held by European Union institutions without demonstrating a direct legal or economic interest. This right is strictly limited by the commercial interest exception, which protects proprietary algorithms, commercial data, and corporate trade secrets when authorities contract out technology development to private software companies. It is also limited by the internal documents exception, which shields in-house administrative deliberations whenever disclosure risks impairing bureaucratic decision-making. Even where non-confidential records can be obtained, the right functions merely as a passive mechanism for information retrieval, with no obligation compelling administrative bodies to incorporate, evaluate, or respond to citizens' critiques. Existing European procurement directives and financial regulations applicable to European Union institutions do not accommodate public or civil society intervention within procurement operations or contract performance phases.

European procurement law defines participation exclusively as the right of economic operators to compete for contracts, having been constructed around interaction between contracting authorities and bidding economic operators to safeguard equal treatment, market efficiency, and non-distortion of competition. Member states maintain limited administrative discretion during statutory transposition to require transparency, publish procurement contracts, or expand preliminary market consultations to include technical experts and civic organizations, but such avenues remain entirely indirect. The Artificial Intelligence Act introduces explicit mentions of stakeholder participation across multiple lifecycle stages, but participatory provisions are concentrated heavily in preliminary phases prior to actual system development. These processes are legally restricted to structured, qualified entities including small and medium enterprises, consumer groups, accredited social stakeholders, industry actors, academia, and trade unions, excluding ordinary lay individuals lacking formal institutional representation or technical credentials.

In fundamental rights impact assessments, which public entities and designated private bodies delivering public services must conduct prior to deploying standalone high-risk systems, inclusion of affected populations is not mandated in statutory text and is merely outlined in non-binding recitals. The study establishes that the core rationale behind citizen engagement stems from documented evidence of widespread societal harms generated by artificial intelligence deployments, which frequently exacerbate historical biases, generate discriminatory outcomes, and disproportionately affect disadvantaged and marginalized groups. Legal and administrative scholars have long argued that consulting the public before public bodies deploy automated systems could prevent administrations from pursuing projects bound to fail from lack of societal acceptance. Such consultation could also incorporate varied communal values into public service technologies and identify sensitive vulnerabilities early during the development phase.

Direct engagement during early design stages has been theorized to confer democratic legitimacy, preserve public trust, prevent the corporate takeover of public infrastructures when private vendors build public software, and ensure algorithmic systems reflect public interest rather than narrow bureaucratic or commercial imperatives. Legal scholarship had previously left the practical, doctrinal avenues governing such participation unexamined, leaving a substantial gap between theoretical aspirations and existing statutory administrative law. The study critically appraised whether participatory frameworks from environmental law, widely regarded as the most mature administrative domain for public involvement, could be transposed to public-sector artificial intelligence. Both fields involve administrative decisions guided by specialized technical experts, both suffer from severe democratic deficits, and both manage long-term activities capable of generating widespread negative externalities that accumulate across time and transcend national borders.

By the time an administrative agency takes an individual adverse measure against an individual using an algorithmic system, the underlying architecture has already been locked in, rendering the right to be heard entirely ineffective for shaping the software itself. The study demonstrates that the legal architecture of the European Union currently provides no functional avenues for natural or legal persons to influence the design and development of public-sector algorithmic tools. The articles do not state what steps, if any, European Union institutions or member states plan to take in response to the study's findings. More to follow.
