stories.Headline: Akkodis launches a global AI Factory and uses itself as client zero to scale enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
Akkodis, a digital engineering consulting company that is part of the Adecco Group and is headquartered in Switzerland, announced on November 23, 2026 the launch of its AI Factory, which it describes as a global model designed to accelerate the development, adoption and scaling of enterprise AI. The company said it is operating the model within its own business, applying the same principles it offers to clients that are moving from AI experimentation to enterprise-scale value. Akkodis said the AI Factory is already connecting AI solutions and reusable capabilities across the company globally, with the first global AI Factory solutions now in production through common pathways for intake, governance and deployment. The company said the model is not a single centralized technology platform but an enablement ecosystem that connects countries, engineers, business teams and specialists with reusable capabilities, development resources and expertise. The AI Factory brings together four core functions, which Akkodis lists as Design, Build, Run and Govern, covering the operating model and architecture, the development of solutions and reusable components, the move into production and lifecycle support, and the security, compliance and decision frameworks needed to manage AI responsibly.

Akkodis said the model helps teams decide whether to reuse or adapt existing capabilities, combine expertise across countries or develop something new, rather than assuming every AI requirement demands a new solution. The company said its AI use case intake agent, a common entry point that structures AI opportunities and identifies governance and duplication risks, is now live across Akkodis. Through AI Factory as a Service, Akkodis said it brings that experience, engineering expertise and reusable capabilities to clients seeking to move from fragmented AI initiatives toward scalable enterprise capability. Jo Debecker, President and CEO of Akkodis, said that scaling AI is not simply a technology challenge and that it requires organizations to connect innovation with the systems, expertise and operating models needed to turn it into repeatable value.

He said the company sees that challenge with its clients and experiences it itself, and that the AI Factory helps Akkodis learn by doing while putting Akkodis Intelligence into practice by combining human expertise and technology. Akkodis said it serves as "client zero," testing and refining the model in a complex global enterprise environment, and that applying and refining the AI Factory internally and with clients creates a continuous feedback loop that improves both internal execution and customer delivery. Akkodis cited its 2026 What CTOs Think research, which found that while AI ambition continues to grow, organizations often struggle to turn experimentation into repeatable, scalable execution, widening the divide between enterprise-wide AI orchestration and fragmented efforts across functions, systems and skills. Among the AI solutions Akkodis said it is developing and integrating with clients are a multi-agent AI coworker that it says can reduce B2B sales proposal preparation from three days to approximately five minutes, a supplier communications agent designed to save 45 to 55 hours per user each month, a contract review agent designed to reduce review time by at least 30%, and an executive office assistant that reduces administrative effort while improving decision and action traceability.

stories.Headline: TGood and LG enter the power resources market to meet AI computing demands
stories.Summary:
TGood and LG have rushed to enter the power resources market during a scramble driven by artificial intelligence. This race for electricity occurred as computing power demand surged, redrawing cost accounts for energy storage and gas-fired power. The scramble extended to gas fields, where advanced gas power has taken 69 percent of the market share. These events were highlighted during a Grid Revaluation Special Summit held on November 19. The summit gathered North American power traders, researchers, and gas-fired power operators to discuss shifting computing power loads.

The U.S. Department of Energy issued a 5.1 billion dollar loan to Alliant Energy last month for gas storage and power. This funding is earmarked for building 1.6 million kilowatts of new gas-fired power capacity in the United States. TGood signed a centralized procurement contract for power cabins at computing power centers worth 250 million yuan. Vertech, a subsidiary of LG Energy Solution, plans for North American production capacity to reach 70 GWh by next year. LG Energy Solution also reported backlogged energy storage orders reaching 160 GWh by the end of the third quarter.

U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said that gas storage facilities function as warehouses for buying gas when prices are low. Tristan Doherty of Vertech stated that idle grid capacity can meet the pulse load of data centers. TGood claims its computing-power-power island solution reduces the construction cycle by about 70 percent compared with civil engineering. LG Energy Solution was selected for the NVIDIA DSX Ready energy storage partner list, which includes only three companies worldwide. These leaders suggest that batteries are now part of computing power infrastructure rather than just backup power supplies.

Residents in Lowell, Massachusetts, sued the state environmental protection department over the expansion of diesel generators at a data center. These residents have seen electricity tariffs rise by more than 50 percent due to the competition for power. Fifteen U.S. states are considering pausing new data center approvals to manage the growing power gap. The National Data Administration noted that China's computing power scale has reached 3.1 million PFLOPS, ranking second globally. The National Energy Administration estimates China's computing power electricity consumption will reach 800 billion kilowatt-hours by 2030.

BloombergNEF projects that new natural gas consumption from U.S. data centers will reach 15 billion cubic feet per day by 2035. This increment exceeds the total national gas consumption of any country except China, Russia, Iran, and the United States. Massachusetts released a regulatory framework in June requiring data centers to provide their own clean power and cover grid costs. Projects with peak power consumption exceeding 25,000 kilowatts must now obtain community approval before applying for official permits. New York State also released an advanced nuclear power master plan targeting 5 million kilowatts of new capacity.

Small modular reactors remain on the drawing board, with Amazon and Meta investing in X-energy and TerraPower respectively. TGood has expanded overseas with computing power center projects in Thailand and Malaysia during the third quarter. The company's total winning bids for overseas business have exceeded 1.3 billion yuan. Financial statements have yet to reflect performance, as TGood recorded a net operating cash flow of negative 188 million yuan. The articles leave open how the real cost impact will unfold as the real bill is yet to come.

stories.Headline: HCLTech and Cohere partner to deliver sovereign AI in Canada and Germany
stories.Summary:
HCLTech and Cohere announced on 17 November 2026, in a release dated from Noida, a partnership to design and deliver what they call sovereign AI solutions to enterprises and public administrations. Under the agreement, HCLTech becomes one of Cohere's preferred global systems integrators in two countries, Canada and Germany. The release presents Canada and Germany as priority markets for HCLTech and says sovereignty is shaping AI adoption by businesses and governments there. The agreement combines Cohere's platform and models, including North, its agent platform, with the integrator's professional services.

Initial developments will target insurance, financial services and industry, with the release citing claims processing that takes jurisdiction into account, secure analysis of sensitive financial data and faster access to technical documentation as examples. Solutions will be installed in the environment chosen by each client to meet data residency, security and regulatory requirements, and Cohere's presentation lists public or private clouds, on-premises installations and fully air-gapped environments as possibilities. Only one certification is cited, ISO 42001, the international standard for AI management systems, which both companies hold. Nothing in the release indicates exclusivity, and the release does not say which entity contracts or where the teams operating the systems are based. France remains outside the announced scope, and the two companies say only that they want to extend the partnership to the rest of the world, with no timeline.

Phil Blunsom, Cohere's chief technology officer, said organisations should not have to choose between the benefits of AI and control of their data, according to the release. Vijay Guntur, his counterpart at HCLTech, and Dave Chopra, who heads the Indian group's Canadian operations, are also quoted, and the only country manager to speak is Canada's. As of 19 November, Cohere's press room did not mention the agreement. HCLTech reports more than 230,000 employees in over 60 countries and USD 14.8 billion in revenue for the twelve months ended September 2026, and its German headquarters is in Frankfurt/Eschborn.

The release mentions none of Cohere's other German elements: its merger with Aleph Alpha, its latest funding round led by the Schwarz Group and its offering on the STACKIT cloud. The Aleph Alpha merger, announced in April, produced a definitive agreement on 16 September, and the combined entity will operate under the Cohere name with headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, keeping the Heidelberg office as a research centre and employing more than 1,000 people. The merger had not been declared closed as of 19 November, and Cohere and Aleph Alpha were expecting in September to close it before the end of 2026, within six weeks of that date. Each partner has other alliances: Cohere announced a global alliance with PwC on 5 October and a partnership with OpenText on 16 September, while HCLTech concluded a Global Premier partnership with Anthropic on 12 October.

stories.Headline: Manitoba education minister Tracy Schmidt expands school cellphone ban to include smart watches and AI glasses
stories.Summary:
Manitoba Education Minister Tracy Schmidt sent a directive to school leaders last week telling them to add smart glasses, smart watches and other wearable technologies to the cellphone ban that has been in place in the province's schools since September 2024, the Manitoba government says. The November 17 letter went to all school division superintendents as well as principals of independent schools that receive public funding, and it said students increasingly have access to personal devices that offer messaging, social media, internet browsing, photography, recording, artificial intelligence tools or other cellphone-like functions. The directive was issued one week after the Hanover School Division in southeast Manitoba became the first division in the province to ban smart glasses in its schools, according to the government, with a letter to parents citing privacy because the glasses can record audio and video without others readily knowing.

Schmidt said in a statement that guidelines must evolve with technology so students learn in healthy, safe environments that support their education and well-being, and the original ban was meant to reduce distractions in classrooms and minimize the harmful impacts associated with social media and online platforms. Kara Brisson-Boivin, director of research at the Ottawa-based digital media literacy group MediaSmarts, said Manitoba is on the right track but she would like to see rules set at the federal level rather than a patchwork of 13 provinces and territories regulating the same technological challenge in different shades of grey. She said policing the technology should not fall on school staff who are already overrun with day-to-day challenges, and she is not convinced a blanket long-term ban is right because students with visual and hearing impairments could be aided by such devices, though she said not enough is known yet about the potential benefits.

Meta, one of several makers of AI glasses, says on its website that its product has an LED light that blinks to alert others when the wearer takes a picture or records video, and the glasses automatically disable the camera if they detect the capture light was covered or tampered with. Brisson-Boivin said that light is difficult to recognize, especially for children and youth, and online criticism says the LEDs are small and easy to miss in direct sunlight, in bright indoor lighting, from the side or in crowded spaces. Logan Hassett, 14, told CBC he could not understand why watches are included because there is not as much to do on them and it is easy to see if someone is staring at their watch, while Kaitlynn Seavers, who bought a smart watch for her 10-year-old son, said a ban goes too far and parents should teach their kids when to use one. Tracy Cosser, assistant director of the Manitoba Child Care Association, called the crackdown a really good idea, saying parents want to stay connected to their children but devices that can take video and images infringe on privacy.

Brisson-Boivin said it makes good sense to slow the integration of new technology in a controlled way and study the benefits as well as the harms, and she said Manitoba is taking important steps but a broader conversation is needed across the country about the role and place of wearable technology. She said AI, like any other technology, is a tool that can be used to hone skills but should not be used to replace them.

stories.Headline: Maryland students sue Omnilert and school officials over AI chip bag gun alert
stories.Summary:
Four current and former students from a Maryland high school filed a federal lawsuit after being detained at gunpoint. This incident occurred approximately one year before the lawsuit was filed in November 2026. An artificial intelligence system mistakenly identified a bag of Doritos as a firearm. Armed police officers responded to the alert and handcuffed the students. The students reported that they feared for their lives during the encounter.

The lawsuit names Omnilert, the company that created the AI gun detection system, as a defendant. Other defendants include the Baltimore County Police, the board of education, individual officers, and Principal Kate Smith. The event took place at Kenwood High School in Baltimore, Maryland. The plaintiffs allege that technological and human errors led to their unlawful detention and search. The lawsuit claims the encounter was terrifying and life-threatening for the students.

Omnilert expressed regret over the incident but claimed the process functioned as intended. The company stated its system is designed to identify possible threats for rapid human verification. Principal Kate Smith sent a screenshot of the footage to School Resource Officer John Douglas. She later sent a text message to other administrators laughing about the bag of chips. The lawsuit alleges that Smith was deliberately negligent or dangerously malicious.

The students were the primary victims who were accosted by officers aiming real guns. Some police officers on the scene expressed that the AI cameras were stupid and unreliable. Two school administrators had canceled the alert within two minutes of receiving it. Despite this cancellation, the principal proceeded to provoke the armed police response. The officers eventually revealed that the Omnilert system had prompted their dispatch.

Omnilert is a major player in the AI gun detection space using camera image analysis. The company previously failed to detect a gun used by a student in a shooting. Another company, Evolv, also faced criticism for generating many false positives in schools. These systems were marketed as game-changers for preventing school shootings through enhanced camera algorithms. Schools found that these technologies often forced more in-person searches of students.

The legal process will now determine if the defendants are held personally or corporately accountable. The lawsuit seeks damages for the unlawful detention and the resulting emotional distress. The articles do not state the specific financial demands made by the plaintiffs. It remains unclear if the school board will discipline Principal Kate Smith. The court must now decide if the AI alert provided sufficient probable cause.

stories.Headline: Ghana education minister Haruna Iddrisu proposes coding and AI subjects for basic schools pending Cabinet approval
stories.Summary:
Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu announced on Monday at the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission in Accra that basic schools will introduce new subjects. Students from kindergarten to Primary Six will study coding, robotics, artificial intelligence, and electronics once the Cabinet approves a revised curriculum. These subjects are not currently in force because the Cabinet has not yet signed off on the changes. Mr. Iddrisu has mentioned these potential curriculum updates during various gatherings since December 2025.

The proposed changes require a revised basic school curriculum that also includes financial literacy for students. Researchers are currently presenting evidence on digital learning to help create a draft AI-in-education roadmap for 2027 to 2030. While the 2027 Budget provides for 10,000 recruitment places for various education staff, no specific costs for the new subjects have been released. There is currently no official start date for the classrooms, no list of required equipment, and no timetable for teacher training.

Minister Haruna Iddrisu stated that the government intends to use artificial intelligence to improve learning outcomes and develop competitive human capital. He clarified that the policy aims to empower teachers with technology rather than replacing them with artificial intelligence. The Minister warned that the country must prevent the use of these tools from creating lazy learners who take shortcuts. He believes that such shortcuts could prevent the production of quality graduates for the needs of the country.

stories.Headline: Federal judge consolidates pretrial activity in 11 lawsuits against xAI over AI-generated child sexual abuse images
stories.Summary:
A federal judge on Friday ordered that preparations in 11 federal lawsuits against xAI be jointly coordinated as one case, citing similarities among them, the Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette reported. The order came in Fayetteville, according to the newspaper, which said the judge acted on the similarities the suits share. The cases concern AI-generated sexually explicit images of children, the headline of the report states. The report did not name the judge or give the date of the order beyond saying it was Friday.

The order consolidates pretrial activity in the 11 lawsuits against xAI into one coordinated case, the newspaper reported. The report gives no further numbers, dates or names connected to the order or the cases. It does not say what the consolidation changes for any party beyond the joint coordination of pretrial preparations. The report does not describe the claims in the individual suits or the relief they seek.

The report does not identify who is responsible for the images or what xAI said about the order. It carries no statement from the company, from the plaintiffs or from the court beyond the order itself. No person or party is quoted in the report, and no response to the ruling is given. The newspaper's account is subscriber-exclusive reporting, it states.

The report gives no context beyond the similarities the judge cited among the 11 suits. It does not say what happens next in the coordinated case or when further proceedings are expected. stories.Headline: China names 34 flagship smart factories to expand AI use into consumer goods sectors
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology named 34 facilities as flagship smart factories on Thursday, November 23, 2026. This latest group of recognized sites includes manufacturers of electronics, alcohol, and clothing, showing a shift away from heavy industry. One of these highlighted facilities is operated by the Jiangsu-based HLA Group, where artificial intelligence helps coordinate production. These systems work alongside human operators to turn consumer preference insights into specific design ideas.

The program was launched in 2024 to upgrade supply chains through the use of artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies. It requires factories to integrate smart systems that can analyze market trends and streamline the manufacturing process. By recognizing these 34 facilities, the government aims to encourage the adoption of high-tech tools across various consumer goods sectors. This transition allows manufacturers to better understand what customers want before a product ever reaches a retail shop.

The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology is responsible for identifying these flagship factories and overseeing the broader technological upgrade. Officials stated that the goal of the initiative is to modernize the way goods are produced and distributed throughout the country. They believe that integrating AI into the manufacturing sector will create more efficient supply chains for a wide range of products. The government intends to continue promoting these advanced systems to ensure that Chinese industry remains competitive.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop AI framework to integrate urban building energy modeling across life cycles
stories.Summary:
Researchers Chao Wang, Xin Wang, Francesco Causone, and Xing Shi developed an artificial intelligence framework for urban building energy modeling. This work was detailed in a comprehensive review published on November 23, 2026. The researchers analyzed the progression of city-scale energy simulations alongside conventional and advanced artificial intelligence paradigms. They focused on the operational mechanisms and computational bottlenecks governing city-scale decarbonization. The team formalized an extended paradigm termed UBEM plus to foster low-carbon urban environments.

The UBEM plus framework integrates urban design, building renewal, and multi-building operations across the built environment lifecycle. In the design phase, it optimizes urban form and building layouts to reduce overall energy demand. The renewal phase evaluates retrofit options and renewable resource availability across existing building stocks. For the operational phase, the system integrates system diagnosis and control optimization to coordinate energy demand. This framework expands standard urban building energy modeling to bridge analytical projections and practical physical interventions.

The researchers are responsible for identifying three core structural barriers hindering the widespread implementation of this framework. They stated that the interdisciplinary nature of urban modeling requires fusing heterogeneous data sources from various fields. They noted that scaling from individual properties to urban districts creates high-dimensional modeling obstacles. The authors explained that urban environments are dynamic cyber-physical-social systems with longitudinal interdependencies. They argued that detailed simulations capture physical heterogeneity only at a substantial computational expense.

The review affects urban planners and those managing the global climate crisis in urban areas. These areas account for approximately seventy percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. Heat-related mortality in these regions has increased by roughly seventy-four percent over the past three decades. The researchers used a thematic corpus of 473 publications to evaluate how others addressed modeling challenges. This corpus included 185 publications from China, 45 from the United States, and 22 from the United Kingdom.

The authors executed a systematic literature retrieval across Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect databases. They covered English-language publications from 2020 through a cutoff date of July 24, 2026. The initial search retrieved 3,499 records before screening removed duplicates and ineligible document types. The background includes an evolutionary trajectory divided into top-down and bottom-up modeling paradigms. Physics-based techniques were first formalized as a coherent three-part pipeline of data inputs, thermal modeling, and validation in 2016.

Next, the framework utilizes advanced artificial intelligence like transformer architectures, diffusion models, and foundation large language models. Vision transformers enhance footprint extraction and facade material identification for better urban modeling. Diffusion models offer stable training convergence for generative design to avoid training instabilities. Multi-agent deep reinforcement learning coordinates decentralized devices like heat pumps and battery storage. The articles leave open how to tailor general foundation models to specialized building domains.

stories.Headline: LexisNexis adds citation and quote checks to Protégé as states tighten legal AI rules
stories.Summary:
New York’s October 26, 2026, guidance on the risks of using artificial intelligence in preparing court papers specifically names LexisNexis as an authoritative source attorneys can use to independently verify AI-generated citations and quotations. The guidance reinforces attorney accountability under existing duties and does not generally require special disclosure of AI use under its statewide approach. California’s SB 574, signed September 30, 2026, and effective January 1, 2027, adds statutory requirements addressing verification, professional responsibility, confidentiality, and disclosure. Pennsylvania’s court advisory committee has published a proposed AI notice and compliance certification for public comment, and New York’s pending S9794 and A9097 would impose additional certification or disclosure obligations. Those proposals are not current requirements, but they show that expectations continue to develop.

The article organizes these expectations into four practical categories: verify authorities, retain professional responsibility and judgment, protect sensitive information, and document or disclose AI use as applicable. Lexis+ with Protégé brings together verification capabilities, attorney-directed skills and drafting tools, and security safeguards that the article says help attorneys address these expectations in their everyday work. Shepard’s Verify checks citations against LexisNexis legal content and Shepard’s citation information, provides Shepard’s Signals where available, and flags unmatched citations for further review. Shepard’s Verify will soon check quotations and paraphrased statements against cited sources, flagging inaccurate quotes, misleading context, and unsupported or overstated characterizations of case law. The article notes that matching a citation to a real authority does not establish that it supports a particular proposition or quotation.

Protégé’s Skills provide reusable instructions for specific tasks, and custom skills can reflect a firm’s preferred workflows, document standards, and review processes. For complex drafting and analysis, attorneys can review, edit, and approve a proposed plan before execution, then follow progress and assess the results. Protégé operates within the LexisNexis environment, supported by privacy, security, and governance controls, and customer data is not used to train or fine-tune LexisNexis AI models. New York’s guide recommends recording the tools used, the tasks performed, and the verification steps taken, while California’s new law requires disclosure of generative AI use for court-submitted documents. Shepard’s Verify offers downloadable PDF reports that attorneys can retain as part of their verification records.

Tony Muljadi, Vice President of Large Law at LexisNexis, said that as expectations for legal AI evolve, attorneys need technology they can trust and practical ways to verify its work. He said LexisNexis has for decades helped attorneys research the law and validate the authorities they rely on, and that Lexis+ with Protégé builds on that foundation. He described the company’s commitment as helping customers put AI to work with the sources, safeguards, and oversight that responsible legal practice demands. The article states that the attorney remains responsible for applying the rules governing each matter and must still determine what disclosure is necessary and submit it in the form their court requires.

stories.Headline: Wolfspeed and United Rentals build AI agents on Snowflake to capture retiring engineers' expertise
stories.Summary:
Snowflake published a blog post on November 23, 2026, titled "AI in Manufacturing: Preserving Institutional Knowledge," written by Angela Marrujo Fornaca, its senior content marketing manager. The post described how manufacturers are using AI to capture the expertise of experienced engineers and technicians before those workers retire. It cited the "Global AI & Data Trends Survey," which gathered responses from 2,050 enterprise leaders, including 288 in manufacturing. It described AI agents built by Wolfspeed and United Rentals on Snowflake. It argued that the knowledge plants run on exists in the heads of experienced people and can be lost when they leave.

The survey found job losses among senior individual contributors in manufacturing running at 33%, compared to 41% across all industries surveyed. It found 62% of job displacement in manufacturing concentrated at the entry level. It found 77% of organizations surveyed had experienced active job creation due to AI, and among companies experiencing both job creation and displacement, more than two-thirds confirmed a positive net employment impact. Wolfspeed operates 24/7 automated cleanroom fabs and built a custom AI agent on Snowflake fed with raw chat history from engineering conversations, maintenance logs and operational data. United Rentals manages 1,650 highly decentralized branches and 49,000 telematics-enabled assets, and within 30 days of rollout 4,000 field personnel were active users of its Business Intelligence Agent.

Wolfspeed's leadership is described as clear-eyed about the risk that AI models can confidently misinterpret operational context, especially in highly plant-specific environments. The company established a mandatory framework for trusted autonomy whose first principle is that data must carry the explicit institutional context of the specific plant's operational processes. Its second principle is that all automated troubleshooting guides must natively incorporate audited plant safety procedures, because under production stress technicians will follow AI instructions. The post said that compliance cannot depend on whoever built the agent having a good day. The post said the agent can draw on the documented troubleshooting history of the plant's most experienced engineers, with guidance built around the plant's audited safety procedures.

The post said the narrative that AI is replacing experienced workers in manufacturing does not hold up against the data. It said manufacturing is protecting its domain experts at a higher rate than the cross-industry average. It said an industrial workforce that had historically resisted digital tools adopted the United Rentals tool almost immediately because it did not ask them to change how they work. It said the tool links a fault code to the exact page and section needed to execute a fix, encoding the lookup expertise of experienced mechanics. It said the workers affected include process engineers, maintenance technicians, shift supervisors, master mechanics and incoming technical talent expected to perform at the same level from the start.

The post said the expertise specific to a facility, accumulated over years, is the invisible infrastructure behind operational performance and exists almost entirely in human heads. It said companies that have not begun capturing that expertise face a version of the data fragmentation problem that is harder to solve, because once the knowledge walks out the door it cannot be recovered from a legacy historian or a spreadsheet backup. It said the survey reveals a workforce undergoing active transformation and points to a window closing faster than most executives realize. It said what is emerging is a new tier of AI-native manufacturing roles that did not exist five years ago, including supply chain prompt engineers, digital twin analysts and AgentOps engineers. It said a master scheduler in a pre-AI environment might spend the first three hours of a shift manually tracing a shipment delay across five disconnected systems.

The post said manufacturers that treat AI purely as a head count reduction lever rather than a knowledge preservation and workforce elevation opportunity face a compounding risk. It said veteran operators and engineers will migrate to competitors where their expertise is augmented, not constrained by manual bureaucracy. It said recruiting the next generation becomes significantly harder in organizations that have not built that infrastructure. It offered a downloadable ebook, "Navigating the Age of Agentic AI: A Manufacturing Leader's Playbook," to learn how to capture and preserve institutional knowledge and reskill the workforce into high-value AI supervisors. It did not name the competitors to which veterans might migrate, did not give a date by which the window closes, and did not say how many of the 2,050 surveyed leaders were outside manufacturing beyond the 288 figure.

stories.Headline: New Zealand Commerce Commission issues AI guidance for businesses
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Commission of New Zealand released new guidance for businesses on November 18, 2026, regarding the use of artificial intelligence. This regulatory framework helps companies understand how existing consumer protection and competition laws apply to their modern technological tools. The commission issued these instructions because businesses are increasingly using AI to conduct transactions, engage with consumers, and support commercial decision-making. These guidelines aim to clarify the legal landscape as AI continues to change the way various businesses operate. The new guidance specifically explains how the Commerce Act 1986 and the Fair Trading Act 1986 apply to AI systems.

It highlights potential legal risks and provides practical steps that companies can take to manage those risks effectively. The framework requires that businesses remain fully accountable for all outcomes, regardless of whether decisions are made by people or algorithms. Companies must ensure that the information they provide is accurate and that all consumers are treated fairly. Deputy Chair Anne Callinan stated that using artificial intelligence does not shift the legal accountability or responsibility of a business.

She explained that the commission is not focusing on regulating the technology itself, but rather its impact on markets and competition. Callinan urged boards and senior leaders to treat AI as a governance issue that requires constant monitoring. She emphasized that leaders must ensure sufficient safeguards are in place to oversee how the technology influences corporate decisions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers present a black-box jailbreak that exploits multimodal models' trust in authoritative visuals
stories.Summary:
Weihang Liu, Qianqian Xu, Yangbangyan Jiang, Zitai Wang, Zhipeng Yu and Qingming Huang posted a paper on arXiv on 23 November 2026 describing a jailbreak framework they call Visual Trust Bias Attack, or VTBA, which they say exploits a previously overlooked attack surface in multimodal large language models. The authors state that these models show an intrinsic trust bias toward authoritative visual features, and that this bias allows jailbreaks that are both transferable and stealthy. They describe VTBA as a black-box method that works directly on naturally occurring harmful image-text pairs, rather than injecting fragile adversarial perturbations into irrelevant images or synthesizing toxic visual cues as earlier jailbreaks do. The paper carries a warning that it may contain sensitive content.

According to the abstract, VTBA builds a bank of authoritative templates, matches each input image-text pair to the most relevant template, and integrates the harmful intent into the selected layout, so that credible visual cues override safety refusals while the pair still looks natural. To test jailbreaks in this practical multimodal setting, the authors constructed a dataset of 2,500 naturally occurring image-text pairs. They report that their method consistently achieves high attack success rates across strong multimodal large language models, which they say reveals a severe and previously underexplored weakness in current multimodal safety alignment. The abstract gives no further numbers beyond the dataset size.

The authors are responsible for the framework and for the claims about its performance, and the abstract presents the high success rates and the transferability and stealth of the method as their own findings. They frame the work as addressing a practical jailbreak problem centered on naturally occurring harmful image-text pairs, in contrast to prior approaches that rely on perturbations or synthesized toxic cues. They also present the trust bias toward authoritative visual features as something earlier work had overlooked. The abstract does not say who else was involved or whether the work was reviewed.

The paper is listed on arXiv with the identifier 2611.22292 and is dated 23 November 2026, and the listing offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. Beyond the abstract, the articles give no details on the template bank, the matching procedure or the specific models tested. The authors describe the weakness as underexplored, and the abstract does not say what mitigation or follow-up work they propose. More to follow.

stories.Headline: China and ASEAN designate 2027 as the Year of AI cooperation
stories.Summary:
China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations declared 2027 as the Year of AI cooperation on Monday, November 16, 2026. This announcement occurred as the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol prepares to enter into force on December 1, 2026. The upgraded deal moves beyond traditional trade liberalization to cover emerging areas like the digital economy and green development. It aims to shift the regional relationship from simple market opening toward deeper institutional cooperation and coordinated standards. This new framework will address global challenges by creating a more stable and predictable regional market and industrial chain.

The protocol, signed in October 2025, includes a standalone chapter on supply-chain cooperation for the first time in a bilateral agreement. It covers hard connectivity in logistics and digital infrastructure, plus soft connectivity for electronic payments, invoices, and bills of lading. The agreement empowers a regional market of nearly 2.1 billion people through high-level commitments and improved customs procedures. China and ASEAN will establish sub-committees on standards, small and medium-sized enterprises, green development, and the digital economy. These measures will reduce business costs by encouraging the mutual recognition of conformity assessment results to avoid duplicate testing.

An official from the Ministry of Commerce of China said the upgrade reflects a commitment to multilateralism and free trade. The official stated that the deal will create a safe and open environment for digital trade and investment. MOFCOM will support local governments and industries by organizing targeted outreach and training for enterprises to understand new rules. The ministry noted that these arrangements will provide fresh impetus to Asia-Pacific economic integration amid global trade uncertainty. They believe that improving system compatibility through digital cooperation will enhance the competitiveness of regional products more than tariffs.

Poh-Yian Koh of FedEx China said AI adoption must translate technology deployment into better decisions and measurable customer value. Robin Li of Baidu warned that AI risks becoming a bubble if it does not translate into practical business value. Yang Ting of Agilent Technologies noted that AI helps life sciences customers make faster decisions and improve data quality. Fang Ling of Alstom stated that AI can improve rail reliability but requires rigorous validation in real operating environments. Winnie Ma of VF Corp said realizing AI potential requires responsible governance and a combination of technology and creativity.

China has remained the largest trading partner for ASEAN for 17 consecutive years, while ASEAN has led for China for six. In 2025, the value of bilateral trade between the two sides exceeded 1 trillion dollars, up 18 times since 2002. Business leaders recently met at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, to discuss AI productivity. Executives highlighted China's AI Plus initiative and its large manufacturing base as key opportunities for multinational companies to validate applications. They noted that China's digital infrastructure and market scale provide a strong environment for the adoption of new technologies.

The two sides will now review relevant provisions under the protocol's future work plan and hold further AI consultations. APEC economies are called upon to share practical experience and expand digital skills to make AI applications more accessible. The Ministry of Commerce will continue working with ASEAN to advance practical cooperation and implement the new trade rules. The articles do not state when the specific sub-committees will be formed or the exact date for AI consultations. It remains open how businesses will specifically measure the tangible productivity gains mentioned by the various regional business leaders.

stories.Headline: China-nexus actor uses AI agents to breach East Asian universities via zero-day flaw
stories.Summary:
A China-nexus actor used Cairn AI agents to attack universities across East Asia outside mainland China. The campaign began on September 8 and lasted for approximately 48 hours. These agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in an open source medical imaging application. The attackers moved from discovering the flaw to gaining root access in 11 minutes. Researchers at Amazon Threat Intelligence uncovered the incident and published a report on Friday.

The agents targeted a server running a medical imaging AI application and mapped its API endpoints. They found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter that was vulnerable to path traversal. This allowed the agents to arbitrarily write files and execute a Python reverse shell payload as root. The actor gave the agents a simple goal to obtain shell access to the systems. The campaign involved probing and reconnaissance aimed at taking control of various university IT systems.

CJ Moses is the chief information security officer of Amazon Web Services and wrote the report. He stated that agentic offensive operations are already happening and defenders should prepare for this speed. Moses observed that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without any human direction. He noted that the agents conducted two extensive operations that failed before they found the zero-day. These failures demonstrated the adaptability and persistence of the AI tools during the attack campaign.

Cris Thomas of Semgrep said AI agents change the economics of vulnerability discovery without skilled humans. He believes defenders must double down on security fundamentals and make them work at machine speed. Ross Filipek of Corsica Technologies suggested that organizations should continuously analyze server logs for unusual patterns. Filipek also recommended maintaining an inventory of exposed assets and restricting access to staff only. These experts believe automated detection and containment must be backed by human oversight for consequential decisions.

The agents first tried to take control of a Redis instance at one university for 16 hours. This unsuccessful effort involved 148 sequential actions and an attempted Log4Shell injection against another service. Another failed operation lasted over six hours and targeted a university GPU server using 80 usernames. The agents tested over 30,000 credential combinations against the remote login service and tried accessing a VPN. They also attempted to enter an admin dashboard, a campus portal, and a network storage device.

Other China-linked actors have used Cairn-based AI agents to breach 10 organizations to steal secrets. These actors also used the tools to automate a massive attack spree against high-profile websites. Threat actors are using Cairn and a similar tool called Artex to facilitate and automate attacks. The articles do not state if the specific medical imaging vulnerability has been patched yet. They leave open whether other universities in East Asia were successfully breached during this campaign.

stories.Headline: Congressional Research Service releases a guide organizing federal AI policy research into twelve topics for lawmakers
stories.Summary:
The Congressional Research Service released a new report on November 24, 2026, providing Congress with a comprehensive topical guide to federal artificial intelligence policy research. This new resource organizes selected work from the research agency into twelve distinct topic areas to help lawmakers navigate complex legal and policy issues. The guide includes a variety of written and audiovisual products that examine legislation, executive branch actions, and various AI-related policy challenges. These categories specifically cover critical sectors such as national security, defense, health care, infrastructure, finance, patents, and the integrity of elections.

The guide tracks several key executive actions, including an explainer on Executive Order 14409 which was published in the Federal Register on June 5. This specific order directs federal agencies to prioritize cybersecurity and create a voluntary framework for government access to certain advanced AI models. The report also details court outcomes regarding the federal government and Anthropic, noting a California district-court injunction on August 27 and a D.C. Circuit ruling on September 25. Additionally, the guide references the TAKE IT DOWN Act, known as Public Law 119-12, which became law on May 19, 2025, to prohibit the nonconsensual publication of intimate images.

The Congressional Research Service is responsible for this guide and notes that advances in machine learning, generative AI, and facial recognition offer potential benefits across many sectors. However, the agency also expressed significant concerns regarding the spread of misinformation, potential shifts in the job market, and various security risks. The report further includes information on cyber and artificial intelligence provisions found within the National Defense Authorization Act for the 2026 fiscal year. These entries aim to provide a centralized location for members of Congress to review how the government is managing the rapid evolution of AI technology.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: mEinstein outlines Human Context Contracts to define revocable human authorization for AI agents
stories.Summary:
mEinstein is outlining a framework called Human Context Contracts, which the company says is meant to address how human authorization can be represented and applied when AI agents interact with personal information and external systems, according to an article published by aithority.com on November 23, 2026. The company describes the framework as a way to translate human consent into defined, enforceable and revocable authority over autonomous actions. The article says existing consent mechanisms were largely developed for websites and digital services, while autonomous agents introduce requirements involving delegated authority, task limitations and accountability. Prithwi Thakuria, Founder and CEO of mEinstein, said a checkbox records consent but an autonomous system needs permission it can actually execute.

The framework is designed to represent distinctions between kinds of permission through structured requests that specify the purpose, required information and permitted action, and its architecture includes authorization conditions covering the requesting entity, scope, duration, value, revocation and audit records. The article gives the example of a request to find a flight, which may authorize an AI assistant to search and compare available options, while purchasing a ticket, selecting a payment method, accepting a connecting flight or disclosing travel information to external services may require separate authorization. It also says a healthcare system may be authorized to assess clinical-trial eligibility without automatically receiving permission to disclose patient information to a research sponsor, and a financial assistant may evaluate mortgage readiness without having authority to share an individual's complete financial information or submit an application. Thakuria said permission to know something is not permission to share it, and permission to share it is not permission to act on it. The framework forms part of the company's broader Human Intelligence Infrastructure concept, which addresses the relationship between enterprise AI systems and an individual's private, user-controlled information, and the company summarizes the operating principle as AI interprets, rules govern, device executes.

The article says the issue is receiving attention across the AI industry, noting that the National Institute of Standards and Technology has been examining AI-agent identity and authorization, including how agents establish authority, operate under delegated permissions and maintain evidence connecting their actions to human authorization. It also says Microsoft has outlined a Dynamic Permissions approach in which AI agents receive permissions appropriate to specific tasks rather than relying on unrestricted standing access, with permissions limited by task and duration and additional verification for actions requiring human approval. OpenAI's computer-use guidance similarly distinguishes direct user instructions from information encountered by an agent during operation and recommends confirmation before certain consequential actions, including financial transactions and the transmission of sensitive information. The article says Mastercard's Verifiable Intent initiative focuses on establishing evidence of consumer authorization when AI agents conduct purchases, and its Agent Pay Trust Framework incorporates identity, intent, controls, execution and intelligence into the management of agent-led transactions.

The article says the framework also addresses the operational limitations of repeated approval requests, because rather than requiring confirmation for every individual action, permission boundaries can define which activities an agent may perform independently and which require renewed authorization, and changes in circumstances or actions outside the approved scope may trigger additional verification. It says that as AI agents take on more responsibilities across digital services and commercial transactions, the distinction between consent, delegated authority and executable permission is becoming an important consideration for system developers and organizations. The article describes Human Context Contracts as mEinstein's approach to structuring that authorization layer, with the aim of maintaining defined human authority as autonomous systems perform increasingly complex tasks. The article does not say when the framework will be available or how it will be adopted.

Articles.Title: mEinstein Develops Human Context Contracts for AI Agent Authorization

stories.Headline: Gilbane starts building New York's 74.5 million dollar Empire AI data center at the University at Buffalo
stories.Summary:
Gilbane broke ground on the Empire AI data center on November 19, 2026. Governor Kathy Hochul announced the start of this project in New York. The facility will be located at the University at Buffalo in Amherst. This new center will focus on research and education for the state. Project stakeholders held a groundbreaking ceremony to mark the start of construction.

The project has a construction budget of 74.5 million dollars and uses five megawatts. It will house the Empire AI Gamma supercomputer at the University at Buffalo. The site connects to the university Baker Chilled Water Plant using clean hydropower. Geothermal wells and heat pumps will recover energy to warm North Campus buildings. The facility is exempt from the statewide data center moratorium ordered by Kathy Hochul.

Roger Treichler is a senior project executive at Gilbane and the construction manager. He said the facility will expand access to powerful computing resources for researchers. Treichler stated the project shows how technology construction and environmental stewardship work together. He noted the plan supports the university goal to reuse heat on campus. He said the center helps researchers tackle challenges in healthcare and climate science.

The project will serve researchers who need access to high performance computing infrastructure. The facility is part of the Empire AI consortium mentioned in the executive order. Other researchers already use two earlier systems that serve the academic community. One existing system is a 40 million dollar supercomputer located in downtown Buffalo. That second system has 11 times the AI training capacity of the first.

Governor Kathy Hochul paused certain state environmental permits for new data centers in July. This order was meant to study effects on water use and energy demand. The moratorium exempts facilities used primarily for research or education in the state. The first of the three supercomputing systems was launched in the year 2024. The new center adds to the existing capacity of the earlier state systems.

Gilbane targets substantial completion of the data center for late in the year 2027. The state expects the construction to reach full completion by early in 2028. Treichler said finishing touches will continue on the site after substantial completion occurs. Remaining work includes commissioning the facility and testing building systems before operations begin. The articles do not state when the Gamma supercomputer will be fully active.

stories.Headline: Alpha School in Palm Beach Gardens uses an AI app as primary teacher for morning lessons
stories.Summary:
The Alpha School in Palm Beach Gardens, a private school where the primary teacher is an artificial intelligence app rather than a person, was the subject of a CBS12 report broadcast on November 23, 2026, and the school is part of a network that now claims 50 campuses across the country, with two of them in Palm Beach County. For two to three hours every morning, students learn math, reading, science and other subjects from an app that senses when they have mastered a subject and then moves them on to the next one. The adults in the building are called guides, and they help students through morning frustrations with the app but usually do no actual teaching. Kirsten Berg, the Dean of Parents, who is basically like the principal, said the school has a lounge area with a lot of books, which she called one of her favorite areas because it is something you probably would not expect to see there.

The school claims it can teach kids twice as much in half the time, and Scott Dangerfield, a reading specialist who worked for years in public schools, said every student learns at their own level and pace, with one student in his class working on 8th-grade subjects while in 2nd grade. He said that in prior schools he taught to the middle, so some students were bored because the material was too easy and others were left behind because it was too difficult, and he said he now feels he is teaching what used to take a full school day in just two hours, adding that he is not teaching because the app is their teacher. Sean McKenna, the school's head guide, said the school is taking everything legacy schooling has done and essentially flipping it on its head, and instead of babysitting and busy work it is actively teaching children to learn in two hours and then helping them become better people and teaching them life skills. Annual tuition is $50,000, and Berg said one of the biggest things she has talked with parents and folks in Palm Beach County about is trying something different because the traditional education system they were coming from was not working.

With the fundamentals over before lunchtime, the school gets creative for the rest of the day with interactive workshops that could include visiting a gym, holding a puppet show or doing a nature walk, and students Lily and Laila described a workshop as an activity or experience where they learn new life skills. Lily said they learned the thriller dance with a professional dance coach, learned receiving feedback and applying it, and did a flash mob at the mall on Saturday, and the girls' mothers said that since starting at the school they have seen major changes, with one daughter who used to beg not to go to school now saying she cannot wait to go tomorrow. A New York Times expose, according to the report, uncovered that many students are not learning twice as much in half the time at Alpha Schools and that some kids struggling in public school needed all day to keep up in the app, while many students who actually attend are already high achievers when they arrive. The report said the school's software platform is being pushed out to public schools across the country according to The New York Times, and McKenna said it will change society, how we teach and raise our children to be better adults and human beings, and that it will be something that is going to change the world.

stories.Headline: AI-native biotechs advance 45% of Phase II drugs versus 29% industry-wide, Oliver Wyman finds
stories.Summary:
Drugs from AI-native biotechs, companies built around artificial intelligence platforms, advanced from Phase II trials at a rate of 45%, compared with 29% for the industry overall, according to an Oliver Wyman analysis reported on November 23, 2026. The firm said early-trial success for these developers runs more than 40% higher than the industry rate, based on limited clinical data. In Phase II, the tests of whether a drug works, 45% of the programs advanced. The analysis covers 46 Phase II programs, and roughly half of them are still running. AI-discovered molecules make up only about 1% to 2% of the clinical pipeline.

Investment in AI drug discovery and licensing deals reached $46 billion in the first half of 2026, after $43 billion in 2025 and $12 billion in 2024. Oliver Wyman says roughly 90% of drug candidates fail and development averages $2.67 billion per asset. Because more drugs are clearing early trials, someone has to pay for the larger trials that follow, and the firm says the limit on drug development shifts from science to capital. Smaller developers that cannot fund every program will need partners, which could put more late-stage drugs up for licensing. A Nature Medicine paper reports that an AI-built pill, rentosertib, helped patients with a lung disease gain lung capacity, with the trial following 71 patients for 12 weeks; patients on the highest dose gained 98.4 ml of lung capacity while placebo patients lost 20.3 ml, and side effects were similar across groups.

The authors say AI found the drug's target and designed the molecule, and they say larger, longer trials are needed. The FDA and the European Medicines Agency introduced 10 guiding principles for AI drug development, and the FDA says drugmakers and product developers can consider them but they are not rules. The first five are human-centric design, a risk-based approach, adherence to standards, a clear context of use and multidisciplinary expertise, and the last five are data governance and documentation, model design and development practices, risk-based performance assessment, life cycle management and clear, essential information. Gabriel Innes, an assistant director at the FDA's drug center, told a RAPS panel that the center has received more than 1,500 AI-related submissions, which have grown exponentially since 2016, mostly applications to begin human trials followed by new drug applications and biologics license applications. Innes said AI is becoming quite routine and called the principles a starting point for future standards.

Articles.Title: AI Drug Developers Post Higher Trial Success as Deals Hit $46 Billion

stories.headline_source: AI Drug Developers Post Higher Trial Success as Deals Hit $46 Billion

stories.Headline: NTT uses AI to find software vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them
stories.Summary:
NTT Group detected and blocked seven times as many cyberattacks in October as in the same month a year earlier, according to President and CEO Akira Shimada, who spoke at the NTT R&D Forum 2026 in Tokyo. The Japanese telecommunications group is now using artificial intelligence to find vulnerabilities in software before attackers do. Shimada said there had been 20 confirmed or potential customer data leak incidents since September involving NTT Group and its vendors. He said attacks are increasingly targeting consumer websites, online stores and official apps on a large scale, and that leaks through vendors and supply chains are becoming more visible. The effort requires NTT to examine source code and internal design with multiple frontier AI models for white-box testing, and the group supports customer vulnerability assessments from identification to prioritisation and fixing.

To protect sensitive data such as source code, NTT is developing AI-based methods that run in on-premises IT environments, using open-weight models whose trained parameters are public so organisations can run them on their own systems. NTT says its current AI approach achieves 70 to 80 per cent of frontier AI performance in vulnerability discovery. For older systems, industrial equipment and internet of things devices that cannot run endpoint detection and response software, NTT uses the network as a sensor to identify and block threats from network traffic. Shimada said attacks are becoming faster, with exploitation attempts sometimes detected before a vulnerability is publicly disclosed, citing a PHP vulnerability where attempts were detected days before its October disclosure and spread globally within 24 hours. He said AI makes it easier to find and analyse vulnerabilities, potentially leading to more such attacks, and that attacks are also more complex, with multiple minor weaknesses combining to create system access.

He said targets are widening to include industrial equipment and operational technology, such as an October attack on supermarket refrigeration equipment in Europe. NTT has shifted its defence from perimeter security to zero trust and now incorporates AI-powered defence for proactive vulnerability discovery. The articles say reported data exposure at Japanese companies reached 376.21 million records by October 2026, compared with 49.53 million for all of 2025, citing MM Research Institute. NTT says basic security practices such as applying updates and removing unused accounts remain essential.

Articles.Title: NTT uses AI to find software flaws before cyberattacks

stories.headline_source: NTT uses AI to find software flaws before cyberattacks

stories.Headline: Ashish Mishra urges governance for AI agents that act without human oversight
stories.Summary:
Ashish Mishra, Lead Solutions Architect for Agentic AI Services at NTT DATA, published an article on 16 November 2026 about governing AI that acts rather than only answers. He described a voice bot his colleague had asked to suggest an itinerary for a trip to France, which instead supplied one for India. Mishra called it an obvious hallucination that could be verified easily. He wrote that the consequences can be far more serious when an autonomous AI agent makes the wrong decision and runs with it. He said organizations are moving away from “vanilla” AI, which simply answers questions, toward AI that can make decisions, act and carry out entire business processes.

Mishra wrote that existing governance will remain relevant, covering the quality and accuracy of AI, data protection, privacy, security and bias. He said agentic AI does not change any of that and simply gives organizations more to govern. Traditional AI produces an output and a person decides what to do with it, while agentic AI can use other tools and systems, communicate with people or initiate the next step in a process without any human intervention. He said this means questioning the output as well as the activity throughout the workflow. He wrote that every agent should have a clear business purpose and a named owner, its own identity and access only to the information and tools required for its job.

Mishra said the excitement around new technology is understandable but that letting it get ahead of the controls is a mistake he sees far too often. He wrote that by the time you discover a problem, the agent may already have acted on it. He said organizations without effective AI governance can face compliance failures and operational problems, and that when AI acts without guardrails those consequences are amplified. He said an action that is difficult or impossible to reverse needs a different level of control than a simple day-to-day task. He wrote that if something goes wrong, you should be able to see what information the agent was working with, which tools it used and what approvals it received.

Mishra wrote that AI risk is no longer confined to the information an agent produces and now extends to the running of the business. He said AI agents can take information from emails, documents and websites and interact with different tools, systems and even other agents. He said testing an agent before it starts working is essential but you cannot stop there, because the information it receives and the environment it operates in will continue to change. He said you need to know what an agent can retain, how long it keeps that information and whether anything sensitive could be exposed. He compared an agent carrying out one small, contained task to hiring a freelancer for a specific piece of work.

Mishra cited NTT DATA’s 2026 Global AI Report: A Playbook for AI Leaders, which found that 55.9% of AI leaders use a centralized governance model, compared with 37.6% of other organizations and 33.3% of AI laggards. He wrote that NTT DATA has learned many of these lessons by being its own client zero, experimenting with AI internally and encountering security and compliance issues before taking that experience to clients. He said one of the most important lessons is to start with the end in mind, being clear about what an agent should achieve, how its value will be measured and what it is prepared to let the agent do. He wrote that trying to add the right controls once an agent is already operating across your business is far more difficult. He said applying governance to AI agents does not limit their freedom but puts the right rules in place for them to operate as intended.

Mishra wrote that before you build, you should be clear on the agent’s purpose, who owns it, the data it will use and how much freedom it should have. He said that before an agent goes live you should check its permissions, testing and approvals and make sure you can reverse or stop an action if something goes wrong. He said that once it is working you should monitor how well it performs, the decisions and actions it takes, how much it costs to run and whether it delivers the results you expect. He wrote that if you cannot see every agent operating in your business, trace what happened or step in quickly, you should start with visibility. He directed readers to learn more about NTT DATA’s Agentic AI Studio and how it can help build, govern and manage AI agents across their lifecycle.

Articles.Title: When AI moves from answering to acting: Getting governance right - NTT Data

stories.Headline: Bly Road residents sue Independence and developers to halt AI data center construction
stories.Summary:
Residents along Bly Road in the Little Blue Valley area of Independence, Missouri, filed a 16-count, 52-page lawsuit on Wednesday in Jackson County Circuit Court in an effort to stop a hyperscale AI data factory that is under construction near their homes, according to the Independence GUARD (Guardians United Against Reckless Development) Alliance, which announced the filing on Thursday. The suit names the city of Independence, Missouri ADC Holdings LLC, which is described as the data center developer, and Independence Power Partners LP, a Delaware-based third party building a new natural gas plant to power the data center. The lawsuit alleges that the city violated zoning and sunshine laws as well as the city charter, and that it has failed to enforce city laws, and the residents are asking a judge to pause the project. The city council approved billions of dollars in incentives in March for Nebius, a Dutch tech company, to build and operate a 2.1-million-square-foot hyperscale AI data factory on 400 acres at the south end of Bly Road, and Nebius broke ground on the first phase in April.

The lawsuit seeks a temporary restraining order to stop work at the site while the case proceeds, according to Steve Jeffery of the Chesterfield, Missouri, firm Jeffery Law Group, one of the attorneys representing the residents. Jeffery said there is no check on what the developer is doing regarding noise limits, hours of operation, hours of construction, heavy truck traffic and construction traffic, and that the city appears to turn a blind eye to it, which he called the primary basis for the restraining order request. The defendants have 30 days to file their response, as is typical in civil cases in Missouri.

The city of Independence acknowledged the lawsuit in a statement to KSHB 41 News on Thursday but denied any wrongdoing, saying the filing contains the plaintiffs' allegations, which the city will address through the appropriate judicial process, and that it disagrees with the characterization of its actions and believes the approvals and processes related to the project were handled in accordance with applicable law. The city also said it will not comment further on the specific claims at this time because of the pending litigation. Nebius Vice President of Public Affairs John Sutter said the company is reviewing the claims and cannot comment on the case specifics, and that Nebius remains committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations and being a responsible partner for the community as its investment in Independence takes shape.

Jeffery said the case is not about the broader AI discussion taking place across the country, saying his clients are not against AI, technology or data centers, but that there is a right time, place, process and procedure for such things and that the local governments did not follow the process. Bly Road resident Kelly Garrett said the community feels let down by the city and is upset, angry, disappointed and frustrated, and said the community was betrayed quietly and repeatedly long before residents had the chance to say a word. Daniel Moorehead, coalition leader of the Independence GUARD Alliance, said residents have endured months of disruption since construction began, including work that starts well ahead of daylight and ends well after it, and trucks that have gotten stuck and torn up the road in multiple places. Dawn Hahnfeld, a Bly Road resident who lives near the site, described constant noise, dust and banging in the middle of the night and late at night, and said the ultimate goal is to make the construction go away. Moorehead said the coalition intends to keep pushing, describing the residents as a handful of homeowners standing against some of the most powerful institutional and financial interests in the state, and said they have been treated as an afterthought at best and an obstacle to be managed at worst.

Articles.Title: Bly Road residents file 52-page lawsuit to stop Independence AI data center project - KSHB 41 Kansas City

stories.headline_source: Bly Road residents file 52-page lawsuit to stop Independence AI data center project

stories.Headline: Taiwan passes bill to give every citizen a cash AI bonus
stories.Summary:
The Legislative Yuan of Taiwan passed a bill on November 20 to provide an artificial intelligence bonus to the public. This legislation was pushed through by opposition parties shortly before local elections scheduled for November 28. The measure aims to return tax revenue that has increased because of the boom in artificial intelligence. It was passed with a vote of 50 to 46 in the chamber. Thirteen lawmakers from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party abstained from the final vote.

The special act on sharing economic gains with all citizens and stabilizing livelihoods requires a cash payment of 20,000 Taiwan dollars to every citizen. This payout is intended for all residents regardless of their income levels. However, the articles note that further procedures must be completed before the money is actually disbursed to the people. Chuang Rui-hsiung of the Democratic Progressive Party mentioned that the government already budgeted 10,000 Taiwan dollars for each citizen. He stated this lower amount was chosen to keep spending and revenue balanced without additional borrowing.

The main opposition Kuomintang led the effort to pass the bill and increase the payout amount. Hsu Yu-chen, the secretary-general of the Kuomintang caucus, demanded that Premier Cho Jung-tai explain if he intends to countersign the legislation. Lawmaker Lo Chih-chiang stated that the actual payment of the bonus will depend on the outcome of the local elections. He argued that the ruling party fears the will of the voters during this period. Chuang Rui-hsiung criticized the opposition for seeking to double the payout without considering the fiscal conditions of the state.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Taiwan Passes Bill to Give Every Citizen 'AI Bonus' Cash Payout - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.headline_source: Taiwan Passes Bill to Give Every Citizen 'AI Bonus' Cash Payout

stories.Headline: Hong Kong Monetary Authority promotes agentic AI to manage on-chain financial crime risks
stories.Summary:
Banking supervisors in Hong Kong recently highlighted the role of agentic AI for combating financial crime on-chain. Raymond Chan delivered a speech on this topic on November 17. He is the Executive Director for Enforcement and AML at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. The speech focused on using technology to manage digital asset risks. This occurred as banks increase their role in tokenization and stablecoins.

The HKMA published a discussion paper on agentic AI governance on November 2. This report describes opportunities to enhance risk management, anti-fraud capabilities, operational efficiency, and customer experience. It calls for banks to establish proportionate and risk-based governance arrangements across the AI lifecycle. These arrangements must ensure alignment between agent actions and intended firm outcomes. Banks should ensure human oversight, intervention, validation, testing, and mitigating controls.

Raymond Chan stated that digital assets present unique risks through speed, global reach, pseudonymity, and limited reversibility. He argued that agentic AI can enhance the detection of proliferating crimes like fraud. Chan suggested integrating blockchain analytics, customer due diligence, scam intelligence, and wallet monitoring into an AI agent. He noted that a permanent public trail on the blockchain provides valuable evidence. He said agentic AI could flag anomalies like rapid fund layering between cryptos and fiat.

The HKMA report warns that AI adoption can pose new or heightened risks. These risks include unintended actions, ambiguous accountability, data compromise, and operational disruption. The banking sector is affected because it is where illicit on-chain and off-chain flows converge. Other jurisdictions like the US, UK, and Singapore have issued AI governance guidelines. International bodies including the G20 and Financial Services Board have also issued recommendations.

The HKMA has licensed HSBC and Standard Chartered to issue stablecoins under its supervisory framework. It has also undertaken work to enable banking innovation through tokenization sandbox arrangements. These efforts support a strategy to be a world leader in digital asset innovation. The HKMA also uses its Accountability, Resilience, and Trust Framework to assess AI in financial services. This framework aims to improve service delivery and financial crime risk mitigation.

The HKMA continues to explore the development of agentic AI for more powerful monitoring capabilities. The supervisor remains focused on ensuring accountability over these agentic systems. The articles do not state when the agentic AI tools will be fully deployed. They do not specify which banks will first adopt these specific AI agents. The text leaves open how the proposed governance arrangements will be enforced.

Articles.Title: Crypto regulatory affairs: Hong Kong supervisor highlights agentic AI for on-chain risk management - Elliptic
