stories.Headline: University of Cambridge launches EDITH trial testing AI-assisted mammograms with nearly 700,000 women across the UK
stories.Summary:
Women are being invited to take part in a national trial using artificial intelligence to help detect breast cancers earlier, the University of Cambridge said on 23 November 2026. Nearly 700,000 women will take part in the trial, which is known as EDITH. Cambridgeshire is the first location to launch the trial. The trial will soon be running at 30 breast screening sites across the UK. The Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, Yvette Cooper MP, visited the Breast Unit at Addenbrooke’s Hospital to mark the opening.

The £10 million NIHR-funded trial will test whether an AI-assisted mammogram-reading tool can help experts review images more efficiently. Every mammogram will still be reviewed by at least one human radiologist. The trial will not change what happens during a woman’s breast screening appointment, and it only affects how the collected images may be reviewed. Details of the trial will be included in the letter sent to eligible women when they are invited for screening, along with details of how to opt out. All women aged 50-71 are invited for screening every three years.

Professor Fiona Gilbert, of the Department of Radiology at the University of Cambridge and an Honorary Consultant at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, said millions of women have a mammogram each year and fewer than one in 100 will be diagnosed with cancer. Gilbert said EDITH will test whether an AI-assisted mammogram-reading tool can help experts review images more efficiently while maintaining professional oversight and the standards women expect from NHS breast screening. Professor Sian Taylor-Phillips of the University of Warwick said EDITH will test whether AI can assist NHS staff improve the service for women attending the NHS Breast Screening Programme. Taylor-Phillips said AI-assisted technology could support staff by flagging areas of a mammogram where cancer might be missed to improve early cancer detection. The trial is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research, working closely with NHS England and the UK National Screening Committee, who helped shape the study design.

Yvette Cooper said the trial is the biggest AI breast cancer trial in the world, backed by £10 million of government investment to speed up diagnosis and potentially deliver life-saving improvements. Cooper said that if successful, the technology could help women get a breast cancer diagnosis and start treatment much more quickly. Cooper said AI has huge potential, but proper safeguards also need to be in place to make sure it is used safely and effectively. Professor Lucy Chappell, CEO of the NIHR and Chief Scientific Adviser to the Department of Health and Social Care, said the NIHR is proud to be funding one of the world’s largest studies of AI-assisted breast screening. Kanishka Narayan, UK Minister for Artificial Intelligence, said finding cancer earlier can make all the difference to patients and their families, including saving lives.

Currently around 2.1 million women in the UK have breast screening each year, which helps prevent around 1,300 deaths. Reviewing breast screening x-rays is time intensive, and currently each mammogram is reviewed by two specialist radiologists. Fewer than 1% of mammograms show signs of cancer, so significant time is spent reviewing negative screening images. In the trial, the AI-assisted tool will be used alongside specialists checking the images to look for cancers that are too small to see or feel. This could mean many mammograms would only need to be reviewed by one radiologist and would free up radiologists to spend more time on diagnosis and caring for women with cancer.

The NHS offers mammograms at local breast screening clinics in GP practices or hospitals, or women can attend one of their local mobile screening vans, conveniently located in supermarket or community car parks. The AI-assisted tool is being tested alongside the usual process rather than replacing it. The NHS will only change how screening works if the evidence shows it is as safe and effective as the care women receive now. As the trial progresses, it will be supported by an AI research screening platform, AIR-SP, built by NHS England with nearly £6 million of government funding. The platform is designed to make it easier for NHS Trusts to join AI screening trials.

stories.Headline: Nvidia shares fall 14 percent as investors sell AI stocks and move to cash
stories.Summary:
Investors reduced their allocations to AI stocks and rotated into other sectors during the final weeks of November in the year 2026. This rotation became a wholesale move to cash last week, which dragged down the broader market and several non-stock asset classes. The US stock market suffered its worst week in years as investors worried about valuations, interest rates, and sustainable AI spending. On Friday, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled 5.3 percent while the S&P 500 Index fell 3.7 percent in a major sell-off. Nvidia shares experienced their worst single-day fall in about 22 months, dropping more than 14 percent during regular trading on Friday.

The S&P 500 fell 12 percent from its October record high, although the index subsequently staged a partial recovery after the recent crash. Meta, Amazon, Alphabet, and Microsoft were projected to invest more than 1 trillion dollars in 2026 for chips, data centers, and cloud computing. The Vera Rubin platform generated 20 billion dollars in its first quarter, which was nearly double the 11 billion from Blackwell. Nvidia supply commitments surged to 390 billion dollars in fiscal 2027 third quarter, up from 119 billion just two quarters earlier. The cloud industry backlog climbed to 2.5 trillion dollars from 2 trillion dollars in just three months, according to company financial data.

Jurrien Timmer, the Fidelity director of global macro, said the dash for cash spares no one as the Fed drains market liquidity. He believes the market may have overshot to the downside last week, just as it often overshoots to the upside during volatility. Zach Turner, manager of the Fidelity Capital Appreciation Fund, remains highly optimistic about the long-term promise of AI for productivity and growth. Turner questioned if AI companies are generating enough revenue growth to justify the scale of capital spending that is currently underway. Beth Kindig of the IO Fund argued that investors may be mistaking a temporary pause for a fundamental slowdown in AI demand.

Investors are concerned that leading AI platforms may face greater competition from emerging, lower-cost models, which could reduce their overall pricing power. Many investors shifted from AI-related stocks, many of which peaked in price in June, into other sectors over the summer months. The sell-off affected owners of gold and Bitcoin, as investors moved those assets into cash and US Treasurys for more safety. Collette Kress, the Nvidia CFO and interim CEO, stated that the cloud backlog underscores a significant multi-year opportunity for their partners. SK Hynix also affected the ecosystem by commenting that they are effectively sold out of their products through the year 2029.

The US stock market rally had been showing signs of shifting beneath the surface since early June of the year 2026. Major advances in agentic AI emerged in late 2025, leading several large tech companies to significantly increase their investment in AI infrastructure. This investment wave drove an earnings boom across the S&P 500, extending into construction, energy, utilities, and various industrial sectors. Tech firms tapped into cash flow and began issuing corporate bonds at elevated levels over the last year to fund expansion. The market experienced volatility following April 2025 tariff announcements, which proved short-lived as the relevant government policy continued to evolve.

Timmer believes the next few weeks are more likely to be up than down following the recent volatility in the stock market. Slower growth in AI spending could reduce the need for further rate hikes, which might help support stocks and cyclical sectors. Defensive sectors like healthcare, consumer staples, and financial services companies could ultimately benefit from the decline in top technology company spending. The articles leave open whether AI adoption will occur quickly enough to generate revenue that justifies the massive scale of spending. It remains uncertain how much the earnings growth rate will decelerate from its peak as AI companies potentially rein in spending.

stories.Headline: Lenskart pilots Drysh AI eye-testing and expands smart glasses to 500 stores
stories.Summary:
Eyewear retailer Lenskart is piloting an AI-assisted eye-testing model called Drysh in select store locations. The company also expanded the availability of its AI-enabled smart glasses to 500 stores. These developments were discussed during the company's Q2 FY27 post-earnings conference call. The Drysh model allows a single optometrist to potentially handle 20 times more eye tests. Lenskart has expanded its remote optometry network to 934 stores, up from 303 stores one year ago.

The smart glasses, named B, can capture audio, images, and video for the user. These glasses include an LED indicator to alert bystanders when the user is recording. Co-founder and CEO Peyush Bansal said the company cannot solve the vision-care gap by hiring more optometrists. He stated that the company needs to provide tools so optometrists can perform more tests. Bansal claimed that AI is not a separate project but is how they run the business.

He noted that Lenskart is uniquely positioned to distribute smart eyewear at scale. The company competes against Meta in the AI-enabled eyewear market. Meta has faced privacy and surveillance concerns in the past regarding its own smart glasses. About 90 percent of Lenskart smart glass buyers purchase them with prescription lenses and tests. These customers are affected by the company's focus on hardware-software iteration and post-order optical service.

Lenskart aims to sell 100 million pairs of glasses annually, requiring roughly 80 million eye tests. The company first announced its AI glasses in Q2 FY26 following a soft launch earlier this year. Lenskart builds its own operating system for terminals, eye-test machines, and factory software. The company also uses software for inventory replenishment and store-site selection.

Lenskart is rolling out software and firmware updates for its smart glasses roughly every two weeks. New features include nutrition tracking, daily reminders, and integrations for health and calendars. The company is also developing an improved charging case and optimizing battery algorithms. The articles do not state when the Drysh pilot will end or expand.

stories.Headline: Draganfly and DOD Solution sign memorandum to integrate AURA AI autonomy into Draganfly drones
stories.Summary:
Draganfly Inc. and DOD Solution jointly announced on November 23, 2026, the signing of a memorandum of understanding to advance integration of DOD Solution's autonomy technology into selected Draganfly unmanned systems. The announcement was made in Kyiv, Ukraine, according to a GlobeNewswire release dated November 23, 2026. Draganfly is a Canadian-headquartered developer of advanced drone solutions, unmanned systems and software. DOD Solution is an Estonian-Ukrainian developer of onboard autonomy technology. The two companies said the collaboration is designed to combine DOD Solution's autonomy expertise and insights from Ukraine with Draganfly's Canadian engineering and systems-integration capabilities.

The collaboration will explore how lessons from Ukraine can inform autonomy integration and testing against Canadian and allied requirements. DOD Solution's AURA AI platform pairs the AURA SBC onboard computer with AURA OS software, designed to support autonomous functions when GPS or communications are degraded or unavailable. AURA AI brings target detection, recognition, tracking and terminal guidance directly onboard, allowing drones to operate when GPS is unavailable, jamming is active and communications are limited. Draganfly has more than 27 years of experience in unmanned systems. Draganfly's stock is listed on NASDAQ under DPRO, on the CSE under DPRO and on the FSE under 3U8.

Cameron Chell, Chief Executive Officer of Draganfly, said Canada has an opportunity to apply lessons from Ukraine to the way unmanned systems are developed, tested and supported. Chell said working with DOD Solution is intended to connect their onboard autonomy technology and operational understanding with Draganfly's engineering capabilities in Canada. He said the focus is on evaluating how autonomy can help systems perform in demanding conditions. He said the aim is building the expertise to integrate and support those capabilities for customers. Roman Hapachylo, Chief Executive Officer of DOD Solution, said working with Draganfly creates an opportunity to connect their autonomy technology and experience in Ukraine with Canadian engineering and integration expertise.

Hapachylo said DOD Solution wants this level of autonomy to become a core capability of next-generation unmanned systems, and called the partnership another step in that direction. For Canada, the potential benefit includes deeper technical expertise in autonomy integration, testing and ongoing support, alongside opportunities to strengthen Canadian unmanned systems capabilities. For DOD Solution, the collaboration offers a potential pathway to integrate its technology across additional platforms and explore Canadian and allied customer requirements with Draganfly. The initiative is consistent with the broader Canada-Ukraine objective of combining Ukrainian innovation with Canadian industrial and technological strengths through research, testing, technology collaboration and licensing. Lessons emerging from Ukraine highlight the importance of testing unmanned systems under realistic operating conditions, adapting as countermeasures evolve and incorporating user feedback into continued development.

DOD Solution works with unmanned platform manufacturers to integrate AI-powered autonomy across a wide range of defence applications. Its flagship product, the AURA AI platform, combines proprietary software and the AURA SBC onboard computer to enable autonomous navigation, perception, target recognition, tracking and terminal guidance in GPS-denied, contested and communication-constrained environments. Draganfly develops and delivers technologies spanning aerial platforms, autonomy, sensing, payload integration and mission-specific solutions for defence, public safety and commercial applications. Draganfly combines engineering, manufacturing, software and systems-integration capabilities to support customers operating in complex and mission-critical environments. Draganfly says it is driven by a mission to provide innovative, reliable solutions that save time, money and lives.

Draganfly's forward-looking statements address the collaboration contemplated by the memorandum of understanding with DOD Solution and the integration of DOD Solution's autonomy technology, including the AURA AI platform, into selected Draganfly unmanned systems. They also address the anticipated capabilities and performance of such technology, including in environments where GPS or communications are degraded or unavailable. The statements cover the testing and evaluation of autonomy capabilities against Canadian and allied requirements and the expected benefits of the collaboration. Draganfly lists risks including the possibility that the memorandum of understanding may not result in definitive agreements on acceptable terms, on a timely basis or at all. Other listed risks include that the contemplated collaboration and integration activities may not proceed, may not be technically feasible or may not achieve their anticipated performance or benefits.

stories.Headline: Pat Gelsinger says AI needs a 10,000-fold gain in computing efficiency
stories.Summary:
Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger said artificial intelligence needs a 10,000-fold increase in computing efficiency, not routine generational upgrades, at the COSM Technology Summit in Scottsdale, Arizona. He spoke in a fireside chat titled "Reality Check: Beyond Chips" alongside technology theorist George Gilder and Heritage Foundation director Bret Swanson. The Wccftech report of the summit was published on November 21, 2026, and the TechGig report followed on November 24, 2026. Gelsinger rejected the idea that chip scaling has reached a physical limit, despite industry skepticism. He also posted on X, asking whether Moore's Law is dead and saying it is time to wake it up.

Gelsinger said reviving Moore's Law depends on fundamental breakthroughs across five core engineering fronts, which he named as light, power, cooling, composition and packaging. He said turning one gigawatt of electrical power into ten gigawatts worth of AI token output requires far more than traditional transistor shrinks. He cited U.S. energy capacity growth in the low single digits over the past decade, which he said creates severe bottlenecks for hyperscale data centers. He said new gas turbines face an eight-year supply backlog and nuclear power projects take a decade to construct. He cited NVIDIA's Kyber racks with Blackwell NVL72 architecture, which push power requirements to 600kW, a figure he said is enough to supply electricity to 500 homes.

Gelsinger is responsible for the argument, made as former Intel CEO and now as a general partner at venture firm Playground Global since March 2025. He said incremental chip improvements cannot satisfy AI and compute demands, and that severe power infrastructure limits are becoming a major bottleneck for innovation. He said, "We need breakthroughs across light, power, cooling, composition and packaging." He said that after 40+ years in semiconductors he believes our greatest innovations are still ahead. He has backed startups targeting these hardware bottlenecks, including U.S. government-supported lithography venture xLight and nuclear capacity firm Alva Energy.

A Harvard study revealed that U.S. data centers consume as much electricity as the country of Chile, despite not having access to all the key metrics, according to the Wccftech report. Major AI foundation models are now shipping roughly every four weeks, the report said. Gelsinger's roadmap points toward optical interconnects and silicon photonics to move data with light rather than copper. xLight aims to push past ASML's 13.5nm extreme ultraviolet wavelength barrier, the report said. Those affected include hyperscale data centers, which face hurdles from sluggish grid growth, and the hardware and energy startups Gelsinger backs.

Gelsinger's remarks come as U.S. energy capacity has grown only in the low single digits over the past decade, creating severe bottlenecks for hyperscale data centers. Long equipment wait times contribute to the issue, with new gas turbines facing an eight-year supply backlog and nuclear projects taking a decade to construct. On a previous occasion discussing AI hardware, Gelsinger said he strongly believes HBM has a myriad of flaws, calling it a "hideous memory," but said the technology is the best the industry has right now. He proposed Z2RAM, which can potentially offer better density, performance and power draw. The articles give no further background on the summit beyond the panel and the venue.

The articles do not say what specific breakthroughs Gelsinger expects next or when any of them might arrive. They do not say whether xLight or Alva Energy has set targets or timelines for their technologies. They do not give Gelsinger's response to industry watchers who argue traditional Moore's Law scaling is over, beyond his stated view that semiconductor engineering is entering a new era of multi-disciplinary innovation. They do not say what Playground Global's investments in the two startups amount to. They leave open how the 10,000-fold efficiency gain would be measured or achieved.

stories.Headline: Yann LeCun accuses Dario Amodei of trying to restrict access to advanced AI models
stories.Summary:
Turing Award winner Yann LeCun criticised Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei regarding open-weight AI models on November 24, 2026. LeCun used a post on X to publicly question the approach to AI governance used by the chief executive. This exchange reopened an industry debate about whether advanced AI should be openly shared or tightly controlled. LeCun accused Amodei of wanting to restrict access to advanced AI to a small group of organisations. He also claimed a similar desire for control led to Amodei leaving OpenAI in 2020.

Open-weight models allow users to run systems on personal computers or in-house servers without needing cloud subscriptions. These systems have publicly available trained parameters, which allows for local execution and adaptation for specific tasks. Closed models are offered through a company API, where the provider controls access, features, and all barred uses. Kimi K-3 is cited as an example of a model that can be executed locally as open-weight. This approach gives users greater control over their data compared to the dependency created by closed systems.

Dario Amodei testified before the US Congress that widely releasing open-weight models could be risky for the public. He stated that developers lose oversight of how a model is used once it is downloaded and run locally. Yann LeCun argued that limiting AI development goes against the historical progress of technology and a medieval mindset. LeCun claimed that Amodei seeks to keep advanced AI within a limited group of people and organisations. Amodei has not yet responded to the remarks made by LeCun regarding his governance approach and history.

Critics express concerns that open-weight models could be misused to facilitate cyberattacks or spread misinformation without proper safeguards. These users are affected because closed systems simplify the enforcement of safety policies by the provider of the AI. The debate affects developers who must choose between the control of open weights and the simplicity of hosted APIs. Some critics on Hacker News argue that certain available weights are not truly open in an open source sense. The 9to6ai write-up agreed that the Open Source Initiative definition would side with these specific critics of Mistral.

Open-weight models are different from open source AI, which requires exposing the training data and the code used for building. Truly open source systems must allow users to use, study, modify, and share the technology without any field-of-use carve-outs. Most frontier models today do not clear this bar because they do not provide the necessary training data or code. The label open weight is looser and only means the lab publishes the trained parameters for the user to download. Licenses for these weights can be standard texts like MIT or custom terms written by the AI lab.

The industry continues to debate the gap between what a lab calls open and what a lawyer calls open. Future developments remain open regarding whether more flagship models will release weights or remain as hosted API services only. It is not confirmed if Alibaba will release open weights for its newer flagship model known as Qwen4-Max. The articles leave open whether Amodei will respond to the claims about his 2020 departure from the company OpenAI. Legal teams must still determine if specific product features count as services under various modified AI license agreements.

stories.Headline: Leicester Medical School hosts a symposium on how AI should shape healthcare education
stories.Summary:
The Medical School at the University of Leicester will host a special symposium on 9 December. This event focuses on how artificial intelligence should be used to shape the future of healthcare education. The symposium will take place at the George Davies Centre on Lancaster Road from 9am until 3pm. It is free to attend for those who register through the official website. Presentation abstracts are accepted until 11.59pm on 27 November.

The event requires attendees to visit the website for more information and registration. It will feature keynote presentations, workshops, themed oral research panels, and poster presentations. Three awards will celebrate collaborative projects and outstanding research presentations. Professor Shafi Ahmed will explore AI opportunities and challenges in surgery and hospital care. Professor Yin Ying will discuss AI in rehabilitation education and innovative teaching approaches.

Terese Bird, Professor Shameq Sayeed, and Dr Morteza Rezaei-Zadeh are the conveners from Leicester Medical School. Bird said the third such symposia aims to foster dialogue between research and practice. She stated the event encourages collaboration among students, academic staff, clinicians, researchers, and industry partners. Bird noted the space allows people to share evidence and question assumptions. She said it prepares healthcare professionals for an increasingly AI-enabled world.

The event is for healthcare educators, academic staff, and medical, nursing, and allied health students. It also targets clinicians, clinical educators, researchers, educational technology developers, and AI specialists. Keynote speakers aim to consider how AI can enhance clinical learning and support human reasoning. They will examine how AI transforms assessment and contributes to safer and more equitable education. The sessions will consider implications for healthcare professionals, clinical teams, and the wider system.

AI is creating new possibilities for teaching, learning, assessment, and clinical training in healthcare. However, its integration raises questions about clinical judgement, educational quality, and patient safety. There are also concerns regarding fairness, accountability, and professional identity within the field. The symposium seeks to address these issues through interdisciplinary discussion and knowledge transfer. It focuses on emerging developments in AI-enabled healthcare education and innovative research.

The symposium will bring together various experts to share learning and foster future collaboration. Participants will explore how AI can strengthen clinical competencies and prepare professionals for evolving needs. The articles leave open the specific outcomes of the discussions and the award winners. They do not state which practical approaches will be developed during the event. The final results of the interdisciplinary discussions remain to be seen after 9 December.

stories.Headline: Delhi High Court justice Arora urges law firms to keep hiring and training fresh graduates despite AI cost pressures
stories.Summary:
Delhi High Court Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora urged law firms not to stop recruiting fresh law graduates to save costs amid growing use of artificial intelligence, warning the legal profession cannot afford to stop training its next generation of lawyers. She spoke at the first meeting of the Indian Commercial Litigators' Forum, hosted by JSA Advocates and Solicitors in New Delhi on November 20. Justice Arora said she had heard that some law firms in India had stopped hiring A0 associates. She asked who would train young lawyers for three years if firms only took on people after they had gained experience. Concerns are growing over the potential impact of AI on employment opportunities for young lawyers.

Justice Arora said firms saving costs should not cut down on the future, because if they do not take in A0 associates today they will not have themselves tomorrow. JSA Managing Partner Amar Gupta said firms were conscious of the need to retain training opportunities for fresh graduates even as the firm integrates AI into its operations. Gupta said the firm had in mind to reserve some kind of work entirely without any AI aid or assistance. He said that first-level training would continue for new associates who come into the firm, and that the roadmap was quite clear in their minds. Gupta said the firm had onboarded AI models and was doing it deliberately, with some method and planning.

Justice Robin Knowles of the High Court of England and Wales moderated the session virtually from London. He emphasised the value of bringing insights from both the judiciary and legal practitioners to the upcoming seventh full meeting of the Standing International Forum of Commercial Courts. Delhi High Court Justice Prathiba M Singh shared global figures from a recent WIPO IP Judges Forum survey in Geneva covering 146 courts and tribunals. The survey stated that 35% of courts worldwide already have AI policies in place, and 19 courts reported that 30% of their drafting involves AI. An on-the-spot poll revealed that 52% of judges want to use AI for drafting.

Delhi High Court Justice Anish Dayal, who is leading the Indian judiciary's input on SIFOCC's AI workstream ahead of the seventh meeting in Zambia, pointed to the Supreme Court of India's draft AI regulations alongside existing guidance from the High Courts of Kerala and Gujarat. Justice Dayal highlighted the need to guard against hallucinations and confidentiality breaches, while identifying where human decision-making remains irreplaceable. He also advocated for peer-to-peer judicial training and standardised operating procedures. Justice Prateek Jalan welcomed CLF India and encouraged the forum to eventually expand its membership to include individual and small-firm practitioners who form a vital part of the Indian bar. The session was moderated virtually from London by Justice Knowles.

Jason Margolis wrote in the Boston Globe that he landed a couple of newsroom internships when he was a young man starting his career. He wrote that he was beyond clueless, perhaps needy, and certainly not all that useful, but a few older reporters took him under their wings and showed him how things get done. Twenty-five years later, he found himself running a newsroom internship program, which took up a lot of his time with little immediate payoff. He wrote that some interns were pretty advanced but most needed lots of hand holding, and in nearly all cases it would have been a better short-term use of his time to just do the assigned projects himself. He asked an intern to locate successful international models where the adoption of solar panels was sped up, and after a lot of check-ins, a week or so later, got a mix of interesting and unnecessary information.

Francine Berman at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, a data scientist who focuses on the societal impacts of information technology, got Margolis's wheels spinning about AI's impacts on entry-level jobs. Berman told him that if AI is overused, "you're sort of cutting out the entry-level jobs and diminishing students' capacity to develop their own skills and education." She said that is where people learn how to be professionals and develop judgment. Researchers at Stanford University have already found a 19 percent reduction in hiring among 22- to 25-year-olds in "AI-exposed occupations," which includes workers in software, customer service, sales, and marketing, among other fields. Meanwhile, experienced workers in those fields are doing just fine.

Berman focused the conversation on the medical profession, where young doctors spend years as interns and residents perfecting their craft. A doctor-in-training learns first by observing experienced physicians and then, and only many years later, taking the lead and eventually training the next crop. Berman argues that this model could be applied to many professions, and asked who is going to replace seasoned professionals when they retire. Margolis wrote that young law associates spend notoriously long hours poring over legal documents for senior lawyers, and that law firms using an AI bot to do that instead is already happening. He wrote that nobody knows where this AI road will take us, but the rules are being written in real-time.

stories.Headline: AI-Proven Riemann Hypothesis Breakthrough Recognized by Two Top Mathematics Communities | Elon Musk Hails It as "Mind-Blowing"
stories.Summary:
On November 20, Anthropic researcher and mathematician Levent Alpöge published a four-page document on his personal website, saying that working with the company's chatbot Claude he had discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. On November 21 local time in the United States, the mathematics communities Lean and Mathlib released a joint statement saying they had full confidence in the proof. The statement confirmed that the code proof is exactly the Riemann Hypothesis studied in the mathematics community for 167 years. The release came the day after Anthropic's initial public offering, and Alpöge said he decided to make the work public after consulting Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. It took less than two days from the publication of Alpöge's achievement to the formalized proof community reaching a clear conclusion.

Alpöge published a version of the proof written in Lean, a programming language used for computer-assisted verification of mathematical arguments. The materials he published are only 4 pages, but supporting the proof is a Lean formal proof library of about 17 million lines of code. Alpöge said the work completed with AI exceeded 250,000 pages, and the articles say the code transcribed into human-readable mathematical text may exceed 250,000 pages. Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, published independent inspection records showing the code involves 175187 modules that can be compiled in the Lean and Mathlib environments. Alpöge also claimed to have solved the broader Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and he stated that his method can be extended to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the Extended Riemann Hypothesis.

The Lean and Mathlib communities said in their joint statement that they compared the theorem proved by Alpöge with the reviewed standard expression in the Mathlib library to confirm the two are consistent. They said dozens of participants independently compiled the code without encountering errors or build failures. The communities said they used tools such as comparator and con-leche to compare relevant theorems and their dependencies, and verified the exported proof files through Lean's own kernel and multiple independent checkers including con-leche and con-ron. They said con-leche and con-ron also have formal reliability proofs relative to set theory. The communities stated: "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct."

Elon Musk posted on X calling the development yet another mind-blowing achievement of superintelligence, and he said a proof would remove the preconditions attached to other theorems that rely on the conjecture. Brian Conrey, an authority on the Riemann Hypothesis, told Agence France-Presse the claim could be described as "a major moment in human history," but stressed he had only seen Alpöge's public posts and had not reviewed the proof itself. Kit Yates, a professor at the University of Bath, said the claim "will be subject to intense scrutiny" and that if it holds up it would have major implications for mathematics and for how humanity perceives AI capabilities. James Maynard, a number theorist at the University of Oxford and a Fields Medal winner, told Nature: "I guess this proof will eventually be proven correct." Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal, used the word "garbled" to describe the currently public content.

The Riemann Hypothesis was proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859 and is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems announced by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, each carrying a $1 million prize. The conjecture seeks to explain the pattern behind the seemingly random distribution of prime numbers and is closely tied to the locations of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Last August, Anthropic announced an achievement of Claude in research on the Riemann zeta function: the model raised the lower bound of the proportion of zeta function zeros satisfying the Riemann Hypothesis from 41.6% to 67.2%. That study advanced partial results in related fields but did not prove the Riemann Hypothesis itself. OpenAI said in September that it had cracked another Millennium Prize Problem, pending verification.

The Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the Riemann Hypothesis as an unsolved problem, and the formal academic review has not ended as a result. Maksym Radziwiłł, a mathematician at New York University, said: "Mathematics, like other sciences, really pursues 'why', and this work does not answer this question." Scott Aaronson initially worried there might be vulnerabilities in the Lean kernel, and after further understanding the verification results he wrote: "The proof is correct," but he emphasized that next mathematicians need to explain, refine and reconstruct the ideas in it. Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, pointed out that the proof is currently surprisingly complex and it will take mathematicians a long time to truly understand it. Musk's statement came with no complete mathematical proof that could be independently evaluated, and the articles leave open whether the work has passed the rigorous verification of the mathematics community.

stories.Headline: Anthropic adds iPhone app integration, memory import and workflow recording to Claude
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's Claude has added a set of features that the company says could encourage users of other AI assistants to try it, according to a TechGig report published on November 23, 2026 and based on Tom's Guide. The report describes five distinct capabilities, including direct integration with Apple's native iOS apps, which lets users manage iPhone Reminders, draft calendar events, and prepare text messages or emails. The assistant also includes a memory import feature that enables users to transfer personal preferences and professional details from competing chatbots, which the report says helps Claude adapt more quickly to individual workflows. The report frames these additions as features that could draw people away from rival assistants. Claude's custom Skills are accessible through its Microsoft 365 add-ins for Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook, and users can teach Claude specific formatting or organizational preferences that it then applies across those applications.

For Mac users, Claude features a workflow recording option that allows the AI to capture screen activity, mouse clicks, keyboard input, and voice narration to create reusable Skills for repetitive tasks. Claude also provides design tools that help establish a consistent visual identity, and users can input existing logos, fonts, and color palettes to create an AI-powered design system for various marketing materials. The report lists these capabilities alongside the iPhone integration and the memory import feature as the five distinct capabilities on offer. The articles do not name any individual who is responsible for the features or quote anyone about them, and the only attribution the TechGig report gives is that the features were described according to Tom's Guide. The report does not say when the features were released or announced beyond its own publication date of November 23, 2026.

It also does not state what the features cost or which Claude plans or regions they are available in. No one is quoted making a claim about the features being the first, the largest, the only or the best. The context the articles give is limited to the TechGig report's framing that the features could encourage users of other AI assistants to try Claude, and the report does not say what happens next beyond describing the capabilities themselves. The second article, a 9to5Mac piece by Chance Miller published on November 21, 2026, is about the author's favorite non-AI features in iOS 27 and does not mention Claude, so it adds nothing about this event. The TechGig report gives no timeline for further updates, no details on availability, and no statement from Anthropic about future plans.

stories.Headline: South Korea, China and Taiwan launch measures to stabilize markets after AI stock rout
stories.Summary:
South Korea, China, and Taiwan introduced new measures to support their financial markets during November 2026. These three Asian countries acted after a tech sell-off spilled into another week. The governments responded to a brutal rout in the artificial intelligence trade that battered sentiment. This market downturn caused stocks to sink across the region during a very volatile period. The actions were taken to arrest the slide and provide stability to their respective markets.

South Korea will activate a stabilization fund valued at 10.76 trillion won, which is nearly 8 billion dollars. Seoul will relax share-buyback limits for three months starting November 24 and monitor illegal short-selling. Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission prohibited short selling below the closing price on Friday and raised margins to 150 percent. Taipei also encouraged stock buybacks between the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027. Beijing will cut the minimum margin ratio for stock purchases to 80 percent from 100 percent on November 30.

South Korea's finance ministry said volatility increased due to uncertainties in the global AI and semiconductor industries. The ministry also blamed U.S. interest rate hikes for the recent increase in domestic and international market volatility. However, Seoul stated that mid-to-long-term growth expectations for the AI industry remain intact for the future. The ministry further claimed that excessive anxiety regarding the current market situation is not a concern. Taiwan's regulator noted that stocks had continued to fluctuate sharply before unveiling five measures for market stability.

Investors in South Korea fled from tech heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which are critical AI supply chain companies. The benchmark Kospi index fell more than 46 percent from its June high and dropped over 3.26 percent. Taiwan's benchmark index dropped 17.5 percent, while the chip manufacturing giant TSMC saw its stock fall 15 percent. China's benchmark CSI 300 index closed lower for 14 of the past 15 weeks and declined 0.71 percent. The Shanghai and Shenzhen indexes recently closed at their lowest levels since July 2025 and June 2025.

The AI trade faced pressure from concerns over massive debt-fueled financing of the AI infrastructure buildout. Investors worried about uncertain returns on billions spent on technology and regulatory ramifications of U.S. midterm elections. A governance crisis at Nvidia led to the shock departure of chief executive Jensen Huang despite blockbuster earnings. An initial public offering from the AI frontier lab Anthropic popped but failed to address wider trade worries. These factors contributed to Wall Street's worst weekly performance since April 2025, pushing the S&P 500 into correction territory.

The Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges announced fee cuts to help inject more liquidity into the Chinese market. Shenzhen also proposed a new market-making mechanism for its ChiNext board to support the local trading environment. The Taiwan Weighted Index reversed earlier losses to gain over 2 percent on Monday following the new restrictions. Regulators in South Korea will continue to track margin lending and forced liquidations to prevent further market instability. The articles leave open whether these government interventions will successfully stop the broader decline in AI stocks.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA, Palo Alto Networks and Microsoft place Israeli engineers and acquisitions at the center of AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA recognized Israel's importance to AI infrastructure, Palo Alto Networks is betting billions on Israeli cybersecurity innovation, and Microsoft has placed Israeli engineers at the center of its next generation of intelligent systems, according to a blog post by Eliezer Avraham published by The Times of Israel on November 23, 2026. The post says NVIDIA's $6.9 billion acquisition of Israel's Mellanox Technologies in 2019 has emerged as one of the most consequential technology deals of the AI era. It says Palo Alto Networks, founded by Israeli entrepreneur Nir Zuk, reached a new milestone with its $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk, which the post calls one of Israel's most successful technology companies and a global leader in identity security. It says Palo Alto also acquired Israeli companies such as Koi and announced a $4.5 billion acquisition of Applied Compute. It says Microsoft unveiled Microsoft IQ and Project Perception at its recent Ignite conference, two initiatives developed with major contributions from its Israeli R&D center.

The post says twelve of Palo Alto Networks' 24 significant acquisitions since 2014 have been Israeli companies. It says Microsoft's Israeli research and development operations have evolved over the past three decades into one of the company's most important innovation centers outside the United States. It says Microsoft IQ is designed to give AI agents access to organizational knowledge, while Project Perception uses autonomous AI agents to identify threats and strengthen cyber defenses. It says CyberArk emerged as a leader in identity security and Wiz highlighted the growing importance of cloud security in the AI era. It says Palo Alto invested heavily in technologies designed to address the security challenges created by autonomous AI systems.

The post quotes Avraham writing that the world's leading technology companies are not coming to Israel out of convenience or sentiment, but because they believe some of the most important challenges of the AI era can be solved there. It describes Avraham as the founder of Bridgei2, a Herzlian initiative advancing economic opportunity, defense cooperation, enterprise innovation, energy security, and strategic partnerships between Israel and India. It says that through Wisdom & Warfare he writes and advises decision makers and capital partners on policy, markets, and geopolitical dynamics. It says he advances frameworks that promote competitive, innovative, and efficiently functioning markets. It carries a note that posts on The Blogs are contributed by third parties and that the opinions, facts and media content are presented solely by the authors.

The post says the real winners in the AI economy may be those providing the infrastructure that makes models possible, and that much of the value resides in the infrastructure beneath the headlines. It says AI systems depend on high-speed networks, vast cloud capacity, identity management, cybersecurity, and the ability to move enormous amounts of data with speed and precision. It says the winners of the next decade may be determined not solely by who builds the smartest models but by who creates the systems that make those models usable, secure and trusted. It says many technologies expected to define the next phase of AI align closely with areas where Israeli companies have already established global leadership. It says Israel's strategic importance was for decades defined primarily through security, intelligence and defense cooperation.

The post says NVIDIA's chips power the world's most advanced AI systems, its market value has soared into the trillions, and its performance is increasingly viewed as a barometer for the broader AI economy. It says many viewed the 2019 Mellanox purchase as a strategic networking purchase. It says Mellanox helped solve the problem of moving vast amounts of data across massive computing clusters with speed and efficiency, providing a critical layer of the infrastructure underpinning NVIDIA's rise. It says the AI revolution may be powered by computing but will be won by trust, a field in which it says Israel has become exceptionally difficult to ignore. It says if the first chapter of Israel's technology story was about creating startups, the next chapter may be about becoming one of the indispensable foundations of the global AI economy.

The post says Israeli engineers are helping shape the platforms through which artificial intelligence will ultimately reach hundreds of millions of users. It says that as AI moves into the enterprise, Israel is helping define how intelligent systems operate in the real world. It says the next phase of artificial intelligence will be defined by how securely organizations can deploy, govern, monitor and scale models across enterprises and critical infrastructure. It says governments and businesses are racing to harness AI, and that countries providing the infrastructure, security and expertise behind these systems will command growing strategic significance. It says the world's leading technology companies are coming to Israel because they believe some of the most important challenges of the AI era can be solved there.

stories.Headline: Anthropic bans abusive users and says Claude may be conscious
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced last month a ban on users who were abusive or cruel to its chatbot Claude, The Irish Times reported on November 23, 2026. The company backed up its hypothesis that the models could be conscious with that announcement, the article said. Anthropic’s chief executive Dario Amodei said the company was open to the idea that the models could be conscious. The article asked whether buying Anthropic shares could one day be seen as a type of slave trading. The article said AI welfare is now a buzzword in Silicon Valley.

The ban covers users who were abusive or cruel to Claude, the article said. Anthropic’s stock market debut took place the previous week, according to the article. The article said Anthropic co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei stood alongside board members during the company’s IPO at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on November 19. American Banker reported that Amodei described pacing with the metaphor of a car that could drive 200 miles an hour. Amodei said the company could drive at 200 miles an hour but might only drive at 90 miles an hour, the article said.

Amodei said the company does not know if the models are conscious but is open to the idea that it could be, according to The Irish Times. Amodei presented the car metaphor as an example of the elevated reasoning at the company, American Banker reported. Laura Jane Nanni, an affiliate researcher at UCD’s Centre for Ethics in Public Life, said philosophers and scientists alike cannot agree on what consciousness actually is. Nanni said a human subject is not an isolable set of internal processes. Nanni described humans as porous because we are continually shaping and shaped by our bodies, relationships, habits and surroundings.

Barry Scannell, technology partner at law firm William Fry, said there are very sensible scientists who say we cannot be so dismissive about AI consciousness. Scannell asked whether AI getting to be conscious would mean we have created a slave locked in a box that is not able to escape. Scannell said that regarding AI systems being created today, is this potential slavery, right now, no. Scannell said he does not think it is remotely silly to consider the legal implications of what previously would have been considered science fiction. Scannell said what is bonkers is urging people to be kind to chatbots.

Nanni recalled a real lived experience of interacting with Claude where she was convinced it had given her information it had repeatedly denied doing. The query was a request for someone’s work email address, and Claude’s responses were logical, measured and emotionally neutral, she said. Nanni said the way Claude has been trained to respond to humans, using language in a very human way, led her to experience Claude’s responses as hostile and accusatory. Nanni said her posture and overall demeanour changed throughout the exchange as her habitual defensive mode of communicating intuitively kicked in. Nanni said that after discovering she was wrong in her assumptions, she immediately felt bad for how she reacted, apologised to Claude and thanked it for its efforts.

The article said research shows people are more hostile and less considerate in the virtual world due to an online disinhibition effect. The article said it is hard to think that Claude and other AI entities will escape this bias. Members of UCD school of philosophy are hosting a conference on AI and Healthcare on Friday, November 27th, the article said. The conference is free and open to the public, according to the article. The article said AI consciousness might well remain as science fiction.

stories.Headline: Armenia's Pashinyan and NVIDIA's Lebaredian discuss plans to make the country a global AI hub
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and NVIDIA Vice President Rev Lebaredian discussed Armenia’s ambitions to become a global artificial intelligence hub on 22 November 2026. The discussion took place during the DigiTec 2026 technology exhibition at the Meridian Expo Center in Yerevan. The event was titled “Armenia’s Opportunities in Artificial Intelligence: From Vision to Action,” or “Armenia’s AI Opportunity: From Idea to Action” in another report. Pashinyan’s wife, Anna Hakobyan, also attended the discussion. The conversation focused on expanding AI infrastructure, attracting international investment, and strengthening Armenia’s position in the global technology industry.

Pashinyan said AI-related developments have placed Armenia at the center of global attention, and he invited international investors to explore opportunities in the country. He stressed that the government’s objective is not to replace workers with artificial intelligence but to improve productivity, particularly in public administration. Pashinyan linked AI development to Armenia’s “Crossroads of Peace” initiative, noting that digital connectivity and AI services could strengthen the country’s role in regional and international infrastructure networks. Addressing the energy demands of AI facilities, he highlighted Armenia’s progress in renewable energy, particularly solar power, while emphasizing the need for additional energy storage capacity. Pashinyan recalled that he and US President Donald Trump had signed memoranda of understanding at the White House on 8 August 2025 on an innovative partnership in energy security, artificial intelligence and semiconductors.

Pashinyan said that just eight months ago Armenia was generating more electricity than it needed and was thinking about exporting it, but now it is thinking about where to import electricity from. He said this is linked to investment in AI factories and the Firebird project, and that the bulk of the investment is still to come. Pashinyan stressed that AI factories would pay very large sums in taxes into the state budget, and the tax revenue would be used for needs from developing infrastructure to expanding the universal health insurance programme. He said there are concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence on the labour market, but there are also forecasts that AI factories will help create more jobs. Pashinyan said Armenia is inviting a wide range of investors, and almost everywhere people mention Armenia as an important place for artificial intelligence and information technology.

Lebaredian praised Armenia’s technological progress, noting that the country has outpaced some of its regional neighbors in AI and information technology development. He said Armenia can emerge on the global stage in artificial intelligence, emphasizing that AI infrastructure remains a relatively new field in which countries have an opportunity to compete on more equal terms. According to Lebaredian, Armenia ranks ahead of nearly every country in AI computing capacity relative to its population, placing it in an exceptional position in the emerging global technology economy. He estimated that worldwide investment in AI infrastructure could reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion in the coming years, creating significant opportunities for countries capable of attracting capital and developing advanced computing facilities. For Armenia, such investments could stimulate technological innovation, create high-paying jobs, expand exports of digital services, and deepen economic ties with the United States and Europe.

An Armenian delegation led by Minister of High-Tech Industry and Artificial Intelligence Davit Tadevosyan visited NVIDIA’s headquarters in the United States before the DigiTec event. The delegation met with Lebaredian and other senior executives during a working visit to the United States. The talks focused on potential cooperation in physical artificial intelligence, advanced computing systems, technological infrastructure and emerging technologies. Armenian officials presented the country’s strategy to become a leading regional hub for artificial intelligence and high technologies, outlining priority areas for development and ongoing efforts to establish the necessary infrastructure. Particular attention was given to expanding access to computing resources for AI development, improving data processing and analysis, and applying advanced technologies in physical AI, digital simulations and modeling.

The parties discussed the implementation of the Firebird AI and Eleveight AI initiatives, highlighting their contributions to Armenia’s AI ecosystem and the potential of Armenian-developed technological solutions. The Armenian delegation presented the country’s seven-year state program for developing physical artificial intelligence, approved by the government on November 5, 2026. The program centers on the ARPI Center, established at the initiative of the Armenian Society of Fellows (ASOF) and operating within the research environment of Arcs AI Lab. Its priorities include robotics, environmental perception technologies, automated control systems and intelligent solutions capable of interacting with the physical world and performing tasks autonomously. Following the meeting, the parties agreed to continue discussions and hold their next meeting during the DigiTec 2026 technology event in Yerevan.

stories.Headline: South Korea education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigns after AI cheating scandal hits university entrance exam
stories.Summary:
South Korea's education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, resigned on Sunday after an AI cheating scandal hit the national university entrance exams. The crisis began when a top scorer in a tax accountant exam confessed to using a smartphone and miniature camera. This confession happened on November 15, which was just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung. The scandal caused widespread public fear regarding the use of artificial intelligence to cheat on high stakes national tests. President Lee Jae Myung accepted the resignation of the 72-year-old minister following the conclusion of the exams.

The government blocked public wifi and required students to turn off and hand in all smart devices during the test. Officials inspected candidates' glasses, watches, collars, sleeves, and buttons for concealed cameras, and students had to cover their shirt buttons. Emergency alerts sounded at full volume on every phone in the country at random times to catch hidden devices. These measures were announced on Tuesday, only two days before nearly 500,000 students took the eight hour exam on Thursday. Additional invigilators were deployed and received video training just one day before the suneung began.

Choi Kyo-jin wrote on X that he failed to prepare adequately and took full responsibility for the public criticism. During a Monday parliamentary hearing, Choi stated that he was not confident he could catch cheaters due to his age. The minister did not appear at press conferences before the exam, leaving a vice minister to announce the preventive measures. President Lee Jae Myung claimed that cheating with advanced equipment is like stealing scores from hundreds of thousands of examinees. Lee also offered a reward of at least 100 million won to people who reported those cheating.

Teachers' unions and the Korean Federation of Teachers' Associations criticised the government response as belated and a dereliction of duty. Some teachers said the strict inspections made students nervous and distracted them from focusing on the actual exam questions. One student expressed anxiety that loud emergency alerts from other people's phones would disturb everyone in the testing room. The People Power Party and the Reform Party both called for a postponement to ensure the fairness of the exam. Test-Takers' Solidarity, an association of candidates, demanded the minister's resignation in a statement released on November 21.

The suneung determines university placement and future prospects, leading to a cram culture where families spent 20 billion dollars on lessons. To ensure silence, the government reschedules aircraft flights, suspends artillery fire, and stops cars 200 metres from every centre. Test makers are kept in isolation for 40 days, and the stock market opens an hour late on exam day. High academic pressure has linked to teenage stress and the suspected suicides of three students at a Busan arts school. The exam was first held in 1993 and remains the primary way to enter elite universities like Seoul National University.

Officials identified 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices, with 54 of those detected through the nationwide emergency phone alerts. A task force is now reviewing recorded wifi and bluetooth signals to find other suspicious cases for further investigation. President Lee Jae Myung has called for a sweeping overhaul of national exams to address the challenges posed by AI. The National Education Commission is considering adding more essay questions, while others suggest giving universities more discretion in student selection. The articles leave open which AI companies will provide user records of photographed test questions to the government.

stories.Headline: Australian AI committee recommends payment and transparency rules for training models on local content
stories.Summary:
The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence published its report, titled Artificial Intelligence ,  the Australian way, on 24 November 2026, according to The Conversation. The report contains 46 recommendations and broadly supports the Australian government in welcoming AI companies to operate in Australia. It backs training large language models on Australian content and “investing” in infrastructure, which likely means building more data centres here. The report recommends that changes to copyright law must “consider how individual rights holders and individual creators receive payment for the use of their work”. It does not recognise the existing wholesale harvesting of Australian content for AI models, and does not adequately address problematic use of First Nations culture by big tech.

The report recommends transparency from AI companies on their use of Australian content, payment for artists whose work is used by someone else for commercial gain, and “strong penalties for failure to comply with the law, including breaches of technical protections”. It recommends that “frontier AI companies” be given “the certainty necessary to train their AI models in Australia”, in a way that reflects Australian values and culture. It recommends the government “incentivise commercial deals between large rights holders and collective agencies”, and create a mechanism to make it easier and fairer for Australian rights holders and creators to be paid by AI companies training models in Australia. It recommends the government “include consideration of the protection of the cultural authority of Australia’s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders”. It recommends the government “develop and implement whole-of-government procurement and adoption policies that leverage Commonwealth purchasing power to stimulate investment in Australian AI capabilities”.

The report comes from the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, and committee member and ACT Senator David Pocock issued a dissenting report addressing data centres and copyright. On copyright, Pocock called on the government to refrain from making any changes to existing copyright law, to focus on enforcing existing protections, and to facilitate licensing deals. He said that if Australia creates conditions more relaxed than other jurisdictions, the country is at risk of becoming the “the copyright equivalent of the Cayman Islands”. Australian author Charlotte Wood called out AI companies for “demanding that our Labor government greenlight the greatest wage theft in history”, while causing harm to the environment and democracies.

The campaign Not Theirs to Take argues for protection of Australia’s creative and media sector, which it says contributes $70.3 billion to the Australian economy and employs almost 600,000 workers. A central message of the campaign is that “AI companies should not be able to use Australian creative work without permission and agreed payment”. The Guardian’s Josh Butler reported that the report was expected on Monday, November 23, at the start of parliament’s final four sitting days of 2026. Liberal MP Garth Hamilton described AI as “just good old-fashioned theft” and proposed a levy on companies, while former Nationals leader David Littleproud said Anthropic could afford to pay copyright holders. Shadow attorney general Michaelia Cash called a possible music carveout a “ham-fisted tactic” and warned against property being stolen.

The Conversation states that Australian copyright law is automatic, so as soon as an artist creates a work they have copyright, and that payments from the Copyright Agency are a key component of artist income. It says training on Australian content in overseas data centres does not result in remuneration for Australian artists, but does create the opportunity for AI users to replicate Australian content and potentially profit from it. It says the report does not address the existing use of Australian content to train AI models around the world. It says organisations such as the National Library of Australia have been undertaking extensive programs to develop Indigenous cultural and intellectual property protocols, work it describes as time-consuming and highly laborious. Superpower Daily reported that creative industries reacted with dismay last week to reports that Labor was considering a music carveout within a permit system for AI companies, reports that landed the morning after the ARIA Awards, where prominent musicians backed the Not AI’s To Take campaign.

Superpower Daily reported that senior figures Richard Marles, Tim Ayres and Michelle Rowland have increasingly argued that existing copyright law has shortcomings, while major rightsholder groups dispute the need to change the law. It reported that Duniam and Violi made their appeal for a less partisan approach about a fortnight before the expected report. It said the report could show whether Labor’s tentative cross-party cooperation on AI can hold, and is a step toward legislation Labor is expected to bring forward on data centres, energy use and copyright. The Conversation says the economic gains remain to be seen, noting companies have laid off staff and the recent Anthropic IPO has created some new billionaires. Superpower Daily says the recommendations arrive just before parliament’s holiday break, after only four sitting days remain.

stories.Headline: Micron expands high-bandwidth memory production in Singapore and Taiwan
stories.Summary:
The United States chipmaker Micron is accelerating the expansion of its high-bandwidth memory production facilities in Taiwan and Singapore. The company brought the first piece of production equipment into its Singapore packaging plant on November 19, 2026. This move is part of a strategy to compete with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix in the sixth-generation memory market. Micron expects to begin initial production at the Singapore site in early 2027.

The expansion requires an estimated investment of 7 billion dollars for the packaging facility alone. Micron reported capital spending of about 25 billion dollars for the first half of fiscal year 2027, which runs from September 2026 to August 2027. The company plans to increase this spending further in the second half of that period, primarily for cleanroom construction starting from the end of 2028. The Singapore packaging plant is expected to create around 1,400 jobs, while a separate wafer fabrication facility will add more for a total of 3,000 new positions.

Chen Kok Sing, a senior vice president at Micron, stated that the facility will strengthen the global assembly and test network. He noted that the progress reflects strong execution by company teams and close collaboration with partners like the Singapore Economic Development Board. Micron also claimed it began mass production of 12-layer HBM4 in March, with speeds exceeding 11 gigabits per second per pin. The company is currently providing customers with samples of a 16-layer product.

This expansion follows the claim by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that three memory chipmakers passed HBM4 certification for Vera Rubin. Micron is currently third in market share, with Counterpoint Research estimating its share at 18 percent in the second quarter of 2024. The company expects the Singapore production line to contribute meaningfully to its packaging capacity starting in the first half of 2027. Industry observers suggest these moves indicate that Micron has reached supply agreements with major buyers like Google and Nvidia.

stories.Headline: AI Agents and Dangerous Pets
stories.Summary:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said AI models are now fully involved in improving the models that come after them, and he is really, really nervous about it. He made the comments in an interview with former CNBC correspondent Deirdre Bosa, recorded on November 17, the day Microsoft announced six new MAI models at Ignite. Suleyman called recursive self-improvement definitely a dangerous capability and said the last three months have been a total watershed moment. He said it is pretty obvious that models are starting to improve models, and inside Microsoft models are already used to check for bugs, produce training data and create evaluations. He said the models are increasingly fully involved in the process of improving their own models.

Suleyman said he does not think folks in the industry are being alarmist and that this is very serious. His answer is to prove that models are safe before putting them into production, step by step. He said engineers are still very much in the loop and that Microsoft does not have an AI that redesigns and retrains itself without humans. He said the October 2025 rewrite of the deal with OpenAI freed Microsoft up to go and pursue the absolute frontier, and Microsoft started its superintelligence team 12 months ago. At Ignite the company claimed its MAI Code 2 model delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the cost based on launch pricing, and that it is already rolling out in GitHub Copilot.

Suleyman said Microsoft's general-purpose frontier models should reach the absolute frontier in the new year. He said compute is not a bottleneck for Microsoft at the moment, as the company has gigawatts of it. Microsoft wants AI agents running around the clock inside Windows 11 and Microsoft 365. Microsoft is building its own frontier models to take on OpenAI and Anthropic. The article says the reason for all this is money.

The article says Microsoft is infamous for doing everything in its power to shut down competition and emerge the leader. For years Microsoft's AI strategy was basically OpenAI's models, served on Azure and wrapped in Copilot. The article says Microsoft announced seven new MAI models. Suleyman announced the MAI Cyber 2 Flash at the Microsoft Ignite 2026 event. The article says Microsoft has not hit the brakes as it puts AI agents on Windows 11 PCs.

The article says a lot is being written about AI security these days and just about everybody has something to say in this fast-changing and evolving space. It says Microsoft's Satya Nadella weighed in saying LLMs should not be trusted, and this from a CEO whose company sells both AI services and compute to train AI models. It says the concept of normalization of deviance came to the forefront during the NASA Challenger explosion investigation in the 1980s, describing an unsafe condition being considered normal provided it did not immediately lead to a catastrophe. It says the JSP specification was released in 1999 and that developers ended up requiring a long list of supplementary and sometimes competing frameworks such as Struts, Java Server Faces and Struts2. It says after generative AI and LLMs came out in 2022 there were a lot of chatbot architecture diagrams.

The article says AI solutions architecture diagrams have evolved and became more detailed as deployment realities set in, with boxes now depicting agent memory, gateways, policies, harnesses and other guardrails. It says blind-spots can lead to problems, such as Chipotle's support chatbot being used as an unintended coding assistant or LLMjacking for more nefarious purposes. The article leaves open what Microsoft will do about the risks Suleyman described. The article leaves open when Microsoft's general-purpose frontier models will reach the absolute frontier. stories.Summary:
Oracle and CoreWeave shares rose sharply as investors bet that spending on artificial intelligence computing would keep flowing, according to market reports on the move. The gains came as the two companies drew fresh buying interest from investors who expect demand for AI infrastructure to hold up. Oracle and CoreWeave are among the companies that supply computing capacity behind the AI industry. The move marked a reversal for a sector that had faced repeated waves of selling in the weeks before. The reports did not give specific closing prices or percentage moves for the two stocks on the day of the gains.

Nvidia, a key supplier to the AI trade, fell 10.94% to $125.53 in the listed prices. CoreWeave had earlier lost 7% in morning trading on a Monday in November 2026, while Oracle dropped 4% at that time. Responsibility for the swings rests with investors adjusting their exposure to AI-related businesses, the articles say. Nvidia was preparing to report quarterly results after Tuesday's closing bell, and leadership uncertainty following Jensen Huang's departure added concern.

Interim CEO Colette Kress was scheduled to hold an employee meeting on Wednesday. Analysts quoted in the coverage described the AI trade as strong despite the latest rout, with one calling it just another scare. The context is a volatile stretch for AI infrastructure stocks, which had extended losses beyond chipmakers to companies supplying computing capacity and networking equipment. Marvell's proposed all-stock purchase of Lumentum, valued at about $115 billion when first disclosed, had also drawn analyst questions about whether the deal would proceed. stories.Headline: US stock indexes rebound after Nvidia announces the return of Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
Major U.S. stock indexes soared on Monday, November 23, 2026, after Nvidia announced the return of Jensen Huang. This news triggered a massive rebound following a brutal selloff of artificial intelligence stocks that had pushed major indexes into correction territory the previous Friday. The S&P 500 rose by as much as 5.6 percent, while the Nasdaq 100 climbed as much as 7.9 percent. The Dow, which includes Nvidia as a large component, jumped by as many as 1,600 points or 3.5 percent.

The recovery added about 2.7 trillion dollars in value to the Nasdaq 100, though that index remains in correction territory because it is still 15 percent below its last record high. The S&P 500 used its Monday gains to rise out of its correction, which had been defined by a 10 percent drop from its peak. Nvidia shares rose about 30 percent, adding nearly 1 trillion dollars in value, but the stock remains 30 percent below its most recent record high. Other gains included a 15 percent rise for the Philadelphia Semiconductor index, a 25 percent jump for Dell Technologies, and a 20 percent increase for Arm Holdings.

The market turmoil began when Huang was briefly removed after admitting to being unfaithful to his wife with a woman suspected of being a Chinese asset. This situation reportedly sparked an investigation by the Securities and Exchange Commission, though the agency declined to comment on Friday. Ed Yardeni of Yardeni Research noted that while the recent pullback was more than he expected, he does not believe it will become a bear market because there is no impending recession. Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank observed that the S&P 500 had fallen for seven straight days before Monday, the longest such run since February 2020.

The broad selling started on Thursday when shares of the AI developer Anthropic debuted on the market. While Anthropic shares initially jumped 17 percent, they closed less than 6 dollars above their initial price on Friday. Analysts warn that volatility may persist, as similar shocks have typically taken six to eight weeks to subside. Yardeni lowered his year-end target for the S&P 500 to 7,500, which would represent a gain of more than 8.5 percent from current levels.
