stories.Headline: Nick Bostrom says AI could let humans live 1,200 to 1,400 years
stories.Summary:
Nick Bostrom, a Swedish philosopher and former professor at Oxford, discussed the potential for extreme human longevity during an A16z show episode released on Thursday, November 20, 2026. He suggested that artificial intelligence could enable humans to live for more than a millennium by eliminating aging and creating biomedical breakthroughs. This technological advancement would allow people to potentially reach a life expectancy of 1,200 or 1,400 years. Bostrom noted that these figures are conservative estimates because AI might also reduce mortality risks from accidents. Achieving this lifespan requires AI to unlock radical research in antiaging and biomedicine to fundamentally change how the human body ages.

Bostrom previously led the Future of Humanity Institute, which he founded in 2005 at Oxford before it closed in 2024. He believes that the ability to extend life so drastically depends on the successful integration of emerging technologies and human enhancement. The process involves a complex balance between rapid development and the implementation of safety guardrails. Bostrom explained that the trade-off between speed and safety is a difficult evaluation for researchers to make. He acknowledged that spending more time on AI alignment research could lower existential risks and make the transition safer.

However, he argued that delaying these advancements means millions of people continue to die every year. He believes that the potential to save lives must be weighed against the risks of developing advanced AI too quickly. This discussion occurs as many researchers call for a slowdown in AI development to address alignment issues and ensure the technology remains beneficial to humans. Bostrom continues to study how emerging technologies can enhance human existence while managing the inherent dangers of artificial intelligence. The debate remains focused on whether the immediate benefits of life extension outweigh the long-term risks of an unaligned AI.

stories.Headline: Stanley urges faster integration of super intelligence capabilities at Department of War
stories.Summary:
Cameron Stanley, the chief super intelligence officer for the Department of War, called for faster integration of super intelligence capabilities during a keynote address at the AFCEA DC Luncheon Series on November 19, 2026, in a talk titled "Decision Dominance Through Awareness." He said the only way to fight an agentically enabled and very nefarious threat environment is to get agents yourself, and he urged the department to integrate SI and use its domain and subject matter expertise to fight fire with fire. He warned that the longer the department waits, the further behind it will be. The Department of War announced the previous week that it had redesignated the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office as the Department of War Super Intelligence Office.

Stanley said the redesignation focuses attention on the administration's intent to deliver super intelligence tools into the department at speed and at scale. He noted that since his last visit in May, the department has expanded its GenAI.mil platform, which now offers three models at Impact Level 5 and lets personnel work on U.S. government data at the controlled unclassified information level. He said the department's objective is to use SI to process large volumes of information so it can make better decisions more quickly, because there is usually too much data. He described open-source data as a treasure trove in volume and quality for those who can parse it, and said commercial solutions offer access to larger datasets and processing capabilities than the department has internally, though he acknowledged they do not work for everything. He also said the commercial industry has overtaken the military in areas such as space-based intelligence and Military Satellite Communications, which is no longer considered the gold standard.

Diane Staheli, chief scientist for AI and cybersecurity at MIT Lincoln Laboratory, said during a panel discussion after the keynote that the Department of War now has 100,000 agents created using GenAI.mil, about 500,000 power users and approaching 2 million casual users of the technology, and that the desire for rapid experimentation carries risk. She recalled an incident in which intelligence imagery was misinterpreted and a commercial vessel was misidentified as a nuclear submarine, which she called a high consequence decision, and she stressed the need for human accountability and checkpoints along the way. Sarah Pearson, director of strategic initiatives at the Defense Innovation Unit, said closer partnership is needed between operators on a battlefield and the engineers at the companies building these capabilities. Stanley said adopting the capabilities at scale will require changes within the department, and he pledged to identify every policy barrier that prevents integration of these technologies and to destroy every barrier that slows the department down, adding that it needs to lean forward and take risks, especially in this domain.

stories.Headline: Board Compensation Committees Need Reimagining for the AI Moment
stories.Summary:
Leo E. Strine, Jr., of counsel at Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz and a former Chief Justice and Chancellor of Delaware, and Kirby M. Smith, an academic fellow at Columbia Law School and former CEO and general counsel of Bridgeport Partners, published the article on November 24, 2026, in Bloomberg Law’s Insights and Commentary section. They argue that the independent committees US-listed companies must keep focused on top management pay have failed to check soaring executive take or restore fairer gainsharing among corporate leaders, stockholders, and workers. They write that CEO pay has risen by over 1,300% over the past 47 years while the stock market rose 1,400% and the typical worker’s pay grew by just 28%, with labor’s share of overall income now at an all-time low in the post-World War II period. They say AI has the power to accelerate these worrying trends, that industry leaders predict major job losses even though AI has yet to cause them, and that only about a third of AI projects are actively delivering a positive return on investment.

The authors propose transforming the compensation committee of the corporate board into a workforce committee, which they say is efficient because boards face time pressures and reorienting an existing committee lets them see the big picture. Instead of addressing only top executive pay, they write, the committee would track and improve gainsharing among shareholders, top executives, and workers over time, understand management’s pay-setting process, monitor employee-related metrics such as satisfaction, turnover, promotions, training, safety, and culture, and bring workers’ voice into strategic planning and budget processes. They say the committee could require management to provide it and the full board with information about what jobs workers do at each quartile of compensation and the median and mean pay and benefit packages of those jobs. They also say the committee could tackle AI’s implications for the quality of work, since without thoughtful implementation AI can increase workloads, erode personal collaboration, and cause skill atrophy.

The authors write that Congress and the stock exchanges mandated that company boards focus on top executive pay and that this accelerated, not arrested, take at the top. They say that if lawmakers are serious about promoting pro-worker policies and sharing the blessings of capitalism more fairly, broadening the mandate of that existing committee is a simple and sensible way to ensure that boards and management pay attention to the workers who drive a company’s success. They acknowledge that a board-level workforce committee is no panacea but say it helps address something long overdue by requiring that the best interests of American workers receive consideration at the boardroom table. They add that at a time of great political divide, leading figures in both parties agree that the American economy is failing ordinary workers, and that companies which do not create good jobs for American workers are not great companies.

The authors say AI forces boards to confront two key questions: whether available dollars are best used for executive compensation or spread among the workers most responsible for the company’s success, and how to balance investing in workers while deploying AI most productively. They write that companies wanting to maximize their AI potential and employee AI fluency need to rethink how they train and structure their workforce, and that a reconceived committee could encourage investment in workers’ AI-related skills on the promise that wages will rise if productivity does. They argue that boards which understand their workforces will make better decisions about where to invest compensation dollars and capital to deliver sustainable profits, and that the idea is pro-worker and benefits stockholders too. The article states that it does not necessarily reflect the opinion of Bloomberg Industry Group Inc., the publisher of Bloomberg Law, Bloomberg Tax, and Bloomberg Government, or its owners.

stories.Headline: NTT DATA embeds over 500 Microsoft engineers in clients to build AI-native industry solutions
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA plans to mobilise more than 500 Microsoft Frontier engineers globally to build AI-native industry solutions with clients in four sectors, the company said on 23 November 2026. The engineers will be embedded directly with clients, working alongside NTT DATA industry specialists, global AI and engineering teams, and Microsoft field and engineering staff. The initial focus is on insurance, manufacturing and automotive, healthcare and life sciences, and telecommunications and media. The initiative reflects a services model in which engineering teams are placed inside client environments to redesign business processes around AI, rather than simply adding AI tools to existing workflows. The work will draw on more than 400 reusable AI assets and pieces of intellectual property, alongside the AI Vista platform and other internal tools.

NTT DATA describes AI-native industry solutions as systems designed around AI from the outset to address a specific industry problem or transform a business process, while still working with existing enterprise applications, data and technology environments. Forward Deployed Engineering is a model in which software engineers work alongside client teams within the customer's operating environment, and those teams remain connected to NTT DATA's broader industry and technical resources as well as Microsoft expertise. Examples cited by NTT DATA include claims handling and underwriting in insurance, production quality and response decisions in manufacturing, workflow orchestration in healthcare, and network and customer operations in telecoms. Edwina Fitzmaurice, Corporate Vice President for Industry Solutions Delivery at Microsoft, said that combining Microsoft's cloud and AI platform, software engineers and enterprise-grade trust with NTT DATA's deep industry expertise and global engineering scale can help clients build AI-native industry solutions that reimagine how work gets done and deliver meaningful business outcomes. NTT DATA is also using Microsoft AI tools across its own operations, including employee productivity, IT service management and marketing, and it has about 120,000 Microsoft Copilot users globally, including in Japan.

According to NTT DATA, that internal use has given it experience in adoption, governance, identifying where human judgement remains necessary, integrating AI with enterprise systems and data, monitoring performance and measuring business value. The collaboration builds on a long-standing relationship between the two groups spanning more than 25 years, and it includes more than 24,700 Microsoft certifications, six Microsoft Solutions Partner designations and 23 advanced specialisations. The commitment of more than 500 Frontier engineers suggests both companies see embedded engineering as a key delivery model for large-scale enterprise AI projects. With the initial programme focused on four industries, NTT DATA is seeking to combine repeatable technical assets with on-site engineering and sector expertise. The teams can adapt existing agent patterns, architecture, controls, connectors and industry knowledge to specific client requirements, rather than starting each project from scratch.

stories.Headline: NTT DATA launches AKM to turn scattered enterprise knowledge into shared assets for AI agents
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA INSTITUTE OF MANAGEMENT CONSULTING, Inc. announced on November 20, 2026 the launch of AI-era Knowledge Management, known as AKM, as the second offering under SPARK, its AI-powered consulting service. The company, headquartered in Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo, with Shigeki Yamaguchi as President and CEO, said AKM connects institutional knowledge to enhance business operations with AI agents. SPARK was described as comprising three offerings, with AI Foresight & Intelligence launched in October 2026 and Agentic AI Adoption Practice still planned. AKM collects and organizes knowledge and experience dispersed across an enterprise and transforms it into institutional knowledge that serves as a shared asset for AI agents to use in business operations. The offering provides end-to-end support, from organizing internal information to building mechanisms that connect knowledge and establishing foundations for AI adoption.

The company said AI use at many companies remains limited to preliminary applications such as summarization, translation and idea generation, and that turning it into business transformation outcomes remains a challenge. It said internal information is scattered across documents, systems and departments, with relationships and business context often left undefined. AKM follows three steps: defining the knowledge to be used and its purpose, connecting and structuring knowledge for practical use through a knowledge graph and operating rules, and validating AI applications in actual business operations while developing an implementation plan. Junhao Zhong, a Senior Consultant in the Global Business Development Center, said what he finds most compelling about SPARK is not simply what AI can do but how human knowledge can be combined with AI capabilities to create business value. He said consulting must increasingly take on the role of a Human, AI Orchestrator, bringing together continuous AI-driven information gathering, analysis and learning with human expertise, contextual understanding and strategic judgment.

He said that through a cycle in which people and AI continuously learn from one another, SPARK transforms fragmented information into actionable intelligence for decision-making. He said he sees potential in evolving AI beyond a productivity tool into a strategic capability that continuously improves. The company said it plans to launch Agentic AI Adoption Practice as the third offering under SPARK, which redesigns business processes and decision-making around AI agents and supports proof-of-concept testing and implementation. Through the three offerings, the company said it will support clients across the full transformation journey, from anticipating change and putting knowledge to work to deploying AI and generating tangible business outcomes. The company was established in 1991 and describes itself as the strategic consulting firm of the NTT DATA Group.

stories.Headline: Most firms without AI fraud tools cite false positives as adoption barrier
stories.Summary:
A September PYMNTS Intelligence report, produced with Bottomline and titled “Prevention First: Building a Smarter Defense Against Payments Fraud,” found that 57% of surveyed firms did not use artificial intelligence to detect fraud in outgoing payments. Researchers surveyed 150 treasury and finance executives in the United States at companies with at least $100 million in annual revenue. Among the 85 firms that did not use AI for fraud detection, 89% cited the risk of flagging a legitimate payment as a barrier to adoption. By comparison, 62% of those firms cited cost as a barrier, a gap of 27 percentage points.

Among firms without AI fraud tools, 74% expressed hesitation about automating without human sign-off, while 55% said manual reviews already handled fraud well enough. Among firms not using AI fraud detection, 24% said they were already putting it in place, 9% planned to do so within six months and 25% within a year. Taken together, 58% were either implementing the technology or expected to do so within 12 months, and just 2% said they had no plans to adopt it. Across the full survey, 83% of firms used bank account validation to detect fraud, 79% required approval from two or more people and 77% used staff reviews.

The report describes an opening for tools that act like a second pair of eyes, flagging a change in a supplier’s bank details while an employee who knows the account decides whether to release the money. It says a system can flag a payment in seconds, but an employee still must establish that the supplier should get paid. For a finance team that knows its suppliers well, the report says, that gives AI a specific job to do. It can draw attention to the payment that deserves a closer look while leaving the decision with the people responsible for sending it.

stories.Headline: Alaska stroke coalition uses RapidAI to speed clot removal across the state
stories.Summary:
A neurointerventionalist in Anchorage received an alert just after lunchtime on a summer Wednesday, the article says. It concerned a patient three hundred miles away at a hospital deep in Alaska's interior, where a clot in a major artery was blocking blood flow to the brain. The patient, in his mid-60s, had arrived at a nearby emergency room after a morning fall, suddenly weak on his left side. He needed the clot removed, and would have to come to the state's biggest city to get it done. The article was published by STAT on November 24, 2026.

The patient got a head CT, which helps diagnose a stroke and determine whether a clot can be broken up with drugs or needs to be extracted. Normally it could take 45 precious minutes just to send the scans to Anchorage for review, the article says. This summer day, the tool from RapidAI analyzed his CT scan nearly instantly for signs of a large vessel occlusion, or LVO. The app alerted the doctor with results just seconds after the scan was complete: suspected LVO. Less than a half hour after the patient arrived at his local ER, the team had called Providence for a transfer, two minutes before their on-call radiologist delivered their official CT report.

The article attributes the account to Kelly Isaacs, Providence's stroke program manager, and to Kevin Myrick, one of the coalition's founders and Providence's stroke program coordinator. The article says the Alaska Stroke Coalition was established in 2023 by a small group of stroke coordinators and neurointerventionalists as a volunteer nonprofit. Lucy He, a neurointerventionalist in Alaska, found funding from a family foundation to buy RapidAI for six additional hospitals at a cost of about $450,000, the article says. The article quotes David Stoffel, RapidAI's chief business officer, saying the challenge was that hospitals existed in different systems but were not coordinated.

The article says the resulting network spread from Utqiagvik, Alaska's northernmost tip, south to the capital Juneau, which can only be accessed by air or water. In return for the coalition paying for the AI tool, the health systems agreed to report their performance over the next three years, the article says. The article quotes Stanford neurologist Greg Albers, co-founder of RapidAI, calling those earlier years "the wonder years." It also quotes Casey Pelzl, a researcher at the Harvey L. Neiman Health Policy Institution, saying many patients seek initial treatment at noncomprehensive stroke care centers. The article quotes UC Health neurologist and stroke researcher Joseph Broderick saying "Time is brain" is still very much the case.

The article says that in 2026 it is not rare for a hospital to use AI to triage stroke patients. Eight years ago, clinical trials showed automated image analysis could extend the clot removal window to as late as 24 hours after patients were last well, before which the window was just six hours, the article says. At the same time, the Food and Drug Administration approved the first AI to detect large vessel occlusions. The article says stroke is the fourth-leading cause of death in the United States, the majority caused by occlusions that block blood flow to the brain, and survival rates are significantly worse for rural patients. It says Alaska is more than double the size of Texas, most of it inaccessible by road, and has five neurointerventionalists in the entire state.

The article says that four hours and 23 minutes later, the clot was out, and that without the AI assist it would have taken at least an extra hour. It describes a second patient, a man in his 80s with a large vessel occlusion and severe symptoms, whose CT perfusion images showed far more green tissue than pink. Myrick said of that patient, "This patient was definitely a go," and the article says he traveled 750 miles and was shuttled into Providence's catheterization lab within a few minutes of arrival. The article says he remains weak with impaired speech after the mechanical thrombectomy and has a long way to go. It does not say what happens next for either patient or for the coalition's three-year reporting.

stories.Headline: Kyndryl opens an AI innovation lab in Dallas to move organizations past experimentation
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl has opened an AI Innovation Lab in Dallas, according to a contributed article by Chinh Vo of Kyndryl that was published on November 17, 2026. The Dallas lab is part of a larger network that also has locations in Liverpool in the United Kingdom and in Luxembourg. Vo wrote that organizations regularly ask how they can move beyond AI experimentation and identify where AI can actually deliver measurable business impact. He said that is exactly the type of challenge the Dallas lab and the wider network are designed to address.

The lab starts with a meaningful use case rather than with technology, and it brings business and technology leaders together with Kyndryl experts to understand the challenge. From there the work involves redesigning how the work gets done, developing a working prototype and creating a roadmap to production and scale. Vo encouraged California government leaders to identify one meaningful agency challenge or workflow where AI could improve operations or service delivery. He said he would welcome the opportunity to connect and explore whether such a challenge could be a candidate for moving from an idea to a practical, scalable solution.

Vo is the person named in the article as making the case for the lab, and he presented it as a way to move organizations past experimentation toward measurable impact. He invited interested leaders to connect with him on LinkedIn and to explore the Kyndryl AI Innovation Labs. The article describes Kyndryl as helping state and local government agencies modernize mission-critical technology, strengthen resilience and deliver more secure, seamless services to constituents. It says the company has deep expertise across infrastructure, cloud, applications, data and AI, and helps agencies transform complex environments while maintaining reliability and trust.

The article gives no further details on the Dallas lab itself, such as its size, cost or opening date beyond the publication of the piece. It also does not say which agencies or organizations have used the lab or what results any of them have seen. The next step it describes is for leaders with a specific challenge in mind to reach out to Vo and explore whether that challenge could be a candidate for the lab. Beyond that invitation, the article does not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Maine labor center rates office and finance jobs as most exposed to AI
stories.Summary:
Maine's Center for Workforce Research and Information, a part of the state Department of Labor, has categorized careers by how much of the work could be done by artificial intelligence and how much already is, according to a recent report. The report found that jobs related to office and administrative support, business and financial operations, sales and related occupations, and computers and mathematics are the most exposed to AI. More than 171,000 jobs in Maine fall into those categories, based on data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, including positions at banks, call centers, schools, libraries, hospitals, engineering companies and graphic design firms. Mark McInerney, the center's director, said at an October meeting of the state's Consensus Economic Forecasting Commission that high exposure does not necessarily equate to job losses. McInerney said there is a lot of nuance among the occupations that rate very highly, and that the state could see a mix of some that experience job displacement and some that experience productivity gains, as well as lots in between.

He also said the ratings do not factor in how the technology might affect productivity or wages. Some impacts are already apparent in Maine, according to the report. Last spring, Lewiston-based Central Maine Healthcare, which employs about 2,748 people, laid off 50 IT workers while transitioning to Epic, a cloud-based health records system with AI features. In July, Portland-based MaineHealth, which has about 25,000 employees and also uses Epic, announced it would cut 83 IT and analytics positions. At the University of Maine in Orono, staff and students are challenging the administration's plan to eliminate hundreds of positions to address an expected $19 million budget shortfall.

That plan comes just months after the UMaine System entered a two-year, $1.4 million contract in July to provide access to the AI platform ChatGPT across all campuses. Chancellor Dannel Malloy described the contract as a strategic investment that will help strengthen teaching and research, modernize operations and improve efficiency. Thomas Leighton, owner of Chair Salon in South Portland, said he is not worried that AI will eliminate his job after cutting hair for 28 years. He said he is confident that his skill and his passion cannot be replaced by AI, though he knows people who are very worried. A client who is a graphic designer shared their fear with him just last week, telling him their job is going to be toast.

Articles.Title: AI could eliminate jobs. Which ones in Maine are at risk?

stories.Headline: Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive, lifting AI stocks
stories.Summary:
On Monday morning, November 23, 2026, the board of Nvidia announced that it had unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive of the AI chip company, a move the article describes as a stunning turn of events. After the announcement, shares of the AI cloud providers CoreWeave and Nebius rose more than 22% as investors grew optimistic that Nvidia would keep investing across the AI trade. Nvidia is a major investor in both CoreWeave and Nebius, which build data centers and offer computing capacity for AI workloads. Other stocks also moved up on the day, with Applied Digital and the Nvidia-backed IREN jumping by double-digit percentages.

The optical equipment maker Coherent, which holds a partnership with Nvidia, surged 15% on Monday, and Bloom Energy shares rose more than 18% as investors looked for possible beneficiaries of continued spending on AI infrastructure. The article gives no other terms of the reinstatement and does not say what the board's decision requires of Huang or changes at the company. It reports the price moves as of Monday and gives no further figures beyond the percentage gains for each stock named. The article also does not say when Huang had left the chief executive role or why the board acted as it did.

The article attributes the board's action to the board itself, which it says announced the unanimous reinstatement on Monday morning, and it quotes no statement from Huang or from the companies whose shares rose. It describes the market reaction as optimism that Nvidia will continue to invest in nearly every corner of the AI trade, without naming any investor who said so. No responsible official is quoted on the decision, and the article gives no comment from CoreWeave, Nebius or the other companies mentioned. The only words it places in quotation marks come from the headlines of related stories listed on the page, not from anyone speaking about Monday's news.

The article presents the gains as part of a broader lift for the AI trade after Huang's return, and it notes that Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave and Nebius. It does not say what happens next at Nvidia or at the neocloud companies, and it gives no date for any further step. The related headlines shown on the page refer to earlier coverage of Huang, CoreWeave and Nebius, but the article itself reports nothing beyond Monday's announcement and the share moves. No further details on the reinstatement, its terms or its effect on Nvidia's investments are given in the article.

stories.Headline: Travel executives discuss AI readiness and accountability at Phocuswright roundtable
stories.Summary:
Travel leaders met at The Phocuswright Conference last week for a session titled "Pressure Into Power: Leading AI When Everyone Says They're Ready," which was moderated by Melissa Maher, founder and CEO of Pinnacle Enterprises Group, and Kimberly Newbury, vice president of sales for Phocuswright. The session was structured as a working roundtable, and the moderators opened it by citing three tensions leaders face: confidence versus candor, speed versus trust, and adoption versus transformation. Participants then broke into small groups to discuss leadership challenges including culture, return on investment, governance, leading AI-human teams, customer experience and trust, and the talent pipeline. The groups were led by travel leaders from hospitality, technology providers, online intermediaries and investors, with companies represented including Hilton, Expedia Group, American Express Global Business Travel, Cloudbeds and Unlock Advisors. Session discussions were governed by the Chatham House Rule, which allowed participants to share without attribution.

Data from Phocuswright's forthcoming research, Rebuilt or Bolted On: Travel's Agentic AI Divide, put numbers to the trends the session addressed. The research found that 74% of surveyed travel industry executives say leaders are accountable for AI outcomes, yet only 48% set formal key performance indicators for AI initiatives. Sixty-three percent of respondents have data demonstrating productivity gains, but only 22% are able to quantify revenue or conversion lift. Fewer than one in 10 surveyed companies, or 9%, said they feel fully prepared for AI, compared with 12% in 2025, a difference the article describes as within sampling error. The group focused on human-AI teams discussed empowering employees to redefine their roles and identify where they bring value compared with AI systems.

The culture conversation reported success in driving organizational adoption of AI by allowing employees to use every tool in nearly any way they wanted, with problems addressed only as they arose. The customer experience and trust group concluded that AI can help make customer interactions feel less commoditized by enabling more personalized and consistent responses, giving the example that a family traveling with two toddlers has very different needs than a family traveling with two high schoolers. Other conversations addressed sustaining a talent pipeline when AI can replace entry-level roles and using AI to help visualize and rethink complex processes. Speaking after the event, Mike Coletta, Phocuswright's senior manager of research and innovation, told PhocusWire that while companies are making progress, including implementing agentic AI and building self-improving loops, most aren't feeling any more prepared than they were a year ago. He said the small share feeling fully prepared speaks to how difficult this is and how early the industry still is in the process.

stories.Headline: Aidoc CTO Michael Braginsky frames RSNA debate on AI drafting radiology reports
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence can analyze X-rays and CT scans and draft radiology reports, and the question of whether it will make care better and safer is in sharp focus as the Radiological Society of North America meets in Chicago, according to STAT. For more than two decades, artificial intelligence has played a growing role in the practice of radiology, and today nearly every radiologist uses AI tools to triage the images they interpret, dictate their reports, or detect findings in the dozens of X-rays and CTs they read every day. Last year, radiology experts and developers at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America began to foreground a new paradigm in AI, with business acquisitions and debates centered on technology powered by vision-language models that can do the core work of a radiologist by looking at an image and drafting a report of the clinical findings within it. Michael Braginsky, chief technology officer of Aidoc, said last year's RSNA was mainly focused on whether it is actually possible that an AI model will write a draft for radiologists that would look like an actual radiology report and would be accurate enough to be even considered by a radiologist.

The article does not say what the technology requires, what it changes, or which specific products, dates or figures are involved beyond the meeting and the prior year's discussion. It gives no numbers on accuracy, no cost figures and no named health systems adopting the drafting tools. The only named person is Braginsky of Aidoc, and the only named event is the RSNA meeting in Chicago. The article does not say how many radiologists use drafting tools specifically, only that nearly every radiologist uses AI tools for tasks such as triage, dictation and detection.

Braginsky is the person the article quotes on the shift in focus, and his comment frames the prior meeting as a test of whether a model could produce a report accurate enough for a radiologist to consider. The article does not say who else is responsible for the technology or who would oversee its use in care. It does not say what regulators, hospitals or radiologists have said about the drafting tools. No other developer or expert is named in the available text.

The context the article gives is the long rise of AI in radiology and the turn at last year's RSNA toward vision-language models that draft reports, with this year's meeting in Chicago as the setting for the debate. The article does not say what happens next, what studies are planned or when the tools might reach patients. The rest of the story is behind a subscription to STAT+, so the published text ends before any further details. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Short sellers rank Nebius seventh most overvalued AI stock as capex outpaces revenue
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group N.V., which trades on Nasdaq under the ticker NBIS, ranked seventh on a list of the ten most overvalued AI stocks according to short sellers, as reported by Yahoo Finance on November 21, 2026. The broader market suffered a sell-off heading into year-end, driven by renewed concerns about elevated AI valuations and uncertainty over whether AI investments will prove profitable. Short sellers are increasingly scrutinizing Nebius amid concerns that its valuation reflects aggressive expectations for AI infrastructure growth despite the enormous capital the company requires. As of November 18, Nebius traded at approximately 22 times forward earnings and 13 times trailing sales, a premium that reflects expectations of exceptionally rapid growth as the company invests heavily to become a major provider of AI computing infrastructure.

The company's third-quarter revenue surged 571% to $980.8 million, with AI cloud revenue coming in at $973.8 million, yet it spent approximately 7.4 times its quarterly revenue on capital expenditure at $7.3 billion. Nebius expects capital expenditure of $27 billion in 2026, which could rise to $45 billion in 2027, and funding these investments through asset-backed financing, debt and equity issuance could increase borrowing costs and financial obligations while exposing existing shareholders to potential dilution. Nebius has already lowered its 2026 revenue forecast to between $3 billion and $3.2 billion, with delays pushing some planned capacity openings into the first half of 2027. Investors are also concerned that delays in bringing data center capacity online could undermine the company's growth targets.

Michael Burry, the investor made famous by The Big Short, has raised concerns about the financial structure supporting the AI boom, warning that AI infrastructure companies could be relying on increasingly complicated financing arrangements that may become unsustainable. RSM Chief economist Joe Brusuelas is wary of a wholesale bursting of the AI bubble as uncertainty surrounding Nvidia undermines confidence among lenders and investors financing the massive data-center expansion. Barclays Chief Market Strategist Julien Lafargue has warned that the AI sell-off is exposing a fundamental weakness in the investment cycle, the growing cost of financing AI infrastructure, and according to Barclays, AI demand remains strong but investors are questioning who will finance the enormous investments required. Billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller has also become increasingly cautious about the stock market amid the AI sell-off.

The market rout wiped out about $3 trillion in S&P 500 market capitalization in early November, as the Nasdaq recorded its largest single-day decline in 19 months. Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO raised $81 billion and attracted substantial demand, but its successful debut failed to reverse the broader weakness in AI-related stocks. Morgan Stanley argued that the November AI sell-off was excessive and presented a buying opportunity, while Goldman Sachs strategists warned that the outlook for AI investment and corporate profit margins in 2028 and beyond remains highly uncertain. The article does not say what happens next for Nebius beyond these pressures.

stories.Headline: OpenRouter removes three AI providers and urges users to rotate API keys after security breaches
stories.Summary:
OpenRouter removed three inference providers from its platform on November 22, 2026, following findings from the Dragos canary study. The service also stripped 125 endpoints of their Zero Data Retention eligibility, which is a label for endpoints that do not store requests. Some of these removals were taken as a precautionary measure, although the company did not name all three providers. OpenRouter stated that the findings did not show any unauthorized access or breach of its own systems.

Users who sent requests to MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, or Kimi K2.6 at Together AI must replace every password, token, and API key included in those requests. Those who used DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 through OpenRouter between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should also rotate their credentials. This requirement includes any keys that were part of log files or pasted code. Affected users are advised to check their accounts for any unauthorized activity.

Together AI CEO Vipul Ved Prakash wrote that the review of affected prompt contents is currently ongoing. Together AI reported that an AI coding agent committed a credential to a public GitHub repository, allowing an unauthorized party to download prompt samples from June and July. Phala reported that an attacker used a legacy service to reach unauthenticated management interfaces and later took over a GPU server. This breach made in-flight request data visible for the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model.

Together AI has now made zero data retention the default setting for all new accounts. OpenRouter confirmed that it has notified all potentially affected customers about these security incidents. Together AI also plans to contact its direct customers regarding the leakage of prompt samples. Developers who use coding agents are encouraged to scan their GitHub repositories for leaked passwords.

stories.Headline: Arklex.ai's Zhou Yu says dynamic simulations test non-deterministic AI agents across development stages
stories.Summary:
Zhou Yu, co-founder of Arklex.ai and a computer science professor at Columbia University, discussed using dynamic simulations to evaluate AI agents in a report published by TechGig on November 24, 2026. He said the approach addresses the challenges that non-deterministic large language models and multi-turn conversational agents create for testing. In such agents, each action depends on the prior response, and the non-deterministic nature of LLMs makes static benchmarks unreliable. The report describes dynamic simulations as crucial for evaluating these non-deterministic agents.

The simulations can be used across the software development lifecycle, from prototyping and design by product managers to testing in CI/CD pipelines by engineers. They also help monitor production for model drift or third-party tool failures and ensure compliance with regional laws. Simulations incorporate different personas, goals and corner cases, so testers can see how conversations shift with factors such as moods, preferences, accents or environmental conditions. Rather than simple pass or fail results, rule-based task verifiers measure task completion and threshold metrics for cost, efficiency, safety and compliance. For non-deterministic systems, the report says testing focuses on goal completion rather than turn-by-turn checks, and task verifiers can be rule-based or use LLM judges to assess whether the agent met the user's ultimate goal.

Arklex.ai offers an open-source Python package called ArkSim for individual developers to begin agent simulation and evaluation. Scenarios for the simulations can be manually designed, automatically generated using machine learning algorithms, or derived from existing data and social media. The simulations can run at various stages, including product design, pre-production for unit and integrated tests, and post-production for continuous drift detection. The report says the approach is evolving for agent improvement and synthetic data generation, which helps fine-tune models and reduce costs by covering more scenarios than real user data.

stories.Headline: E2E Networks reports Rs 72.70 crore Q2 profit as revenue reaches Rs 223.76 crore
stories.Summary:
E2E Networks Limited reported a Q2 FY27 net profit of Rs 72.70 crore, the company announced in results published on 16 October 2026. The company reported revenue from operations of Rs 223.76 crore for the September 2026 quarter. Net profit rose 65.68% from Rs 43.88 crore in the June 2026 quarter. The company had recorded a loss in the comparable Q2 FY26 quarter. The results were reported by Multibagg AI on 12 November 2026.

Revenue from operations rose 410.87% year on year from Rs 43.90 crore in the prior-year quarter. Revenue rose 42.74% sequentially from Rs 156.76 crore in Q1 FY27. Total income reached Rs 233.69 crore, against Rs 168.18 crore in Q1 FY27 and Rs 52.11 crore a year earlier. Operating profit was Rs 171.46 crore, up 45.43% quarter on quarter and 852.56% year on year. Profit before tax was Rs 97.12 crore, up 65.68% quarter on quarter and 625.26% year on year.

The reported EBITDA margin was 76.6% and the reported net profit margin was 33%. Earnings per share were Rs 3.54, against a loss per share of Rs 0.68 in Q2 FY26. The company disclosed a Rs 1,000 crore binding multiyear sovereign AI GPU contract running through June 2029. The company is expanding its Blackwell GPU-powered AI factory by 5.4 MW, taking capacity to 14.6 MW. Management has not provided formal financial guidance, focusing commentary on technology adoption, infrastructure expansion and capacity scaling.

The discussion attributed the improvement to higher revenue and scaling of AI-focused cloud services. The growth was linked to rising demand for AI infrastructure and a larger GPU deployment base. MarketsMOJO's cited view was a Hold rating as of the provided market update. The stock was described as moving sideways as of 10 November 2026. The stock fell 3.25% in one day, 30.51% over one month, 1.69% over one week and 14.94% over three months.

Net sales were stated to have expanded at an annualised rate of 74.03%. Operating profit grew at an annualised 100.54%. The company recorded three consecutive quarters of positive results, according to the supplied discussion. Over a three-year period, average earnings per share growth was cited at 10% annually while the share price increased 146% annually. The discussion around Q1 FY27 raised concerns about margin durability and rising interest costs.

Investors will next watch execution of the Rs 1,000 crore sovereign AI contract through June 2029. They will watch progress on the 14.6 MW AI factory capacity target. They will watch whether margins hold as infrastructure scales. With no formal financial guidance, future quarterly revenue, profitability, interest costs and capacity utilisation will be important measures of delivery. The articles leave open the company's capacity utilisation levels and how it has funded its GPU capacity expansion.

stories.Headline: Sheryl Sandberg joins Nscale board to help scale the British data center start-up before its public flotation
stories.Summary:
Sheryl Sandberg joined the board of the British data center start-up Nscale in February 2026 after being recruited by Paul Daversa. The company was founded by Josh Payne, a former cryptocurrency entrepreneur and coal miner who sought Sandberg's help to scale his business. Sandberg originally declined the offer but changed her mind after reading a memo from Payne that reminded her of Mark Zuckerberg. She has since taken a hands-on role with the firm, which is currently preparing for a public flotation.

The upcoming stock market listing could value the company at up to $35bn, though Payne has expressed a long-term goal of reaching a trillion-dollar valuation. Sandberg has been granted shares that could be worth as much as $90m for her efforts in organizing the business. To strengthen the company, she recruited Sir Nick Clegg, Fidji Simo, Justin Osofsky, Caroline Nolan, and Deborah Crawford. The board also includes Susan Decker and Frank Slootman, while the total staff count has grown from 100 to 1,100 employees over the last year.

Sandberg described Payne as a potentially generationally defining leader and stated that she does not intend to join the company full-time. She responded to claims that the firm is losing its British identity by stating that Nscale is a global company that started in London. Some early employees have complained about losing responsibilities, but Sandberg has focused on bringing experienced executives into the organization. She has used her extensive Silicon Valley network to boost the credentials of the young firm.

The company faces significant challenges, including the downfall of its major backer Jensen Huang and a crashed AI stock market. Nscale recently lost a $3.2bn contract with Microsoft due to grid connection problems at its UK site. While it has over $100bn in deals across Norway, Portugal, and the US, it is dealing with floods in West Virginia and scrutiny over Chinese clients in Norway. These tumultuous conditions have led the leadership to consider delaying the planned public flotation.

Articles.Title: Sheryl Sandberg steps in to rescue Britain’s $35bn AI hope - The Telegraph

stories.Headline: Booking.com engineer details 20 years of data and AI platform evolution
stories.Summary:
Jabez Eliezer Manuel, a principal engineer at Booking.com, gave a presentation at QCon London about the 20-year evolution of Booking.com's data management and machine learning platforms. He described how the company scaled its MySQL topologies, retired Hadoop for a cloud architecture, and built model serving and feature stores that handle 400 billion predictions per day. He also covered personalization, interleaved experimentation, and a new agentic AI foundation. The talk was published by InfoQ on November 18, 2026. Manuel brings two decades of software engineering experience to his role.

Booking.com ran its first A/B experiment in 2005, when the company was nine years old and had not yet joined the Priceline group. Visitors to Booking.com are subject to more than 1,000 experiments at any point in time, and the company has run 150,000 experiments or more. The success rate of those experiments is less than 25 percent. In 2005 the MySQL setup was a single master and four slaves, and 15 years later the company operated one of the largest clusters in the world. Every 60 days Booking.com takes its roughly 7,000 instances out, deprovisions them, and reprovisions them, which means some action occurs every three minutes.

The soft limit for a database is 2 terabytes and the hard limit is 10 terabytes, and point queries took less than 350 microseconds. In 2011 Booking.com built two on-premise Hadoop clusters, using HDFS, YARN, MapReduce, Oozie, Spark, Hive, and Sqoop. Manuel said experimentation eliminated HIPPOs and endless internal debates, and that it created a culture of humility in which no experts sat in the room. He said the goal is not to get it right but to learn fast. He said Booking.com made a conscious decision not to fork MySQL but to contribute upstream, and that GTID-based replication exists because the company proposed it.

He said automation was a necessity because no engineer could sit and perform the reprovisioning by hand. He said the company kept databases small so they would fit into the fast storage of a server blade, which let it effectively use MySQL as a cache. Manuel said machine learning in the early era was Perl scripts, statistical and scientific computing libraries from CPAN, and cron jobs, with a deployment strategy of copying the script and praying. He said that setup solved real business problems, including fraud detection, demand forecasting with regression, and recommendations with KNN. He said Hadoop was a shared environment with mono-version, so a data scientist could not use the version they wanted.

He said that when real-time prediction was wanted, the company faked it with lookup tables, enumerating all possible devices and countries and storing the predictions in MySQL. He said that approach obviously does not work for most cases. Manuel said Booking.com impacts billions of travel decisions, and that a bunch of machine learning platforms work behind each of those decisions. He structured his talk into three layers: data management, machine learning engineering, and domain intelligence. He said the data management layer covers database evolution, scale challenges, and the cloud migration.

He said the machine learning layer covers model serving at scale and feature engineering. He said the domain intelligence layer is a high-level tour of the machine learning platforms, with a deep dive into one of them. Manuel said he drives platform engineering for long-term agentic AI memory and next-generation intelligent application infrastructure. He said the company sunset Hadoop for a cloud architecture.

He said the presentation was 40 minutes and 37 seconds long and that slides were available for download. He said he would pick one machine learning platform and do a deep dive so the audience would have something tangible to take away. He said the talk went back two decades in the spirit of QCon's 20th anniversary. More to follow.

stories.Headline: A company fixes CRM sync echo bugs by tracking one owner and value per field
stories.Summary:
The articles describe an internal audit of a CRM sync conducted this autumn, in which a contact's job title would never match between the company's system and the customer's CRM. The company's system filled the CRM with "CTO", its side picked that up, and a rep changed it to "VP". The rep then switched it back to CTO, and the sync saw a value it had sent itself, decided the change was its own write echoing back, and ignored it. From then on the company's system said VP and the CRM said CTO, and nothing anywhere recorded why. The articles say that bug did not use a model, it was the piping.

The articles say every two-way sync must answer, for every incoming change, whether it wrote the value or someone else did. They say Salesforce's out-of-the-box field history tracking is limited to 20 fields per object and stores a user, a timestamp and an old and new value. They say the company watched its production accounts for five weeks, during which about 93% of changes to leads and deals were made by machines. They say the average active account saw about 46 AI-applied changes per week, and a person made zero edits in the median account-week. They cite Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of 4,050 sales professionals, which found that 54% had already used AI agents.

The articles say the company's integrations first decided echoes by author, and that this broke the second it was tested against a real CRM because its integration writes as the person who linked the CRM. They say the fix was to keep one last known value and one owner per synced field, so that an incoming value the company owns and has not seen return is treated as an echo. They give an example record with the title "CTO", owner "ours" and a sent time of 2026-10-01T09:14:00Z. They say the A-to-B-to-A bug occurred because the company used to keep an ever-growing pile of all the values it had ever sent, and that one owner and one value per field fixed it.

The articles say each AI judgement gets its own row in a table holding the model, model version, prompt version, output, confidence, evidence and decision time, with UPDATE and DELETE revoked from the app. They say evidence is stored as pointers, not quotes, so the ledger does not become a duplicate of everyone's email. They say the default rule is that the CRM wins a clash and the clash is logged for an admin to check, and that this is not done yet, with some field edits still logging only which fields changed. They say undo for AI-made records writes forward, marking the creation record reverted and closing the deal with the reason "promoted in error". They say a person who has worked the record blocks a one-click undo.

The articles say the first version of a bulk-sync undo removed every record the link said it had pushed, and the bug was caught in code review before it shipped. They say the solution was to track, for each push, whether a new record was created or an existing one taken, and only delete the former. They say only 0.6% of AI-generated leads were reverted in production data, and none of the hundreds of deals created automatically. They say routine moves apply automatically, lower-confidence readings are suggestions, and the system never closes a lead or marks a deal Won, Lost or Committed by itself. They say outside agents always need a person, one-time approvals are tied to a hash of the tool and its arguments and can be used only once, and irreversible tools never get a standing grant.

The articles say the system moved a deal stage on its own and a person moved it again within a week 2.4% of the time, and for leads 3.2%. They say reps changed AI-filled deal amounts 0.3% of the time, and suggestions the model was less confident in were accepted 59% of the time. They say a caller's timeout was shorter than the downstream deadline and the HTTP client retried a POST after a read timeout, so a write in progress could go out up to three times. They say the fix was to retry only GET and HEAD once a request has been sent, and to record a mutating call that times out as "may have landed" and never re-send it blind. They say the pre-send duplicate screen now matches on the bare domain plus the name, name-only matches are held for a person, and the write waits if the check cannot run.

stories.Headline: OpenText finds 68% of large Australian organisations use AI in production despite visibility gaps
stories.Summary:
OpenText published research on 24 November 2026 showing that many Australian organisations are expanding their use of AI despite gaps in their operational technology, with 68% of large organisations already using AI in production or at enterprise scale. The report, conducted by DataDriven, surveyed 213 technology decision-makers at large Australian organisations across financial services, government, manufacturing, retail, mining, energy and utilities, which together represent combined revenues or budgets of about AUD $1 trillion. The findings point to a divide between AI adoption and the systems needed to support it, because nearly three-quarters of respondents, or 74%, said they face significant visibility gaps across hybrid IT environments, while only 19% said IT and security endpoint data is fully aligned. This suggests many businesses are building more automation on top of fragmented systems, and the research also found that 72% identified legacy system modernisation as a major challenge, 71% cited hybrid and multi-cloud management as a key concern, and 66% pointed to tool sprawl and complexity.

The figures show how AI deployment is colliding with long-running infrastructure issues in large organisations, since hybrid environments, older systems and disconnected tools can make it harder to maintain oversight of assets, dependencies and service performance as automation spreads across operations. Only a small share of respondents reported full alignment between technology and security endpoint data, although 56% described their data as mostly aligned, and that gap matters because incomplete or inconsistent information can reduce confidence in automated decisions and make incident response more difficult. IT service management also emerged as an area under review, with more than three-quarters of respondents, or 76.5%, saying they plan to review or are considering reviewing their IT service management platforms within the next 12 to 18 months, while 91% agreed that a strong knowledge base improves efficiency and first-contact resolution. George Harb, Vice President for Australia and New Zealand at OpenText, said organisations need to strengthen their foundations before expecting stronger returns from AI, noting that adoption is moving quickly but the infrastructure and information needed to support it are not always keeping pace.

He said many organisations are managing a complex mix of legacy systems, cloud platforms and disconnected tools, and that without a clear understanding of how these systems interact and support business services, adding more automation risks creating another layer of complexity. He said Australian organisations need to focus on connecting information, improving operational visibility and ensuring automated decisions are based on accurate, trusted data, and that getting these foundations right is essential to improving service delivery, managing costs and delivering meaningful returns on AI investment. The research adds to a wider debate in Australia over whether AI investment is moving faster than operational reform, and while adoption rates indicate that many large organisations have already moved beyond pilot programs, the survey suggests basic issues such as data consistency, visibility and system modernisation remain unresolved in many cases. For sectors such as government, financial services, energy and mining, these issues have practical consequences because complex operating environments can make it harder to trace how digital services depend on one another, and as AI becomes more embedded in core processes, the need for reliable operational information is likely to become more pressing.

Articles.Title: Australian firms race ahead with AI amid system gaps - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Gartner survey finds CFOs prioritise efficiency and cost optimisation for 2027
stories.Summary:
A survey of 100 finance leaders by Gartner found that chief financial officers are prioritising finance efficiency, cost optimisation and stronger data foundations for the first half of 2027, according to a report published on 23 November 2026. Improving finance process efficiency was the most frequently selected priority, with 52 per cent of CFOs placing it among their top five, while optimising enterprise costs followed at 50 per cent. Strengthening financial and enterprise data foundations rounded out the top three themes named by respondents. The findings suggest finance functions are trying to balance longstanding operational demands with the impact of rapid AI adoption on planning and execution.

The survey found low preparedness to execute in three of the five most-cited priority areas, namely improving finance process efficiency, improving financial and enterprise data quality, and building digital and AI skills within finance. Finance leaders named three main barriers to delivery, with acquiring and developing AI talent for finance teams ranked as the leading challenge, followed by driving cross-functional execution against enterprise strategy and harmonising finance transformation, technology planning and AI plans. Optimising the finance technology vendor stack ranked at the bottom of priority lists, even though Gartner considers it more important as companies seek to control AI-related spending. The report says process improvement built around mapping existing processes may give way to continuous redesign shaped by AI tools and automation.

Mallory Barg Bulman, a Senior Director Analyst at Gartner, said the rapid acceleration of AI in the past year has changed the typical CFO execution playbook in more traditional priority areas, leading to reduced confidence in areas such as improving finance processes. She said optimising the finance technology vendor stack should be a higher priority for most finance leaders because it is essential to managing costs, preserving flexibility and ensuring AI investments deliver measurable value. She said CFOs still face a challenging environment shaped by persistent inflation, geopolitical uncertainty, higher costs of capital and rising AI investments, while boards and investors put increasing pressure on finance leaders to demonstrate clear, measurable returns. She said a more deliberate approach to vendor-stack optimisation can help CFOs control AI costs as adoption expands, reduce dependence on individual technology vendors and maintain flexibility as the technology landscape evolves.

stories.Headline: PinnacleQM launches a 50-page website with an AI assurance practice and product pages
stories.Summary:
PinnacleQM, an Australian quality engineering and software testing consultancy, launched a new website with a dedicated AI assurance section, expanding its online presence from a six-page brochure site to a library of more than 50 pages, according to a report published by IT Brief Australia on 24 November 2026. The company created separate pages for its services, platforms, industries and proprietary products, with the stated aim of giving technology buyers, programme leaders and procurement teams a clearer view of its work. At the centre of the site is an AI assurance practice page covering six areas: AI business assurance, AI production readiness, agentic AI assurance, continuous AI assurance, AI-enabled quality engineering, and AI governance and assurance advisory. These services are organised around the Pinnacle AI Assurance Framework, which the company says is designed to test AI systems for accuracy, reliability, security and governance before and after production use.

The site also gives standalone pages to three in-house products for the first time: QMFactory, described as a quality management console for test planning, execution and reporting; Enginuity, a no-code AI test automation platform for plain-language test creation and scaled execution; and INsight, a set of consulting tools for delivery maturity assessment and improvement. A Trials and Demos page was added as well, allowing organisations to request demonstrations using their own systems. The site includes service pages covering consulting and advisory, test automation, performance engineering, cyber security and penetration testing, test environment and data management, user acceptance testing, DevSecOps and continuous testing, observability, independent assurance, and managed testing services. Beyond AI-related material, it includes pages on enterprise systems including SAP and S/4HANA, Salesforce, Microsoft Dynamics and Power Apps, Oracle, and IBM Maximo testing, and industry sections covering banking and finance, government, healthcare, natural resources, energy and utilities, transport, and software vendors.

Gary Jenn, Managing Director of PinnacleQM, linked the launch to questions he hears from senior technology leaders, saying he has spent most of his career alongside CIOs and programme directors on IT change that cannot fail, and that their question has never changed: whether the company can show it works. He said the new website is the company's answer, backed by real results, so buyers can understand its capability before the first conversation rather than after it. Jenn also said AI now comes up within the first five minutes of almost every conversation he has with technology leaders, and that it is moving from pilots into production faster than most assurance practices can keep up, with models drifting, agents taking actions on their own, and the same prompt producing a different answer tomorrow. He said the AI testing and assurance practice gives organisations independent evidence that their AI systems are accurate, secure and properly governed before they go live and that they stay that way afterwards.

Niranjan Limbachiya, Director of PinnacleQM, said the website was built through collaboration across consulting, delivery, design and development teams, describing it as the work of many hands and saying he is proud of every one of them. He said the consulting and delivery teams gave the company the substance, while the design and development team, working closely with partners, brought its vision to life, and that the site was built for the way people now find quality engineering and AI assurance services: through search, AI assistants and peer recommendations. PinnacleQM is part of Pinnacle Group and is headquartered in Perth, with offices in Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney, and it works in software testing, quality engineering and digital business assurance for government and enterprise customers. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the launch itself.

stories.Headline: Steve Agi says Australian firms lack internal execution, not AI access, for measurable results
stories.Summary:
Steve Agi, founder of C51 Consulting, wrote in an article published by IT Brief Australia on 24 November 2026 that Australian businesses do not lack ways to buy artificial intelligence but lack the internal changes needed to get a measurable result from it. He said businesses can subscribe to a chatbot, generate marketing content, automate customer messages or commission an agent in days, yet access to capability and the ability to use it well are different things. He argued that software can accelerate a good process but can just as easily accelerate confusion, and that the question facing many Australian businesses is no longer whether they can use AI but what needs to change inside the business for AI to produce a measurable result. Agi used a service business that responds slowly to enquiries as an example, saying enquiries arrive through four channels, nobody owns the initial response, staff enter customer details differently and follow-ups depend on whoever remembers.

He said the first problem there is a broken handover rather than a missing AI assistant, and that an automated response would only help after the business decides which enquiries matter, what information must be collected, who takes ownership and when a human must step in. He said the same pattern appears in finance, administration, sales and service delivery, and that organisations should start by asking which task is wasting time, which decision is delayed and which outcome needs to improve rather than which AI product to purchase. Agi said AI changes the work people must supervise, so a business still needs to decide what a system is permitted to do, how errors are detected and who is accountable when something goes wrong, which matters more as tools move from generating suggestions to taking actions. He said leaders should ask what data a system uses, whether staff can see what happened, whether a person can override it, when the workflow stops for approval and who checks whether it delivers the intended result.

He said smaller businesses have a tighter margin for error, that a subscription saving no meaningful time is another overhead and that an automation creating extra checking work may make a team busier, so a useful first project should be narrow, observable and tied to an existing business measure. Agi set out five questions for business owners before their next AI purchase, covering what work is slow, inconsistent or missed, who owns the process from start to finish, what information is needed and whether it is usable, which steps can safely be automated and which need human approval, and what will be measured before and after the change. He said the winners will not necessarily be the organisations that adopt the most tools but those that can identify a problem, assign responsibility, test a solution and prove work is being done better. He said the next stage of AI adoption is less about access and more about execution, and that this is where the commercial value will be decided.

Articles.Title: Australia doesn't have an AI adoption problem. It has an execution problem - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Nudge Security finds firms spread AI agents across many platforms
stories.Summary:
Nudge Security published research showing that more than half of organisations using AI agents run them across multiple platforms, with the findings based on telemetry from customer environments rather than surveys or self-reported responses. Among organisations using AI agents, half run seven or more and more than four in 10 run more than 10, according to the data, which also found the agents are spread across a range of business platforms rather than concentrated in a single system. The report found that 74% of organisations have at least one Anthropic integration and 67% have an OpenAI integration, with links reaching systems such as email, code repositories, chat and documents. At least 91% of organisations in the dataset used both OpenAI and Anthropic, while Anthropic adoption rose from 77.8% in January to 94.5%, and by October 2026 half of organisations had 27 or more AI tools in their environments. Among organisations with at least one AI browser extension, 67% had Grammarly and 65% had Claude installed, giving those tools visibility into the contents of web pages viewed by employees, and 18% of observed prompts included pasted content or an uploaded file, compared with 17% in an earlier report.

The report argues that much of the resulting risk sits outside traditional security controls, because agents are increasingly embedded in project management systems, customer relationship management software, chat tools and automation platforms, often operating with the access rights of the employee who created them. It recommends that security teams focus less on maintaining lists of approved tools and more on understanding what employees have connected to company systems, identifying where agents are created, who created them and what access rights they inherit. It also highlights OAuth grants as an area for review, saying organisations should check which AI tools employees have authorised, what data each connection can access and whether those permissions are still needed, and it says browser extensions that can read page content should also be reviewed. OpenAI still received more than half of all observed prompts, but its share fell from 67% to 55% as employees spread activity across a wider mix of tools, which the report said suggests prompt traffic is diversifying even as overall use remains concentrated among major providers.

Jaime Blasco, Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer at Nudge Security, said the spread of agent-building functions inside everyday workplace software had changed the visibility challenge for security teams, saying the platforms teams use every day are becoming agent platforms whether or not anyone decided they should be. He said the project tracker, the CRM and the chat tool each now let an employee build something that acts on their behalf, with their access, continuously, and that the question for security teams is no longer whether that is allowed but whether they know it is happening. Blasco said he expected the problem to get harder rather than easier, because every platform teams use is adding agent-building features and each one makes it simpler to hand an agent a person's access. He said that means the gap between what an organisation's identity provider knows about and what is actually acting on its data is going to keep widening.

stories.Headline: SandboxAQ adds onboarding, chat and app connectors to its Switch Rooms workplace AI platform
stories.Summary:
SandboxAQ expanded its Switch Rooms platform for workplace AI agents, adding onboarding, in-app conversations and links to common work software, according to an announcement reported by IT Brief Australia on 24 November 2026. The release is aimed at teams that want to move from individual use of AI agents to shared workflows across a business. It includes a personal onboarding assistant, direct and group conversations inside the Switch Console, and connectors for Google Workspace, Jira, Confluence, GitHub and Datadog. Switch Rooms is designed as a shared environment where staff and AI agents work from the same pool of conversations, documents and decisions, which is meant to reduce the need to repeat instructions or carry context between tools. The update adds a guided setup process in which new users get an onboarding assistant called switch-buddy when they first open the Switch Console, and it can help create agents and rooms, connect messaging applications and answer questions about the system.

The console has been reworked so teams can start conversations with both people and agents inside the application, with each conversation backed by a Switch room that keeps the same history, tools and shared context through connected messaging services. Slack, Microsoft Teams and Telegram integrations can now be installed in a few clicks without configuring bot tokens or application programming interfaces. Newly added connectors cover Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides and Calendar, as well as Atlassian Jira and Confluence, GitHub repositories and pull requests, and Datadog metrics, logs, traces and incidents. Each agent acts through the identity of the employee who connected the service, with read or write permissions assigned for each one, and administrators can decide which connectors are allowed across a workspace. SandboxAQ gave the example of a software incident investigation in which an agent could be given access to Datadog logs, GitHub repositories and a Jira ticket, with staff and agents discussing the findings in a shared room that leaves a record of the investigation and decisions.

Organisations can manage membership, roles and connected messaging applications through a central interface, while a new devices view shows where agents are running, their status and the device assigned to each one. The company said users can change AI agents, models or vendors at any time and keep the context their team has built. SandboxAQ, which emerged from Google and has worked in quantum security as well as artificial intelligence, is positioning Switch Rooms as a way to address fragmented AI use inside companies, where more employees adopting different tools and agents makes it harder to preserve a common record of work and oversee what systems can access. The release builds on existing Switch Trust controls, in which messages are checked before delivery and policy violations are blocked, redacted or flagged according to customer settings. By combining shared rooms, administrative controls and connectors to widely used workplace software, SandboxAQ is seeking to give teams a single place to manage those interactions while keeping control over the context their agents rely on.
