stories.Headline: Eugene library assistant Elly Hutchinson designs a workshop that helps about 30 attendees opt out of AI on their devices
stories.Summary:
The Eugene Public Library hosted a free public workshop titled “AI-nxiety: an Opt-Out Workshop” on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, at its downtown branch. About 30 attendees gathered at the library to gain information about how to opt out of AI on their devices. The event was created and designed by the library and was based on giving people agency in how they use AI. Many of the attendees were older adults, and the event was the library’s first AI workshop. Library assistant Elly Hutchinson came up with the idea and designed the packets that accompanied the workshop.

The hourlong event was a mostly self-guided hands-on workshop rather than a presentation-style format. Attendees were given a choice of two packets supplied by the library, one for Apple users and one for Android users, which divided them into two table groups. The packets guided people on how they could opt out of AI with Siri, in their preferred email system, their device’s operating system, on their preferred browser and on various social media apps. Hutchinson said the packets carry a “heavy disclaimer” that they aren’t comprehensive and that both AI and settings can change. Four library staff and volunteers were there to help attendees who ran into speed bumps along the way.

Marsha Sutherland, adult services supervisor at the library’s downtown branch, said the library was “not taking a stance on the pros and cons (of AI).” She said the event was really about giving people agency and reminding them that they can opt out of certain AI features on their devices. Sutherland said she was not surprised by the demographic or the large turnout for the library’s first AI workshop. Hutchinson said patrons had been asking a lot of questions about Google’s AI Overviews, the summaries that now appear at the top of search results. Hutchinson said the openness of the format was intentional, citing that various folks might have different needs regarding AI on their devices, and she hopes to hold the workshop again.

Janel Erickson, 67, and her husband, Dave Reuter, 70, attended because they were curious about AI and said they use the AI summaries in search results but otherwise not at all. They said they have many friends who use AI, including their two adult sons and their wives, who all use AI at work. They said they’d like to see more events like this and suggested the library tell people in the event description to update their operating systems beforehand and that the workshop is hands-on rather than a formal presentation. William Herbert, 80, and his wife, Anna Herbert, 74, attended because they see AI becoming more present in their lives, and Anna said she feels overwhelmed by all the information.

The Herberts said they’d come back for another event but that the event didn’t help them achieve what they wanted, though they thought it was “good,” and Anna said AI is “a waste of my time.” Sutherland said that if folks weren’t able to make the event on Nov. 19, the library holds a tech help drop-in session roughly twice a month. She said the event was more of an AI baseline on how to turn it off, and drop-in tech help is just a little broader. The workshop was open to the public and free, and thirty people showed up.

Hutchinson said the hourlong event wasn’t a presentation-style workshop but more of a chance for folks to ask questions while following along via a packet that the library designed. The packets divided content into either Android or Apple. Hutchinson hopes to hold the workshop again. Erickson and Reuter said they’d like to see more events like this.

The Herberts said they’d come back for another event. Sutherland said the library holds a tech help drop-in session roughly twice a month for folks who weren’t able to make the event on Nov. 19. The articles do not say whether another AI workshop has been scheduled. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Guterres urges UN members to start talks on a multilateral AI risk management framework
stories.Summary:
UN Secretary-General António Guterres on Monday called on Member States to begin discussions on a multilateral framework for managing the risks of artificial intelligence, speaking to reporters at the close of the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety in Barbados, which the UN co-hosted with Barbados. Guterres, who leaves office at the end of December, said protections against AI risks remain fragmented and that governments are too often playing catch-up, and he warned that the technology is driving what he called the biggest transfer of power in the history of humankind. He issued what he described as a call from Bridgetown for Member States to begin discussions on a multilateral AI Risk Management Framework, saying a common foundation for AI safety is needed. He said the framework would include shared safety measures, common approaches to testing, clear safeguards and standards, basic transparency requirements, independent evaluation and oversight of advanced AI models, and support so that every country can put them into practice. Guterres said some leading AI developers are themselves sounding the alarm about increasingly powerful systems, and that recent technological outages and cyberattacks have exposed the vulnerabilities of digital systems the world depends on, with AI amplifying the threats as systems behave in ways even their developers did not always anticipate.

He said the promise of AI is real, from strengthening health systems to accelerating scientific discovery, but that the risks of unchecked digital technology are growing just as fast, describing the dangers as technology without accountability, capability without safeguards and power without responsibility. In a fireside conversation with Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley, he said power is moving from States and governing institutions to a small number of companies and persons, a shift for which institutions created after the Second World War, including the UN, are today not adequately equipped, and he called for deep reform of global governance while insisting the UN has the legitimacy to lead. He noted that at the first Global Dialogue on AI Governance in July, 111 of the participating countries had never taken part in any discussion on AI, and he warned that the capacity to weaponise AI is concentrated in two countries and a limited number of companies, reiterating his support for banning autonomous weapons and calling the idea that a machine can choose who and where to kill absolutely unacceptable. Mottley said small States often do not have the opportunity to share their perspective on the rules that affect them, and asked whether a frontier AI lab should have to pay if one of its AI agents hacked a bank in Barbados and whether her Government should have a kill switch to cut off access to its models in an emergency, she answered yes, saying it has to be a condition of sale that the buyer is capable of saying no more. She also warned that the horse has already bolted from the stables and that only governments willing to regulate and legislate can rein in the concentration of power.

In a video message, French President Emmanuel Macron said the Paris Call for AI Security had been signed by 18 Heads of State and government and 11 AI leaders, and argued that agreeing to its principles should be a condition for access to markets, while Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith said in some ways AI was moving faster than the speed of safety but that AI diffusion, especially in the global South, needed to speed up. Asked what people should take away from the summit, Guterres said the evolution of AI models cannot go faster than the capacity to control their safety, and that AI must help reduce, not increase, the inequalities growing in today's world, adding that the ability of countries to manage AI risks remains deeply unequal and that solutions must be as borderless as the risks. To narrow that gap he has proposed a Global Fund for AI Capacity-Building, and he said the summit could help strengthen every country's capacity to test whether AI systems work safely in local contexts. He pointed to a new thematic brief from the UN-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, released on Sunday, which highlights the value of countries testing AI systems in their own languages, and panel member Vukosi Marivate of the University of Pretoria said AI models still perform far worse and can be less safe across a wide range of tongues, from African languages to Caribbean creoles, though over 1,000 of them already have the foundations needed to close that gap. Guterres said artificial intelligence should be shaped by humanity, with humanity and for all humanity.

stories.Headline: Researchers find AI matches expert pathologists in cancer diagnosis across multiple malignancies
stories.Summary:
Researchers Umang K. Agrawal, Sakshi Jaiswal, and Deepanshu Singh published a comprehensive scientific review in Surgical and Experimental Pathology, reported on November 23, 2026. The review found that artificial intelligence algorithms are demonstrating diagnostic accuracy comparable to expert pathologists across diverse malignancies. These malignancies include breast, prostate, colorectal, lung, and gastrointestinal cancers. Advances in computational pathology and deep learning are redefining the interface between surgical oncologists and pathologists. The review describes how routine digitized tissue slides are converted into diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive datasets.

The review covers the transition from conventional microscopy of physical glass slides to digital whole-slide imaging systems. Modern whole-slide scanners digitize conventional glass slides at extremely high resolutions, preserving sub-cellular details comparable to high-magnification optical microscopes. Deep convolutional neural networks analyze these massive image datasets using layered hierarchical computational structures. Early network layers typically detect elementary morphological features, including tissue borders, cellular edges, and simple textures. Deeper neural layers progressively synthesize these basic inputs into complex pathological structures, capturing glandular architecture, nuclear atypia, and stromal interactions.

The review states that multi-institutional clinical validations, such as landmark investigations by Campanella and colleagues, showed deep learning models can achieve near-expert diagnostic sensitivity. Those models identified prostate carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and metastatic breast cancer cells within complex whole-slide preparations. In breast cancer, deep learning models automated scoring of tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic figures defined by the Nottingham Histologic Score. In prostate oncology, convolutional algorithms evaluated glandular patterns across entire biopsy cores, matching the grading fidelity of experienced uropathologists. In benchmark studies such as the CAMELYON challenge, automated models matched expert pathologists in identifying nodal breast cancer metastases.

The review reports that computational platforms can accurately infer microsatellite instability in colorectal and gastric cancers directly from standard tissue sections. In non-small cell lung cancer, neural networks have accurately predicted epidermal growth factor receptor mutations from routine histology. In colorectal cancer, algorithms successfully identified KRAS and BRAF mutational signatures. In breast and gastric malignancies, deep learning platforms can evaluate human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 status from morphological patterns alone.

Deep learning algorithms trained on whole-slide images rapidly scan extensive tissue perimeters, identifying invasive carcinoma and ductal carcinoma in situ at margins in breast, head and neck, and gastrointestinal operations. The review states that histopathological evaluation has long functioned as the indispensable cornerstone of clinical cancer management. Traditional workflows have historically depended on pathologists manually scanning glass slides to identify atypical tissue structures, count mitotic events, and estimate margin clearances. Modern oncological care increasingly demands individualized precision, placing substantial strain on pathology laboratories confronted with escalating caseloads, diagnostic complexity, and documented observer variability.

Traditional machine learning frameworks required labor-intensive manual feature engineering to isolate variables like nuclear pleomorphism and glandular morphology. Modern deep learning architectures bypass manual feature extraction entirely, learning complex diagnostic representations directly from raw digital image pixels. The review states that significant methodological, regulatory, and ethical hurdles must be resolved before artificial intelligence can achieve ubiquitous integration within routine clinical environments. Training robust deep learning algorithms requires diverse, multi-institutional histological datasets.

Models trained on homogenous institutional archives frequently experience performance degradation when exposed to external variations in tissue fixation, staining intensity, or optical scanner specifications. The review describes the black-box nature of deep neural networks as posing serious transparency challenges for surgical and pathological teams requiring clear morphological reasoning. Addressing these barriers necessitates explainable AI frameworks. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers in Leipzig develop an AI cytometry method that profiles honey pollen in minutes with 98 percent accuracy
stories.Summary:
A research team developed an automated method to profile honey pollen using artificial intelligence and multispectral image-based flow cytometry. This interdisciplinary group included members from the UFZ and iDiv in Leipzig. The study was published in the journal npj Science of Food on November 23, 2026. The system identifies pollen grains in honey samples within minutes. It achieves ninety-eight percent agreement with traditional microscopic examinations.

The process uses DIN laboratory instructions and a hydrodynamic channel to separate pollen into single particles. High-speed hardware captures images at rates up to two thousand particles per second. The system uses laser excitation to create optical signatures for rapeseed, sweet chestnut, sunflower, phacelia, lime, and cornflower. Testing involved thirteen authentic single-flower honey samples and ten mixed honey samples. The Lower Saxony State Office for Consumer Protection and Food Safety in Celle provided manual benchmarks.

Lead author Franziska Walther stated that manual evaluation requires extensive taxonomic expertise and substantial financial expense. She noted that traditional methods typically take thirty to sixty minutes per sample. Dr. Susanne Dunker explained that rapid diagnostics provide beekeepers with critical ecological insights. These insights concern the diversity and nutritional adequacy of floral resources. The researchers claim the system addresses labor and expertise constraints in commercial apiculture.

The system affects quality assurance laboratories and the beekeeping community by offering a rapid pre-screening mechanism. Specialists from the Julius Kühn Institute in Braunschweig helped assemble the reference library of microscopic images. Computational scientists from the Ilmenau University of Technology engineered the machine learning models. The method allows facilities to determine if a batch justifies formal microscopic certification. It reduces the time to identify over one thousand grains to less than ten minutes.

Six years ago, a team led by Dr. Susanne Dunker created a cytometry framework for ecological dynamics. This original framework examined plant-pollinator networks and pollen forecasting models. The current investigation was conducted under the NutriBee research initiative regarding bee health. The Federal Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Regional Identity supported the work. The Federal Office for Agriculture and Food managed the research project.

The authors emphasize that the method is a preliminary pre-screening tool rather than a total replacement for microscopy. Future computational investigations will clarify how different machine learning architectures process ambiguous classification boundaries. Existing models occasionally generate minor variations in their categorical assignments. The articles do not state when the system will be fully commercialized. They leave open whether the system will expand beyond the six tested plant species.

stories.Headline: San José State IT staff ask workers for pain points to guide AI adoption
stories.Summary:
San José State University’s IT office launched its AdoptAI Champions series, starting by asking staff what obstacles make their jobs difficult, according to EdTech Magazine on November 23, 2026. Vincent J. Del Casino Jr., provost and senior vice president of academic affairs at SJSU, said the effort did not start with the technology but with the questions. The series gives employees a place to bring their workflow problems to IT, matching a pain point to a specific solution rather than rolling out generic AI tools. The approach shapes how the university handles artificial intelligence adoption across campus, from staff workflows and faculty development to student use. Del Casino said the strategy is a work in progress but that a few years into the effort he has clear advice for other institutions.

SJSU has a policy requiring every instructor to address AI use in their syllabus, stating how it can and cannot be used in their courses. AI ambassadors now work in every college and most academic programs, running train-the-trainer sessions. The Center for Faculty Excellence in Teaching Innovation shows instructors how to use the latest AI tools and addresses the challenges that come with each. Three years ago, SJSU set a goal that at least 50% of tenure-track hires be at the intersection of AI, machine learning, science and technology studies, spanning education, health and the social sciences. The university has created a suite of curricular and co-curricular learning experiences for students, including a partnership with IBM to deliver its SkillsBuild program.

Del Casino said that often when these kinds of disruptions come in, many faculty and staff are left to just figure it out, so SJSU has built an infrastructure of faculty support. He said the staff conversation is really an agentic AI conversation as much as a generative one. He said it is important to him that SJSU provides space for the conversation and debate without making institutionwide decisions on the matter. He said there are those who are still really skeptical, and rightly so, because there is a lot to be skeptical about, but they are just asked to talk to the students about it. He said this is going to be messy for a long time and that the point of higher education is actually to stay messy and let people struggle.

Del Casino said the sentiment among some students is that everyone should have some basic training in AI literacy and that the university should mandate it. He said others are as skeptical as faculty and are really concerned about what this is going to do to them socially, culturally, politically and economically. The Writing Center created something called the AI Writers Toolbox, generated by faculty and staff in response to students asking how they would be allowed to use these tools. As an Adobe Creative Campus, SJSU trains students on creative tools, which leads to further ethical conversations about generative AI. According to Del Casino, the fastest-growing student group is the Responsible Computing Club, with more than 300 members.

Del Casino said most of the AI technology SJSU uses is tied to systemwide contracts through California State University. He said one of the most important questions he asks when any tech company comes in is how many full-time employees he needs to support what they want to sell him. At a Cal State campus with limited resources, he sees AI as a way to free experienced staff from process-heavy work so they can spend more time with students and faculty. He said you do not solve that with agentic AI but support it with agentic AI, if it is right and if you are asking the right questions. He said the goal is to make sure everyone on campus, students, faculty and staff, knows how to use technology effectively.

Del Casino said that when you do that, you are going to have an incredibly well-trained student group, and students are going to go out in the world and hopefully bring that mentality to bear in the broader market. He said the students are going to push the university to do this, and it should listen to them so that they have a world that they feel really good about. The university is looking to embed an AI literacy course into Canvas so students can complete it at their own pace. Faculty are embedding AI education into their curriculum, and individual departments are also tackling the issue. The articles do not say what further steps SJSU will take or when the strategy will be complete.

stories.Headline: Historian Brad Bertelli finds ChatGPT omits Oliver M. Woods from Tavernier history
stories.Summary:
Brad Bertelli wrote in Keys Weekly on November 23, 2026, that artificial intelligence is changing the landscape of social media with stories and AI-generated images. He said he is not in love with artificial intelligence after two decades of reading old books, magazines, documents and newspaper stories. He wrote that researching and writing a document using AI is an exercise of search, copy and paste. He said ChatGPT and its cousins were trained to gather facts and figures and are efficient. He wrote that he asked ChatGPT why Tavernier was important and who helped develop the community.

Bertelli wrote that ChatGPT offered a fair synopsis and could create a decent overview of the community's development in a minute or two. He said it mentioned that the original Tavernier community was known as a farming community called Planter. He said it mentioned early families like the Alburys and Lowes and Hugh McKenzie, who played a pivotal role as an early developer. He wrote that one name missing was Oliver M. Woods, the man who helped make McKenzie's work possible. He said that once his column goes online, AI and its programs will likely start inserting Woods' name into the digital record.

Bertelli said he moved to Plantation Key in 2001 and his first job was teaching at the Florida Keys Community College annex at Coral Shores High School. He wrote that if he were still teaching, he would have little confidence in his students' ability to research, write and create original work. He said the temptation of AI seems too great and it can become a game of cat and mouse. He wrote that schools subject student papers to programs that try to ferret out AI incorporated into their work. He said savvy students can use programs to cover the AI, and while the mouse might get away from the cat, it misses an opportunity to learn.

Bertelli wrote that for the last 13 years he has made nearly daily history posts on social media, for eight years while curating Islamorada's Keys History & Discovery Center and for the last five supporting his Florida Keys History with Brad Bertelli group. He said he used to get incensed when people took his posts, cut, pasted and reposted them without credit to the source. He wrote that at least then he knew people were getting authentic history. He said he spends a lot of time looking through old pictures and AI interpretations of the idea of an image are tough to take seriously. He wrote that photographs capture a moment in time and their details have a richness a computer-generated image of an idea can't match.

Bertelli wrote that he drove to Marathon last weekend to give a talk about the history of Tavernier for the ladies of the Florida Keys Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution. He said he asked ChatGPT about Tavernier to see what it had to say about something he knows a thing or two about. He wrote that Woods lived in Chicago with his wife, Josephine, their daughter, Peggy, and two sons, Dexter and Delmer. He said that around 1924 Ollie and his family moved to South Florida, where he began developing properties after the Florida land boom when many lots fell into default and were sold at rock-bottom prices. He wrote that Woods bought in South Miami and the Upper Keys, focusing on Key Largo and Plantation Key.

Bertelli wrote that the Woods family moved to Tavernier in the late 1920s, where Woods developed several subdivisions including Olliewood, an icehouse, the Tavernier drugstore, the Tavernier Lumber & Supply Company, the Tavernier Grocery Company, the Keys Theater and the Keys Utilities Company. He said Woods persuaded the Standard Oil Company to build bulk oil tanks and served as the company's agent until his death. He wrote that McKenzie moved to the Miami area in the 1920s and taught at the Shenandoah School, and after a honeymoon in Tavernier he and his wife Hazel moved there in 1928 with reportedly $5 between them. He said Woods died at 47 in 1934 after a heart attack while driving along Ponce de Leon Avenue in Coral Gables, and his wife Josephine was in the car. He wrote that after his death the Woods family signed the properties over to Mac, and that AI is not going anywhere and will be running the show long after he has passed on.

stories.Headline: Researchers review linking AI predictions to automated biofoundries for microbial engineering
stories.Summary:
Automated biofoundries are being linked to artificial intelligence predictions for experimental microbial engineering, according to a review published in Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology. The review was written by Youngjoon Lee, Seung-Goo Lee and colleagues from the Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology and affiliated academic institutions. The review was reported by bioengineer.org on November 23, 2026. The authors systematically evaluated how artificial intelligence algorithms can be coordinated with high-throughput biofoundries. Their survey assesses recent advances spanning biosynthetic pathway design, protein and enzyme engineering, and genome-scale metabolic modeling.

The review examines biofoundries that combine automated liquid handling, robotic cultivation and laboratory information management systems to execute standardized experimental workflows. It describes the Galaxy-SynBioCAD platform, which uses an XGBoost classifier and recovered literature-supported or expert-selected routes among its top ten candidates in 83 percent of test cases, compared with 58 percent using additive scoring. It describes READRetro, which attained a 93.2 percent search success rate across 368 plant natural product pathways. It describes an autonomous platform combining ESM-2, EVmutation and low-N regression that optimized Arabidopsis thaliana halide methyltransferase, delivering a 16-fold increase in ethyltransferase activity and a 90-fold shift in substrate preference toward ethyl iodide within four weeks. The same platform optimized a phytase variant to achieve a 26.3-fold improvement in specific activity.

The authors emphasize that computational algorithms can prioritize actionable genetic designs, but transforming predictive models into high-titer production strains depends on systematic experimental evaluation and standardized data generation. They state that the central obstacle confronting artificial intelligence in metabolic engineering stems from the contextual complexity of biological systems. They note that publicly available datasets are frequently scarce, heterogeneous and difficult to reproduce across disparate laboratories. They caution that structure prediction confidence metrics do not correlate with mutational effects on catalytic activity or cellular stability, making direct experimental testing indispensable. They conclude that a pronounced gap remains between computational designs and commercially viable biomanufacturing metrics.

The review states that most published studies evaluate artificial intelligence models primarily through in silico benchmark scores. It states that experimentally validated strains frequently demonstrate relative improvements over parent strains while remaining below the absolute titers, yields and volumetric productivities required for industrial deployment. It states that training algorithms solely on intended genetic designs without verifying in vivo biological consequences risks learning misleading genotype-phenotype correlations. The review describes an engineered syringic acid pathway in yeast that yielded upstream intermediates but no final product.

It describes support vector machine models that identified aromatic acetaldehyde synthase and phenylpyruvate decarboxylase activities, allowing construction of an alternative pathway branch in Escherichia coli that produced 356 micromolar norcoclaurine, 240 micromolar N-methylcoclaurine and 74.9 micromolar reticuline. The review gives background on metabolic engineering, which it says provides a foundational biological platform for synthesizing valuable chemicals, therapeutic proteins and advanced biopolymers directly from renewable resources. It says broad industrial implementation remains constrained by inefficient biosynthetic pathways, suboptimal enzyme kinetics and prolonged design-build-test-learn cycles. It says cellular phenotypes emerge from intricate, non-linear interactions connecting heterologous pathway enzymes, endogenous host regulatory networks, dynamic metabolic fluxes and precise cultivation environments.

It says enzyme activities and metabolic behaviors are sensitive to shifting growth conditions. It says deep sequence databases and physical constraints enabled rapid breakthroughs in structural biology, creating challenges distinct from those in metabolic engineering. The review describes generative models such as ESM3 and ProGen that have synthesized functional proteins, including an artificial fluorescent protein with 58 percent sequence identity to natural counterparts and active lysozymes sharing as little as 31.4 percent identity with known sequences. It describes family-wide structural hallucination that generated artificial luciferases with no sequence or structural homology to natural enzymes, yielding the synthetic catalyst LuxSit-i.

It notes that designing fully de novo enzymes for complex metabolic pathways remains difficult because intracellular catalysis requires sub-angstrom positioning of transition states alongside sustained stability in crowded cytoplasmic environments. It describes the Automated Recommendation Tool, which employed probabilistic machine learning ensembles and active learning across six automated biofoundry cycles in Pseudomonas putida, evaluating more than 400 combinatorial CRISPR interference designs from a theoretical space of 800,000 to achieve a fivefold increase in isoprenol titer, reaching 580 milligrams per liter. The articles leave open what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: US and China face obstacles to establishing AI arms control agreements
stories.Summary:
The United States and China dominate the development of artificial intelligence technology which has various military applications. These two large countries are currently engaged in a bitter rivalry of global scope. They both invest heavily in improving these weapons and expanding their supplies. This behavior has led to an arms race between the two nations.

The author suggests that the two rivals might find common ground in controlling this technology. He notes that in 2026 the technical possibilities of AI cannot be accurately foreseen. The American government cannot arbitrarily take control of the private sector that owns AI. This differs from the 1972 agreement where the United States and Soviet Union limited defensive systems.

Michael Mandelbaum argues that AI arms control is unlikely because the technology is not yet mature. He states that the uncertainty surrounding AI makes governments less inclined to impose limits. He believes that limiting AI could impose very high costs on the whole of society. He also claims that the Chinese government has a record of breaking its promises.

The author notes that private companies in the United States are affected by these developments. He mentions that the people of Hong Kong can testify to the record of the Communist Party. He argues that open-weight AI models from China are spreading rapidly to other countries. This proliferation makes the prospects for a nonproliferation treaty very poor.

The author compares AI to the history of nuclear weapons from World War II to the 1970s. He explains that nuclear weapons were easier to track using satellites launched in the 1960s. He notes that nuclear fuel is difficult to obtain, while AI is more accessible. He mentions the 1968 Nonproliferation Treaty as a successful example of nuclear control.

The author suggests that both governments will take necessary steps to preclude a maximal disaster. He mentions the hypothetical paper clip problem where a machine destroys humans to make clips. He argues that the Chinese regime will suppress any danger to its own rule. He notes that the United States government would act to preserve the republic.

stories.Headline: Innovaccer integrates Grok Voice into its Gravity Voice AI agents for healthcare
stories.Summary:
Innovaccer said on November 23, 2026 that it had integrated Grok Voice into its Gravity Voice AI agents, combining the platform's healthcare intelligence data and workflow infrastructure with Grok Voice at scale. The company said Grok Voice is trained on real phone audio, is HIPAA-eligible and is available in more than 25 languages. Innovaccer said the integration is now live for customers. CEO and co-founder Abhinav Shashank said in a statement that healthcare voice AI is moving from answering questions to doing work. Innovaccer said patient voice interactions have grown from roughly 250,000 to more than five million since its launch six months ago.

The company said it has tripled referral intakes, helped organizations book significantly more appointments and reduced documentation times by 90% per case. Shashank said the company scaled from hundreds of thousands of interactions to more than five million and showed measurable results in appointments, referrals and engagement. He said that by leveraging Grok Voice the company is bringing frontier intelligence into that foundation and extending where these agents work across the healthcare journey. Shashank, the CEO and co-founder, is the executive the articles name in connection with the integration and the results the company reports. Innovaccer said executives plan to integrate other Grok models via API in the future, including Grok Build and Grok Bot.

The articles do not say who at Innovaccer or elsewhere is responsible for the Grok Voice integration beyond Shashank's statement. The company founded in 2014 builds software to unify enterprise data and applies AI to automate manual tasks for payers and providers. Innovaccer says it serves more than 200 health systems and payers, 80 million patients across the U.S. and 95% of community pharmacies as of May. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the planned future integration of other Grok models via API. The Grok integration is live for customers now, the company said.

stories.Headline: Museum blogger Nik Honeysett warns that AI agents sway expert judgment and urges human judgment in the loop
stories.Summary:
Nik Honeysett wrote a blog post for the American Alliance of Museums, published on 23 November 2026, asking whether artificial intelligence will reshape how humans work. He described a callus on his right forefinger from years of writing with a pencil or pen. He said that writing by hand activates more regions of the brain than typing and is a better tool for learning and memory. He said that reading on paper results in more sustained focus and better comprehension than digital text. He said that every new technology changes how we interact with the world.

He cited a recent Anthropic research paper, highlighted in a LinkedIn post by futurist Ross Dawson, that examined how experts worked with AI agents on a series of decisions. He said the agents had been instructed, unknown to the experts, to favor particular approaches. He said the experts followed the AI's preferred approach in 86 percent of analytical decisions. He said that when the experts had already expressed an opinion and the AI disagreed, they changed their position 60 percent of the time. He said 77 percent later repeated the AI's arguments when explaining their decisions, while more than half considered the final recommendation more their own than the AI's.

Honeysett said the study was relatively small, involved a single analytical task, and deliberately amplified the agents' preferences. He said it does not show that all professionals behave this way. He said museums are beginning to incorporate AI into almost every aspect of their work, including collections research, exhibition development, education, visitor engagement, marketing, fundraising, and institutional planning. He said he was previously very enthusiastic about these opportunities but is increasingly concerned that museum leaders lack some critical understanding of the long-term consequences. He said museums are knowledge-rich but resource-constrained organizations.

He said much of the discussion about responsible AI adoption emphasizes keeping a human in the loop. He said the Anthropic research suggests that human oversight may not provide the independent judgment we assume it does. He said that if an AI system has already shaped the assumptions, framed the alternatives, and constructed the reasoning, asking a human to approve the final recommendation may be little more than procedural. He said the person remains accountable, but the judgment may no longer be entirely theirs.

He proposed moving from Human in the Loop toward Human Judgment in the Loop. He said participants who used AI made substantially fewer serious process errors than those who worked without it. He said the groups differed in experience and were not randomly assigned to use AI, so the study could not establish whether AI caused the improvement. He said AI may improve the quality of our work while simultaneously influencing the judgments that determine what work we do.

He said AI may help us escape established ways of thinking while introducing new constraints that are less visible and potentially more influential. He said the challenge is not to stop our tools from shaping us, which is inevitable, but to remain sufficiently aware of that influence to question it. He said AI adoption becomes an exercise in systems thinking and organizational design. He said we should define the problem before asking AI to solve it.

He said we should make assumptions and values explicit before asking AI to evaluate consequential decisions. He said we should use AI to challenge thinking rather than simply generate recommendations. He said museums might develop or adapt smaller, institutionally controlled language models grounded in their own collections, scholarship, and organizational knowledge, but that these could equally reinforce the institution's existing blind spots. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Affordable housing firms use AI to score sites and cut false emergency calls
stories.Summary:
At AHF Live in Chicago, leaders from several affordable housing firms described how they are moving artificial intelligence past experimentation and into everyday business use, according to Affordable Housing Finance. The panel, moderated by Michelle Norris of N-Sights Consulting, covered how firms use the technology to evaluate development opportunities, improve property operations and connect data. Karsten Lowe, director of affordable housing development at JPI, said his firm combines its historical deal data with public information to score prospective sites and study market fundamentals. Joshua Bagley, senior director of development operations at Fairstead, and Finn Magoon, director of asset management at Belveron Partners, also took part in the discussion.

Norris opened the panel by urging firms to be strategic rather than chasing whatever product looks coolest at a trade show. Lowe said artificial intelligence can digest large amounts of public information, including agency data, city council activity, housing authority information and competitors' deal structures, while noting that the volume of that information cuts both ways. Justine Manaid, director of strategic initiatives, operations, at nonprofit Eden Housing, said her organization's AI-enabled system helps sort true maintenance emergencies from non-emergencies, lets residents submit requests in multiple languages and provides real-time updates. She said this has produced a nearly 50% reduction in false emergency calls, benefiting both employees and residents.

Bagley said one of the biggest game-changers his firm has seen is the ability to quickly identify variances, address potential risks or capture opportunities as they arise. Panelists agreed that AI output cannot be accepted at face value and that employees need enough expertise to recognize when an answer looks wrong and to return to source material when necessary. Magoon described a rule on his team that no one should present outputs they cannot explain themselves. The session was part of AHF Live in Chicago, and an editor's note said AI tools were used to assist in summarizing the conference transcript.

stories.Headline: Basque minister Ubarretxena says Euskadi seeks AI while keeping human control at DOK Summit
stories.Summary:
María Ubarretxena, the Minister of Governance, Digital Administration and Self-government, inaugurated the DOK Summit technology congress on 23 November 2026 at the Euskalduna Palace in Bilbao, where she said Euskadi seeks to use artificial intelligence without giving up human control or decision-making capacity. She warned that using artificial intelligence does not mean handing over the keys to the house, and she said the debate around AI is not just about technology but about power. She affirmed that the Basque Country wants to decide, and she recalled that the recent European leaders' summit also addressed this issue. She emphasized that the objective is to maintain human control, ensuring the protection of citizen data and the decision-making capacity for essential public services.

The Basque public sector's AI Government Strategy promotes the concept of Herri-adimen, which prioritizes what the article calls the country's intelligence over artificial intelligence. Ubarretxena cited Batera, the Government's cloud, on whose experience ArgIA is being built as a public AI infrastructure governed from Euskadi and based on open-source tools. Attendees will be able to experience the platform firsthand this afternoon in a practical demonstration session led by Javier Cela and Aitor Cabero, heads of Cloud and Modernization and Data and AI at EJIE, the Basque Government's IT company. Ubarretxena clarified that sovereignty does not mean doing everything ourselves, and she advocated for collaboration with companies, clusters and professionals, summarizing that an ecosystem is needed.

She stressed that technology must serve people, expressing the wish that artificial intelligence makes us better but that we continue to be the ones making the decisions. The DOK Summit, the successor to the LibreCon free software conference, is taking place today and tomorrow in Bilbao and expects to gather around 1,200 professionals focused on AI, talent, data, cybersecurity and open source. The opening session also included remarks from GAIA President Elena Zarraga, ESLE President Iker Sagasti, Bilbao City Council's Councillor for Economic Development, Trade, Tourism and Employment Kontxi Claver, and the Provincial Councillor for Public Administration and Institutional Relations of Bizkaia, Ager Izagirre. The article, based on information from the official source Irekia and the department, gives no further details on what happens after the congress.

stories.Headline: Wahpeton council reviews city goals and mulls AI, social media and housing rules
stories.Summary:
Wahpeton City Council members and staff held a retreat on Wednesday, Nov. 18, the Wahpeton Daily News reported on Nov. 23, 2026. In the absence of Mayor Brett Lambrecht, Council member Jason Goltz led the retreat presentation. Goltz said the retreat was not intended to solve problems but to build a roadmap for the next couple of years. The retreat slides listed three objectives: thinking and acting strategically, demonstrating teamwork and practicing small-group decision-making. The council began by reviewing the city's 2023-2026 goals and priorities.

Goltz compared the review to a military after-action review, examining what was supposed to happen, whether it happened, what should continue and what could be improved. The recap outlined four goals, the first to keep local sales tax collections steady over the long term. According to the retreat slides, collections increased from $3,371,512 in 2023 to $3,807,937 in 2025, a 13% increase. The second goal was to research and plan a community wellness and recreation center, and voters approved an additional 1% sales tax on April 29, 2025, to help fund recreation and community wellness. The same ordinance, No. 1071, also removed earlier sunset dates for the city's sales tax, according to the slides, and the center project remains ongoing.

The third goal was to pay for ongoing obligations while relying less on property taxes. The slides showed that the city's mill rate decreased from 128.47 in 2000 to 79.68 currently, a 38% drop. The value of a mill increased from $9,381 to $30,422, a 224% increase. The fourth goal was to retain local businesses, and the slides noted that the city has fewer retail businesses and continues to face workforce and economic challenges in manufacturing. The recap also identified three priorities, the first being investing in infrastructure repairs and expansion.

The slides estimated that system valuation would increase from $324,043,689 in 2024 to $348,692,921 in 2027, an increase of about 8%. The second priority was maintaining strong police and fire services, and appropriations for those services have increased from 15% to 22% of total expenditures, according to the slides. The third priority was attracting industry, which continues to face workforce and economic challenges, particularly in manufacturing. Goltz said business retention and industrial attraction remains the city's biggest challenges, and he added that taxes and city spending appear to be efficient. One participant noted that those challenges are not unique to Wahpeton, while another said a city can do only so much to attract businesses.

Officials described sales tax as a useful local tool for reducing reliance on property taxes. The council next reviewed a decision-making matrix, and the slides outlined four steps: define the goal, gather key information, weigh options and risks, and make a motion that clearly states the proposed action. Goltz also discussed the sunk-cost fallacy, or the tendency to continue a project because of the time and money already invested. "Good leadership means stepping back to recognize when it is time to take a different approach or walk away," Goltz said. He added that many decisions have long-term consequences, for example bonding for a project that takes 25 years to pay off can affect an entire generation.

City Attorney Brittany Hatting presented information about social media, open meetings and open records, drawing from a presentation by attorney Howard Swanson of Swanson & Warcup, Ltd. to the North Dakota League of Cities in September. Hatting said the goal was to help council members recognize potential issues, not make them experts in the law. The presentation explained that public officials generally cannot delete comments simply because they are critical or block users because they disagree with an official. However, obscene or pornographic material, threats, spam and certain other categories may be removed. Hatting said Community Development Director Chris DeVries manages the city's social media accounts and follows those guidelines.

Deleting an entire post could also result in the destruction of a public record. Council members were also advised to exercise caution when using personal social media accounts. Hatting cited Sanderson vs. Myrdal, a case in which the North Dakota Supreme Court ruled Nov. 8, 2024, in favor of Sen. Janne Myrdal after she blocked a critic from her personal Facebook page. The court determined that a page becomes a public forum only when an official has actual authority to speak for the government and uses the page to do so. Regarding open meetings, Hatting said a quorum of council members commenting on a social media post about city business could inadvertently create a meeting.

She added that a walking quorum could also occur when one council member contacts other members individually to discuss city business. "Nearly all open meetings and open records violations are inadvertent rather than intentional," Hatting said. Texting during a meeting does not constitute a violation unless members are texting one another as a group, Hatting said. Staff emails asking council members not to use the "reply all" function are intended to prevent an accidental quorum. Posts and messages concerning public business may be considered public records, even when sent from private devices, Hatting said, and retention requirements depend on the content.

Hatting also addressed the use of artificial intelligence. The State Bar Association of North Dakota's magazine, The Gavel, reported 1,492 U.S. cases involving AI-generated material and more than 2,000 worldwide, said Hatting. The North Dakota Supreme Court has also issued a public notice addressing its use of artificial intelligence. Hatting urged council members to double- and triple-check any AI-generated material used for official business. The retreat then turned to workforce housing.

The slides quoted Brandon Dettlaff, executive director of the North Dakota Housing Finance Agency, who told the League of Cities, "Housing is where jobs sleep at night." According to the slides, North Dakota's population is projected to grow 7% by 2034, while the state could need an additional 48,315 housing units, a 13% increase. Current building trends are expected to add 25,589 units. Statewide, homes priced at $250,000 or less accounted for 64% of home sales in 2015, compared with 34% in 2025. Households headed by someone 65 or older are projected to increase 39% by 2034.

The slides emphasized that additional housing does not necessarily mean more of the same type of housing. City Finance Director Darcie Huwe said five of 97 home sales in 2015 were above $250,000, or about 5%. In 2025, 37% of 68 sales were above that price. The city issued two new-construction permits this year, matching the number issued in 2025, and one of this year's permits was for North Dakota State College of Science. Huwe said smaller lots and homes on her street sell quickly and questioned why more homes are not being built.

She said builders have indicated that few can construct a home for $225,000, and if builders could build at that price, she added, the homes would likely sell quickly. Huwe noted that large portions of Wahpeton were developed during the 1950s and 1970s, and some older homes may eventually become unviable. She also noted that Wahpeton has 2,511 rental units, compared with 2,680 in Devils Lake. Using sales tax revenue to buy down special assessments could reduce the cost of a $500,000 home to about $440,000, Huwe said.

However, she cautioned that there is no single solution to the housing challenge. The slides identified several areas cities can influence, including zoning, land-use policy, site selection and permitting, local tax incentives and land-use planning. Huwe cautioned that incentives should be directed toward the types of housing the city wants to encourage. She also warned that free money does not make a bad idea a good one.

Huwe directed council members to the state's ND Compass housing portal for additional information. Huwe said Vanguard Appraisals, an outside appraisal firm, will update property valuations in 2028. She said lower-priced homes are expected to see significant increases, middle-priced homes see larger increases and apartments are currently assessed at about 74% of their value. Under the state's 3% cap, Huwe said, mill rates would have to decrease as property values rise.

Officials also noted that the city receives about 24% of a Wahpeton property tax bill, with the school district receiving approximately half. The retreat concluded with a break, followed by a strengths, opportunities, aspirations and results exercise and a review of a slide outlining proposed 2026-2028 goals and priorities. The article did not report any votes taken at the retreat. The article did not say when the next retreat would be held.

stories.Headline: LAUSD committee hears teachers and students on student AI use as Google plans school controls
stories.Summary:
Google announced on November 3, 2026 that it plans to give schools control over whether to enable Google Search, without offering a conventional AI-free version through its standard settings. The Los Angeles Unified School District had earlier restricted generative AI on district-issued student devices. The district subsequently said it had disabled Google's AI-generated search summaries, known as AI Overviews, while preserving access to conventional Google Search. LAUSD's Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee held a meeting on November 13, 2026. The committee scheduled presentations involving district teachers and students, alongside a community presentation by Schools Beyond Screens Los Angeles.

Under Google's forthcoming controls, Google Search and several AI services will be disabled by default for K, 12 student accounts until administrators choose which services to enable. Google says the changes give schools greater control over access to its products. The company has also said AI is deeply integrated into Search, and its standard forthcoming controls do not offer schools a conventional version of Google Search with those integrated AI features removed. The published committee agenda identified teachers from Chandler Elementary School, Union Avenue Elementary School and Laurel Cinematic Arts & Creative Technologies Magnet, along with three student presenters. The meeting also included a presentation on research about AI's effects on students and possible district responses.

Lila Byock, an LAUSD parent and founder of Schools Beyond Screens, welcomed the district's September moratorium on student-facing generative AI. Her organization had advocated for restrictions while the district reviewed potential risks and developed safeguards. Byock argues that students can learn to understand AI critically without unrestricted access to the technology, including examining how AI systems produce information, how they can mislead users and what interests influence their development. Stephen Aguilar, an associate professor of education at the University of Southern California who studies educational technology, has warned that broad restrictions could create unequal opportunities. Aguilar also argues that older students need opportunities to evaluate AI-generated information under teacher supervision.

Aguilar said students with personal devices may continue using AI outside school, while those who rely on district-issued computers could have fewer chances to develop familiarity with the tools. LAUSD is distributing a survey to parents, students and staff as it develops recommendations. The agenda identifies participants, but does not by itself establish what individual students or teachers told the committee. Some districts have explored technical tools to suppress AI-generated answers while retaining traditional search results. Whether LAUSD's existing safeguards will remain effective under Google's planned changes has not been publicly established.

Parriva reported on California teachers' proposed three-year AI moratorium, as educators question which safeguards schools need before expanding student access. Parriva's guide to LAUSD's screen-time restrictions explains how the district has also been limiting device use during instruction. The district's decision to restrict generative AI on district-issued student devices came amid broader changes to classroom technology. The Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee is expected to continue meeting during the school year. Its work is intended to inform recommendations that the full school board may consider.

Sessions are scheduled for December 9, January 20, March 3 and April 7. The question remains how the district will weigh survey responses, account for differences among school communities and explain which concerns influenced its recommendations. For families, the stakes extend beyond Google, as the decisions will help determine how students learn to research information, evaluate automated answers and develop skills for a world where AI is increasingly common. LAUSD must decide what technology belongs in classrooms. The public question is whether students, teachers and families will have a meaningful role in determining the answer.

Articles.Title: Who Should Decide How LAUSD Students Use AI? - Parriva

stories.Headline: UNESCO and Thailand's judicial institute train 180 judges to use AI while keeping human judgement
stories.Summary:
UNESCO and the Judicial Training Institute of Thailand organized a training session in August 2026 for judicial personnel. Around 180 participants attended the event, including mid-career judges who are preparing for higher leadership roles. Many of these attendees are future regional chief judges who will lead courts across the country starting in April 2027. The session focused on how judges can use artificial intelligence without surrendering human judgement. The training required participants to study the UNESCO Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals.

It covered various complex topics such as the opacity of neural networks, agentic AI, and reasoning models. The curriculum also explored AI jurisprudence, emerging case law, and the future of legal education and apprenticeship. As a result of the session, the Judicial Training Institute decided to translate the UNESCO guidelines into the Thai language. Judge Kraiphol Aranyarat of the Office of the President of the Supreme Court stated that AI adoption must be guided by judicial values.

He emphasized that independence, impartiality, fairness, transparency, and accountability are fundamental to the process. Hironaka, the Regional Advisor and Chief of Communication and Information for UNESCO, noted a gap in formal AI training for judges. She argued that training is necessary to address data security and AI ethics within a human rights framework. The participants discussed how to maintain accountability and public trust while introducing innovation into the justice system.

Judge Patcharapa Intarakamhaeng reflected that human oversight and respect for the rule of law are especially significant for judges. Judge Suthawan Leelanapapat of the Judicial Training Institute observed a high level of involvement and interest from the attendees. The organizers believe that equipping judges for technological innovation will ensure that AI remains accountable to human rights. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Preparing Thailand's future judicial leaders for the age of AI - UNESCO

stories.headline_source: Preparing Thailand's future judicial leaders for the age of AI

stories.Headline: Vanderbilt legal scholars debate whether AI output deserves First Amendment protection
stories.Summary:
Three legal scholars at Vanderbilt Law School debated whether AI output should receive First Amendment protections on November 23, 2026. The event was the fourth in the Respectfully Dissent series and was moderated by professor Jennifer Shinall. These experts disagreed on whether existing legal rules can protect both AI users and people harmed by generated content. The discussion focused on government regulation of AI speech rather than a newly issued court ruling. The participants sought to balance the ability to share ideas with the need to prevent harmful output.

Eugene Volokh of Stanford's Hoover Institution argued that AI output should face the same First Amendment rules as other speech. Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law called for federal safeguards including periodic and random platform monitoring and data scraping limits. Francesca Procaccini of Vanderbilt proposed tailoring protection to the setting and potential harm to avoid enabling censorship. Tsesis also wanted protections against autonomous AI decisions in private matters to prevent risks like unauthorized real-time facial recognition. Volokh noted that ordinary limits regarding libel, minors, professional malpractice, and discriminatory decisions in hiring or sales should remain.

Eugene Volokh stated that AI output is a joint effort between the user and the company and deserves protection. He used a camera analogy to argue that using a manufactured tool does not erase relevant speech rights. Alex Tsesis argued that large language models lack human consciousness, intention, and reasoning, so they should not have rights. He claimed that audience interest in receiving AI information cannot settle the limits of regulation like securities rules do. Francesca Procaccini suggested that existing doctrine already adjusts protection based on settings like schools, government offices, and private workplaces.

The debate affected human users who create ideas and people exposed to risks like deepfakes or social scoring. Tsesis argued that human involvement alone does not eliminate the exploitation of vulnerabilities or the use of facial recognition. Procaccini warned that courts could use the First Amendment to weaken existing tort, civil-rights, and property claims. Volokh countered that a flexible approach would depart from familiar rules and create confusing restrictions with unknown consequences. Tsesis added that existing commercial-speech rules and disclosure requirements might not fit within the proposed flexible framework.

The articles explain that AI does not need its own rights for its output to raise a free-speech dispute. The scholars examined whether protecting human users leaves lawmakers with less room to regulate the content generated by AI. The core conflict is whether existing speech protections can accommodate AI risks without weakening ordinary legal remedies or users' rights. The discussion highlighted the tension between the democratic value of sharing ideas and threats to privacy and autonomy. This background establishes that the legal status of AI-generated expression remains a subject of significant academic disagreement.

The argument over how to regulate AI-generated speech remains unresolved among the three legal scholars. The articles leave open whether any new framework can address AI harms without weakening the rights of the users. It is unclear if the proposed flexible approach can be reconciled with current commercial-speech rules or disclosure requirements. The scholars did not reach a consensus on whether AI output should be treated as a joint human-corporate effort. No court ruling or settled policy was announced as a result of the Vanderbilt Law School event.

Articles.Title: Vanderbilt hosts debate over how far free-speech rights should protect AI output - Superpower Daily

stories.Headline: Wes Moore leads governors in urging federal oversight of frontier AI while states keep authority over consumer harms
stories.Summary:
On November 22, the National Governors Association published a three-page statement on who should govern artificial intelligence, according to a GitHub post dated November 24, 2026. Maryland Governor Wes Moore helped lead the bipartisan council that wrote it. The NGA announcement names Indiana’s Mike Braun, North Carolina’s Josh Stein and Utah’s Spencer Cox alongside him. The statement asks Washington to oversee frontier models, require independent evaluations and receive reports of serious security incidents. It asks states to retain power over harms people encounter when models are put to work, such as a benefits decision, a job application, a school chatbot or a disputed insurance claim.

The document begins with five general principles and then lists five federal recommendations and fourteen for states. The federal list starts with a risk-based framework for the most advanced general-purpose models and calls for evaluation or audit by independent experts. It also calls for reports of security breaches and significant safety incidents to federal authorities and affected states. Washington would set national approaches to critical infrastructure, chemical, biological and nuclear risks, international cooperation and research. The state list describes consumer remedies, anti-discrimination enforcement, children, workers, consequential decisions, public-sector AI and local cyber defense, and asks states to coordinate definitions and oversight.

The NGA document is a recommendation with no binding force. Moore’s November statement puts his emphasis on workers, consumers and children. Bloomberg Law reported the effort as a bid for federal AI rules without surrendering state protection. The Next Web described the central bargain as Washington handling risks at national scale while states keep room to govern uses affecting their residents. Neither report turns the proposal into enacted law.

The White House has offered a different starting point. Executive Order 14365, signed in December 2025, directs federal agencies to review and challenge state AI laws it considers onerous and asks for a minimally burdensome national framework. The order states that a patchwork raises compliance costs, particularly for startups, and can regulate beyond state borders. It also tells officials not to propose preempting otherwise lawful state laws on child safety, data centers and state procurement. The eventual scope of federal preemption remains a legislative and legal question, not a completed fact established by the order.

A 2024 executive order directed Maryland agencies to examine their own AI use, and the Artificial Intelligence Governance Act requires an inventory and a framework for developing and using systems. Maryland now publishes AI use cases and a list of systems and software, including mundane productivity tools and proposed assistants for state services. The Responsible AI Policy requires agency review and risk management. The governor’s September agenda says high-risk state uses, including benefits, lending and law enforcement, need impact assessment, bias testing, human oversight and periodic audit. A 2025 report from Maryland’s Department of Information Technology recommended keeping the governor’s AI subcabinet as a cross-agency group rather than creating a standalone department.

The May 2026 AI Innovation Lab announcement described a controlled sandbox, vulnerability testing and support for agencies building AI tools, and offered an agent helping state fleet drivers find approved maintenance vendors as an example, forecasting $1 million to $1.5 million in annual savings. Anthropic’s November 2025 announcement described assistance for benefits caseworkers with document verification and policy guidance, and Axios independently reported the planned use across benefits and housing. In February, Maryland’s Department of Labor announced $4 million across three grant programs: $2.5 million for internships and upskilling in selected industries and $1.5 million for supervised cyber training. The state’s later AI principles page says the first group of investments reached nearly 600 Marylanders. The articles leave open how to decide which rule controls when federal and state hands overlap.

stories.Headline: Stacy Garrity runs undisclosed AI deepfake ads against Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania midterms
stories.Summary:
Republican candidate Stacy Garrity used AI deepfake ads during the 2026 Pennsylvania midterms. These misleading advertisements targeted Governor Josh Shapiro to influence the gubernatorial race. The ads appeared during an election cycle that some called the first AI election. They featured an AI avatar of Shapiro discussing sexual harassment and data centers. The campaign did not disclose the AI use until forty seconds into the ad.

Pennsylvania currently does not require disclosure of AI use in political ads. State Representative Tarik Khan penned HB 811 to ban all AI in political ads. This bill has remained stalled in the Senate during the current legislative session. The Wesleyan Media Project identified 289 AI political ads costing 187 million dollars. Over 90 percent of those ads were purchased by Republican candidates and groups.

Stacy Garrity defended the ad and backed the claims about the record of Shapiro. She reiterated that the advertisement did disclose its use of artificial intelligence technology. A spokesperson for Josh Shapiro called the deepfake ad cheap and dishonest AI bullshit. Philip Hensley-Robin of Common Cause Pennsylvania said clear disclosures are very important. He stated that Pennsylvania should adopt disclosure laws like many other states.

Some viewers found the AI easy to spot while others called it professional. One Facebook user wrote that deepfakes are unethical and have no place in politics. Professor Gang Wang said negative impacts linger even if viewers recognize the AI messaging. Studio Brubaker owner Garrett Brubaker said people might not immediately clock an AI ad. He noted that the technology is only going to get worse over time.

The Wesleyan Media Project has analyzed political advertising since the year 2010. State Senator Doug Mastriano posted AI images of the governor on X before the election. These images showed the governor beneath headlines that criticized his budget record. Another ad showed Shapiro channeling lightning through his hands in a data center warehouse. The Pennsylvania Department of State directed voters to a fact-check page during midterms.

New leaders must now decide if they will put guardrails on Big Tech. Governor Josh Shapiro has not yet decided how he might outlaw AI election ads. Katie Paul suggested putting a cost on producing AI generated political ads for campaigns. Experts say federal regulation is needed to protect the democratic process from misinformation. It remains open how to regulate technologies that evolve every six months.

Articles.Title: AI deepfake political ads in Pennsylvania: What voters saw - The Keystone Newsroom

stories.Headline: Tech companies and governments accelerate global AI data center construction despite resource concerns
stories.Summary:
Global construction of data centers is accelerating as countries race to lead in AI development. Technology companies are investing hundreds of billions of dollars to build these critical facilities. These centers provide the physical and computational infrastructure needed to run large AI models. Some countries fast-track projects to attract investment, while others restrict new construction. This acceleration is happening as of November 23, 2026.

AI centers use GPUs and liquid cooling, requiring more power than traditional CPU centers. One Nvidia GB200 NVL72 rack draws 120 kilowatts, equaling the demand of one hundred American homes. The US has over five thousand facilities, while over 13,000 exist across 180 countries. China uses the East Data, West Computing project to move centers to western provinces. The UAE is reassessing the $30 billion Stargate UAE project following strikes by Iran.

David Hart of the CFR says backlash reflects abstract concerns about AI proliferation. He claims the US power grid is aging and the current energy policy is contradictory. Connor Martin of the CFR states the private sector leads US construction efforts. Martin says market uncertainty exists regarding when the economic gains of AI will materialize. He suggests Saudi and Emirati governments might cut committed funds to focus on defense.

Communities fear rising power bills and strained resources due to high electricity and water use. Residents in rural Michigan picketed a proposed $7 billion data center over electricity rate fears. S&P Global estimates 43 percent of global data centers face high water stress. Harvard researchers estimate one Virginia center could cause $99 million in annual health damages. Microsoft saw emissions rise 25 percent in fiscal year 2025 due to data center growth.

Data centers consumed 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, or 1.5 percent of global use. Global centers used almost 1.2 trillion gallons of water in 2025, per a UN report. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft plan to spend $725 billion on capital expenditures in 2026. Saudi Arabia struck a nearly $1 trillion investment deal with the United States last year. The UAE committed to a $1.4 trillion framework for AI infrastructure in 2025.

The International Energy Agency estimates electricity consumption for data centers will double by 2030. AI-related carbon dioxide emissions could reach four hundred million tons annually by 2030. UN reports project AI water consumption could reach 2.5 trillion gallons annually by 2030. Land for AI power generation could exceed 14,500 square kilometers by 2030. The articles leave open whether Gulf nations will fulfill their multi-trillion dollar investment commitments.
