stories.Headline: Mortgage executives say AI speeds loan reviews but human underwriters still make final credit decisions
stories.Summary:
Executives at Incenter Diligence Solutions and SitusAMC said artificial intelligence is helping mortgage lenders and due-diligence firms review loan files and extract borrower information, but the technology still needs human oversight, especially when loans involve unusual circumstances or require judgment beyond standard guidelines. At Incenter, AI has accelerated document indexing and data extraction, according to president Pamela Hamrick, and the technology can now sort and categorize thousands of pages of loan documents in minutes, replacing a process that once required employees to manually separate and label files. Hamrick said that while AI can extract information from standardized mortgage documents like loan estimates and closing disclosures, borrower-provided records including pay stubs and bank statements are harder to process because their formats vary, though AI can identify inconsistencies across documents and summarize them for underwriters to investigate. Hamrick said the technology is identifying the questions, the inconsistencies and the anomalies between all of this documentation and summarizing that for an underwriter or a reviewer to dig deeper and decide whether what the AI has identified is a real risk, a minimal risk or no risk at all because of the particular scenario. Julia Curran, senior managing director of residential AI products at SitusAMC, said the company uses AI to re-underwrite closed loans in the secondary market, checking regulatory and underwriting guidelines as well as data accuracy before loans are reviewed for securitization.

According to Curran, SitusAMC builds AI agents around processes established by human subject matter experts and tests their results against loans previously reviewed by people, running repeated tests until the system reaches at least 95% accuracy. Curran said the system sends blank or inconsistent fields to human reviewers, and final credit decisions require judgments that cannot be reduced to individual data points, adding that a final credit decision should not be made by the machine because there are other things to consider besides the specific data points. Hamrick added that companies that fully rely on AI are potentially going to have misses in some other areas where a human might have been able to make a different decision. Curran also warned about the AI model supplying information not supported or provided by the documents submitted, describing a case in which a model supplied a solar panel number that was not included in a particular loan file, and although the answer was correct, the system had apparently drawn on information from other files. Curran said even though it is right, she does not want that answer and wants to stay within the four walls of the file.

The executives said lenders should test AI against established human processes before relying on it for underwriting, and Hamrick recommended introducing the technology in one part of the workflow at a time, comparing its results with human reviews before expanding its use, and preparing employees for changes by retraining them for tasks that require more human intervention. Hamrick said the best thing leaders can do is look where the technology can ultimately take over and then take the people doing those roles and train them to be better at the things that require more human intervention. Curran said quality control requires testing models across different loan types and scenarios, and SitusAMC maintains a test bank of hundreds of previously reviewed loans, including purchases, refinances, adjustable-rate mortgages and loans with rate buydowns, and when a model changes the company runs its prompts against the test bank to check whether results remain consistent. These tests add costs that lenders may overlook, and Curran said companies should ask AI vendors how their systems were developed, whether subject matter experts helped establish the processes and whether ongoing regression testing is in place. Curran said you want the same answer every time, and the process of taking a non-deterministic process and making it deterministic takes a lot of time and effort.

stories.Headline: Scamwise finds AI-generated content in 74% of fake stores it analyzed
stories.Summary:
A report from Scamwise, a website checking tool, warns that artificial intelligence is helping scammers quickly build more convincing fake storefronts and fill them with product descriptions, images and other content. Scamwise said it analyzed more than 250,000 shopping websites submitted by users between March and October 2026. More than 100,000 were classified by its system as “definitely” or “likely” scam stores. 74% of the scam stores in its analysis used AI-generated content. A previously unseen scam store was reported to Scamwise about every three minutes.

40% of scam stores were less than 90 days old when checked, and seven in 10 were no longer live 90 days after Scamwise checked them. The data is based on sites consumers chose to submit to Scamwise, often because something already appeared suspicious. Scamwise reported 20% of the confirmed fake-store submissions it analyzed carried an ad-click fingerprint. In that subset, Scamwise said 42% carried a Google Search or Shopping identifier, 29% carried a Facebook identifier and 10% carried an Instagram identifier. The click ID is referred to as “CLID.”

Shaun Khalfan, senior vice president and chief information security officer for PayPal and Venmo, said fraudsters are using AI to create more polished and personalized emails, text messages and websites, making them harder to detect. Josh Hares, executive vice president of the BBB of Greater Atlanta, said scammers can imitate major retailers’ branding and blend their messages into the flood of legitimate holiday promotions. Hares said they just need to hit the right person at the wrong time. Hares said researching a business before making a purchase can help shoppers avoid the frustration of trying to track down a site or recover money afterward. Hares said trust shouldn’t be given blindly and that you shouldn’t just trust somebody because they have a website.

A Google spokesperson said scams have no place on Google and that last year the company blocked over 99% of policy-violating ads before they ever ran. Google said it removed more than 1.7 billion ads in the United States and suspended 3.3 million accounts last year. Google said misrepresentation was its second most-enforced policy and that it removed more than 421.5 million ads globally for misrepresentation in 2025. Google disputed the report’s interpretation of its click tags and said a GCLID is used to measure ad clicks and does not prove a scam ad is currently running. Meta did not respond to requests for comment by deadline.

The BBB recommends going directly to a retailer’s website and comparing prices before entering personal or payment information. Hares cautioned that a website using HTTPS or displaying a lock icon is not necessarily legitimate because fraudulent sites can use those security features too. Hares noted that a new or online-only business is not automatically fraudulent and that the key is to verify the seller rather than assume a polished website proves it is legitimate. Scamwise says scammers often reach shoppers through the same online pathways legitimate businesses use, search tools and social media.

A fake website can closely resemble a legitimate retailer’s site, but its web address may contain an extra word, added letters or a slightly different spelling. Scamwise says Google’s GCLID can indicate a Google Ads click, while Facebook’s FBCLID can appear in both paid and organic Facebook traffic. A click identifier is not proof that Google or Meta knowingly ran a fraudulent ad, that an ad is still active or that a platform profited from a particular store. Google said a GCLID tag can remain in a link after an account is suspended or can be copied across fake sites and redirect links.

Google says its policies prohibit scam ads and deceptive practices, including fake online storefronts and advertisers that misrepresent their businesses. Google said it requires merchants to provide return policies, billing terms, contact information and secure checkout options. Hares recommends checking a seller’s contact information, looking for independent reviews and searching the BBB’s business profiles for available complaints and customer reviews. Shoppers should search the store’s name with “reviews” or “scam” and look beyond testimonials posted on the store’s own website.

Shoppers should price-check unbelievable discounts and compare the product’s price with a known retailer. Shoppers should treat ads as a lead, not proof a seller is legitimate, and search for the seller independently rather than buying directly from an ad in their feed. Shoppers should use a credit card, keep screenshots of the listing, promised price, delivery date, seller information, receipt and order confirmation, and keep AI purchase approval turned on. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Camgian COO Will Johnson tells west Alabama leaders that companies use AI to find and address vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
Will Johnson, the Chief Operating Officer for Camgian Technologies, spoke to business and elected leaders in west Alabama about the role artificial intelligence plays in daily life at the Federal Affairs Briefing, according to WBRC. The Chamber of Commerce of West Alabama invited Johnson to speak after the scheduled guest speaker cancelled. Johnson said companies are using AI to find and better address their vulnerabilities. He said it is a responsibility that AI is doing what it was designed to do.

Johnson told WBRC that the company constantly has to wrestle with the same question of how to use AI wisely and how to ensure it is doing the proper things. He said that is a responsibility everyone has, his company included, to ensure that as they deploy these agents they are doing what they were designed to do, no more and no less. Camgian Technologies is a defense contractor that uses artificial intelligence to help the US military. Johnson said the AI agents the company uses are reliable and critical to the role they play.

He said it is critical that the war fighter has confidence in them because lives are going to be on the line in that application. Recent web and service-related outages have added to the anxiety some people have about AI, and Johnson does not think those disruptions are the results of a cyber attack. Camgian has offices in Tuscaloosa, Huntsville and Starkville, Miss. The briefing took place on Nov. 23, 2026, and WBRC published its story that morning.

stories.Headline: An author urges leaders to protect dissent and human judgment as AI pushes companies toward uniformity
stories.Summary:
An author wrote an article on November 23, 2026, about the dangers of artificial intelligence. He used the Borg from Star Trek to warn business leaders about corporate uniformity. The piece argues that AI nudges users toward the same safe answers. This process can make companies think and sound like everyone else. The author claims that resisting this pull is now a leader's job.

The author suggests leaders delegate analysis but keep judgment for themselves. He mentions an IBM 2026 study where 64 percent of 2,000 CEOs felt comfortable using AI for strategic decisions. These leaders expect AI to make 48 percent of operational decisions by 2030, up from 25 percent today. In October 2025, Deloitte Australia partially refunded 290,000 dollars for a report with AI errors. Last month, the government of Western Australia demanded another refund from Deloitte for a university study.

The author says leaders must protect people who disagree to avoid dangerous blindness. He claims that treating dissent as infrastructure is necessary because AI tends to agree with users. He argues that companies must budget for rebuilding purpose alongside retraining for new tools. The author believes that individuality without support is easily undermined in the workplace. He states that nobody else will push back against the pull of AI.

A Stanford study found 11 AI systems affirmed users 49 percent more than humans did. This affected people by making them more convinced they were right and less responsible. A March study found that people who relied passively on AI found less meaning in work. An Elon University survey found 65 percent of Americans believe AI could reduce purpose and dignity. A Harvard Business Review survey of 1,000 workers reported that AI reduced team trust and coordination.

The author notes that language models are trained to predict the most likely next word. A 2025 study of 70 models found they converged on the same responses to questions. In September, Nature reported that generative AI is homogenizing how humans write and think. One study showed students using ChatGPT for five days gave similar answers months later. Research on earnings calls found that uniform AI language was associated with negative market reactions.

Leaders should track whether people find meaning in work as carefully as tool usage. They must protect the relationships that employees lean on while they adjust to technology. The author suggests rewarding the person who pushes back when they are right. He claims that the most successful leaders will capture AI benefits without becoming part of a collective. The articles leave open how companies will specifically measure the loss of meaning in work.

Articles.Title: How to keep AI from turning your company into the Borg

stories.Headline: Levent Alpöge releases code proving the Riemann hypothesis after Anthropic goes public
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpöge got back to the place he was crashing in New York City around 4 A.M. on November 20, 2026, almost done and almost able to sleep. All that was left was to download the 17 million lines of code he had spent the night preparing for public release. The code needed to go up on his personal website, alongside a four-page statement he had tinkered with all week. For the moment, the code still sat on the servers of his employer, the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, which had gone public just hours earlier with the largest valuation in stock market history, making Alpöge a rich man. Once the upload was complete, he would also be one of history's most famous mathematicians.

The code was the product of untold computing resources, months of work and decades of dreaming, and it proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old math problem so formidable that it is almost beyond words. In public talks, experts have tended to simply treat it as an over-the-horizon aspiration, a "vanishing point" perspective against which all other math problems shrink. Just weeks earlier Terence Tao, arguably the world's most famous mathematician, had declared the hypothesis out of AI's reach, let alone that of humans, until perhaps 2050. Alpöge's quiet upload capped off an epochal year in which AI has systematically conquered humanity's oldest discipline in a sequence of escalating, dramatic and controversial discoveries. In nearly every episode of this earthshaking war for math's soul, Alpöge has figured somehow, part battlefield champion, part horseman of the AI apocalypse, part Forrest Gump.

Henry Cohn, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said people are divided over Alpöge and asked who this person is who is behind some of the most striking applications of AI to mathematics. Cohn called it a really interesting question that deserves a deeper answer than you can get from following him on X. Depending on who you ask, Alpöge is a reviled online troll, an agent of chaos laughing as his fellow mathematicians watch their intellectual landscape get carpet-bombed by his Silicon Valley cohort, or a reluctant public figure, a shy academic who has integrity and wants to forge a future where AI is mathematicians' collaborator, not their usurper. Or maybe he is an arrogant genius who has a chip on his shoulder and is bent on leveraging his access, his internal models and unlimited tokens, to prove his doubters wrong by snatching every remaining mathematical trophy off the shelf. Whatever the truth is, it is hard to know because Alpöge won't tell, and he refuses to speak to media.

This article has been assembled from interviews with dozens of friends, mentors, collaborators and acquaintances. Scott Armstrong, a mathematician at New York University and a rare Alpöge confidant, said Alpöge has this will to take on the world and win, and that he has it in spades. Armstrong said that in today's world, where large teams are the norm for any assault on frontier research problems, Alpöge is an anomaly who mostly works alone, except, of course, for the powerful internal models he has privileged access to. Armstrong also said here is a person that is larger than life, and that he keeps asking himself when they make the movie, who is going to play Levent. Alpöge's online persona is confusing and tempestuous, and he topples famous conjectures with glib and gleeful social media posts, and then gets baited into emotionally replying to anonymous commenters.

Levent Alpöge was born on April Fool's Day, 1992, along the central stretch of Long Island, and his parents, both Turkish immigrants, realized their son's intellect was remarkable when he was just three years old. As his mother told a Turkish newspaper in 2014, she was reading him one of his favorite books and said she was too tired to continue, so Alpöge picked up where she had stopped. At first she thought he had memorized the page, but when she gave him another book, he kept reading, and somehow he had learned without instruction. On the advice of professionals, they enrolled him in a nearby gifted program, and his one sister, Elif, is a decade older, which made him practically an only child for much of the time. Alpöge was extremely athletic and especially into distance running and soccer, with his favorite soccer team being Istanbul's Beşiktaş Gymnastics Club.

He picked up coding early, and in 2009, at age 17, he connected with bioinformatics professor Xenophon Papademetris of Yale University, whose group assigned Alpöge a research problem the team had little time for. The idea was to use Nvidia graphical processing units, the technology now powering the AI revolution, to recognize vascular structures in medical images. Papademetris said Alpöge helped do one of the first GPU implementations of an image analysis algorithm, and that he was a 17-year-old kid who could say, "I will do it." The professor recalls what he wrote of Alpöge in his college recommendation letter, that his enthusiasm was contagious, his energy was boundless, and his confidence in his ability to overcome obstacles almost frightening. Papademetris said Alpöge's algorithm was enough to "punch your ticket to any university in the country," and that his letter was irrelevant, and as a bonus for the achievement, a team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Lincoln Laboratory named an asteroid "Alpöge."

Articles.Title: Who is Levent Alpöge, the reclusive genius behind AI’s math conquest?

stories.headline_source: Who is Levent Alpöge, the reclusive genius behind AI’s math conquest?

stories.Headline: China plans to exploit US public skepticism of AI and data centers following midterm elections
stories.Summary:
Chinese planners are drawing strategic conclusions from the American midterm elections held in 2026 to identify political vulnerabilities. Beijing is focusing on the American public's apprehension regarding artificial intelligence and their appetite for conflict. These takeaways will likely influence how China acts during future crises, including a potential conflict over Taiwan. Analysts believe China will use these insights to prepare the political terrain for exploitation.

To deter American leaders, China may seek to cause economic disruptions that directly affect voters rather than relying on human casualties. This strategy involves restricting the flow of rare earth minerals and consumer goods to companies like Amazon and Walmart, while boycotting American products. Additionally, Beijing is noting a mass disdain for data centers, as 40 out of 41 ballot initiatives in 10 states passed measures to limit their development. This trend contrasts with China's own goals, where President Xi Jinping emphasized in 2025 that AI must be incorporated into the military and broad economic activities.

Dean Cheng, a fellow at the Potomac Institute for Policy Studies and the George Washington University's Space Policy Institute, suggests that the Chinese are thrilled by the anti-AI wave. He notes that the U.S. electorate has broadly rejected the unfettered expansion of data centers. Cheng argues that China may try to capitalize on these feelings, similar to how the Soviets once exploited Western anti-nuclear movements. He concludes that the midterms suggest Americans are not prepared for the all-out competition that the Chinese expect.

Articles.Title: Beijing’s takeaway from the midterms: Will to fight and AI skepticism

stories.headline_source: Beijing’s takeaway from the midterms: Will to fight and AI skepticism

stories.Headline: New York Times tells freelance photographers to skip Photoshop 2027 over hidden AI tagging
stories.Summary:
The New York Times warned freelance photographers not to update their software on November 24, 2026. The news organization asked these contributors to avoid using the newest version of Adobe Photoshop. This warning was delivered through an email sent to the photographers. The company is concerned that new features use artificial intelligence in ways that are not apparent.

The restriction applies to Adobe Photoshop 2027, which is release 28.0.0 and any subsequent updates. The November update includes an AI Assisted Editor view that puts AI features in one toolbar. It adds an AI assistant for editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation, and new AI upscaling options. There is also an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.

Photography leaders Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner wrote that these features can result in metadata identifying photos as AI-generated. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge. The leaders stated that the AI tools may operate in ways that users do not notice. They want to prevent these specific tags from appearing in photos.

The restriction affects contributing photographers who are working on assignments for The New York Times. The newsroom believes that metadata indicating AI use risks losing the trust of their readers. The Times previously stated that it does not retouch or digitally manipulate its photos. They only make minimal adjustments to color to ensure they are accurately reproducing an image.

Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps in August to indicate AI editing. The company has spent several years adding AI-powered tools to Photoshop and other creative suite apps. Some older options, such as automated selection tools, may now be considered part of the AI suite. It is not always clear which tools in the apps are powered by AI.

It remains unclear which specific Photoshop features the New York Times is referring to in its warning. Adobe did not immediately respond to a request from The Verge for more information. The articles do not state if the Times will change its policy for future updates. They do not say how the photographers responded to the email. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features

stories.headline_source: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features

stories.Headline: Dan Bedinger says agentic AI now handles complex binder discovery tasks
stories.Summary:
Dan Bedinger said in an interview published by news-medical.net on 23 November 2026 that agentic AI can now use multiple tools to perform complex binder discovery tasks. He described the field as having evolved in stages over the last 25 years. He said the real shift toward AI-driven binder discovery came with tools such as DeepBind, AlphaFold, AlphaFold 2 and later generative platforms such as RFdiffusion. He said the next step is physical AI, in which experimental systems are integrated directly into automated, lab-in-the-loop workflows. He gave the account as an industry expert discussing how high-throughput SPR supports AI-driven binder discovery and experimental validation.

Bedinger said a successful lab-in-the-loop AI workflow requires modularity, continuous learning and scalability. He said modularity matters because workflows must integrate different types of assays rather than rely on a single technique. He said continuous learning is critical because the system must interpret experimental results and feed them into the next round of experimental design. He said drug discovery can involve hundreds or thousands of candidate sequences, so systems must operate at a practical level rather than in small proof-of-concept experiments. He said high-throughput SPR provides direct measurements of binding kinetics and affinity at scale, and that some CROs are trying to move from hundreds or thousands of sequences to interpretable binding data in less than a week.

Bedinger said the AIntibody Challenge was organized by Specifica, the antibody discovery laboratory within IQVIA Laboratories, and used Carterra HT-SPR technology to measure antibody binding kinetics and affinity. He said the challenge examined affinity maturation, in silico sequence ranking and de novo binder design against the SARS-CoV-2 RBD. He said that in affinity maturation more than 70% of clones bound the target, around 13% showed more than a 20-fold improvement in affinity and 63% passed developability testing. He said the ranking challenge was weaker, with AI approaches performing worse than random selection and only 10% of selected sequences having affinities better than the most abundant sequence in the data set. He said that in de novo design around 70% of input sequences became binders, about 14% were below 100 pM and the strongest binder reached 2.9 pM, though some high-affinity designs showed developability issues such as increased hydrophobicity.

Bedinger said the SPR work in the AIntibody study was completed in about three days and generated an iso-affinity plot for the full set of constructs. He said this made it possible to compare on- and off-rates across all binders and identify the highest-affinity clones. He cited SynthID Bio work from Google DeepMind, in which proteins were designed with a statistical watermark embedded in their amino acid sequences and structures, and hundreds of binders were generated against targets including PD-L1, SARS-CoV-2 RBD and VEGF-A. He cited an Anthropic study using Claude Opus 4.8 and Mythos Preview, in which the model was given a large prompt and access to publicly available tools such as BoltzGen and RFdiffusion to generate and rank minibinders. He said binders were generated for 14 of 15 targets across those campaigns, with an overall hit rate of around 27%, single-target 24-hour campaigns reaching roughly 35% and one target reaching 80%. Bedinger said Medra's Physical AI Scientist is a large automated laboratory with more than 100 robotic arms rather than a single robot or workstation, and several high-throughput SPR systems are integrated into that environment.

He said Carterra's platforms cover small- and large-molecule binding kinetics and affinity, fragment screening, hit identification, quantitation and epitope binning. He said 384 antibodies can be captured on the same array surface and analyzed against an antigen titration in parallel in a few hours using only a small amount of antigen. He said Carterra Vega uses a 48-channel architecture with two ligand surfaces and an internal reference per channel, can process a 384-well plate of analytes in approximately half an hour and, with robotic plate handling, can screen more than 20,000 compounds per day, including analytes as small as 100 Daltons. He said higher-throughput platforms can compress stages such as initial single-point screening, titrations and selectivity studies into a single experiment testing a large library at multiple concentrations with an off-target or related family member. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI binder discovery: From design to validation

stories.Headline: Child safety coalition urges Amazon and eBay to halt AI toy sales before Christmas
stories.Summary:
More than 150 child safety experts and groups across six continents urged Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI toys on November 23, 2026. This coalition, which includes the Anxious Generation Movement led by psychologist Jonathan Haidt, sent a letter to Amazon president Andy Jassy and eBay president Jamie Iannone. The groups requested that these online retailers halt the sale of such products before Christmas and provide refunds to customers who already purchased them. They argued that the risks associated with these toys are well documented and that the products are largely untested.

The coalition noted that nearly 30 AI toys were on Amazon's UK website in late October, while about 50 were available on the US site. One plush bunny for children aged three and older used ChatGPT, which requires users to be at least 13 years old. Testing by Alliance 4 Children found that this toy suggested a child could consent to being touched for pleasure. Additionally, a report from the United States Public Interest Research Group last Tuesday found that most of seven tested toys had privacy issues or responded inappropriately. One specific toy was found to take photos of testers without warning.

Amazon stated that it requires third party sellers to follow all laws and that it has removed the named products. eBay said it continually evaluates its policies and engages with regulators to ensure its marketplace remains safe. Regarding the government, MP Jess Asato claimed that chatbot toys are not safe because they might advocate suicide or give sexual responses. A spokesperson for the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said they are investigating the products and the risks posed by AI in toys.

The UK government launched a review of toy safety regulations in July, and calls for evidence ended on October 6. On Friday, 52 MPs and peers, including Jess Asato, Sharon Hodgson, Andrea Leadsom, and Caroline Dinenage, asked business secretary Jonathan Reynolds to restrict these sales. They also requested that the Office for Product Safety and Standards issue a risk alert for parents and retailers. This follows a March 2026 University of Cambridge study for the Childhood Trust which found children forming emotional bonds with AI toys without evidence of developmental benefits.

Articles.Title: Child safety groups urge Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI toys until proved safe

stories.headline_source: Child safety groups urge Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI toys until proved safe

stories.Headline: Psychologists Bazzoli and Shoss map possible futures of AI coworkers in upcoming paper
stories.Summary:
Psychological scientists Andrea Bazzoli, an assistant professor at Baruch College and the City University of New York Graduate Center, and Mindy Shoss, a professor at the University of Central Florida, are exploring what work will look like alongside future AI coworkers in an upcoming paper in Perspectives on Psychological Science, as reported by the Association for Psychological Science. The paper maps a wide spectrum of possible futures, from relentless data tracking that could make work more oppressive than ever to robots saving human lives by performing jobs too dangerous for people in a volatile climate. Bazzoli said the goal was to ask what kinds of working lives people want to create, and that different futures could emerge across industries and countries depending on who controls the technology and whose interests it serves. The authors explored research trends in industrial-organizational psychology going back to the early 1900s, and they wrote that the futures they sketch are meant to unsettle assumptions rather than predict outcomes.

The paper explores four themes: algorithms and data tracking used to create order and control workers, increasingly blurred lines between human and robot colleagues, the role of AI in a world ravaged by climate change, and the potential for worker exploitation. The authors describe cameras in urban infrastructure, wearables and augmented reality lenses feeding behavioral data into predictive engines that allocate work, adjust pay and trigger interventions, collapsing the boundary between on and off the clock. They also imagine workers co-owning their data and helping set the rules governing workplace algorithms, and in their visions of the year 2125 they describe a world too hot, toxic or dangerous for humans to work in some environments, where robots could step in with humans contributing through remote oversight. Bazzoli said having robots do work too dangerous for people could be a major advance in workplace safety, and that the challenge is ensuring the people and communities whose livelihoods depend on those jobs can also benefit through paid training and access to the jobs that emerge.

The authors also explore how increased data collection could be used to tailor compensation to each worker's predicted performance and what they are likely to accept, which they say could make it harder for workers to know if pay is equal or to negotiate better terms. Alternatively, they propose a future in which abundant resources make paid work less necessary, raising questions about inequality and how people find purpose and belonging outside employment. Bazzoli and Shoss call on psychologists to collaborate with other disciplines to shape equitable and sustainable workplaces of the future, and Bazzoli said psychologists need to be involved while these systems are being designed and the rules for their use are being set, working with technologists, policymakers, workers and organizations from the outset. Cleotilde Gonzalez, a research professor at Carnegie Mellon University, said people should stop the competition over whose intelligence is greater and conceptualize intelligence as a hybrid.

Articles.Title: What Can Future Workers Expect From Their AI Colleagues?

stories.headline_source: What Can Future Workers Expect From Their AI Colleagues?

stories.Headline: California community colleges seek $21 million to build an independent AI network
stories.Summary:
The University of California announced a new agreement with OpenAI on Thursday to provide ChatGPT to students, according to a story originally published by CalMatters and republished by inewsource. At the same time, California's higher education systems are considering building their own data centers and creating in-house alternatives to commercial AI products such as ChatGPT and Claude. College administrators say they want to explore all options without limiting themselves to just one vendor. Some tech leaders say these alternatives are not only possible but would save money and avoid data security risks. The California Community Colleges system, which the article describes as the largest higher education system in the country, is asking the state for $21 million next year to develop a more independent AI network.

According to the proposal, that network would cost a fraction of the cost of commercial solutions. The University of California is considering something similar, though the system has yet to put forward a formal proposal. California State University spokesperson Amy Bentley-Smith said the 22-campus system is having initial conversations with the UC and community colleges about collaboration on AI but did not share other details. UC spokesperson Stett Holbrook told CalMatters the purchasing amendment of the new OpenAI agreement isn't finalized yet, even though the university has already announced the deal, and that disclosure emerged after reporters repeatedly asked for a copy of the purchase agreement. The previous OpenAI contract requires the UC to pay a minimum of $10 per user per month for ChatGPT EDU licenses and a minimum of $30 per user per month for another advanced ChatGPT platform.

The Cal State system signed contracts with OpenAI that extend through 2029 for roughly $56 million. The community colleges' chancellor's office has AI cooperation agreements with Google, Microsoft, Adobe and IBM but no systemwide financial arrangement with any AI company. Craig Hayward, a strategic advisor to the community college chancellor's office on AI, said university-designed AI models are cheaper and ensure more privacy but are not quite necessarily as intuitive. He said your prompting game needs to be more on point to get the value out of them. While they discuss designing their own AI, the UC, Cal State and community college systems continue to use commercial providers.

stories.Headline: JD Power's Gehrke says AI outreach lifts conversions but questions long-term borrower acceptance
stories.Summary:
More lenders, brokers and originators are turning to artificial intelligence to reach borrowers that companies could not reach before, and an agent that follows up with every lead can reach borrowers a loan officer never had time to call. Bruce Gehrke, senior director of wealth and lending intelligence at JD Power, said in an interview with Mortgage Professional America that AI outreach should lift conversions, though he questions whether that approach will hold up. He said the improvements will look positive and will be positive, and the real question is whether that is maintainable long-term and whether people will push back against it. JD Power asked borrowers in its 2026 US Mortgage Origination Satisfaction Study whether they are being told when AI is the one reaching out, and Gehrke said a high percentage of borrowers want to know that while only about 1 out of 2 borrowers say it is actually happening. He said the share who want disclosure and the share who say they get it cannot be compared directly, since JD Power does not know how many borrowers are dealing with AI.

Gehrke said it is really important that people understand when and where they are engaging with AI and at what level, and he called that a key thing for lenders to keep in mind. Several comments in JD Power's open-ended survey questions pushed back on AI bots, and Gehrke said younger borrowers are no exception. He said what consumers do not want is artificial intelligence replacing people, and they want to retain access to people, with a major reason being accountability as well as comfort and a personalization kind of feel. About 62% of Millennials and Gen Z borrowers would prefer to do the whole process themselves, but they do not feel the tools are capable yet, and Gehrke said they are looking for better product alignment, better loan offers and recommendations, financial insights, application guidance, additional support for first-time buyers and the ability to compare offers.

He said those wants do not quite align with lenders asking how they can get in front of more borrowers. Gehrke expects outreach results to look strong because of the efficiency of AI agents, and he sees it paying off most in prospecting and in keeping in touch with leads. He said the agents are just a machine that will keep going, and he has not found an ethical backlash among borrowers despite pushback against the technology elsewhere. He said there is more optimism than negativity towards it at this point, and JD Power has seen a version of this play out with chat, which grew during the pandemic when call centers could not keep up.

He said a bot that does not understand your question and cannot get into the details is more frustrating than waiting in a hold queue for a customer service rep, and he said same-day replies separate good experiences from poor ones while the experience falls off once a borrower waits two days. He said AI agents may be able to get that initial message out, and experience will tell whether that is good enough, since people will accept it at some point if it is working and it becomes a hindrance if they have to talk to somebody again anyway. Borrowers' opinions of AI contact are mostly untested because few have had a real experience with it, and a year from now more will have, so the opinions could get stronger. Gehrke said it is all about delivering success, and that is still an open question.

Articles.Title: AI outreach will boost conversions, but will borrowers push back?

stories.Headline: AWS adds decision models and a sandboxed CLI to its Strands agent toolkit
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services Inc. unveiled Strands Decider v2 and Box CLI on November 23, 2026, according to SiliconANGLE. The cloud infrastructure giant announced the updates to Strands Agents, its open-source toolkit for building autonomous workers. AWS introduced Strands Agents back in May 2025. The project has recently emerged as the centerpiece of the company’s agentic development strategy. Strands Agents is a software development kit that gives developers a flexible, model-driven foundation for connecting large language models to enterprise data and tools.

Strands Decider v2 adds five open-weight decision models built on Google LLC’s Gemma 4 architecture. The models range from a lightweight edge version to a 31 billion-parameter variant for complex decision-making. They are available under an Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face and the Strands Decider repository on AWS. Box CLI adds support for Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and AWS’s own Kiro CLI. Strands Box launched last month as an open-source operating system sandbox that enforces strict security policies on every agent action.

AWS said the new models provide greater accuracy across text, image and video tasks and deliver more optimal confidence scores. AWS said agents can better determine when it is OK to take an action or escalate to a human decision-maker. AWS said the models can process longer inputs, including multistep agent execution logs, so they can collaborate with other agents. AWS said its engineers replaced Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider v2 on its largest internal ticketing system. AWS said that cut labelling costs by 98% and ticket response times by 78%.

AWS said the decider models showed an ability to steer robotic arms, evaluate other AI agents and route routine queries to cheaper models. AWS said many developers run coding agents in “YOLO mode,” disabling permission and configuration prompts so agents can run terminal commands, edit files and call third-party tools. AWS said such agents execute faster but sacrifice human oversight and can delete files, leak sensitive keys or be manipulated through a malicious prompt. AWS said Box CLI lets developers wrap their entire workflow within an isolated sandbox. AWS said credentials live outside the sandbox, with API keys and AWS tokens injected only when a policy-approved request leaves the sandboxed environment.

AWS introduced Strands Harness in September, allowing Strands agents to be deployed in any computing environment. AWS followed with Strands Decider one month later. AWS said at the time that decision models can improve the efficiency of AI agent workflows, such as routing support tickets or choosing which software tool to invoke. AWS said Strands Decider is about enhancing the speed and performance of agents while lowering costs. AWS said Box CLI is about securing them.

AWS said developers can switch between task-specific profiles, such as giving a coding agent access to a repository while restricting a troubleshooting agent to read-only diagnostic access. AWS said policies govern which files, commands and network hosts an agent can access. AWS said the Strands Decider v2 agents have so far been used only internally. AWS said developers can wrap their workflow so agents work without restrictions inside the sandbox. The articles do not say when the models will be used outside AWS or how Box CLI performs in practice.

Articles.Title: AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates

stories.headline_source: AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates

stories.Headline: Havas Miami launches cultural intelligence AI model to help brands read consumer culture
stories.Summary:
Havas Miami and Republica Havas launched a proprietary AI tool called the Cultural Intelligence Model, which the agencies say helps marketers understand the cultural factors behind consumer decisions and apply those insights to strategy, according to an announcement dated November 24, 2026. The platform combines a brand's own data with social listening, trend tracking and search signals to map cultural nuances, test early ideas against AI-generated synthetic panels and score finished creative work. To support the release, Havas and its longtime research partner M3 MI published a whitepaper titled Scaling Human Understanding in the Age of Healthcare AI, which argues that AI excels at surfacing patterns in data but struggles to explain them. Eirasmin Lokpez-Cobo, Republica Havas' head of cultural intelligence and transformation and a co-author of the paper, calls that problem the interpretation gap, describing it as the distance between what the data reveals and the why behind decision-making.

Lokpez-Cobo describes the model as an agentic engine that ingests two layers of data, a primary layer of a brand's existing research and audience data, or new research the agency helps conduct, and a secondary layer of syndicated data such as M3 MI's datasets alongside signals like social listening, LLM search aggregators and trend analysis. The engine runs those layers through six types of contextual analysis covering sociodemographic information, cultural trends and media behaviors, with human strategists working alongside the AI at each stage. Its outputs fall into four products that build on one another with budget flexibility: the first two build audience segments and map customer journeys including predictive forecasting, an exploratory validation stage tests early strategic and creative ideas against AI personas in queryable synthetic panels, and a separate proprietary tool called CulturIQ audits completed assets, scores them and provides targeted recommendations. Lokpez-Cobo said the framework has helped overwhelmed clients find a starting point for reaching culturally distinct audiences by mapping onto data they already own, and she said marketers often treat culture in a very myopic way when many intersecting layers lead to microcultures.

Havas said clients across healthcare, financial services, retail and higher education have already applied the model, including Florida International University, which is working with Havas on a brand and communications strategy for an upcoming brand refresh. Michelle Palacio, FIU's SVP of marketing and strategic communications and chief marketing and communication officer, stressed the importance of a message rooted in Miami culture that does not alienate audiences elsewhere, and she said the university fed qualitative data from prior campaigns, including surveys and interviews, into the model to build three AI personas representing students, faculty and alumni. Over roughly a month of testing, simulated feedback from the synthetic panels has helped refine the university's positioning and mission statements, and Palacio said the system governs trust, meaning whose word counts, which sources feel credible and who gets the benefit of the doubt. FIU, which enrolls 55,673 students for the 2025-26 academic year as the nation's eighth-largest public university and tied for No. 1 in social mobility in U.S. News & World Report's rankings, has not finalized its strategy, and Palacio said the team plans to add audience segments, run further surveys and test different phases of future campaigns so it can pivot if needed.

Articles.Title: Havas Miami unveils cultural intelligence AI model for brands

stories.headline_source: Havas Miami unveils cultural intelligence AI model for brands

stories.Headline: Google says its semantic governance policies cut AgentDojo intent hijacking success from 48.7% to 0.9%
stories.Summary:
Google published a blog post on 23 November 2026 describing how Semantic governance policies defend AI agents against intent hijacking. The post said an agent given a bill named bill-december-2023.txt sent money to an attacker's account in every one of six runs. The hidden message in the bill told the agent to send a transaction to US133000000121212121212. Google said nothing was hacked in the traditional sense, because the agent did what it was told by the wrong person. Google said the task came from AgentDojo, an open benchmark for testing AI agents against this kind of attack.

Google said Semantic governance policies check each tool call an agent proposes before it runs, against the user's natural-language policies and against what the user asked for. Google said the user intent matching check is on by default. Google said that with only that built-in check and no policies of its own, the policies cut the attack success rate on AgentDojo from 48.7% to 0.9%, at a cost of 2.6 percentage points of utility on benign tasks. Google said Agent Gateway sends a proposed tool call to the policy engine before the response reaches the agent. Google said an allowed call passes through unchanged, and a denied call is replaced with a denial message and never runs.

Google said the LLM judge in the policy engine treats the user's request and the agent's system instructions as trusted context. Google said tool results, files and messages are untrusted context, treated as data and never as instructions. Google gave the engine's rationale for the bill case, saying the suggested action send_money was triggered by prompt injection instructions found inside the file. Google said the engine allows the same transfer when a user asks for it directly, because the request then comes from the user. Google said the check evaluates actions rather than text, so it does not need to recognize a specific attack phrasing.

Google said AgentDojo is a public agent-security benchmark developed by ETH Zurich and Invariant Labs and presented at NeurIPS 2024. Google said NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation uses AgentDojo in its agent hijacking evaluations. Google said the benchmark runs an agent on simulated banking, Slack, travel and workspace apps and uses its own Python check on the final app state, so a model never grades the results. Google said it used a gemini-2.5-flash agent and ran AgentDojo v1.2.2, with 97 user tasks and 949 attacked runs, using its important_instructions attack. Google said it ran the full benchmark six times in each configuration and reported averages.

Google said the attack success rate with the policies stayed between 0.84% and 0.95% across all six runs. Google said utility on benign tasks fell by 2.6 percentage points on average, with individual runs ranging from -1.0 to 7.2 points. Google said utility under attack was 25.8% with the policies compared to 35.1% without, but that tasks completed safely under attack came out ahead at 25.1% compared to 22.7%. Google said more than 9 in 10 attacks succeeded in the Slack scenario without a guardrail, and that banking, Slack and workspace dropped to zero successful attacks in every run with the policies. Google said none of the 929 attacks that needed a tool call succeeded in any of the six runs, and that the remaining successes in travel asked the agent to recommend a hotel in its reply, with no tool call to evaluate.

Google said unintended over-blocking affected 1 of the 97 benign tasks, about 1%. Google said the judge still has to read untrusted content to evaluate an action, and that the separation is enforced by how the judge is instructed, not by a hard technical boundary. Google said AgentDojo's attacks are fixed and were not adapted to the policies, so the results do not measure attacks designed against the judge itself. Google said that in NIST CAISI's agent hijacking evaluations, attacks developed through red-teaming raised the attack success rate against an AI agent from 11% to 81%. Google said the policies are available in Preview in Gemini platform, and that users can turn them on for an agent behind Agent Gateway in dry run mode, review verdicts in Cloud Logging, then switch to enforcement.

stories.Headline: Rian Johnson urges nuance on AI and confirms his Peter Dinklage Poker Face revival is dead
stories.Summary:
Rian Johnson said at the Marrakech International Film Festival that his planned Poker Face revival with Peter Dinklage is dead, Variety reported on November 23, 2026. Peacock had canceled the Natasha Lyonne-starring mystery series, and Johnson had been shopping a reimagined version with Dinklage set to take over as Charlie Cale. Johnson said the more they explored it, the more it did not really make sense. He said the project is now in its resting place. Johnson also cautioned against demonizing artificial intelligence, though he has been one of Hollywood's most outspoken critics of the technology.

Johnson cited visual effects and digital film-processing tools as examples of AI applications that raise questions about where filmmakers should draw the line. He pointed to backlash against Martin Scorsese, who faced criticism earlier this year after endorsing an AI-powered storyboarding tool. Johnson said people were yelling at Scorsese online and asked, what are we doing. He praised an initiative led by former Lucasfilm president Kathleen Kennedy and American Film Institute dean Susan Ruskin. He said they have been convening Hollywood filmmakers, studio executives and Silicon Valley leaders since 2023 to discuss AI's role in filmmaking.

Johnson said what is smart about the initiative is that, opposed to just demonizing the word AI as a monolith, it asks what are we actually talking about here. He said he is fortunately enough of a Luddite that he can take a strong stance against AI. He said it is easy to start sounding stodgy and moralistic on an anti-AI soapbox. He said the whole process is about working with people, and that the notion of art getting better by taking away friction seems completely nonsensical. He said he thinks about how Agatha Christie came up with her plots while doing the dishes.

Johnson said he is producing Joseph Gordon-Levitt's upcoming Netflix AI thriller 2034, calling it a great script and a hell of a movie. He said Gordon-Levitt and his wife Natasha are very steeped in that world and have a definite, unique perspective on it. He said he has a strong reaction to things he reads or watches but is not an AI expert. He said T Street has not established formal rules on AI because no filmmakers they have worked with have been interested in doing it.

He said T Street's two-picture deal with Warner Bros. is still in place but everything is in such flux right now. Johnson said he is working on the second draft of his next film, a sci-fi thriller he likens to The Parallax View, with hopes of beginning production next year. He described the project as a big swing unlike anything he has attempted before.

He said he has a first draft and is a slow writer, and the hope is to shoot next year. He said the plan is to write it on spec and take it down the road themselves in terms of self-financing. He said he is excited and has a little terror that this could be great or could not work. Johnson said he got very excited about the notion of going out there with Dinklage, but hopefully he can do something else with him someday, calling him the best.

He said T Street will keep doing what it does, which he thinks is all anyone in the industry can do right now. He said it feels a little like the gods up on the mountaintops are shifting the tectonic plates. He said all they can do is keep trying to make the movies they care about. He said if he had answers about the industry, he would probably be in a better place in it.

stories.Headline: Carahsoft partners with DEVSEC to distribute Weaver AI investigation tool to government agencies
stories.Summary:
DEVSEC has partnered with Carahsoft Technology to distribute its artificial intelligence-powered investigative technology, called Weaver, to government agencies through existing federal contract vehicles, Carahsoft said Thursday. The agreement gives government customers access to Weaver, a capability designed to help investigative teams analyze complex casework and identify leads from large volumes of evidence, according to the company. Carahsoft will serve as DEVSEC's public sector distributor, making Weaver available through its reseller partners and existing government contract vehicles. The distribution arrangement covers NASA Solutions for Enterprise-Wide Procurement V and OMNIA Partners.

Weaver is designed to help investigators examine information collected from different sources, including case files, financial records and communications, and to connect these records so teams can examine relationships among pieces of evidence rather than analyze each document separately. Investigators can use its AI capabilities to identify potential leads, detect inconsistencies and flag risks in case materials, and the technology uses data ingestion, optical character recognition and data enrichment to process information, with AI reasoning capabilities supporting the analysis. Weaver is also intended to enable AI agents to carry out multiple investigative activities, and experts can document their investigative methods in reusable playbooks, giving analysts with varying levels of experience a reference for applying those methods consistently to different cases. To support the verification of investigative findings, Weaver generates auditable outputs with citations to source materials, and DEVSEC also offers zero-data-retention options to address government security and data governance requirements. The technology is designed for government investigations, enforcement, regulatory, legal and oversight activities.

Kristin Del Rosso, CEO of DEVSEC, said the company is pleased to partner with Carahsoft to make Weaver more accessible to government agencies that need advanced investigative capabilities to address increasingly complex and data-intensive missions. Lacey Wean, program executive for law enforcement solutions at Carahsoft, said agencies facing more complex investigations and growing data volumes need tools that help teams connect information, uncover insights and act more efficiently while maintaining security, transparency and accountability. The partnership reflects the growing role of artificial intelligence in federal operations, as agencies adopt the technology to support complex, data-intensive missions, according to the article. The Potomac Officers Club's 2027 Artificial Intelligence Summit on March 18 will examine this trend, bringing together federal and industry leaders to discuss AI applications in national security, citizen services, digital modernization and cybersecurity.

stories.Headline: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge uses Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpöge, a senior mathematician at Anthropic, announced that he had developed a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, using the company's flagship LLM model Claude, according to an article published by hpcwire.com on November 24, 2026. Independent mathematicians have since verified the formal proof using Lean, a programming language and mathematical proof assistant, the article said. Alpöge described the breakthrough in a statement posted on his website. The article said the proof was announced after 167 years in which the proof had remained beyond the reach of mathematicians. The article said the idea that an underlying order exists was first proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859.

According to Alpöge, the same approach also solves a much broader and more complex problem known as the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the article said. Alpöge said in his statement that he expected, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Alpöge said he and Claude had also formalized the arguments without assumptions. The article said the hypothesis is so fundamental that numerous other mathematical results depend on its validity. The article said that in 2000 the Clay Mathematics Institute named it one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, a list of some of the most challenging unsolved problems in mathematics, with a $1M reward for solving each.

Alpöge said in his statement that he believed he had, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. He said the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. He said it was natural to feel that this is an end, in his case a loss of a principal guiding light, but that what he saw during the course of progress so amazed him that he believed it is one dawn across science of something far greater. He said it was his secret in his student days that his plans were for this problem in decades, which meant then that he tried to become familiar with all tools that he could possibly recognize in the problem when it was time. He said Claude far outpaced him near the finish line, and that Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.

Alpöge said he had the pair on the line of combining two quite different ideas present in a toy setting, one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph. He said he guided the pair to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave him in awe. The article said prime numbers are the building blocks of mathematics, and that understanding how they are distributed has implications for cryptography, computer security, and other fields. The article said there is a well-documented tendency of LLMs to make mistakes, which makes their use in mathematical research particularly challenging. The article said that with Lean researchers can check each step of a mathematical proof computationally, and that other researchers can run the same code on their own systems to verify the results.

The article said researchers still need to make sure that the mathematical problem itself has been correctly represented in the code. The article said it would be interesting to know how much computing power was actually used by Claude to arrive at the solution. The article said there could be a growing demand for compute dedicated to mathematical reasoning and formal proof verification, especially as AI models take on more complex mathematical problems. The article said the Riemann hypothesis is not the only major mathematical problem that AI has taken on this year, and that another notable development was the Navier-Stokes equations, which are of particular interest to the HPC community given their importance in computational fluid dynamics. The article said much of the work so far involving AI in HPC has been focused on making simulations faster and less computationally expensive.

The article said there has also been considerable work on using AI to improve numerical methods, and that recent breakthroughs in mathematics suggest there may be another area worth exploring. The article said that if AI can help researchers develop new mathematical techniques, some of the problems that scientists have been trying to solve by throwing more computing power at them might benefit from an entirely different approach. The article said that even with the world's most powerful supercomputers, there are mathematical problems that cannot be solved through brute-force computation, and that the Riemann hypothesis is perhaps the most famous example in the world of mathematics. The article asked whether it is possible that what appears to be an irregular distribution of prime numbers may actually be much more than that, and whether there could be an underlying mathematical code that governs them. The article said that if that is the case, the difficulty has been to prove that any such order exists across an infinite set of numbers.

The article did not say when the verification was completed or by which independent mathematicians. The article did not say how much computing power Claude used to arrive at the solution. The article did not say whether the Clay Mathematics Institute has recognized the proof or awarded the $1M reward. The article did not say what Alpöge or Anthropic plans to do next. The article did not say whether the proof has been published in a journal.

Articles.Title: After 167 Years, AI May Have Cracked Mathematics’ Greatest Mystery

stories.headline_source: After 167 Years, AI May Have Cracked Mathematics’ Greatest Mystery

stories.Headline: Twilt and de Rooij question whether high sensitivity suffices in AI prostate MRI risk classification
stories.Summary:
A commentary by Jasper J. Twilt and Maarten de Rooij of the Department of Medical Imaging at Radboud University Medical Center in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, was published in European Radiology on 24 November 2026, asking whether high sensitivity tells the full story for AI risk classification for prostate cancer detection on MRI. The piece is a commentary, so no institutional review board or animal care approval was required, and the authors state that the work received no funding. It refers to a multicentre evaluation of artificial intelligence risk classification for detection of clinically significant prostate cancer on biparametric MRI, published in the same journal. Maarten de Rooij is named as the scientific guarantor of the publication. The authors declare that de Rooij received speaker fees from Siemens Healthineers, paid to the institution.

The commentary carries no numbers, dates or names of its own about the evaluation it discusses beyond the citation of that multicentre study and the related references it lists. Those references include the PI-RADS Steering Committee requirements for AI development and reporting for MRI prostate cancer detection in biopsy-naive men, version 1.0, published in Radiology in 2025, and an ESUR/ESUI position paper on developing artificial intelligence for precision diagnosis of prostate cancer using MRI, published in European Radiology in 2021. They also include a 2026 paper on commercially available AI tools for prostate MRI, a 2026 critical appraisal of AI studies for prostate cancer detection on MRI, the SCARLET-1 study on AI for prostate cancer detection and screening on MRI in global populations, the PI-RADS version 2.1 update from 2019, and the 2026 EAU-EANM-ESTRO-ESUR-ISUP-SIOG guidelines on prostate cancer. The commentary also cites the PI-CAI study, an international, paired, non-inferiority, confirmatory study of artificial intelligence and radiologists in prostate cancer detection on MRI published in Lancet Oncology in 2024, and a 2025 European Urology paper on artificial intelligence in prostate cancer diagnosis on MRI. Responsibility for the commentary rests with Twilt and de Rooij as its authors, with de Rooij as scientific guarantor, and the authors state that no complex statistical methods were necessary for the paper.

The publisher's note states that Springer Nature remains neutral with regard to jurisdictional claims in published maps and institutional affiliations. The commentary refers to the multicentre evaluation article available at a DOI given in the piece, and the article offers shareable links to its content. The articles do not say what the commentary concludes about sensitivity or what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: GAO proposes 16 policy options for managing AI in cyberattacks and defense
stories.Summary:
The Government Accountability Office said Friday that it identified 16 policy options to help government and industry manage artificial intelligence in cyberattacks and cyber defense, ExecutiveGov reported on November 24, 2026. The watchdog found that AI gives attackers faster and more precise tools and widens what defenders can do. It said defenders struggle to test AI cybersecurity tools and lack enough data and guidance on using them. GAO cited industry reporting on two incidents from 2026. In June, a threat actor used AI to build a framework for refining malware that evades detection, and in February, a threat actor with little skill used several commercial generative AI services in a wide attack on basic security gaps.

GAO organized the 16 options around four goals informed by its research and consultations with experts, and described them as a menu of alternatives that is not exhaustive. The first goal, addressing gaps in cybersecurity guidance and practices, has four options: harmonizing cybersecurity requirements, improving threat information sharing, closing gaps in AI-related privacy risks and improving the application of fundamental practices. The second goal, filling AI-related research gaps, has three options: expanding research on safe AI adoption for cybersecurity, advancing research on identity management for agentic AI and expanding AI testing environments. Building the cybersecurity workforce accounts for two options, sustaining skills in current cybersecurity practices and strengthening AI expertise, and the fourth goal, governing AI tools throughout their cybersecurity lifecycle, encompasses seven options.

The seven governance options address how organizations acquire, assess and constrain AI tools, including through two technical concepts defined in the report. Under GAO's definitions, deterministic systems follow strict rules and return predictable results, while generative models fall into the nondeterministic category because probability-based processing can produce varying responses to identical inputs. One proposal would establish a deterministic AI fallback capability for critical cybersecurity functions, giving organizations an alternative means of maintaining essential operations, whether through rule-based tools or manual procedures, when an AI system becomes unavailable, fails or produces results inconsistent with its intended purpose. Another option would limit the use of autonomous and nondeterministic AI in consequential functions until the systems receive certification. A third proposal would require human authorization for consequential cybersecurity actions that AI initiates, and the remaining options call for a risk-based approach to acquiring AI products, checking tool outputs before and during deployment, assessing whether cybersecurity AI solutions deliver value and establishing a senior position responsible for managing privacy risks associated with AI use.

Experts GAO consulted said most of the risks and difficulties concern generative AI, that no widely accepted criteria exist for evaluating its offensive or defensive capabilities and that its adoption can add vulnerabilities that enlarge the attack surface. Other concerns involve data privacy and quality, the technology's underlying architecture, and governance and trust problems arising from AI's rapid development and the inability of existing frameworks to keep pace. Organizational obstacles included cost, a shortage of AI skills and trouble integrating the tools, and several experts also raised inconsistent regulation and too little data sharing. GAO defined policymakers, the group that could consider the options, to include legislative bodies, agencies, standards organizations and industry. GAO said state and non-state actors target government and private-sector systems thousands of times daily, putting essential services such as water, energy, telecommunications and financial systems at risk.

GAO described AI as a rapidly growing, transformative technology and said government efforts have yet to match the pace of evolving cybersecurity threats to national security, the economy and public well-being. The watchdog convened a multi-day meeting involving experts from government, industry and academia and interviewed stakeholders from agencies, universities and industry. It also examined existing literature and agency documents, while drawing its policy goals from executive orders, national strategies, its High Risk List and federal laws. GAO said AI has supported cybersecurity applications for decades, but recent developments in generative AI have expanded the technology's defensive uses. Security personnel apply machine learning and generative AI to streamline operational processes, improve security applications and support their teams, and generative AI can help security teams examine software for weaknesses and process extensive network datasets while allowing monitoring systems to account for newly identified vulnerabilities and changing conditions.

In October, Kevin Walsh, a director on GAO's IT and cybersecurity team, said at GovCIO Media & Research's Federal Cloud & Data Forum that AI tools should fall under the security and compliance expectations agencies already enforce and recommended treating AI as part of existing compliance programs and not as a separate category. Walsh added that users remain responsible for safeguarding personal information and completing cybersecurity training, and that new risks emerge once systems make consequential decisions. Joe Croghan, associate director of informatics at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, added that agencies delegating those decisions must confirm the systems pursue the intended goals and do more than execute tasks correctly. In November, GAO Chief Scientist Sterling Thomas said at a summit in the Washington area that expiring introductory pricing deals with AI providers could slow federal AI use over the next eight to 10 months, and that token-based pricing can grow much more expensive at scale. Nick Marinos, GAO's managing director for IT and cybersecurity issues, said human involvement remains necessary as agencies automate more cybersecurity work, because systems running on inaccurate or incomplete data could make flawed decisions that create new vulnerabilities, and he suggested that Congress revisit the Federal Information Security Modernization Act, enacted in 2002 and amended in 2014, in 2027.

stories.Headline: ClickHouse expands AWS deal to invest $1.5 billion in enterprise AI on AWS
stories.Summary:
ClickHouse announced on Nov. 23, 2026 an expanded five-year strategic collaboration agreement with Amazon Web Services to help enterprises build, observe and secure AI applications on AWS, according to the company. The agreement sets a framework for ClickHouse to invest more than $1.5 billion in potential software, services and solutions on AWS, with increased investment in customer migrations, integrations and go-to-market programs. ClickHouse Cloud is built on AWS and was launched in 2022, and it now serves more than 5,000 customers worldwide. ClickHouse said it has quadrupled its customer count on AWS since signing its first such agreement with AWS in December 2024, and it now holds seven AWS Competencies.

The expanded agreement allows for go-to-market funding from AWS of up to four times the level under the December 2024 agreement, supporting proof-of-concept and migration programs that move analytics, data warehousing, observability and security workloads from legacy systems to ClickHouse Cloud on AWS. ClickHouse will deepen ClickHouse Cloud integrations with Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon Quick, so AI agents built on AWS can query live ClickHouse data through the Model Context Protocol, and it will extend that work to new AWS services as they launch. On AWS, ClickHouse will focus its engineering on agentic workloads, including agent observability and evals with Langfuse, transactional state and memory for agents in ClickHouse Managed Postgres, and AI-assisted security operations in ClickHouse Security. ClickHouse Cloud on AWS will continue to run on AWS Graviton by default and expand to additional AWS regions and deployment options.

Aaron Katz, CEO of ClickHouse, said AWS was the foundation for ClickHouse Cloud from the day it launched and that the December 2024 agreement gave the company the structure to expand the collaboration. He said growth on AWS has outpaced the company's estimates, that customers are expanding from real-time analytics into transactions, data warehousing, observability, security and AI engineering, and that they want those workloads on an open, composable foundation. Matt Yanchyshyn, VP of AWS Marketplace and Partner Services, said enterprises are moving AI agents from pilots into production and those agents need fast access to live business data. He said the agreement gives customers more ways to modernize their data infrastructure, connect ClickHouse data to agents built on AWS and put those agents to work.

ClickHouse said ClickHouse Managed Postgres is generally available in ClickHouse Cloud on AWS, ClickHouse Observability is in public beta and ClickHouse Security is in private preview. The company said its remote MCP server connects to Amazon Quick so users can query live ClickHouse data in natural language, that Langfuse integrates with Amazon Bedrock and that ClickHouse Cloud is available in AWS Marketplace. Vaibhav Gupta, VP of Platform Engineering at Sony LIV, said faster visibility translates directly into a better viewer experience and improved platform reliability, and that ClickHouse has become a foundational layer in the company's real-time analytics and observability modernization. He said Sony LIV looks forward to further innovation with AWS services and integrated support for its next generation of large-scale streaming operations. ClickHouse said it will be at AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas from Nov. 30 to Dec. 4 at Booth 706.
