stories.Summary:
The article is a personal essay by a GrantWatch writer published on 23 November 2026, reflecting on search and AI changes and a Thanksgiving seating chart. The writer says Google's search updates gave a disastrous May and June. The writer made a seating chart with a turkey in the middle and the head of the table saved for the human who came for an answer. The writer describes SEO, AEO, GEO, AIO and SXO as guests at the table. The writer says the person at the head of the table asks whether the content is clear, trustworthy and useful to them.

The writer says the human wants to know three things: whether there is a grant for their nonprofit, what it takes to apply, and whether it can be done by Friday. The writer says GrantWatch researchers verify grants and add new opportunities every weekday. The writer says researchers check who is eligible, when applications are due, and what the funder actually says. The writer says GrantWatch adds new grants and updates existing grant listings daily. The writer says every grant undergoes a scheduled review every 90 to 180 days to verify its information and availability.

The writer says GrantWatch writers and editors tell readers about the newest grants and explain how to write a grant proposal. The writer says GrantWatch Intelligence and the 12-Stage Grant Pipeline are tools readers can use. The writer says readers with 20 minutes before a board meeting can subscribe to search Human Verified grants. The writer says the staff kept showing up for the people who count on them. The writer says the team will make it through what the writer calls this AI tunnel.

The writer says ChatGPT and Claude showed up already knowing what they want to eat. The writer says there is no choice for anyone writing content right now. The writer gives a prompt asking an AI editor to edit a draft for SEO, AEO, GEO, AIO and SXO while keeping the writer's voice, humor and point of view. The writer says the prompt asks for a clear title and headings, an early answer to the reader's main question, easy-to-verify claims, a flagged source list and an obvious next step. The writer says the prompt asks for light edits and a short list of changes.

The writer says the home office is right across from the dining room. The writer says the acronyms would pull up a chair and turn the mashed potatoes into a featured snippet. The writer says the website and the acronyms can sell GrantWatch subscriptions without the writer this weekend. The writer thanks friends Elli and Mel for having the writer and says the writer is bringing the stuffing, family and a clear mind. The writer says GrantWatch is in good hands.

The writer says the good seat comes with Human Verified grants and invites readers to subscribe and pull up a chair. The writer says GrantWatch is a grant research and management service that does not award grants, distribute grant funding or guarantee an award. The writer says GrantWatch distinguishes open opportunities from upcoming opportunities announced by a funder whose opening date has not arrived or whose complete guidelines are not yet available. The writer says forecasted opportunities are based on advance notices published by funding sources, often government agencies. stories.Headline: METR finds Anthropic accelerates AI progress through AI-driven R&D and solves a 167-year-old math problem
stories.Summary:
On November 5, METR released a report from inside Anthropic, according to investinglive.com on November 23, 2026. Anthropic gave METR unprecedented access to internal data on its AI R&D process from August 12 to October 29. Anthropic restricted some details and METR agreed to those restrictions. The report was released at the same time as the US midterms, during a 5% Nasdaq fall. The article says it was seen as pre-IPO hype and did not get the attention it deserved.

METR is described as the best-placed independent evaluator there is. The article says Anthropic is likely improving its models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate it did between March 2024 and October 2025. It says a majority of this acceleration is likely attributable to Anthropic's extensive use of AI to do R&D, which it calls close to recursive self-improvement. METR said it did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks that would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. METR said it was confident the observed acceleration was not simply the result of faster growth in training compute.

The article attributes the acceleration finding to METR and the R&D explanation to its own assessment. It reports METR's conclusion that there is no wall and that AI will continue to progress at an even-faster pace in the next year. It says Anthropic solved a 167-year-old math problem late last week and that the solution has now been verified. Brian Conrey, described as a leading Riemann specialist, told AFP it is really the biggest thing he thinks has ever happened in mathematics. The article calls the solution a validation of CEO Dario Amodei's promise to cure diseases.

The article says not many people in markets understand the gravity of AI solving the 167-year-old math problem. It says the solution is basically the holy grail of math problems and is likely to unlock entirely new ways of looking at math. It says the implications for scientific discovery, from materials science to medicine, are difficult to overstate. It says the significance of the two developments together is hard to overstate. It says there has most recently been talk about a leap in robotics training from AI.

The article says the market had a meltdown over AI fears this month and that there is a real discussion to have about the economics of the AI spend. It says the real story of AI is the technology itself. It says AI is the most important technology in a generation, or it might not be another technological revolution at all. It says AI may be the technology that accelerates every technological revolution that follows or came before. It says the METR report was released in the midst of the 5% Nasdaq fall.

The article says METR has shown that AI is already accelerating the development of AI itself. It says the Riemann hypothesis breakthrough illustrates the kinds of problems increasingly capable models can tackle. It asks whether the gains will go to memory chip makers, graphics chip makers, power producers or hackers, and calls that an entirely different and difficult discussion. It says the author continues to think the HALO trade is the safest bet on AI. It says the greatest winners from AI may not be the companies selling intelligence but the companies that suddenly find intelligence becoming almost free.

Articles.Title: A look inside Anthropic shows there is no ceiling on AI

stories.Headline: New Brunswick communities seek council approval and raise concerns as AI data centers test social license
stories.Summary:
Two communities in New Brunswick are approaching the prospect of AI data center development in different ways, according to an article republished by TechXplore from The Conversation. In Fundy Shores, the mayor has called for new rules governing AI data centers even though no developer has proposed building one in his municipality yet, and the municipality wants future developers to obtain council approval through a rezoning process that would let residents weigh in before construction could proceed. In nearby Saint John, residents have been debating a proposed facility in Lorneville, where at a public meeting they raised concerns about air quality, water consumption and the benefits such a project would bring. After the meeting, one resident told reporters that in their view there is no social license for the project, and the article says the two communities illustrate different points in the debate over social license. The article describes a social license to operate as the ongoing acceptance of a project by the people affected by it, an informal relationship between a developer and affected communities rather than a formal legal authorization like a government permit.

It says the term emerged in the mining industry in the 1990s, when companies recognized that even with government permits in hand, opposition from neighbors could delay or disrupt their operations. As an example, it cites Enbridge's proposed Northern Gateway pipeline, where in April 2014 residents of Kitimat, B.C., voted on the project and 58.4% of those who voted opposed it, after which a political dispute followed about how much weight residents' responses should carry. The article says claims that a project has or lacks a social license often depend on who is speaking for the community and whose views are being counted, since a council resolution, a benefits agreement and a public vote each provide evidence about a different group of people but none necessarily represents everyone affected. The article says this question of representation is especially important when projects affect Indigenous nations, because First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities have distinct rights, governing institutions and authority to make decisions, and their views cannot be subsumed into municipal consultation or treated as another measure of local opinion. It also warns against treating social license as a one-time decision, noting that before a data center is constructed residents have forecasts and promises to consider, and once a facility opens they can measure those promises against their lived experiences, including how the operator responds when something goes wrong.

As an example it cites Sherbrooke, Que., where the city agreed to supply electricity to Bitfarms for a bitcoin mining facility, neighbors soon began complaining to the city about noise, Bitfarms replaced the fans and installed a noise barrier but the problem persisted, and in 2021 the city and the company agreed in principle to move the operation to an industrial park. The article concludes that a social license is not something a developer keeps indefinitely and largely depends on whether a project continues to meet the expectations of the people affected by it. It says residents' views may change as a project develops and its impacts become clearer, and that a council's approval may allow construction to proceed but does not guarantee lasting community acceptance. It adds that residents must have opportunities to hold operators accountable as they experience the project's effects.

stories.Headline: Sam Altman backs Jakub Pachocki's plan for industrywide AI development limits
stories.Summary:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman gave his backing to a proposal for industrywide limits on artificial intelligence development on November 23, 2026. This support follows a plan outlined by OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki on Sunday, November 22. The proposal suggests that rival developers should agree on specific thresholds they will not cross until stronger safety safeguards are established. Altman warned that the capabilities of artificial intelligence could advance faster than companies are able to safely monitor them. The proposal focuses on a measurement called perplexity, which tracks how accurately models predict the next piece of text.

OpenAI reported that GPT-3.5 had a log-perplexity score of around 0.99, while newer models have dropped below 0.8. Pachocki expects potentially transformative capabilities to emerge when scores reach between 0.68 and 0.70, though the exact nature of these changes is unknown. He argues that improvements in this metric have already led to advances in mathematical problem solving and cybersecurity abilities. Jakub Pachocki is responsible for the proposal and warned that AI could improve its own training methods as early as 2027.

He believes this could accelerate development beyond the current capabilities of existing safety measures. Sam Altman endorsed the essay by Pachocki, calling it the most important publication from OpenAI in some time. Altman believes that coordinated restrictions could eventually influence the pace of infrastructure spending and the training of frontier models. No binding industrywide agreement has been announced among the competing developers at this time.

The immediate challenge is whether rivals can agree on enforceable safeguards and common measurement standards. Companies must decide if they can implement these limits without surrendering their own competitive advantages in the market. It remains unclear if other major AI developers will join OpenAI in this effort to slow development. More to follow.

stories.Headline: PCS Software’s Villegas says AI should assist dispatchers with repetitive tasks while people make final decisions
stories.Summary:
Danielle Villegas, chief product and technology officer at PCS Software, said on FreightWaves’ What the Truck?!? that artificial intelligence should multiply the efficiency of a dispatch team rather than replace the people on it. She described AI as a tool that takes on repetitive work so dispatchers can spend their time on decisions that matter. Her starting point is the tasks dispatchers repeat every day, such as routine on-time or delayed delivery notifications and load entry. Automating those tasks gives dispatchers room to find more freight and handle exceptions, like a truck breaking down and a replacement driver having to be arranged.

Villegas said the approach changes what AI is for, framing it as a way to expand what a dispatch team can do rather than only as a way to cut costs. She said anyone who has spent time with AI tools knows their limits, and that sometimes AI is confidently wrong when it is wrong. That is why PCS builds its products around human oversight, particularly for consequential decisions, and she said you have to keep the human in the loop especially when dollars or safety are concerned. Rates are the clearest example, because a wrong one lands directly on the bottom line, and her model is for AI to recommend and speed up decisions while a person makes the final call.

To explain why visibility matters, Villegas pointed to the passenger display inside a Waymo, which she said is there to build confidence rather than because the vehicle needs it. She said the same logic applies in freight, where users need to see what the AI is proposing and why. That transparency principle shapes how PCS designed driver assignment in Cortex, which she said draws on more than 40 data elements to recommend which driver should haul which load. Those inputs include dispatcher knowledge, according to the article.

stories.Headline: Teradyne grows robotics revenue 28% as AI automation demand rises
stories.Summary:
Teradyne is benefiting from growing adoption of artificial intelligence-powered robotics, expanding automation demand and increasing investments in AI data center infrastructure, according to an article published by Zacks Investment Research and carried by Yahoo Finance on November 23, 2026. The article was written by Nilanshi Mukherjee and appeared at 10:04 AM CST. Teradyne's expanding robotics portfolio strengthens its competitive position against KLA and Cohu in the AI space, the article states. Growing investments in physical AI and robot-assisted assembly and testing are creating significant opportunities for the company's Robotics business, according to the article. The article asks whether Teradyne can outpace KLA and Cohu.

In the third quarter of 2026, Teradyne's Robotics revenues increased 28% year over year to $96 million, marking its highest third-quarter revenues on record, the article states. The segment also turned a profit during the quarter, reflecting improving demand and operational performance. Electronics and semiconductor manufacturing has emerged as Robotics' largest vertical, supported by growing automation needs in complex server and rack assembly processes. Teradyne's Universal Robots Gen 7 collaborative robot platform and PolyScope X software are strengthening its competitive position, and these solutions are designed to support physical AI applications and improve automation flexibility across electronics assembly operations. The company is expanding its physical AI ecosystem through partnerships with NVIDIA, Analog Devices, Scale AI, Generalist, Bright Machines and Sereact, collaborations expected to accelerate adoption of intelligent robotics solutions across industrial applications.

Teradyne expects continued Robotics revenue growth in the fourth quarter of 2026, according to the article. Broader automation deployments by a major customer are expected to support growth in 2027, while emerging physical AI applications could create additional opportunities in 2028 and beyond. The article states that Teradyne's expanding AI-powered robotics portfolio, strategic partnerships and growing automation demand strengthen its long-term growth prospects, positioning it favorably against competitors like KLA and Cohu. Teradyne currently carries a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), the article states. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for fiscal 2026 earnings is pegged at $9.41 per share, which has increased 3.29% over the past 30 days and suggests 137.63% year-over-year growth.

KLA is benefiting from growing demand for AI through its leadership in process control and ability to address growth markets in wafer fab equipment, including high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging, the article states. Cohu's exposure to AI infrastructure is expanding through adoption of its Eclipse handler and active thermal-control technology for high-power processors, according to the article. Cohu's management raised the estimated annual high-performance computing opportunity pipeline by 18% sequentially to approximately $1 billion in the third quarter of 2026, including about $230 million in qualified opportunities, $440 million in qualification and $330 million in engagement. Cohu also raised its fiscal 2026 high-performance computing revenue outlook to approximately $120 million from $100-$110 million, the article states. Eclipse supports multiple processor generations, helping customers manage capital investment and accelerate production ramps.

Teradyne shares have gained 5.8% year to date, outperforming the Zacks Computer & Technology sector's 6% decline and the Zacks Electronics - Miscellaneous Products decrease of 5.7%, according to the article. Teradyne stock is trading at a premium with a forward 12-month Price/Sales of 5.06X compared with the Computer & Technology sector's 4.27X, and Teradyne has a Value Score of D. The article states that Teradyne is facing stiff competition from KLA and Cohu, and that both companies are expanding their footprint in the AI space. The article originally published on Zacks Investment Research. The article carries a trading disclosure linking to Coinbase and states that Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser.

The article leaves open whether Teradyne can outpace KLA and Cohu in AI, posing the question in its headline without answering it. It gives no date for when Teradyne might outpace its competitors or what measure would settle the comparison. It does not state the size of KLA's or Cohu's AI-related revenues for comparison with Teradyne's $96 million in third-quarter Robotics revenues. It gives no figures for Teradyne's total company results, only the Robotics segment. It does not say what the major customer's broader automation deployments in 2027 involve or name that customer.

stories.Headline: Organized crime groups steal high value AI hardware during transport to data centers
stories.Summary:
Transnational organized criminal gangs have stolen high value AI hardware during transport to data centers. These thefts occurred in recent weeks and throughout the past year. The criminals include cartels that operate with their own finance and human resources departments. They target shipments moving across the country on roads leading to facilities. Some of these thefts involved losses in the tens of millions of dollars.

The stolen cargo includes Blackwell chips on pallets worth 15 to 20 million dollars. Some truckloads moving across the country carry a total value of 100 million dollars. Other targeted components are generators, transformers, bus bars, and high voltage or low voltage switchgear. Criminals use fake paperwork, signal jammers, and resprayed trucks with changed license plates and DOT numbers. Some gangs buy legitimate trucking companies to gain traction on load boards.

David Warrick is the executive vice president of enterprise at the risk detection company Overhaul. He stated that the economics of these thefts have become crazy from a criminal perspective. Warrick said that chips are easier to move than narcotics because they are legal goods. He noted that some large thefts remain private because there is a level of embarrassment. He advised shippers to treat their inventory as if it were cash.

Hyperscalers and neo cloud providers are affected because stolen components are part of just-in-time builds. These thefts can delay compute capacity that has already been contracted by customers. Warrick noted that the monetary value of the cargo is often not the primary worry. Instead, shippers fear brand damage, empty shelves, and a loss of customer satisfaction. The scarcity of components means there is no automatic way to replace stolen items.

The AI infrastructure boom has created a threat landscape shaped by scale and scarcity. Global spending on this infrastructure now runs about double the cost of the U.S. interstate highway system annually. A secondary market for these components has emerged because supply is very tight. Criminals target handoffs in the supply chain where weaknesses are most common. Destinations of concern for stolen hardware include Russia, Iran, and China.

Overhaul recently recovered a fraudulent load by using analytics and working with local law enforcement. Warrick expects the trend of theft to continue as more money flows into the build-out. He believes more work is needed regarding legislation to ensure that punishments for offenders stick. Shippers are shifting some loads to smaller transit vans or box trucks to reduce risk. The articles leave open how legislation will change to deter these organized gangs.

stories.Headline: Providence cuts internal hiring admin effort 90% with agentic AI tool RITA
stories.Summary:
Providence, a health system with 51 hospitals and more than 1,000 clinics across Alaska, California, Montana, New Mexico, Oregon, Texas and Washington, revamped its internal hiring with an artificial intelligence, powered tool called RITA, or Requisition and Internal Transfer Agent. Providence Vice President of Talent Acquisition Carol McDaniel said the organization decided to automate the process. RITA was built on IBM watsonx Orchestrate and connected to existing systems, including Providence’s Oracle HR environment. The organization has about 119,000 caregivers, which Providence calls its employees. McDaniel said it was easier for internal caregivers to leave and come back as new employees than to transfer to a new opportunity.

Since its rollout, RITA has reduced administrative effort for hiring managers by 90% and allowed internal transfers to start their jobs 12 days sooner, on average. Providence worked first on collective bargaining agreement, governed roles, which are typically assigned by seniority. The tool covers three simple questions: Is this a replacement, is this a new position, and is this CBA-governed. The tool delivers qualified candidates to the hiring leader and takes candidates through the offer process for the position. Providence had five releases of RITA with improvements and enhancements along the way.

McDaniel said the organization stopped and said it had to fix the process because retention is a big part of its recruiting. She said Providence shifted the administrative burden away from its day-to-day caregivers and gave them time back, with big time and cost savings since the launch. She said the entire process took about 18 months, and that Providence made some mistakes in the beginning and had to go back and solve a larger problem than originally thought. She said the first iteration was just about the transfer, and all it had done was shift the problem to another department. She said the enhancements come directly from key operational leaders and the people actually doing the work.

McDaniel said Providence brought stakeholders into the conversation, which it calls human-centered design, and that feedback is critical. She said Providence is an Oracle shop with Oracle Fusion Cloud HCM, implemented about four and a half years ago, and felt it important not to introduce a new system to its stack. She said the building of the requisition process seemed to be where the biggest problem was, secondary to making the transfer happen. She said adoption and communication are hard in a very large organization like Providence, and getting the message to the hiring leader at the front line or in the clinic is really difficult. She said Providence decided to look at administrative effort first and wanted to lessen the time to fill roles today.

McDaniel said that before RITA, Providence’s time to fill for internal transfers rivaled its external hiring, which should not be the case. She said Providence was also interested in addressing hiring costs, with a cost per hire for external hires and for internal, and in redeploying those savings. She said Providence wanted to redeploy the time saved by clinicians to give more time for patient care. She said Providence had not done anything like this before and was a little unsure. She said the metrics are the ones Providence is watching that will hopefully improve its program.

McDaniel said Providence began with internal transfers to start with a smaller scope of what will be a project for more general internal work. She said that today the talk is about department-to-department roles, and tomorrow it will be about going from clinical to nonclinical or moving from one ministry to another. She said Providence had to start smaller so it could grow bigger. She said Providence will expand RITA next year into a larger scope of work. She said it is critical to understand what stakeholders want next and how to make the experience more personalized for caregivers, who are getting automated messages about opportunities.

stories.Headline: Pew Research Center rejects AI tools for coding religious restriction data after tests show inaccuracy
stories.Summary:
Pew Research Center ran two experiments to see if artificial intelligence could help code data about restrictions on religion. The researchers tested these tools to determine if they could make the manual coding process faster for human coders. One experiment took place between December 2024 and February 2025. The second experiment occurred between July and August 2025. These tests compared AI results with data already hand-coded in prior studies.

The first test used Google's NotebookLM to review 2021 sources for Germany, Iceland, Jamaica, Nigeria, and Singapore. It also reviewed Canada, China, India, Saudi Arabia, Turkmenistan, Indonesia, Serbia, and Syria for specific questions. The second test used LexisNexis' Nexis+ AI on 2020 and 2022 data for eight countries. These countries were Canada, Egypt, Germany, Jamaica, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, and South Korea. The process involves answering over 30 questions to produce a Government Restrictions Index and a Social Hostilities Index.

The researchers stated that the tools did not make things up but failed to find all relevant information. They noted that the AI tools did not calculate reliable incident totals across the various sources. The team found that verifying AI citations took more time than the tools saved during the search. They observed that identical prompts often produced different answers at different times or on different days. Consequently, the center is not planning to adopt either tool into the coding workflow.

Human coders are affected because they must manually review laws, policies, or events to ensure data integrity. For example, human coders found 119 detention cases in Nigeria, while the AI tool listed only four. The researchers found that verifying NotebookLM's results for Singapore took 10.5 hours, compared to 4.5 hours for manual coding. Nexis+ AI missed local reporting not translated into English and struggled with bureaucratic topics. The tool also cited Pew Research Center data back to the researchers through news stories.

The center releases an annual report measuring how governments and societies restrict the free exercise of religion. This data covers 198 countries and territories and goes back to 2007. Coders typically spend four months combing through constitutions and publications from the United Nations and U.S. government. They also use documents from nongovernmental organizations like Human Rights Watch. Two coders independently review each case and reconcile disagreements to create annual scores.

The center may explore using AI to produce quick summaries to orient coders before they start researching. They might also test AI as a second coder to help reconcile disagreements on some question types. Future tests could involve updated tools to identify reliable sources for new or related research questions. The articles leave open whether future versions of these AI tools will improve in consistency. They do not state when any further experiments with these tools will begin.

stories.Headline: Mercedes-Benz deploys Arena Physica's Atlas AI agents to speed electrical repairs at its Alabama plant
stories.Summary:
Mercedes-Benz and Arena Physica announced on Nov. 23, 2026, a global agreement to deploy Arena's Atlas platform, which applies AI agents that reason about complex hardware to speed up electrical and electronic repair on the production line, according to the press release issued by Arena Physica. The release said deployment starts at the Tuscaloosa plant in Alabama for the new GLE and GLS, with pilot deployment planned at additional Mercedes-Benz plants. According to the release, Atlas is integrated as an add-on into Mercedes-Benz's existing electrical and electronic rework assistance system and runs a closed-loop optimization that aims to direct technicians to the most likely root cause, refine the repair plan as new measurements come in, and capture causes and repair outcomes. The release said that in the initial testing phase Atlas enabled technicians to diagnose and repair 20 to 30 percent faster, across both new and experienced skill levels.

The release said the expected results are higher first-time-fix rates, reduced rework and disassembly costs, faster onboarding of new technicians, and improved production quality through quicker root cause detection and prevention of repeat electrical and electronic issues. According to the release, Atlas learns to understand hardware the way an experienced engineer does by combining deterministic and probabilistic reasoning, and it is underpinned by the Metagraph, a digital representation of pins, connectors and wires in the vehicle and the mapping of their functional importance and physical location. The release described the Metagraph as a flexible foundation that grows richer as new data comes in and extends to new systems and applications over time. The release said Mercedes-Benz plans to bring Atlas's diagnostic intelligence directly onto global production lines, complementing its existing engineering and quality systems.

Jason Hoff, CEO of Mercedes-Benz North America, said in the release that as the company's vehicles grow more sophisticated, so does the expertise required from technicians on its lines, and that Atlas puts additional diagnostic intelligence into the hands of its teams so they can repair complex electrical systems with greater speed and precision. He said this aligns with the company's global AI strategy of using AI wherever it empowers team members and benefits customers, according to the release. Pratap Ranade, Co-Founder and CEO of Arena Physica, said in the release that one challenge in advanced manufacturing is encoding decades of engineering expertise and scaling it across an organization to support all team members, and that Atlas helps capture deep diagnostic knowledge that takes engineers years to build and makes it available to every technician on the line. He said working with Mercedes-Benz, which he described as a company that has defined the industry standard for automotive quality, shows what is possible when AI is deployed to help skilled people be even better at what they do, according to the release.

The release said the partnership follows a human-centered approach to AI in production at Mercedes-Benz, in which AI provides additional support to experts performing diagnostic tasks as electrical complexity in modern vehicles increases. According to the release, Arena Physica, which calls itself the electromagnetic superintelligence company, was founded in 2019 and is based in New York City, and its Atlas platform is described as the agentic harness for hardware engineering that applies physics-informed AI to verify, debug and optimize complex hardware across its lifecycle. The release said the company works with hardware companies including AMD, Anduril, Bausch + Lomb and Mercedes-Benz. The release did not say when the pilot deployment at additional plants would begin or which plants would be involved.

stories.Headline: Arrive AI sells $100,000 of stock to strategic investor at 50% premium
stories.Summary:
Arrive AI Inc., a company listed on Nasdaq under the ticker ARAI, announced on November 23, 2026, that a strategic investor had completed an initial purchase of $100,000 of its common stock at a 50% premium to the stock's closing price on November 20, 2026. The investor also received one-to-one warrant coverage, exercisable for cash at a 75% premium to that same November 20 closing price. The investor has the ability to purchase up to $400,000 in additional common stock, which could raise its aggregate direct equity investment to $500,000. Any future stock purchases would be priced at a 50% premium to the market price at the time of the applicable transaction.

The arrangement contemplates one-to-one cash warrant coverage for any investor share purchase, and the investor holds an initial tranche of warrants that have not yet been exercised. If all contemplated additional share purchases and cash warrant exercises occur, Arrive AI could receive greater than $1 million in aggregate gross proceeds, though future purchases, warrant issuances and exercises are not assured. The new investment follows Arrive AI's recent exchange of debt into preferred equity, which the company said eliminated its debt and strengthened its balance sheet as it pursues additional growth capital. Additional details of the transaction are set out in the company's Current Report on Form 8-K, filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission concurrently with the announcement.

Piyush Phadke, Chief Financial Officer of Arrive AI, said completing the initial investment at a 50% premium brings fresh capital into the company on terms reflecting its disciplined approach to issuing shares. He said the company continues to believe there is substantial value to unlock at Arrive AI and that the investment reflects confidence in that opportunity. He also said the premium pricing reinforces the company's commitment to securing capital on terms that support its shareholders as it executes its growth strategy. The release describes Arrive AI as a physical AI and autonomous logistics infrastructure company building a network of intelligent delivery endpoints.

The release states that the forward-looking statements in it, including those about potential additional equity investments, future transaction pricing, future warrant tranches, cash warrant exercises and potential aggregate proceeds of up to $1 million, are contingent on future transactions or the exercise of warrants for cash, none of which is guaranteed. It says these statements reflect management's current expectations and assumptions as of the release date and that risks and uncertainties may cause actual results to differ materially. Readers are directed to review the risk factors in Arrive AI's registration statement and other filings at www.sec.gov and to avoid undue reliance on these statements. Al Awadi said du brings together something no other provider in the nation can offer, namely complete ownership of the data centers, national connectivity, sovereign inference compute and an end-to-end delivery journey under one roof. He said du is proud to stand as a trusted partner supporting the UAE's AI ambitions by enabling government entities and enterprises to turn AI opportunities into practical and measurable outcomes. stories.Summary:
A whitepaper published on November 23, 2026 by AFL examines how fiber infrastructure should be planned across edge, regional and core tiers as AI workloads spread out, and it asks when a brownfield retrofit stops making sense compared with a greenfield build. The paper describes AI infrastructure as a distributed system, with training in hyperscale campuses, inference in metro facilities and small models at the edge. It says every tier depends on fiber, which raises the retrofit question for existing sites. The whitepaper was announced by datacenterdynamics.com on the same date.

The paper asks operators to plan edge, regional and core fiber infrastructure as one connected strategy rather than as separate projects. It sets out the capacity, density, resilience and connectivity that each tier of AI infrastructure demands, so planners can compare requirements across the whole system. It also asks operators to assess existing pathways, installed fiber and route diversity before choosing between a retrofit and a new build. On design, it recommends separating long-life and short-life elements so that future speed upgrades can add capacity without pulling new cable.

AFL is responsible for the whitepaper, which appears in the DCD whitepapers and reports section under the compute, storage and networking channel. The articles do not quote any named person, so no individual is credited with specific remarks. The paper frames the retrofit or greenfield decision as a practical question that existing sites must answer before committing. It presents the connected planning approach as guidance for operators weighing that choice.

The articles give no figures, dates or named sites beyond the November 23, 2026 publication date, and they do not say what any operator has decided to do. They also do not describe next steps beyond the planning and assessment the whitepaper recommends. The paper is tagged under AI, AI infrastructure, architecture, brownfield, DCI, distributed infrastructure, fiber, greenfield and retrofit. No outcome or follow-up announcement is reported.

stories.Headline: Can AI help with manage your money? What to know before you ask - WKMG
stories.Summary:
More consumers are turning to artificial intelligence for help with their finances, and one of them is Toni Moore, who is blind and said she began asking AI about her money after using it to answer other questions. The conversations led her to budgets and spreadsheets and helped her review recurring charges, and she said the tool helped her organize subscriptions and cut costs by dropping ones she did not need. Moore said text-based AI tools make financial information easier for her to access because the format is already accessible to her. She said AI helped her learn how to talk with creditors, negotiate and keep a budget, skills she had to teach herself. Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling agency, reported that the number of clients who found it through organic generative AI searches, primarily ChatGPT, rose 48.8% year over year through September 2026.

That increase came as more people sought help with debt, and MMI said its counseling volume was up 9.5% year over year through September. Its clients carried an average of $40,200 in unsecured debt year-to-date, up 4.8% from $38,300 during the same period in 2025. Ted Rossman, MMI's principal consumer finance analyst, said in the release that the story behind the numbers is about the rising cost of living and that on average the price of everything we buy has risen 30% since the pandemic. He said credit card debt often stems from medical bills, car and home repairs, and everyday expenses such as gas and groceries. The article says AI can help users organize expenses, build a basic budget, understand common debt-payoff approaches, or prepare questions to ask a creditor.

The article warns that AI-generated answers can be inaccurate or incomplete and says they should be treated as a starting point, not a substitute for advice from a qualified financial professional or a nonprofit credit counselor. It advises checking important information against trusted sources before making a financial decision, especially when it involves debt, taxes, investments or legal rights. It also says to protect personal information by not entering a Social Security number, date of birth, account numbers, passwords or other details that could identify you or give someone access to your accounts, and it suggests asking general questions with rounded or hypothetical figures instead of sharing exact identifying details. For Moore, the article says, AI is not making her financial decisions but is helping her make more informed ones. The article's tips include starting with a general task, verifying the answer with a bank, creditor, government agency or qualified counselor, keeping control of decisions, and considering nonprofit counseling for anyone struggling with debt.

stories.Headline: South Korea builds a national research base to develop AI scientists for the K-Moonshot project
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT held a meeting with experts from industry, academia, and research on November 23. This gathering took place at the National AI Science Research Center to discuss linking national science AI resources. The participants focused on advancing the AI scientist mission under the K-Moonshot project. They aimed to move beyond using AI as a support tool to using it for setting hypotheses and designing experiments.

The government is building a national science AI research base by combining computing resources, training data, AI models, agents, and skilled personnel. This initiative requires the National AI Science Research Center, established this year, to work with government-funded institutes in fields like nuclear power, nuclear fusion, and biotech. The plan includes running a pilot integrated science AI platform service before the end of this year. Experts also discussed securing dedicated computing resources, such as supercomputer No. 6, and establishing a standard system for training data.

Yong-kyun Yoo, the head of the National AI Science Research Center, presented missions to consolidate resources, operate the integrated platform, and foster an ecosystem. Seong-bin Lim, a PD, presented the specific roadmap for the K-Moonshot AI scientist mission. Deputy Prime Minister and Science and ICT Minister Gyeong-hun Bae stated that an era is coming where AI scientists verify hypotheses alongside human scientists. He promised full government support to ensure the research center becomes a hub and the K-Moonshot project delivers results.

stories.Headline: AMD and US Energy Department unveil Lux supercomputer at Oak Ridge to advance AI-driven science
stories.Summary:
AMD, working with the U.S. Department of Energy and Hewlett Packard Enterprise, unveiled the Lux supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, according to a Small Business Trends report published on November 23, 2026. The system is designed to support advanced artificial intelligence and scientific research, and it is ranked 14th on the TOP500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers. Lux is now accessible to scientific users working on the Genesis Mission, a Department of Energy initiative aimed at advancing AI-driven science. The machine combines AMD EPYC processors, AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD Pensando networking and AMD ROCm software, all built by HPE. The Genesis Mission projects include AI-assisted design of fusion power plants, development of materials for advanced manufacturing, and predictions of earth systems to assess water availability and forecasts in regions such as the Tennessee Valley Authority area.

Small businesses in tech-driven fields like manufacturing, energy or environmental consulting could use Lux to run simulations, refine AI models and analyze large datasets that typical in-house computing resources may not handle. Accessing the system requires navigating the application processes set forth by Oak Ridge's Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, and the report notes that the supercomputer is primarily aimed at researchers and may cater more to academic and governmental initiatives. Small business leaders should also weigh whether their projects align with the goals of the Genesis Mission, since work in fusion technology or environmental prediction may fit Lux particularly well. Thomas Zacharia, AMD's Senior Vice President, said the partnership builds on a strong foundation at Oak Ridge and supports an open, sovereign AI stack with tools that can benefit researchers across the country. Georgia Tourassi, Associate Laboratory Director for Computing and Computational Sciences at ORNL, said that by expanding the computational resources available to the scientific community, Lux will help accelerate the integration of simulation, modeling and experimental data to advance discovery.

Trish Damkroger, Senior Vice President and General Manager at HPE, said the company, together with Oak Ridge and AMD, had delivered breakthrough engineering innovation to advance the nation's scientific computing resources. The report frames access to high-performance computing as a possible advantage for smaller companies seeking to stay competitive in an increasingly tech-centric landscape, while cautioning that the barriers to entry must be weighed against the potential for breakthroughs. Businesses interested in using Lux can visit the ORNL Lux resource page, and the report suggests speaking with the OLCF team to streamline the process and clarify essential considerations. Engaging with advanced computing resources can also foster connections within the scientific community and open the way to partnerships that enhance business operations, according to the report.

stories.Headline: Nvidia adds AI motion generation and RTX updates for game developers
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA published its monthly game development update on 24 November 2026, describing new graphics, animation and local AI capabilities for game teams. Gaijin Entertainment integrated NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering into the Dagor Engine for War Thunder, the article says. NVIDIA Kimodo became the first AI motion-generation model integrated into Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview's guided animation framework, according to the article. The NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8, RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2, Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0 and RTX Path Tracing 1.9 also received updates. The article says the updates help teams balance image quality, performance and creative intent.

Gaijin adapted its color management pipeline to evaluate DLSS 5 in sRGB before post-processing and UI, then map results back to linear HDR. Kimodo lets animators generate character motion inside Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview's Sequencer using text prompts, spline paths and target poses at specific frames. In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8 adds hardened RTX Spark platform support, updated llama.cpp and whisper.cpp backends, Parakeet automatic speech recognition through whisper.cpp, and Vulkan priority API integration. RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 adds stratified low-discrepancy sampling for ReSTIR DI spatial resampling, a fallback sample feature, enhanced reservoir visualization and RTX Spark support. RTX Path Tracing 1.9 adds a nine-step introductory sample combining ReSTIR DI, SHaRC radiance caching and DLSS Ray Reconstruction, plus real-time subsampling and GPU-side acceleration-structure instance generation.

Gaijin said DLSS 5 delivers improved highlights and shadows while introducing a new level of microcontrast the team had not been able to achieve before. The team said the result is a more natural, lifelike image with finer detail and a stronger sense of realism. Gaijin also said it tuned DLSS 5 against its reference look to preserve vehicle markings, surface wear and material properties. The team said it evaluated image quality and performance separately across air, ground and naval combat. The article says the interview offers developers practical lessons on balancing lighting and material enhancements with art direction.

The article says ON/OFF comparisons highlight rainy, overcast scenes in War Thunder. The article says Kimodo pairs GPU-accelerated motion generation with the familiar timeline editor workflow, so teams decide where characters move and how they pose at key moments. The article says the In-Game Inferencing SDK supports multiple inference backends across GPU and CPU hardware, giving teams a common interface for running AI alongside game graphics. The article says the Real-Time BVH Viewer helps developers understand TLAS and BLAS contents, validate acceleration structure updates and debug geometry-related ray tracing issues. The article says RTX Path Tracing 1.9 gives developers a more accessible starting point for adding ray-traced lighting and studying a real-time path tracing pipeline.

The article says the Real-Time BVH Viewer integrates at the graphics API level through Direct3D 12 and Vulkan libraries, displaying results in a separate window with its own camera. The article says developers can use the included sampler to attach the viewer to a running D3D12 or Vulkan process without changing a title's code. The article says the viewer offers visualization modes for primitive, geometry, instance and cluster IDs, BLAS addresses, instance masks and flags, and acceleration structure update state, plus per-pixel trace time heatmaps. The article says RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 is available on GitHub with enhanced reservoir visualization for direct illumination, global illumination and path tracing. The article says the RTX Path Tracing intro sample uses a hybrid deferred renderer to introduce lighting features one at a time across nine selectable steps.

The article directs developers to read the War Thunder DLSS 5 developer interview for practical lessons on balancing lighting enhancements with art direction. It directs developers to explore the Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview release notes and the Kimodo research project to understand the guided animation framework. It directs developers to download Nsight Graphics and Nsight Systems to analyze DLSS Frame Generation workloads and use agentic AI tooling for graphics development. The article says Nsight Graphics 2026.4 and Nsight Systems 2026.6 introduce support for analyzing applications using DLSS Frame Generation, requiring Streamline SDK 2.12 or newer. The article says a new Nsight Graphics MCP server enables compatible AI agents to capture applications, inspect and debug captures, and analyze GPU traces.

stories.Headline: National Governors Association proposes splitting federal and state AI oversight
stories.Summary:
On November 22, 2026, the National Governors Association published bipartisan principles for artificial intelligence governance. These principles split regulatory authority between the federal government and the individual states. The federal government would oversee frontier models, cybersecurity, and international AI. States would maintain authority over workers, children, privacy, and daily AI deployment. This coordinated signal came just before a new session of Congress.

The plan requires a risk-based framework for frontier models, which are the most advanced general-purpose systems. It calls for independent audits of these models and reporting of safety incidents to federal and state authorities. Washington would set national standards for threats to financial systems and chemical, biological, or nuclear security. Maryland Governor Wes Moore and Indiana Governor Mike Braun lead the Governors Council to Secure American AI Dominance. North Carolina Governor Josh Stein and Utah Governor Spencer Cox serve as co-chairs.

Governor Moore stated that humans must stay in control while protecting kids, consumers, and workers. Governor Braun linked the technology to efficient government services, jobs, and wages. Governor Cox argued that states already run thoughtful policies that protect consumers and foster adoption. Governor Stein urged federal action that preserves state authority as states retool service delivery. CEO Brandon Tatum said no federal policy works without input from the governors.

The plan affects AI builders who must now navigate both federal audits and state disclosure rules. It specifically impacts developers of frontier models who face new reporting and evaluation obligations. Workers are affected by state-led efforts to address job disruption and fund transition infrastructure. Small entrants are protected by rules that prevent large incumbents from using compliance as a moat. Consumer protection agencies in states like New York may continue their own testing programs.

The association previously established a cybersecurity advisors institute and a working group on AI and work. They also created a one million dollar RAISE US partnership regarding the future of work. These existing resources provide the infrastructure for implementing the new governance principles. The framework responds to a fragmented legal landscape where states already regulate hiring and health. It also overlaps with the safety frameworks suggested in the SAFE AI Act outline.

Congress will return in January to develop a federal framework consistent with these federalism principles. Developers are advised to tag features by regulator type and draft unified incident templates. The articles leave open whether Congress will adopt these specific separation-of-powers recommendations. It remains uncertain if federal preemption will override state child-safety and privacy statutes. The document is a coordinated signal rather than a statute or law.

stories.Headline: Irish startups need clearance or a licence to train AI on copyrighted works in 2026, guide says
stories.Summary:
The article is a guide published by Global Advisory Experts on November 23, 2026, about training AI on copyrighted content in Ireland. It was written for founders, CTOs, heads of machine learning, product managers and in-house counsel at Irish startups building, fine-tuning or deploying AI models. The guide was last updated in September 2026 and lists Dean Cunningham of Cunningham Solicitors in Ireland as its featured expert on the matter. It sets out the legal framework, the situations in which training on protected content is lawful, how to license data properly, a risk matrix, sample contract wording and a 30/60/90 day action plan. The guide states that in 2026 training a model on copyrighted works in Ireland will in many cases need clearance or a licence.

The guide says the Copyright and Related Rights Act 2000, as amended, is the foundational statute and gives rights holders exclusive rights including reproduction. It states that copying a protected work, even temporarily and even into a training pipeline, needs authorisation unless a statutory exception applies. It names the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, which applies across member states on a phased timeline with different obligations starting at different dates. It says the Act requires certain general-purpose and generative models to have a policy to respect EU copyright law and to publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content. It adds that the GDPR applies where training data holds personal data, supervised in Ireland by the Data Protection Commission.

The guide states that Ireland has transposed the EU Digital Single Market Directive, which introduced text and data mining exceptions. It says one exception covers scientific research by research organisations and cultural heritage institutions, and a broader one covers other mining subject to rights holders reserving their rights in machine-readable form for online content. It says Ireland follows a fair dealing model rather than the open-ended fair use doctrine familiar from the United States, and that fair dealing applies only to listed purposes. It advises startups to follow legislation and statutory instruments through the Oireachtas for final text, the designation of competent authorities and enforcement mechanisms. It warns readers not to assume a particular bill title, section number or penalty figure.

The guide says the cleanest basis for training is an express licence from the rights holder that specifically allows the work to be used to train an AI model. It states that content being publicly accessible does not make it free to copy, that publication is not a waiver of copyright, and that most website terms of service prohibit automated collection and reuse. It says commercially licensed datasets are the lowest-risk source provided the licence expressly permits AI training, and that many older data licences predate generative AI and say nothing about model training or weights. It says open licences often impose attribution, share-alike or non-commercial conditions, and that a non-commercial restriction is incompatible with a revenue-generating model. It says scraping carries the highest content risk and can trigger copyright infringement and breach of contract.

The guide says copyright applies automatically under the Copyright and Related Rights Act 2000, and that most text, images, code and audio scraped or ingested is protected. It says databases have their own protection, including the sui generis database right, which is directly relevant when scraping structured content. It says authors keep moral rights, including attribution and the right to object to derogatory treatment, which survive a sale or licence and must be dealt with expressly in contracts. It says an output that reproduces a substantial part of a protected input can itself infringe, so risk attaches to what a model produces and not only to what it ingests. It says Ireland is building its national governance and enforcement structure for AI, largely to give effect to the EU AI Act.

The guide recommends that startups build dataset manifests and provenance metadata now, and keep one compliance record covering copyright, AI transparency and data protection. It sets out a decision path asking whether an express licence covers AI training, and if not, whether a specific exception clearly covers both the copying and the intended commercial use. It says that if neither is satisfied, a team should not ingest the data but should seek a licence, find a compliant substitute or leave it out. It advises deciding how to respond to a demand letter before one arrives. It states that because the detail of national governance is still developing, readers should check the current position whenever they start a project.

Articles.Title: Training AI on Copyrighted Content in Ireland: 2026 Guide for Startups - Global Advisory Experts

stories.Headline: Corporate real estate leaders expect AI and economic pressure to reshape teams within three years
stories.Summary:
Corporate real estate leaders are expecting a shakeup to their teams over the next three years as AI, economic pressure and M&A activity force changes, CBRE said in a report released Nov. 17. Currently, 10% of corporate real estate departments are undergoing a major reorganization and 33% are exploring one, according to CBRE's 2026 corporate real estate organizational design study. Another 35% added roles in the past year to support what CBRE calls the industry's changing remit. The top five new or in-demand skills that teams are looking for are technology and AI, cited by 77% of respondents, and change management, cited by 52%, with reporting and analytics, financial acumen and CRM also named. As internal corporate real estate teams shift their focus to strategy and business enablement, named by over 90% of leaders as their department's top priority, organizations are shifting delivery to service providers, according to CBRE.

On average, 23% of staff are internal and 77% are Tier 1 service providers, with departments typically using one or two providers for each core function, like facilities, project and transaction management. One change already happening is an increase in outsourcing of real estate management services that were previously done by internal teams, according to CBRE. Real estate analytics software company Tango surveyed leaders at large enterprises, mostly in the C-suite or at the senior level in facilities, and all companies represented had over $500 million in revenue, with the majority in North America. The Tango survey found that the top challenges facing leaders are capital costs, volatile demand, lease inflexibility and limited high-quality space that meets their requirements. These issues are costing organizations, Tango says, with 53% reporting a shrinking set of acceptable compliant space and 43% having renewed or extended a lease on unfavorable terms due to a lack of time or decision support.

Just under 90% of respondents in Tango's survey said they have delayed at least one portfolio decision in the past year, and more than half said external factors were the most common reason a decision gets delayed. Leaders at CBRE, JLL and Cushman & Wakefield all said economic uncertainty did push at least some amount of deals to later in the year. CBRE CFO Emma Giamartino said on an earnings call that the volatility is what's driving a pause or a hold or even delaying deals to 2027, and that the firm expects stability to come in the back half of next year, though results will differ if that doesn't come or things change. Still, the market has so far been surprisingly resilient, with 60% of U.S. markets showing positive net absorption over the past year, and Cushman & Wakefield CEO Michelle MacKay said during her firm's earnings call that companies are starting to make longer-term commitments.

stories.Headline: Small and midsized businesses adopt edge AI to cut latency and bandwidth needs
stories.Summary:
Small and midsized businesses are exploring how to run artificial intelligence workloads at the edge, positioning data storage and computation closer to where it is needed, according to BizTech Magazine. Many of these businesses have relied on cloud platforms to access AI capabilities, while others have run AI workloads in on-premises data centers. Edge computing can reduce the need for bandwidth and lower latency in their workloads. The shift toward edge AI is happening rapidly at the enterprise level, and SMBs are looking to keep pace.

Cisco notes that by 2027, 75 percent of enterprise data will be created and processed at the edge due to evolving AI workloads. Edge AI processes data locally on devices such as smartphones and IoT sensors, at or near the point where it is created, rather than sending it to a service provider's servers. In a September 2025 white paper, IDC's Brandon Butler and Jennifer Cooke write that edge infrastructure minimizes latency, optimizes bandwidth utilization and enhances data privacy. Running workloads locally generally requires less power than cloud data centers, and sensitive data remains on local endpoints rather than traveling across a network. SMBs can scale by pairing cloud-based platforms with native edge capabilities on local devices.

Jeremy Foster, senior vice president and general manager for Cisco Compute, says AI is not waiting for the data center anymore and is happening right now in factories, at ports, in hospitals and in stores, where milliseconds matter. Butler and Cooke write that building an effective strategy for edge infrastructure begins with understanding the unique needs of highly distributed IT landscapes and industry-specific needs. They add that infrastructure and architecture choices need to consider the level of use case criticality and prioritize platforms that ensure data and physical security requirements. SMBs may face challenges, since existing edge infrastructure generally is not optimized for modern AI workloads and many sites have low power and limited footprints. Edge projects often take longer and cost more than planned as businesses deal with configuration drift and poorly managed large-scale updates.

Manufacturing and retail are two segments where edge AI may hold significant promise for SMBs, with edge devices monitoring machinery health, detecting defects and optimizing production, while retail uses it for personalized customer experiences, inventory management and loss prevention. A hybrid model may benefit retailers, with the cloud training large models and aggregating insights across locations while the edge handles real-time inference behind in-store intelligence. By rightsizing their computing infrastructure, SMBs can avoid overprovisioning while keeping performance and costs in check. For SMBs with lean IT teams, working with a trusted partner can make complexity manageable and speed up edge AI deployments.

stories.Headline: Everbridge earns ISO/IEC 42001 certification for its AI management system
stories.Summary:
Everbridge announced on 24 November 2026 that it has achieved ISO/IEC 42001 certification, which the company describes as the world's first international standard for artificial intelligence management systems. The company said the certification makes it one of the first critical event management providers to meet that standard. The certification covers the Everbridge CEM platform, xMatters and SnapComms, along with the corporate office, according to the company. Everbridge said the certification demonstrates an independently assessed AI management system covering the development, deployment and oversight of its AI-powered solutions, including Everbridge 360 AI.

The standard, published in December 2023, provides a certifiable framework for organizations to establish, implement and continually improve how they govern AI across its lifecycle. It addresses risk management, accountability, oversight and continuous improvement, and adds AI-specific requirements such as AI impact assessments, algorithmic risk management and oversight of the AI system lifecycle. Everbridge said just 100 ISO/IEC 42001 certificates were reported in the United States in the latest ISO Survey, compared with more than 5,000 ISO/IEC 27001 certificates there. The company also noted that the EU AI Act is now in effect, establishing what it calls the world's first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence.

Everbridge said it believes investing in AI governance early is an important part of building technology customers can trust, and that it made governance part of its approach from the beginning rather than addressing it after AI capabilities are developed. The company said the certification does not eliminate every risk associated with AI but shows that an organization has implemented an AI management system independently assessed against an internationally recognized standard. It said its commitment to AI innovation goes hand in hand with its commitment to accountable AI practices, and that the certification reflects investment in the processes, oversight and accountability needed to manage AI. Everbridge said organizations that invest in both innovation and structured AI oversight will be better positioned to earn and maintain customer confidence.

Everbridge said AI is rapidly changing how organizations operate, make decisions and respond to challenges, and that questions about how AI is developed, deployed and managed grow as adoption accelerates. The company said these questions matter especially where technology supports time-sensitive, high-stakes decisions, and that regulatory bodies worldwide are signaling structured AI oversight is no longer optional. It said adoption of the newer AI standard is still in its early stages but its importance is growing as organizations increasingly incorporate AI into their operations. Everbridge said organizations that invest in governance frameworks today will be better prepared as these expectations become the norm.

Articles.Title: AI innovation is accelerating. AI governance can’t wait.

stories.Headline: Cox Automotive leader says dealers adopt AI faster than they see its value
stories.Summary:
Micah, who leads the Kelley Blue Book Instant Cash Offer business at Cox Automotive and has spent 17 years in the automotive industry, wrote a piece published on November 24, 2026, describing how he used a large language model to shop for a heavy-duty pickup for his family. He said the AI searched daily for more than four months across major shopping sites such as Autotrader and brought him the right vehicle at the right price, after which he stepped in to negotiate the deal and complete the transaction himself. He wrote that he could have found a truck without AI, but that the value it added was undeniable, and that his career had taught him that anything adding value is here to stay. He said his own experience matched what shoppers have been telling Cox Automotive for months. Cox Automotive's 2026 Content Influence Study found that about seven in 10 new-vehicle shoppers said they use AI at least weekly, and that the share who find AI content trustworthy roughly doubled since 2023, from 27% to 55%.

Among shoppers who use AI search, the study found AI sources lead at the start of the journey by 31% versus 22% for non-AI sources, but non-AI sources lead by the final decision by 36% versus 25%. McKinsey's 2026 Mobility Consumer Pulse found that haggle-free pricing at 44% and longer test drives at 40% outranked generative AI in the buying process at 18%. The third-quarter update to Cox Automotive's AI in Auto Retail Tracker shows dealer AI use holding near current levels, with growth coming mainly from standalone tools rather than AI built into the systems dealers already use. Micah wrote that dealers are reaching for AI faster than they are realizing value from it, and that many still cannot tell whether it is working, while their expectations are shifting from revenue toward productivity before reality has caught up. He recalled that at Digital Dealer in September, he was in a room with 35 dealers and asked for a show of hands from those whose AI investments were meeting their expectations, and zero hands went up.

He set out six takeaways for dealers and brands, including using AI to match the right buyer with the right car and the right deal, keeping inventory, pricing and vehicle details accurate and current everywhere shoppers and their AI tools look, and being clear about when a shopper is engaging with AI and when with a person. He also urged dealers to train, deploy and supervise their AI on accurate dealership data, to bring measurement into vendor conversations from the start, and to let shoppers approve before AI acts, since AI may open the journey but trust closes the deal. He wrote that the Cox Automotive AI Tracker Study found most errors shoppers hit in AI answers trace back to listing data rather than the AI itself, and that because shoppers keep using AI anyway, the exposure sits with the data feeding those answers. He said shoppers want to approve what an AI agent does before it acts, and that those most ready to use AI are the most insistent on that step. He concluded that AI is becoming the first stop in car shopping but that people still make the final sale, and that the winners in auto retail will not have the most AI but will be the easiest for shoppers to find and trust, wherever the journey begins.

stories.Headline: Report urges federal policymakers to give health care workers a voice in AI rollout
stories.Summary:
A report published by the Center for American Progress on November 24, 2026 examines how labor-management training partnerships can support health care workers as artificial intelligence spreads through the sector. The report focuses on one such partnership, the 1199 Service Employees International Union Training and Employment Funds, which trains and supports up to 40,000 workers a year in health care. The authors describe these partnerships as sector-based training programs governed jointly by unions and employers, built on the principle that sustained performance improvement comes through investment in cooperative relationships. The report says the health care industry is driving job growth in America and is expected to be a main contributor of new jobs in the coming decade.

The report says the spread of AI is not expected to reduce the number of health care jobs but could worsen the quality of jobs and care, for example through increased algorithmic management, less time with patients, reduced experience levels needed to catch errors and depressed wages. It cites Pam Brier, former CEO of Maimonides Medical Center in Brooklyn, New York, who attributed cooperation through the 1199SEIU fund to a 50 percent reduction in hospital-acquired infections, a 50 percent reduction in patient falls and a 75 percent increase in unpaid bill collection, among other results. It also cites Kaiser Permanente, described as a nearly three-decade-old partnership including workers across the country, which the report says has achieved more than $602 million in organizational savings. The report recommends that federal policymakers reform the public workforce system to increase worker voice in decisions about how AI is implemented in health care, create cost sharing with employers for training, build more sustainable funding for training and design programs with career navigation and other supports.

The report was written by authors at the Center for American Progress, which says the positions of American Progress and its policy experts are independent and that the findings and conclusions are those of American Progress alone. The authors thank Livia Lam and Samir Fayyaz at the 1199SEIU Training and Employment Funds. The report also recommends that policymakers require public workforce investments to prioritize support for labor-management training partnerships and other training models that include workers in program design and demonstrate good outcomes, such as long-term earnings gains. It says greater cooperation with and encouragement of these partnerships can help solve sectorwide training problems and assist workers navigating AI and other technology-based job displacement.

Articles.Title: How To Support Health Care Workers Amid AI Disruption and Labor Market Changes

stories.headline_source: How To Support Health Care Workers Amid AI Disruption and Labor Market Changes

stories.Headline: Trump threatens penalties for US companies building data centers abroad
stories.Summary:
President Trump threatened penalties for American companies that build data centers in other countries. He made these remarks to reporters at the White House on November 20, 2026. The president specifically cited Finland as a destination for this offshore investment. He claimed that China would take the facilities if this trend continued. He stated that the United States would not allow companies to build abroad.

The president promised tremendous penalties but named no specific rate or tax base. He did not provide a start date or a legal authority for these actions. No implementing document had appeared as of November 23, 2026. The White House summary of the briefing repeated the remarks without setting a policy. Trump admitted he had not yet spoken to his staff about the plan.

Trump is responsible for these statements and the intent to penalize companies. He told reporters that the government would not allow the building of overseas centers. He warned that such actions were necessary to prevent China from taking the capacity. He singled out Finland as a place where American computing capacity was escaping. He suggested that communities should make the companies pay them.

American companies building data centers abroad are the ones affected by these threats. Some companies have already faced delays in Finland due to environmental and water plans. Google's subsidiary Tuike Finland suspended work at sites in Muhos and Kajaani in October. Police in Oulu opened an investigation into suspected environmental damage at the Muhos site. Finnish authorities found that required impact assessments were incomplete.

The articles state that Finland moved data center electricity into a general tax class. This change occurred on July 1, 2026, raising the energy tax per kilowatt-hour. The articles note that electricity, water, and local consent are major bottlenecks. Many AI data center projects in 20 states were canceled due to community opposition. Voters in 40 of 41 local ballot measures recently favored limiting development.

The threat remains a statement of intent rather than a formal law. A new federal tax would require authorization from Congress to be implemented. Other penalties would need an applicable statutory basis to be legally enforceable. The articles leave the specific legal mechanism for these penalties open. It is unclear how the administration will resolve domestic electricity and water constraints.

Articles.Title: The Geography of AI: Why Penalizing Offshore Data Centers Won't Build Capacity at Home - IndraStra Global
