stories.Headline: Google finds an AI system that autonomously writes and launches software exploits
stories.Summary:
Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported that they had uncovered an AI system that autonomously finds software flaws and launches exploits, according to TechGig on November 23, 2026. Investigators found an unsecured staging server that hosted a system called exploit_agent, which links to advanced cloud-based and locally run language models. This framework examines software code to identify differences related to flaws, writes working exploits, and launches them automatically. Scripts on the machine also handled later steps, including mapping internal networks, guessing passwords, planting webshells, and deleting webshells installed by rival attackers. The report describes this as a significant shift in cybercriminal operations, moving from chatbot assistance to independent attack systems.

In August 2026, attackers exploited two PaperCut print server flaws, CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078, which allowed remote command execution without logging in when chained together. A campaign launched four days after disclosure hit hundreds of organisations through these flaws, expanding an initial foothold to domain administrator within minutes. Google also tracks open source attack frameworks such as ARTEX, CAIRN, PentAGI, CyberStrikeAI, and HexStrike AI, and the company confirmed that CAIRN and PentAGI were used against live targets. One actor ran a customised PentAGI platform that probed many Asian organisations for weaknesses from August through early October 2026.

Google recorded at least 8 zero-day exploits per month in 2025 and 11 per month in 2026, with August reaching 22. Mandiant responded to several LLMJacking incidents in 2026 where criminals drained victims' cloud computing and model quotas. Daily fraudulent bills exceeded $100,000 in these cases, with some losses reaching $1 million before cleanup. The articles do not say who is responsible beyond the actors described or what happens next.

stories.Headline: Alexandr Wang publishes essay warning about human control of AI
stories.Summary:
Alexandr Wang published an essay titled "Superintelligence is Arriving" on a Sunday afternoon, according to a Digg report dated November 23, 2026, and the post drew 35,000 likes along with 1,900 comments and 29,100 saves. In the essay Wang ties his warning about human control to a claimed AI-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a claim the article presents as his own. He rejects what he describes as a handover of society to AI and argues that a positive future is possible, though he says it likely requires the industry to change course. The Digg report says the essay was first seen about ten hours before publication and was shared through a link to his article on X.

Jon Favreau reacted sharply to the essay, urging elected leaders to stop frontier labs from handing control to superintelligent machines, according to the report. Commenters on the post included one who wrote that superintelligence is arriving and another who called the Sunday afternoon timing a power move and asked to see the compute to back the headline. The article lists eleven sources for its account, including Wang's X article and several posts reacting to it. The report does not say what specific changes Wang calls for beyond the industry changing course.

The Digg article places the essay in the context of an ongoing debate about superintelligence, recursive self-improvement and loss of control, which its headline names. It gives no further detail on the content of Wang's argument beyond the points above, and it does not say how the industry or elected leaders responded to Favreau's call. The report also does not say what happens next with the essay or the claimed proof. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Elon Musk claims an unequivocal super intelligence has arrived and welcomes the Singularity
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk said on November 23, 2026, that what he called an unequivocal super intelligence had arrived, and he welcomed people to what he called the Singularity, according to a post published by Investment Watch Blog. The blog presented his statement as a wire item under its On Wire category, and it gave no further detail about the system he was referring to. The post did not say where Musk made the statement or what prompted it. It also did not identify any company, laboratory or model behind the claim. The blog framed the remark as a signal to brace for another extremely volatile week.

The statement as published asserts that a super intelligence has arrived, and it treats that arrival as the start of the Singularity, the term for a point at which machine intelligence is imagined to change life beyond prediction. The articles give no date for when this arrival supposedly happened beyond the November 23, 2026 posting date. They give no technical description of the system, no measure of its capability and no independent confirmation of the claim. They also give no number, such as a benchmark score or a parameter count, that would back it up. Nothing in the articles says what the arrival requires of anyone or what it changes in practice.

Responsibility for the claim rests with Musk, who is presented as the person making the statement, and the blog carried it without adding verification of its own. The blog did not say whether it had contacted Musk or anyone else about the remark. It offered no comment from Musk beyond the few words in the headline. It also gave no response from any company, researcher or official to the claim. The post included only the usual notices about subscriptions, tips and corrections.

The context the articles supply is thin, consisting of the blog's own framing and a list of its recent posts. That list mentions other items, including one about a mathematical mystery and one about a film comparison, but the articles do not connect them to Musk's statement. The articles say nothing about what happens next, and they announce no follow-up reporting on the claim. The blog's only guidance to readers is its line about bracing for another extremely volatile week. More to follow.

stories.Headline: New Yorkers warned of holiday scams, AI shopping traps
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James issued a holiday scam warning on November 24, 2026, as reported by Long Island Business News. The warning tells New Yorkers to guard their personal information and to be careful when using artificial intelligence tools while shopping. James said she encourages holiday shoppers to protect themselves, their families and their private information by staying vigilant about potential scams. She also said no one should hesitate to report suspicious activity to her office. The warning covers receipts, buy now pay later loans, subscriptions, devices, phishing emails, fake deals, AI shopping tools and surveillance pricing.

James advised consumers to check that register prices match advertised or shelf prices. New York law requires retailers to charge the lowest advertised, posted or marked price and to keep at least 98% price accuracy during inspections by weights and measures officials. She said shoppers should review interest rates, payment schedules and fees on buy now, pay later loans before buying. Some of those loans charge interest even when payments are made on time, and missed payments may bring late fees and hurt credit scores. New York law requires businesses to clearly disclose subscription terms, obtain consent for automatic renewals, send post-purchase confirmation and offer an easy way to cancel.

James said consumers should update their home Wi-Fi password, avoid public Wi-Fi for purchases, install the latest software updates and keep antivirus software active. She warned that emails promoting exclusive holiday deals or free gift cards may be phishing attempts. She said shoppers should verify senders of unexpected holiday e-cards or invitations before clicking links or opening attachments. She advised shopping only on reputable websites, verifying URLs before entering payment information and checking for a working customer service number, a physical business address and positive customer reviews. She said retailers that list only a P.O. box or have no working phone number deserve caution.

James said shoppers should review all charges before purchasing because some websites add hefty delivery, processing or subscription fees, particularly during the holiday season. She said people using AI tools to make purchases should review what accounts and personal information the tool can access and limit permissions whenever possible. She said anyone whose AI tool can buy on their behalf should set clear spending limits and purchasing rules and require approval before purchases whenever possible. New York's Algorithmic Pricing Disclosure Act requires most businesses that use personal data to set prices to display a clear disclosure near the price. Consumers who encounter undisclosed algorithmic pricing should file a complaint with the attorney general's office.

James said shoppers should compare prices across retailers and platforms, use private or incognito browsing and check prices when logged out of loyalty accounts. She warned about inflated discounts and crossed-out prices and said shoppers should check price histories to judge whether a deal offers real savings. She said consumers should keep order confirmations and receipts, contact the retailer if an item does not arrive as promised and file a complaint with her office if the company does not respond. She said people should review credit card and bank statements regularly for unauthorized charges, which may go unnoticed amid increased holiday spending. Suspected scam victims can report to the attorney general's office by submitting a complaint online or calling 1-800-771-7755.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: New Yorkers warned of holiday scams, AI shopping traps - Long Island Business News

stories.Headline: House committees warn Chinese AI models in US businesses pose national security risks
stories.Summary:
The House Committee on Homeland Security and the Select Committee on China released a joint report on Friday. This report warns that Chinese artificial intelligence models in American businesses create national security and cybersecurity risks. The committees launched their joint investigation in April 2026 to examine these emerging technology patterns. They studied how American companies use models developed in the People's Republic of China. The investigation lasted over seven months and included reviews of documents and classified briefings.

The 50-page report, titled Beijing’s AI Playbook, examines companies including Airbnb, Anysphere, and DoorDash. It notes Chinese models accounted for 41% of downloads on the leading open-model repository last year. The report identifies a Zhipu model capable of building cyber exploits comparable to a restricted American model. It recommends a national American open-weight AI initiative and a model provenance standard for federal contractors. It also proposes prohibiting Chinese models in federal information systems and high-risk critical infrastructure functions.

Chairmen Andrew R. Garbarino and John Moolenaar wrote that developers of these models answer to Beijing. They stated that bringing in a model also brings in the influence of those who trained it. The chairmen noted that AI models execute automated tasks deep inside corporate networks without most Americans knowing. They argued that the priorities and assumptions of Chinese developers shape how these models process information. The report claims that the U.S. lacks competitive open-weight alternatives at required price and performance levels.

The report says that American businesses, government agencies, and critical infrastructure are all affected by these risks. It notes that some Chinese models generate less secure code when prompts reference U.S. government users. The report mentions that South Korean banks were breached using a tool powered by DeepSeek and Zhipu. It claims that the same tools are available to anyone targeting American hospitals, utilities, and banks. The committees found that U.S. data-labeling firms earn about 500 million dollars annually selling data to China.

The committees found that Chinese developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest American model outputs. They claim that six leading Chinese developers conducted industrial-scale distillation campaigns to accelerate their own system development. The report states that the Chinese State Council wants an open-source AI ecosystem with international influence. It notes that Chinese developers sustain losses through state funds, state-owned shareholders, and subsidized compute resources. The report claims that the highest-ranked American open-weight model placed 10th behind six Chinese models.

The committees recommend that NIST and CISA develop an AI bill of materials for high-risk infrastructure. They suggest modernizing the Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation program to inventory AI models running on federal networks. The report suggests a narrow waiver process for research, testing, and defensive security work regarding Chinese models. It remains open how the federal government will track the deployment of these models across the economy. The report leaves open how the U.S. will build a credible alternative to these low-cost models.

Articles.Title: House report flags Chinese AI models embedded in US businesses, cites cybersecurity and national security risks

stories.Headline: York County school board approves $107,100 for education software including AI platform MagicSchool
stories.Summary:
The York County School Board heard updates on a Spanish-language program, gifted education and artificial intelligence during its Tuesday meeting in Yorktown, according to Williamsburg Yorktown Daily. The Spanish program is a grant-funded pilot that operates at Bethel Manor Elementary School and Tabb Elementary School, which were chosen because they are the division's two schools with the most military-connected families. At Bethel Manor, students in kindergarten through fifth grade learn foundational Spanish language skills and explore Spanish culture in a world language resource class. Principal Anthony Friedman said students are building communication skills, curiosity and an appreciation for different perspectives that will help them in a changing world. A Bethel Manor student, Gabe Lugo, told the board he thinks other students should have the chance to learn Spanish because it helps people connect across different backgrounds.

The pilot depends on funding from a Department of Defense Education Activity grant, and Superintendent James Carroll said the division would be open to discussing expansion if the board wants the program in more schools. Carroll also said the division would consider local funding for the program. On gifted education, the board heard that more than 100 students are in the current referral cycle, and the Gifted Education Advisory Committee is reviewing the division's gifted education plan ahead of its 2027 expiration. The board unanimously approved October financial expenditures, Tabb High School additions and renovations totaling $38,100,000, and $107,100 for education software that includes the artificial intelligence platform MagicSchool and the digital learning platform ClassLink. Chief Academic Officer Candi Skinner said the division wants students prepared to use AI appropriately and responsibly in college or the work world, and she confirmed the AI program is monitored and has safeguards for student safety.

The board also reviewed a resolution on a policy called Equal Access to Public Education and Protection of Immigration and Citizenship-Related Information, which establishes that no student can be denied access to any division activity or benefit based on perceived immigration or citizenship status. The board approved consideration of a lease agreement between the school board and the Tabb Lakes Homes Association for the association to use school property for community meetings. The board's next meeting will be its Dec. 14 work session at 7 p.m. in York Hall.

stories.Headline: OX Security finds prompt injection and tool poisoning in 22% of flagged MCP servers
stories.Summary:
OX Security published research on November 23, 2026, saying it had analyzed 542,207 components across npm, PyPI, MCP servers and Agent Skills between July and October 2026. The company said the research revealed two fundamental shifts, with attacks moving from execute to instruct and the traditional signals organizations use to establish trust in software no longer being enough. It said AI agents are taking instructions from third-party tools, servers and packages, and that attackers are learning how to exploit that trust. It described how prompt injection and tool poisoning exploit the instructions agents follow and the permissions they already have. The research said prompt injection and tool poisoning appeared in 22% of flagged MCP servers, compared with 16% for install or import-time execution.

It said nearly one-third of tracked MCP servers have no identifiable source owner, and just 0.4% disclose usage information. It said 82% of researcher-confirmed malicious components were already malicious in their first observed version, meaning they did not turn bad through a later update. It said one account published 2,364 servers in just 17 days, and that a handful of publishers can create common points of failure across thousands of seemingly independent tools. It also said the code you review is not necessarily the code that runs, because remote infrastructure and repository mismatches undermine traditional security reviews. OX Security is responsible for the research, and it presented the findings as its own analysis of the components it tracked.

The company said the OX Security platform is a game changer for application security teams, that it is easy to adopt and integrate into the CI/CD pipeline, and that it provides the visibility and focus needed to develop fast and secure. It said the platform supports the need for transparency and end to end traceability, giving greater control by blocking vulnerabilities and improving accuracy during the development lifecycle. It described the platform as enterprise-grade, securing applications from code to runtime and embedding real-time protection directly into AI editors and IDEs, with an autonomous security agent that connects with AI coding tools. The articles give no further context on the event and do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Security practitioners share AI prompts that help CISOs audit policies, vet vendors and red team runbooks
stories.Summary:
The article, published by CSO Online on 23 November 2026 and written by John Edwards, sets out AI prompt ideas that security leaders can use, gathered from security practitioners. Dzmitry Romanov, cybersecurity team lead and senior security engineer at the Belarusian State University of Informatics and Radioelectronics and cybersecurity team lead with Vention, advocates a prompt that acts as a second security reviewer. Philippe Dourassov, AI pentest lead at Aikido Security, offers an adversarial agent prompt aimed at agent helpers. Brandyn Fisher, senior penetration testing technical lead at Centric Consulting, offers three prompt ideas for CISOs to deploy regularly. Kevin Surace, described as a Gen AI pioneer, offered a similar prompt idea to attendees of this year's CSO Conference and Awards in May.

Romanov says his adversarial prompt works most effectively when analyzing architecture or code, reviewing penetration test results, auditing cloud configurations, modeling threats and assessing risks. Dourassov says a second agent deployed to analyze another agent's work and correct its output can be surprisingly efficient, with the task of eliminating noise, rectifying claims and highlighting the true importance of the first agent's result. Fisher's first prompt is a vendor due diligence prompt that takes the organization's risk thresholds and the vendor, benchmarks the vendor, sweeps the Internet for security pages, breach history, customer reviews, complaints and recent news, and returns a structured report. Fisher's second is a professional writing prompt that reframes technical analysis into language a CIO or board will engage with, and his third is a tech debt reduction prompt that lists the technology stack and has AI flag underutilized tools, overlapping capabilities and consolidation opportunities. Surace's example prompt tells the model it is writing the cyber risk section of the board deck with four minutes of board time and ninety days of security operations data, producing three slides for a board that does not know what lateral movement means.

Fisher advises building each recommendation as a standing agent, project or skill, or whatever the AI platform supports, so there is a static, repeatable spot to run it instead of rewriting the prompt each time. He adds that people should not wait for a perfect first version, should get an initial prompt working even if rough, should have AI help draft the instructions, and should expect to revise it several times before it is reliable. Surace told the CSO Conference that CISOs can use AI prompts to audit policy libraries, with an example prompt casting the model as a compliance auditor given the policy library and the current text of NIST CSF 2.0, ISO 27001:2022 Annex A, SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 and the EU AI Act, producing three lists of contradictions, gaps and stale language. He noted that this is the kind of analysis big firms do for six figures in 12 weeks. Surace also advised attendees to red team their own runbook, with an example prompt casting the model as the operations lead for Scattered Spider and giving it the incident response playbook, detection coverage matrix and on-call tree to identify the five places the runbook fails.

Olivia Brännlund, CISO at Outpost24, a cybersecurity and risk management firm, regularly uses a similar prompt that turns AI into an internal auditor and security advisor reviewing policy, processes, risk assessment, incident reports, contract clauses and specific customer requirements. Brännlund believes organizations that treat AI as an expert reviewer typically obtain more value than those that treat it as a content generator, and says the key isn't using AI to write content but using it to challenge content. Chris Hughes, who teaches in the CISO and Leading Enterprise Agentic AI Development Certificate Program at Carnegie Mellon University's Heinz College, advises asking the model what AI agents can actually do by giving it an agent's configuration, tool manifest or MCP server definitions and asking it to summarize the agent's effective permissions, the blast radius if it is compromised, and whether a human approval step exists anywhere in the workflow. Hughes says most organizations are deploying agents faster than they are documenting what those agents can reach, and that this closes the gap in minutes. Steve Tait, CTO at cloud security firm Skyhigh Security, suggests a prompt response inspection that understands both data and intent, so CISOs can determine not only whether sensitive information is entering or leaving an AI service but whether a user or agent is attempting something risky such as prompt injection, jailbreaks, policy evasion, credential exposure or unauthorized data access.

The article says that for all the talk of AI use by attackers and defenders, little attention is paid to ways CISOs and their security pros can leverage AI uniquely to expedite tasks, cut through the noise, facilitate decision-making and potentially save big on auditing. It says several specific AI prompts can help security leaders and staff handle multiple critical tasks not typically associated with AI for cyber defense, such as risk management, compliance, policy development and critical thinking. It says developing truly useful prompts isn't particularly easy, because it often requires a significant amount of research and effort, not to mention lots of fine-tuning, which can take security teams away from other critical tasks. It says the security community is here to help, with advice on unique prompt ideas that have greatly aided them in strengthening security, facilitating decision-making and saving time for hands-on defense. The article is by John Edwards, who it says has likely written more articles focusing on technology industry issues than anyone else in history.

Surace said of red teaming the runbook that it is totally worth doing and that you will have more information in an hour than you have ever had. Hughes says the model turns work that normally requires a senior architect into something an analyst can run at design review, before deployment and after every change, and that it surfaces assumptions the team stopped questioning. Hughes notes the model doesn't share your blind spots, so it tends to flag the over-permissioned tool or the missing approval gate that everyone walked past, and that once tuned the prompt becomes a control in its own right rather than a one-off exercise. Tait believes CISOs should think of prompt security as a platform control that needs to work across every major access path to AI, including Secure Web Gateway, zero trust network access, browser-based access and APIs, and says the goal should not be to plug a single gap for one AI application but to establish a consistent policy and inspection layer wherever users or agents interact with AI services. Tait adds that this means choosing an approach that can support hybrid environments, including organizations that still rely heavily on on-premises SWG infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Guterres tells Security Council killer robots must have no place in our future
stories.Summary:
The Security Council met on Tuesday to weigh how artificial intelligence and drones are reshaping warfare, with UN chief António Guterres telling ambassadors that killer robots must have no place in our future. The session examined how new technologies now spread globally within months rather than decades, and how disinformation is fuelling record levels of conflict. The council heard that artificial intelligence is already assisting in targeting and that drones are changing the way wars are fought. The meeting was held at UN headquarters and was carried live on UNWebTV. Guterres told council members they have a special duty to ensure that competition over emerging technologies does not destabilise international peace and security.

Last week in Geneva, a push by around 100 countries to negotiate a legally binding instrument on lethal autonomous weapons fell short. The Secretary-General's July review of UN peace operations made closing the technology gap a priority. A new informal council expert group on technology, peace and security met for the first time on 18 November, and in 2021 the council recognised technology as a potential force multiplier for UN peacekeeping. The Secretary-General is responsible for the July review of UN peace operations, which made closing the technology gap a priority, and he addressed the council directly on the duty of members. The council itself set up the informal expert group on technology, peace and security, which held its first meeting on 18 November.

The council also recognised technology in 2021 as a potential force multiplier for UN peacekeeping. Around 100 countries pushed in Geneva last week for a legally binding instrument on lethal autonomous weapons, but that effort fell short. The meeting comes as the UN marks more than eighty years since its founding in 1945, when computers, the internet and satellites were the stuff of science fiction. The articles do not say what the council will decide or when it will next take up the issue. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Law firm leaders propose a single budget to fund junior associate training as AI takes over first drafts
stories.Summary:
A Bloomberg Law commentary published on November 23, 2026, by Kristina Bakardjiev, a former partner and current director of emerging AI at Cozen O’Connor, and Vincent R. McGuinness Jr., the firm’s president and managing partner, argues that law firms must decide who pays to build judgment in junior attorneys now that agentic AI performs the document review, summarization and first drafts that once justified billing first- and second-year associates at a multiple of cost. The authors point to Fortis Advisors LLC v. Krafton in the Delaware Court of Chancery, where a South Korean gaming company’s CEO asked ChatGPT how to avoid a $250 million earnout owed to the founders of the studio behind Subnautica, locked the founders out of the publishing platform and fired them for cause, and the court admitted records of the AI-assisted strategy as evidence of pretextual intent, reinstated the studio chief and extended the earnout. The parties settled the case this June, and the authors say a privileged call to a lawyer could have exposed the flaw in a plan that depended on the acquired company failing. The authors describe the economic exposure firms face, noting that juniors carry the lowest realization rates, that 82% of associates leave within five years and that BigHand puts the cost of each third-year departure near $1 million.

They say firms’ spending on technology tools and associate training is diffuse and duplicative, with recruiting, professional development, knowledge management, innovation and legal technology each holding separate budgets and claims on the same lawyers’ hours, and they propose a single professional advancement budget. They trace pricing history, noting that firms closed engagements with a single line for professional services rendered until hourly billing became more standard after the US Supreme Court struck down minimum fee schedules in Goldfarb v. Virginia State Bar in 1975, and they say nearly three-quarters of US law firms now offer alternative fees while AI-native entrants publish flat per-document prices for work once assigned to first-years. They suggest a transparently negotiated flat fee for associate-level work, reasonable under Model Rule 1.5 and consistent with Virginia Legal Ethics Opinion 1901, might keep AI-driven efficiency inside the firm. The authors recommend tying every approved tool to a specific use case and realistic practice problem, using AI simulators as aviation uses flight simulators, and they cite the 2026 Citi Hildebrandt Client Advisory reporting that 86% of large firms plan to grow associate ranks through 2027, only 35% intend to grow first-year classes and 25% expect AI to change their leverage model, up from 9%.

They propose making supervision a compensated bridge role for senior associates and junior partners, with billable-hour credit capped near 100 hours a year and tied to outcomes clients recognize such as satisfaction, delivery against milestones and fewer revisions. They suggest financing this from a reinvestment pool built on measured realization gains, using 24 months of billing data to baseline first- and second-year time, tracking AI use with task codes and running a control group against a test group. In their example, 20 junior associates billing $13 million and losing about $2 million to write-downs show a realization rate near 85%, and improving realization by five points returns $650,000 while reducing departures from four a year to three avoids roughly $250,000 in hard replacement costs. Against that, they say five supervisors each earning up to 100 credited supervision hours at a collected rate of nearly $600 represent roughly $300,000 in forgone collections, assuming they already meet their hourly targets, leaving a net pool of about $600,000, or $30,000 per junior associate, and even a pessimistic three-point gain recovers $390,000, leaving a pool near $340,000, or $17,000 per associate. They also urge returning some recovered time to the lawyers carrying the load, and they say a cross-functional steering group should own any AI pilot, start in two practice groups, report quarterly and expand to groups clearing realization thresholds while experimenting with fixed fees for AI-streamlined matters, restructuring toward fewer execution hours and a stronger supervisory middle tier if the pilot works and running a post-mortem if not.

stories.Headline: Guelph officials use AI to find city efficiencies and improve services
stories.Summary:
City officials in Guelph are turning to artificial intelligence to find efficiencies, according to a presentation made at a Guelph Chamber of Commerce breakfast event on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. Chief Administrative Officer Tara Baker spoke at the event at the Victoria Park East Golf Club, where about 100 local business people attended along with several city staff and councillors. Baker was joined by deputy CAOs Colleen Clack-Bush, Terry Gayman and Stephen O'Brien, who each presented on the areas of city governance they oversee. The CAO's breakfast took the place of the chamber's annual municipal budget event because the 2027 budget update has not yet been presented due to last month's city election.

According to the articles, the city is using AI to identify mis-sorted residential waste as it is collected by trucks, to track whether buses are on schedule and potentially to assess the grip of municipal equipment on wintry roads. AI is also being used to assess infrastructure risks, model the repercussions of failures and plan how to lessen the impact or reduce the risk. Baker said the city is measuring its performance and how it does business, where it invests money, and is using those performance metrics to drive business decisions. O'Brien said part of the work includes breaking down departmental silos and removing redundant pages or information on the city's website, which he described as dated old legacy systems with highly siloed pockets of data and very low integration across platforms.

Baker said the city is trying to improve those abilities through its focus on data management and business intelligence. Clack-Bush said the city is focused on being efficient, finding ways to eliminate bureaucracy if it can and delivering services in a customer friendly way, noting the city is always looking at how technology can improve customer service. Gayman said the number one thing the city hears about is the housing need, along with transit, active transportation and the ability to provide options for people to get to work reliably. O'Brien said AI searches return a deeper analysis of results than a traditional Google search, making it all the more important that official city details are presented at the top of results pages, and that the city's data governance work matters because the business community needs confidence that the information it uses is accurate, timely and understood.

Budget details are expected to be released in the new year, according to the articles.

Articles.Title: City hall turns to AI in attempt to improve efficiencies - Guelph News

stories.Headline: OX Security finds AI agents follow unverified instructions from tools with no identifiable owner
stories.Summary:
OX Security said its research team analyzed 542,207 open-source software components between July and October 2026, using its early-warning system OX.Radar to track four ecosystems: npm, PyPI, MCP servers and Agent Skills. The company said researchers then investigated the suspicious components the system identified. According to OX Security, the findings point to a new attack path and a growing verification gap, in which instructions are becoming an attack path alongside code execution. The company said attackers can now manipulate an agent into taking actions with permissions it already has, and that security teams cannot verify what their agents connect to. OX Security said AI agents connect to MCP servers, load Agent Skills and pull packages from public registries, then act on what those components tell them, often with access to files, credentials, development tools and enterprise systems.

The company said many agents are taking orders from strangers, meaning tools with no identifiable owner that run code no one can verify before it is already in the environment. It said the attack surface is expanding from code that runs to instructions that agents follow. OX Security compared the situation to the old warning against plugging in a USB drive found somewhere, saying agents break that rule every day. Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security, said companies are giving AI agents access to critical systems while relying on trust signals built for a different era. He said the problem is not just what a tool can do, but who controls it, what code it actually runs and what instructions it can give an AI agent.

Ziv said a new model for software trust is needed. The company said it published a full report on the findings. OX Security said the research covered npm, PyPI, MCP servers and Agent Skills, and that its researchers investigated the suspicious components OX.Radar identified. The company presented the results as evidence of a growing verification gap rather than a single incident. It did not say in the article what specific malicious components were found or what happens next.

stories.Headline: Carnival CEO Josh Weinstein says U.S. travel disruptions cost the company a few hundred million dollars in revenue
stories.Summary:
The second and final day of Center Stage at The Phocuswright Conference 2026 closed the event at the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, with sessions on who will sell travel once AI agents can book on a traveler's behalf, on the race to power banks, airlines and loyalty programs with travel technology, and on the policy pressures weighing on U.S. travel. Carnival Corporation President and CEO Josh Weinstein told U.S. Travel Association President and CEO Geoff Freeman that this year's disruptions have cost the company probably a few hundred million dollars in revenue, not counting fuel, and that the hit took a point or two off yields. Freeman described government shutdowns, hours-long TSA lines, air traffic controller shortages and a 25% drop in Canadian visitors as man-made problems, and said the U.S. will welcome around 12 million fewer international visitors than in 2019. Weinstein said tourism has a cabinet seat in every other major economy and should have one in the U.S., given it accounts for about 3% of GDP, and he said Princess Cruises was the first cruise brand to launch plugins for ChatGPT and Claude, a claim made by him.

Booking Holdings is uniting its B2B operations into a single Booking Partner Division ahead of a January go-live, Agoda CEO Omri Morgenshtern told PhocusWire Executive Editor Linda Fox, and he said Priceline's B2B business is not part of the new division because of an ongoing FTC investigation. Morgenshtern said he expects each major product line to be among the best in the world within six to 12 months, and that success will mean not losing partners to competitors on technology. Expedia Group is now launching B2B partners about 75% faster than before, and its new AI-powered front end has cut launch times from three or four months to three or four days, said Alfonso Paredes, President, B2B and Chief Commercial Officer, who also said agentic booking is overhyped in the short term but underhyped in the long term. Under an expanded partnership with Qantas, Expedia now powers the technology behind Qantas Holidays' own hotel contracts with chains such as Accor, Hilton and Marriott.

Hopper CEO and co-founder Frederic Lalonde said Amex, Chase and Capital One sell around $30 billion of travel a year, a business growing about 22% annually compared with 4% to 6% for travel as a whole, and that Hopper's B2B platform HTS now connects to about 400 million cardholders in 23 countries, which he expects to double next year. He said Hopper did not sell itself to Capital One, which licensed its software and remains a customer, and he questioned whether travel marketplaces of any kind survive the shift to AI agents, saying blocking agents that act for customers is unlikely to work when more than half of internet traffic is no longer human. In a session on who powers travel when AI becomes the seller, panelists Brett Burgess of ATPCO, Niklas Andréen of Sabre and Steve Domin of Duffel predicted AI agents could book anywhere from 15% to 50% of airline tickets within two years. Burgess suggested United's recent decision to stop AI agents booking its flights is likely linked to verifying who the buyer is, and an ATPCO study found AI agents answered questions about flight offers accurately only about 6% of the time, because fare rules and product details are often not machine-readable, while Domin said the booking itself already works smoothly and the harder work is handling changes and cancellations after booking.

New Phocuswright research presented by Mike Coletta found that while 43% of U.S. travelers familiar with AI say they would book inside an AI platform, only 28% of travel companies are working or planning to become bookable there, and a survey of around 150 travel companies and start-ups found 45% are scaling or have scaled agentic AI, up from 28% in 2025, with start-ups further ahead than established companies. Companies that rebuilt core workflows around AI were more than twice as likely to report a major positive impact, at 92% versus 40%, and panelists said the technology to complete an agentic booking already exists but questions over who is accountable when something goes wrong are holding back volume. Google Group Product Manager James Byers told Phocuswright's Mitra Sorrells that AI Overviews now reach 2.5 billion monthly users and AI Mode can take a traveler from research to a completed hotel booking, and that AI queries are three times longer than traditional searches, with one in five using voice or images. Meta's Sanjay Bhatia, Head of Industry, Travel and Auto, showed how brands can use Meta Business Agent and WhatsApp, now used by 100 million Americans each month, to handle bookings and service in a single conversation. Zerolook CEO Simone Lini showed an example in which an AI agent ran around 881,000 flight searches on Etihad's website, and the Zurich-based start-up, which predicts airfares without querying live systems and has raised $1.9 million, reported 96% pricing accuracy for one U.S. carrier. Pintours was named Travel Innovator of the Year at the Innovation Awards, with Groupize runner-up and ZentrumHub winning the audience-voted People's Choice award, and the conference featured 199 speakers across 42 sessions, with session recordings to be released over the coming weeks.

stories.Headline: FACT Coalition policy director urges US to end offshore tax breaks in AI supply chain
stories.Summary:
Zorka Milin, policy director at the FACT Coalition, published an article on November 23, 2026, in Bloomberg Tax arguing that the US must break the AI supply chain’s addiction to offshore tax breaks. The article says Anthropic’s record-setting initial public offering underscores enormous investor enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence. It says the company’s newly released financials have revived a question that has hung over the industry for years about whether companies like Anthropic and OpenAI will ever turn a profit. It says that even if Anthropic turned profitable tomorrow, it might be years before it owed any tax. It says that if the company became hugely profitable, history suggests those profits might simply be moved offshore to avoid US tax.

The article says the AI supply chain has three broad parts: hardware, cloud computing and training data, and foundation models and customer-facing applications. It says Micron reported that its operations in Singapore cut its total tax bill by nearly $6 billion, the largest savings from a tax haven yet seen in newly expanded tax disclosures. It says Micron reported only about 5% of its global profit in the US in 2026, even though nearly 70% of its revenue comes from US customers. It says Broadcom reported saving about $2.7 billion through tax incentives in Singapore and Malaysia in fiscal 2025, before accounting for US taxes on foreign income. It says Marvell, Qualcomm, and KLA reported savings of $396 million, $195 million, and $135 million, respectively, from Singapore last year.

The article says Microsoft saved $3.5 billion last year through its Irish operations, and Oracle saved more than $1 billion through Bermuda, Malta, and Switzerland. It says Dell and IBM also reported hundreds of millions of dollars in savings from tax havens, and Apple reported more than $5.2 billion in tax benefits from Ireland and Singapore. It says 10 companies deeply embedded in the AI supply chain used offshore tax havens to shave more than $20 billion off their tax bills last year. It says the US taxes the foreign income of its multinationals at 12.6%, well below the statutory 21% rate for domestic income. It says Singapore’s implementation of the global minimum tax shaved more than $9 billion off Micron’s projected savings from tax incentive arrangements in the country.

The article says the US has not adopted the OECD standard agreed to by more than 140 nations, so it collects none of the new revenue the minimum tax has unlocked. It says Broadcom’s financial statements indicate that weaker US rules for foreign income recouped only around half of the $2.7 billion the company saved from Singapore and Malaysia in 2025. It says the deduction for foreign-derived intangible income taxes income from sales abroad at a preferential rate of 14%. It says FDII saved Google nearly $4 billion last year and Nvidia more than $4.2 billion, while Qualcomm reported more than $1.6 billion in benefits across 2025 and 2026 and AMD and KLA each saved hundreds of millions last year. It says defenders of FDII say it raises revenue by drawing taxable income back to the US.

The article says recent proposals to tax AI companies directly include taxing energy consumption or compute, or denying certain corporate tax subsidies to AI data center investments. It says economist and UCLA Law School professor Kimberly Clausing proposed raising the corporate tax rate to 27%, tightening tax rules for foreign income, and repealing the FDII export subsidy, raising nearly $4 trillion over the next decade. It says international tax reforms alone could raise as much as $1 trillion, much of it from hyperscalers. It says Congress failed the same test after the internet and social media booms. It says voters are increasingly anxious about AI, opposed to new data centers, and eager to see the largest corporations finally pay their fair share.

The article says tightening US rules for foreign income by raising the rate and aligning more closely with the OECD standard could bring in hundreds of billions of dollars in revenue. It says the 15% global minimum tax is already clawing back billions in savings that many American companies once enjoyed in low-tax countries. It says the article does not necessarily reflect the opinion of Bloomberg Industry Group, Inc., the publisher of Bloomberg Law, Bloomberg Tax, and Bloomberg Government, or its owners. It says Milin leads international tax policy and other transparency priorities at the FACT Coalition. It says readers interested in writing can review author guidelines and submit pitches to Insights@bloombergindustry.com.

stories.Headline: Imperial College London hosts 48-hour biotech hackathon with Claude support for 120 builders
stories.Summary:
Imperial BioHack, an event brought by the Imperial College Computational Biology Society with the Entrepreneurship Society, is set to bring 120 interdisciplinary builders together at Imperial College in London for 48 hours of hacking, tentatively on 28 and 29 November at the City and Guilds Building. The gathering is supported by Claude, and its stated goal is for teams to leave with a working MVP, benchmark, pipeline, or even a preprint in under 48 hours. Teams will compete across three industry-led tracks set by biotech companies, with workshops, sponsor keynotes, and presentations rounding out the schedule. The listing says the venue and dates are tentative and subject to change, and that overnight hacking in the building is not expected to be permitted.

Every participant is guaranteed $100 in Claude API credits, $200 in Cognition credits, Nebius compute credits, $250 in Amass platform credits per team, and a free ThinkCell subscription. The three tracks and their prizes for the top three teams are Adaptyv Bio with £1k cash, $20k in Adaptyv platform credits, 100 designs validated in the lab, and $1k Claude credits, Helical Bio with £1.5k cash, a fast-track to an internship, Helical swag, Nebius credits, and $1k Claude credits, and Novogaia Bio with £1.5k cash, Nebius credits, and $1k Claude credits plus more to be confirmed. A £200 ThinkCell side challenge for best presentation is also up for grabs, and full prize and track details will be announced on the day of the hack. On Saturday registration opens at 9:00am, introduction and sponsor keynotes run from 10:00am to 11:15am, team formation and networking run from 11:15am to 12:00pm, hacking starts at 12:00pm, workshops run from 12:00pm to 2:00pm, and lunch and dinner follow, while on Sunday hacking ends at 12:00pm, judging and lunch run from 12:00pm to 1:30pm, presentations run from 2:00pm to 4:00pm, and awards follow from 4:00pm onwards.

The event is organised by the Imperial College Computational Biology Society in collaboration with the Entrepreneurship Society, and the listing states that details come from the event listing and the organizer page, with registration managed by the organizer. The listing advises people to confirm the venue with the organizer before traveling and to confirm current availability before making plans, and it says the organizer page was checked on 24 November 2026. It also notes that the exact schedule is to be determined, and that doors will be open to everyone on 29 November from 2pm onwards so people can see the projects and final presentations even if they are not hacking. The listing describes the event as an interdisciplinary platform for software engineers, biologists, statisticians, and anyone curious about hackathons or science to build solutions to real challenges set by biotech companies.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Zurich and St Gallen warn shared AI logic keeps client risks correlated
stories.Summary:
New research from Zurich Insurance Group and the University of St. Gallen warns that a client can switch AI vendors or deploy multiple systems and still carry the same underlying risk as a competitor using a single provider. The report, titled The AI Resilience Challenge, draws on 50 expert interviews that University of St. Gallen researchers conducted between July and September 2026. It identifies two ways AI-related losses can spread, the first being concentration risk, which arises when many organizations depend on the same provider, model or infrastructure and a single failure causes simultaneous losses across unrelated businesses. The second, correlation risk, comes not from a shared provider but from shared logic, because separate AI systems may draw on similar training data, architecture or decision rules and fail in similar ways without any common outage or identifiable trigger. The report says that connection is behavioral rather than structural and may only become visible through claims, complaints, regulatory action or litigation appearing across separate organizations.

The report says the conventional assumption that using different systems or providers creates independent exposures can break down, so two clients placing their AI risk with separate insurers may still be exposed to the same underlying vulnerability if their systems share training data or decision logic. The Lloyd's Market Association, drawing on a 2025 survey of 144 managing agent respondents, 94% of them underwriters, found boards were ranking AI risk second only to geopolitical risk on their risk registers, and the survey identified a significant absence of underwriting and claims data to price AI exposures, particularly in professional indemnity. The report uses the July 2024 CrowdStrike outage as an illustration of how concentration risk propagates, when a faulty software update crashed approximately 8.5 million Windows devices globally and disrupted airlines, banks, hospitals and broadcasters, with direct losses to US Fortune 500 companies alone estimated at approximately $5.4 billion by technology downtime insurer Parametrix, though that event was not AI-related. Unlike the EU, which has adopted a risk-based legislative framework through the EU AI Act, the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority are applying a principles-based, technology-neutral approach to AI oversight, relying on existing rules rather than introducing AI-specific legislation.

Mario Greco, group chief executive officer at Zurich Insurance Group, said companies need to know where they depend on AI, what can happen when it fails, and be prepared to respond and recover quickly. The report recommends that organizations map AI dependencies beyond direct suppliers to uncover shared points of failure, assign clear accountability for AI decisions, and test whether critical activities can continue when systems fail or need to be overridden. It frames insurability itself as a diagnostic tool, arguing that when coverage terms tighten, premiums rise or reinsurance appetite narrows, those shifts can indicate that exposure is outrunning the evidence available to price it, and that the limits of insurability reveal where broader resilience needs to be strengthened. The Zurich AI Lab, launched in October 2025 as a collaboration between Zurich, the University of St. Gallen and ETH Zurich's Agentic Systems Lab, describes this as a continuing research programme, and the report was produced as a contribution to discussion ahead of the Geneva Summit 2027.

stories.Headline: AidFinder uses AI to match disaster survivors with aid programs as founder seeks first state customer
stories.Summary:
When the Palisades fire tore through Jonathon Nostrant’s Los Angeles neighborhood in January 2025, his house was damaged but still standing, while many of his neighbors’ homes were destroyed. After the fire, Nostrant found a tangle of federal, state and local assistance programs, each with its own forms, eligibility rules and deadlines. Survivors with insurance must also report their payouts to every agency they apply to, because FEMA cannot pay for losses an insurer already covers. Insurance was already a sore subject in the Palisades, and a year before the fire State Farm dropped roughly 1,600 policies in the neighborhood, Fortune reported as the fire burned. Nostrant said in an interview that his own insurance claim was fighting with him.

That experience led to AidFinder, a Miami-based startup Nostrant co-founded that uses AI to match disaster survivors with programs they may qualify for, explain eligibility rules and prepare applications, with survivors reviewing everything before submission. The intended customers are states, which would offer the platform to residents under their own banner. For now it is a pitch: AidFinder has not signed its first state customer and survivors have yet to use the platform, Refresh Miami reported on Nov. 17. Nostrant told the outlet the company is in talks with 30 states, including Florida, and that Craig Fugate, who ran FEMA under President Barack Obama, has accepted a seat on its board.

Nostrant has spent much of his career teaching machines to listen, launching the voice-activated alarm clock Moshi at the University of Southern California in 2008 and later founding Ivee, an early AI-powered home assistant. AidFinder applies the same idea to turning a survivor’s account of what happened into the right applications for the right agencies. The pitch arrives as Washington pushes more of the recovery burden onto states, and FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton has told state emergency managers to prepare to handle more of the work themselves. Recounting Hamilton’s remarks at a National Emergency Management Association gathering, Nostrant described the federal message as wanting to empower states, counties and cities to be equipped not just to respond to the disaster but to help people recover.

AidFinder’s answer is a branded front door, and Nostrant said the company is giving states the ability to launch a landing page powered by AidFinder that matches residents with recovery programs. FEMA advises survivors to photograph or film damage inside and outside their homes before cleanup and to list damaged belongings, records that support both an insurance claim and a federal aid application. AidFinder is built around the same principle, letting residents store identification, tax records and photos of their homes in a secure digital vault before disaster strikes. The question now is whether a state will pay to offer it.

stories.Headline: Democratic governors in Texas, Ohio and Georgia vow to pause data center development
stories.Summary:
Newly elected Democratic governors have vowed to pause the development of data centers. Gina Hinojosa of Texas and Amy Acton of Ohio both called for moratoria. Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia plans to sign an executive order pausing development. These actions follow elections where voters passed dozens of anti-data center initiatives nationwide. The events occurred around the November 2026 election cycle.

Texas requires new guardrails for hiring union workers and protecting water resources. These rules would give Texas communities the power to approve data center projects. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 affects all new data centers. It requires builders to pay for their own power and invest in local communities. Utilities must obtain financial guarantees to cover incremental energy and infrastructure costs.

Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said she will issue a ban on all data center approvals. She stated this moratorium will last until the legislature passes laws to protect Texans. Democratic leaders in Ohio and Georgia also expressed a need for these pauses. They want regulations to address electricity prices and the impact on local communities. These officials seek to ensure that data centers do not harm residents.

Public opposition to AI data centers reached a crescendo leading up to the elections. Average American households are affected by concerns that these centers hike electricity costs. The Chinese regime is accused of using AI to sow division in the United States. Chinese operators allegedly used ChatGPT to create comic strips suggesting AI centers raise costs. A bot farm of 200 accounts reportedly manipulated debates about American energy policy.

Texas ranks second only to Virginia in data centers due to reliable energy. Texas was projected to exceed 40 gigawatts of data center capacity by 2028. Governor Greg Abbott previously ordered a pause on permits to audit interconnection processes. This was done to maintain power grid reliability and protect water resources. The U.S. faces a bottleneck because gas turbine production cannot meet demand.

The U.S. Senate began discussing a data center bill on November 9. Developers are turning to used turbines and repurposed engines due to shortages. These older units are cheaper but raise questions about maintenance and long term reliability. The articles do not state when the Democratic governors will implement their pauses. They leave open whether the Senate bill will be passed into law.

stories.Headline: Data center developers and senior housing operators can explore partnerships that reuse waste heat, Dham says
stories.Summary:
The article asks whether AI data centers could help with the US senior housing crisis, and it was published by CIO on 23 November 2026. It was written by Ankush Dham, who is CEO of Dataknox Solutions, a global IT infrastructure services company. The piece is an opinion article, and Dham says he believes there is an opportunity to explore partnerships between data center developers and senior housing operators. He describes two trends creating infrastructure challenges in the United States, rising senior housing demand and the rapid expansion of AI data centers. He says the oldest baby boomers turn 80 this year and the shortfall of senior housing units is growing more severe.

According to NIC MAP's 2026 Senior Housing Market Outlook, the need for additional senior housing will reach approximately 576,000 units by 2030. The same outlook says the need will exceed one million units by 2035 if construction continues at its current pace. A 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, up from an estimated 4.7% in 2024. NIC MAP estimates that meeting future senior housing demand will require more than $1 trillion in cumulative investment through 2050. In Groningen, the Netherlands, data center operator QTS has partnered with local energy provider WarmteStad to supply recovered heat to a district heating network.

Dham says the system uses heat pumps powered by renewable energy to circulate hot water through an existing underground district heating network. He says that network supplies residual heat to 10,000 households, buildings and knowledge institutions. He says the community gets access to a heat source that would otherwise be discarded, and the data center benefits from the cooling provided through the energy exchange. He says the engineering requires more than connecting two buildings, because data center cooling systems generally operate at temperatures below those required for conventional building heating. He says heat pumps would likely need to raise the temperature, and a distribution network must transport the energy to where it can be used.

In Chicago's Bronzeville neighborhood, developers have proposed Metropolis Pointe, a mixed-use development combining a data center with residential, commercial and community facilities. Griffin Venture Group, the project's developer, announced additional infrastructure milestones in August 2026, including plans for a 170,000-square-foot data center and a 42,000-square-foot central utility plant. Dham says the proposed utility system would integrate heating and cooling across the campus with the goal of reducing energy costs for residents. He says the project is still in the proposal stage, and he says its design reflects an important evolution in thinking. He says senior living communities may be particularly well suited because they operate 24/7 with substantial year-round energy requirements.

Dham says heating, hot water, kitchens, laundry facilities and common areas all contribute to operating expenses in senior living communities. He says traditional HVAC or electric heating can be an especially high cost in colder climates. He says construction costs have also increased, financing remains costly and challenging, and many older Americans cannot absorb higher housing expenses on their fixed budgets. He says a senior living community located near a suitable data center could potentially receive recovered heat through a shared thermal network. He says senior housing developers with available land might be able to lease a portion of their land to a data center operator to create an additional revenue stream.

Dham says large hyperscale data centers won't always be appropriate, and he thinks smaller computing facilities and strategically located data centers connected through district heating networks will prove more practical. He says data centers would still need adequate space, zoning, electrical capacity and commercial demand to make each arrangement work. He says brownfield opportunities could be identified within existing senior housing developments, and multi-state operators could evaluate their portfolios for facilities with available land, suitable heating systems and access to electrical infrastructure. He says retrofitting older facilities can be expensive and potential savings would need to justify investments. He says a small number of promising projects could test the models, measure their results and demonstrate where these partnerships can deliver meaningful benefits.

stories.Headline: Automated checks help finance teams stop most accounts payable fraud, survey finds
stories.Summary:
Accounts payable fraud often begins with a single fake supplier request that redirects company cash to the wrong account, and PYMNTS Intelligence surveyed 150 U.S. treasury and finance executives to learn how businesses fight this problem as artificial intelligence makes scams harder to spot. The survey, released in a report produced with Bottomline, examined where manual checks fall short and how finance teams can strengthen their defenses. The findings show that automated checks are linked to stronger fraud prevention, and that connected payment data gives teams a stronger defense. The report also found that payment approvals struggle to keep pace with the speed and volume of payments. Among teams with mostly or somewhat automated verification, 65% stop at least 90% of fraud attempts before a loss occurs, according to the survey.

Fifty-five percent of companies with integrated data stop at least 90% of fraud attempts, the findings show. Only 12% of executives strongly agree that their approval controls keep up with payment speed and volume. The report presents these figures as evidence of where manual checks fall short and how finance teams can strengthen their defenses. The survey was conducted by PYMNTS Intelligence, which explored how businesses fight payables fraud, and the report is a collaboration with Bottomline. The findings reveal where manual checks fall short and how finance teams can strengthen their defenses, according to the report.

The report directs readers to download the collaboration with Bottomline for the details. The articles do not name any individual who commented on the findings. The context given is that artificial intelligence is making scams harder to spot, which is why the survey examined how businesses fight payables fraud. The articles do not say what happens next beyond offering the download of the full report with Bottomline for the details. No further steps, dates or responses are given in the articles.

stories.Headline: Venture capital investors weigh proprietary data and deep tech as AI reshapes startup competition
stories.Summary:
CTech launched its VC Survey 2027 project on November 23, 2026, drawing on a survey conducted over the past several weeks among more than 100 executives, managing partners and investment partners at venture capital funds active in the Israeli market. The project is a series of articles and data analyses that examines changes in the venture capital industry in Israel and around the world, with a focus on the impact of artificial intelligence on companies and investment models, fundraising conditions, and the economic and geopolitical challenges facing the industry. Over the coming weeks the project will feature in-depth articles, statistical analyses and interviews with senior figures in the venture capital industry, drawing on survey findings and the perspectives of fund managers and investors. The coverage will address the changes those investors see in the market, the strategies they are adopting, and the opportunities and risks they expect to shape the industry in the years ahead.

One central theme is how the AI revolution affects the way technology companies are built, what gives them a competitive edge, and how venture capital investors evaluate potential investments. Because AI tools make software and digital services faster and cheaper to develop, the competitive landscape for startups is changing and raising new questions about the sources of their long-term advantage. The survey examines the importance investors place on proprietary data, deep integration into customers' workflows, and hard-to-replicate technologies including semiconductors, robotics and computing infrastructure. It also explores changes in venture capital business models and the funding environment, including the challenges of raising capital for new funds, shifts in investment volumes and investor expectations, and the growing gap between the capital requirements of software companies and those of hardware and deep-tech ventures. Another focus is the state of the exit market, where limited IPO opportunities are making mergers and acquisitions and secondary transactions increasingly important routes to liquidity.

A further major part of the project will examine Israel's position in the global venture capital industry, exploring how geopolitical developments affect investment decisions and the ability of Israeli companies to attract foreign capital. The analyses will look at the sectors in which the local ecosystem continues to draw international investor interest, including cybersecurity, defense technology, Physical AI and computing infrastructure, alongside the challenges facing early-stage startups. The project will also look at how venture capital funds themselves are adapting, including their use of AI tools to source companies, screen investment opportunities and conduct due diligence, as well as changes to investment strategies and portfolio management. This year's survey builds on CTech's annual VC Survey, which last year brought together the views of more than 60 leading investors and examined the Israeli tech industry's transition from survival mode to a focus on execution and growth. Against the backdrop of rapid advances in artificial intelligence and ongoing challenges in the capital markets, the project aims to provide an up-to-date picture of the venture capital industry and how its leading figures are preparing for the years ahead.

stories.Headline: Connecticut police use AI with few statewide rules as lawmakers plan updates
stories.Summary:
Connecticut police departments are using artificial intelligence with few statewide rules, according to a report published by CT Insider on Nov. 23, 2026. The report was written by staff writer Jordan Nathaniel Fenster. It says artificial intelligence is entering almost every professional sector, including policing. It says Connecticut has no common set of rules, state-level tracking or guardrails on how police departments are using artificial intelligence. The report says state officials have moved to track and disclose AI use among utilities and in the job market.

Earlier this year, Connecticut prosecutors announced a moratorium on AI programs that draft, author or narrate criminal reports, the report says. That pause addresses one use case of AI and is, at present, the only statewide guidance on AI use for police, according to the report. Beyond automated license plate readers, which are a specific exception with separate state rules and public reporting requirements, there is no general statewide inventory showing which AI systems local police use, how they use them or what safeguards apply, the report says. The state's Responsible AI Framework was created in 2023 and calls for agencies to consider accuracy, privacy, fairness, transparency and human oversight, according to the report. The report says the document applies to state agencies and their contractors, while local governments are "encouraged to adopt" it, leaving cities and towns to decide whether to create separate rules for their police departments.

Mike Lawlor, an educator and former legislator who serves on the state Police Officer Standards and Training Council, said AI can be very useful as an administrative and investigatory tool, the report says. Lawlor said there is a role for this to play and that it is inevitable it will be a major part of everything, including law enforcement. He said it is a question, since it is new, of how you test it, how you figure out what the potential problems are and how you protect against those things happening. State Sen. James Maroney, D-Milford, said he was planning on going back and updating the government use of AI bill this year because of learnings since 2023. Maroney said lawmakers will likely look at it and ask the judiciary branch to do so as well.

Vahid Behzadan, an associate professor at the University of New Haven who researches AI safety and security, said AI is not a single technology, according to the report. Behzadan said police uses can range from transcription and translation to report writing, facial recognition and predictive systems that forecast where crime might occur. With report-writing tools, Behzadan said the model might end up excluding relevant facts, including potentially exculpatory information. He said software could theoretically turn an unclear or ambiguous account into a smoother, more confident-sounding narrative, changing how events appear to have happened.

Behzadan said an officer's review remains essential but does not by itself show which parts of the report came from the software or what the software left out. The report says few municipal police departments in Connecticut have any guidelines for officers' AI use, or publicly disclose how and if police officers are using it. It says academics and advocates have raised concerns that artificial intelligence may create errors in police reports, that AI used for facial recognition can create false matches and that predictive systems might create disproportionate surveillance in communities of color. An NAACP issue brief on predictive policing warns that systems trained on historical crime and policing data can reproduce unequal patterns in surveillance and enforcement, the report says.

The report says the brief calls for oversight and public disclosure and is a statement of risks and recommendations, not evidence that a Connecticut police department uses predictive policing. According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology, facial recognition can produce false matches, and the error rates of tested systems can vary across demographic groups, producing higher error rates when examining Black persons' faces, the report says. A presentation last year by the Connecticut Criminal Justice Information System governing board included a bullet point explaining how the agency was planning to use AI to "do a lot more with less," the report says. The presentation said the agency is automating more of its testing of new code to reduce costs, exploring possibilities of adding AI for Connecticut Information Sharing System Analytics and renegotiating maintenance agreements or instead leveraging time and materials contracts.

The report says lawmakers admit that the 2023 law that created the AI framework is already outdated, and it notes that ChatGPT became available in public previews on Nov. 30, 2022. Prior to the moratorium, New Haven had a 2024 contract with Axon that included Draft One, which can use body-camera audio to generate a draft police report, according to the report. The report says there are no reports of this technology being used in Connecticut. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Saudi princess urges leaders to pair AI growth with power and public consent
stories.Summary:
Princess Maha bint Mishari Al Saud, chief executive of the FII Institute, wrote an op-ed for Formiche and Decode39 arguing that artificial intelligence needs energy, investment and public trust, and the piece was published on 23 November 2026. She wrote it after attending B20 meetings in Washington, where business leaders from the world's largest economies advised G20 governments while the United States held the G20 presidency. In the op-ed she said the discussions were dominated by artificial intelligence and the energy needed to run it, and she argued that training and running AI models demand enormous computing power, which in turn requires energy. She wrote that Saudi Arabia has both abundant energy and investment capital, so it makes sense to build data centers close to the energy that powers them.

She cited figures showing why the issue is sensitive, noting that United States residential electricity prices have risen almost 30% since 2021 and that New Jersey's average bill jumped more than 20% last year alone. She said data centers are not the only cause of such increases but that voters see them as part of it, and that in Ireland data centers now consume more than a fifth of the nation's electricity. She referred to the FII Institute's fifth edition of the PRIORITY Compass, which polls more than 60,000 people in 32 countries each year and finds that the cost of living is the top concern for 56% of people worldwide and 68% of Americans. She added that worry about energy and fuel costs rose nine points in a single year and that 43% of Americans now count it among their biggest cost pressures.

She said the Washington meetings made three things clear, the first being that the United States and Saudi Arabia have a deep and growing economic partnership, with the United States Chamber of Commerce's Saudi program its second largest international program after India's. She wrote that Saudi Arabia has invested $170 billion in the United States, supporting 172,000 American jobs, and has committed a further $1 trillion. The second point was that productivity gains from AI are accelerating, so that energy, capital and the time it takes to approve projects will become the brakes on growth rather than human productivity. The third was that those gains will not survive a loss of public trust, since 77% of people in the institute's polling expect big technology companies to put profit before safety.

She urged leaders to make data centers bring their own power rather than plug into the grid and leave households to pick up the bill, with dedicated energy from natural gas, nuclear power, renewables or storage built alongside new projects. She noted that Washington has already asked America's biggest technology companies to build or buy their own power and said that should become the norm everywhere. She also called for faster permitting, citing speakers who argued for a shot clock on approvals under which a decision that takes too long would be presumed approved. She said citizens should be kept in view by tracking the effect of AI investment on household bills, jobs and the environment and acting before it becomes a grievance, and the articles say her op-ed comes ahead of a potential visit to Italy by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, expected in December.
