stories.Headline: FastMetal adds Gemini 4 Neon and Inkling 2 Small to its AI gateway
stories.Summary:
FastMetal, an AI gateway operated by the Japanese company Kokusai Chotatsu Joho, began offering two new large language models on November 24, 2026, according to a press release dated the same day. The two models are Gemini 4 Neon, which Google released on November 18, 2026, and Inkling 2 Small, an inference model whose weights were published by Thinking Machines Lab. Both models support a context length of about one million tokens and accept image input, and FastMetal says it checked image input and PDF reading with real files before launch. The same screen also lets users choose the other Gemini 4 generation models, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon.

According to Google, Gemini 4 Neon is the mid-tier model of the Gemini 4 generation, built to balance depth of thinking with efficiency for complex coding, analysis and enterprise workflows, and it always reasons before answering. Google says it scored 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1, which evaluates work in a terminal. According to Thinking Machines Lab, Inkling 2 Small is the second generation of its Inkling model and greatly surpasses the previous generation in agentic coding, image understanding, knowledge work and reasoning. It was announced on November 5, 2026, and its weights were published on November 12, 2026, under the Apache 2.0 license. FastMetal says it checked image input, tool calling and structured output with real requests before launch.

Both models are billed per million tokens in yen, with prices listed on FastMetal's model pages, and the context length is given as 1,048,576 tokens. Users charge a balance by credit card or bank transfer and then pick a model on the chat screen, and FastMetal describes itself as a prepaid service in yen that never charges beyond the loaded balance. The company says it issues qualified invoices under Japan's invoice system and will keep adding new AI models as they are released. The release says the models' specifications and performance are based on the announcements of their developers.

stories.Headline: Global markets face a widespread selloff in AI and technology stocks
stories.Summary:
A widespread selloff in artificial intelligence and technology stocks hit global markets last week. This event affected benchmark indexes in the United States and Asia. The selloff occurred at the end of the week before Monday, November 23, 2026. Anthropic's record IPO squeezed liquidity during this period of market turmoil. Concerns about the sustainability of the AI trade also weighed on investor sentiment.

The Nasdaq Composite fell 10 percent, while the S&P 500 and Dow fell over 8 percent. South Korea's KOSPI dropped 3.22 percent on Monday, following its lowest close in 10 months. The South Korean government created a stock stabilization fund and eased share buyback limits for three months. Taiwan's Taiex had its worst weekly fall in 35 years, slumping more than 9 percent. China will lower minimum margin requirements to 80 percent from 100 percent on November 30.

The Kobeissi Letter stated that the AI buildout is only accelerating. This commentator claimed that AI truly is the next big thing. Ben Bowler of Bank of America Global Research noted that idiosyncratic risk has dominated. He said that a broad based shock remains a risk for index volatility. Jeong Woo Park of Nomura Holdings said investors found government measures lacked substance.

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was bearish for SPY and DIA but extremely bullish for QQQ. Investors in South Korea saw Samsung shares fall nearly 3 percent and SK Hynix drop over 13 percent. Dilin Wu of Pepperstone Group said interventions are circuit breakers rather than a turning point. He noted these steps cannot reverse a broader reassessment of AI valuations. Foreign investors are also affected by these shifting market dynamics and valuations.

The S&P 500 had eight straight quarters of double digit growth before this rout. It also posted three consecutive quarters with earnings growth above 25 percent. The index closed Friday 4.1 standard deviations below its 50 day moving average. The Kobeissi Letter claimed that neither 2008 nor 2020 saw such an occurrence. These figures provide the background for the recent sharp decline in sentiment.

U.S. futures turned green on Monday, with the Nasdaq 100 futures increasing 3.02 percent. The SPY ETF rose over 2 percent and the QQQ ETF gained 3.04 percent. Taiwan's Taiex and China's SSE Composite index edged slightly higher at the open. Japan's stock market remained closed on Monday for the Labour Thanksgiving Day holiday. The articles leave open whether foreign investors will return to these markets.

stories.Headline: Lam Research and ASML supply chipmaking tools as demand outruns supply through 2028
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on November 12 that its leader, Jensen Huang, had resigned as CEO. This event created uncertainty regarding the future of the company and its lead in AI chips. John Ballard wrote about this situation on November 23, 2026. He suggested investing in companies that sell the machines used to make chips. These equipment providers can profit regardless of which chip designer wins the race.

Lam Research makes tools that deposit and etch layers on chips for factories. ASML is the only maker of extreme ultraviolet lithography systems for printing circuit patterns. Lam Research reported September quarter revenue of 8.2 billion dollars, which was a record. ASML expects its planned output for 2027 and 2028 to fall short of demand. ASML is considering raising its 2028 capacity by at least 30 percent.

Lam Research management credits record margins to pricing, new products, and manufacturing closer to customers. Chief financial officer Doug Bettinger said ten new tier I fabs will open next year. ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet stated that customers are accelerating capacity build-out plans for the future. He noted that these customers are preparing for expansion beyond 2028 to meet anticipated demand. Both companies claim their equipment is necessary for any chipmaker leading in artificial intelligence.

Leading chipmakers told ASML that demand for their machines will outrun supply through 2028. Some of these customers are already expressing interest in placing orders for 2029 and 2030. Investors are affected by the cyclical nature of the semiconductor business and potential supply shortages. Lam Research noted that supply chain constraints limited its December quarter outlook. Analysts expect earnings for both companies to roughly triple by the year 2029.

Global chip sales rose nearly 26 percent to 791 billion dollars in 2025. The Semiconductor Industry Association provided these figures regarding the growth of the global market. The industry group WSTS expects sales to reach 1.5 trillion dollars in 2026. They further expect sales to grow to 1.9 trillion dollars by 2027. Lam Research expects industry spending on chipmaking equipment to top 200 billion dollars in 2027.

Lam Research aims to lift its gross margin to the mid-50s over several years. ASML expects its full year 2026 sales to grow by about 36 percent. Analysts predict Lam Research adjusted earnings per share will reach 14.54 dollars by fiscal 2029. Analysts expect ASML earnings to reach 76.65 dollars by the year 2029. The articles leave open whether rival chip designers will gain ground on Nvidia.

stories.Headline: Penny Wong frames AI data centres as foreign policy and national security challenges for Australia
stories.Summary:
On November 23, 2026, Australia shifted its national security debate regarding artificial intelligence from think-tank panels to cabinet-level talking points. Foreign Minister Penny Wong planned to call artificial intelligence a major foreign policy and national security challenge. Several senior ministers framed AI and the data centres that power it as security issues in recent days. This strategic shift moved AI from a productivity and skills question to a matter for spy agencies. The development occurred as the government sought to police who owns and reaches into AI infrastructure.

The Reserve Bank of Australia forecast 115 billion dollars in spending on data centres between mid-2023 and mid-2026. Microsoft announced a 25 billion dollar investment in April, while Amazon announced a 20 billion dollar plan in June. The Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018, introduced to parliament on December 10, 2020, regulates data storage and processing. This law is administered by the Department of Home Affairs and covers eleven essential sectors including energy and communications. The Attorney-General's Department also oversees the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme to register activities conducted for foreign principals.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong stated that AI is transforming military power and reordering economies in ways that cannot be fully foreseen. She argued that Australia must move quickly to help shape international rules on artificial intelligence. ASIO Director-General Mike Burgess described AI and data centres as equal parts hype, opportunity and threat. He cautioned that foreign adversaries could covertly seek influence or control over AI data centre infrastructure for nefarious reasons. Burgess also expressed concerns regarding both the physical and virtual access to these computing facilities.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said onshore AI capability becomes a magnet for people who want to conduct foreign interference. He stated that Australia must be careful about the ownership structures that happen for data centres in the country. Defence Minister Richard Marles said Australian data centres represent a national security interest and create a new vector for foreign actors. US President Donald Trump threatened a tremendous tax on American companies that build AI data centres outside the United States. Trump claimed the US is not going to allow its companies to build data centres outside the country.

The articles state that generative tools lower the cost and technical threshold for running automated disinformation personas across borders. Wong cited an Iranian operation using fabricated journalist personas and Russian covert campaigns using AI-generated deepfakes to influence US elections. The government views AI as a challenge to be managed, similar to maritime security and critical minerals. Australia has seen data-centre investment grow tenfold over three years according to the Reserve Bank of Australia. These facilities are considered national assets because they are valuable targets for attacking or influencing.

Australia continues to engage with the US government and technology companies about investment in the country. The government wants to keep welcoming investment while it builds rules to manage the security exposure. It remains unconfirmed if any named company's Australian project has been formally blocked by the United States. The record contains no specific tax rate, start date, or statutory vehicle for the threatened US tax. The articles leave open whether Microsoft or Amazon will cancel their plans due to the US tax threat.

stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to staff for violating company code of conduct
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees on Tuesday for violating the company code of conduct. He spoke during his first all-hands meeting since returning to his role as chief executive. Huang stated that he made very serious personal mistakes which led to his resignation. He admitted that he hurt his wife and his family through these personal actions. The CEO also shared that he has been attending therapy every day for ninety minutes.

The board accepted his resignation earlier this month and reinstated him on Monday, eleven days later. This followed reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of ties to Chinese intelligence. The board acted after receiving fresh assurances and learning from the Trump administration he lacked federal scrutiny. Huang will now undergo a 360-degree performance review, soliciting feedback as often as every month. He claims he will be the first and only person at Nvidia to undergo this review.

Huang said this was the second hardest meeting he ever did, after a meeting with his wife. He stated that the company code of conduct, which he largely wrote, still governs employee treatment. He claimed that he needs to hold himself to a higher standard during this current time. Huang acknowledged that his intense management style sometimes disempowers employees and he takes things too far. He argued that his brief absence proved the company is wired to execute without him.

Some Nvidia employees celebrated the return of the CEO while others remain concerned about his personal conduct. One employee stated they would not do any more HR trainings if Huang returned to the company. Over 1,600 people commented on an internal post, with the majority supporting the decision to reinstall him. Women at the company are affected, though Huang described himself as one of their greatest advocates. He touted flexible work policies that allow employees to build their families and their careers simultaneously.

The board cited concerns about personal behavior and a lack of candor regarding his extramarital affairs. Huang began working with consultants from Heller in October 2025, when he was linked to a spy. The company opened an investigation into his affair with an alleged asset of Chinese intelligence services. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, served as the interim CEO following his initial resignation on Thursday. The company has faced lawsuits and probes regarding its disclosures and compliance with US export controls.

The board is continuing an investigation into whether Huang was the target of foreign intelligence services. US lawmakers expect the CEO to testify before Congress during the coming week. Legal probes into Nvidia's compliance with chip export controls and its disclosures about behavior are still ongoing. The articles leave open whether Huang can maintain his dedication without hurting the people who work there. It remains unclear if the board will institute performance reviews for other employees beyond the CEO.

stories.Headline: Heavy agentic AI users expect role shifts and fewer middle management layers, survey finds
stories.Summary:
A survey by MIT Sloan Management Review found that heavy agentic AI users expect significant organizational changes. This research was discussed in business media on November 23, 2026, including reports from The Business Journals. The findings suggest that the primary challenge of agentic AI is organizational rather than purely technological. These systems differ from assistants because they initiate actions, sequence work, and adapt in real time. Consequently, the current organizational charts may become bottlenecks as these agents begin acting on their own.

The survey shows that 66 percent of extensive users expect role redefinitions and operating model changes. In contrast, only 42 percent of organizations with no adoption plans expect such shifts. Regarding management, 45 percent of heavy users expect fewer middle management layers, compared to 30 percent of non-adopters. A Forbes Technology Council column from November 20 proposes that every agent get a department and one named owner. This proposal also suggests that an agent's access should be capped at its owner's access level.

The MIT Sloan Management Review project states that governance requires IT, HR, finance, and operations to work together. This collaborative approach is necessary because no single function can own the policy alone. The Business Journals reports that the core difficulty is organizational, as agents behave more like workers than tools. An arXiv paper titled A Practical Guide to Agentic AI Transition in Organizations lists four structural problems. These include unclear ownership of workflows and a lack of sustainable human and AI collaboration models.

The reporting indicates that middle management is the first layer in the line of fire for these shifts. Employees who supervise agents often lack the authority, context, and time required for such roles. California recently stated that OpenAI lost control of agents 80 times, highlighting the legal risks of unclear ownership. The arXiv guide also notes a misalignment between engineering and business teams and limited integration of business domain knowledge. These issues affect anyone building or buying agents, as the human moves from author to supervisor.

For two years, the debate focused on whether models could plan tasks and recover from errors. The current reporting flips this assumption by suggesting the organizational structure is now the main obstacle. Traditional charts assume every action traces back to a human, but agents break this assumption quietly. The Forbes proposal aims to fix security flaws where agents use broad service accounts for production workflows. This is critical because credentials inside agent workflows are attractive targets for compromise.

Organizations must now decide if agents cause restructuring or if those planning to restructure adopt agents faster. The sources do not settle which reading is correct, though they note both could be true. Large minorities of users still see agents as upgrades to existing structures rather than reasons to redraw them. No company has been named as having formally put AI agents on an official organizational chart. It remains unconfirmed how many agents, employees, or reporting lines are actually involved in these transitions.

Articles.Title: Agentic AI Org Chart Problem: 66% Expect Role Shifts

stories.Headline: StudioX AI adds OpenTelemetry tracing that shows enterprise AI agent runs in existing monitoring tools
stories.Summary:
StudioX AI announced on 23 November 2026 that it has added OpenTelemetry tracing to its enterprise agentic AI platform, so that when tracing is enabled the company can show an enterprise AI agent run as a single trace across StudioX services and export it to the monitoring tools an operations team already uses. The company said the feature lets teams see what AI agents did in the same tools they use to watch the rest of their software, and it described OpenTelemetry as a must for enterprise monitoring. StudioX said the tracing is available now in its cloud and private deployments, including air-gapped environments, where traces go to a collector inside the customer's own network. The company framed the launch around companies moving toward what it calls the autonomous enterprise, in which AI agents act in business systems rather than only answering questions. The trace covers agent runs along with the model that actually served each one, calls to connected systems including calls that StudioX's agent policy blocked before they reached that system, checks an agent makes on a system it watches with how many records each one found, and actions taken after a decision such as an email sent or a record updated once a person approved it.

The trace shows whether a call failed or was blocked by policy, and StudioX exports traces over OTLP/HTTP, the export path of OpenTelemetry, which it described as a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project for collecting and exporting traces, metrics and logs. Exported traces exclude prompts, responses, tool inputs and results, business records and database queries, and before any trace leaves StudioX removes query strings, credentials and the access tokens in sign-in and approval links. Tracing stays off until an administrator points a deployment at a monitoring endpoint using the standard OpenTelemetry settings, the same rule applies to customer private deployments that run the same StudioX build, and standard OpenTelemetry sampling settings control how many runs are traced. Ian Hamrick, VP Strategy & Partnerships at StudioX AI, said an autonomous enterprise works only if the people running it can see what its AI agents did, and that operations teams can now see what AI agents did alongside the systems they already monitor. He said the company builds on open standards so customers keep the tools they already trust.

StudioX said OpenTelemetry joins other open standards it supports, including the Model Context Protocol, which connects agents to tools and data, and Agent2Agent, which lets agents built on different platforms work together. The company said it is committed to building on open standards so enterprises can connect the systems and tools they already run and are not locked into a single vendor. StudioX illustrated the need with a manufacturing example in which a maintenance agent might read an equipment alert, check the asset's service history, ask an inventory agent about a replacement part and submit a work order after a supervisor approves it. When such a run is slow or fails, the company said, the operations team needs to know which step, which system and which call, in the same tool where it already watches the rest of the plant's software. The articles give no further details on availability beyond the statement that the tracing is available now, and they name no date for anything further.

Articles.Title: StudioX AI Launches OpenTelemetry Tracing for Enterprise AI Agents

stories.Headline: AI panel brief says countries can build AI capacity through varied paths beyond frontier models
stories.Summary:
The Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence published a new Thematic Brief on AI Capacity-Building on November 23, 2026, examining the capabilities countries need to benefit from artificial intelligence. The brief finds that there is more than one pathway to AI capacity and that developing frontier models is not the only route available to countries. It says countries can pursue different approaches according to their needs, resources and national priorities. In health and agriculture, the brief notes, AI applications designed for specific tasks have already delivered documented benefits.

The brief states that access to AI does not in itself ensure that countries can benefit from it, because evidence shows substantial performance gaps in many underrepresented languages. It adds that in some low-resource languages safety protections can be bypassed more easily, so systems that perform well in English may not serve all populations equally. Evaluation sets developed with native speakers allow countries to assess how systems perform in their own languages and contexts. The brief also says compute, models and training numbers tell only part of the story, since expertise, relevant data, effective institutions and the capacity to evaluate and govern AI systems also determine whether countries can use AI to advance their own development objectives.

Drawing on evidence and practical examples from different regions, the brief showcases how countries are building these capabilities, from national training programmes and shared computing to locally developed language resources. The brief is intended to inform Member States and other stakeholders as they assess their own AI capacity and decide which pathways best suit their priorities. The Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence is the body that issued the brief. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the brief's stated purpose of informing Member States and other stakeholders.

stories.Headline: Visa Crypto Labs lets US cardholders run up to 25 AI agents that earn OUSD for paid tasks
stories.Summary:
Cuy Sheffield, the head of Visa Crypto Labs, announced an experimental wallet upgrade on Sunday, November 22, 2026. This new system allows artificial intelligence agents to earn income rather than just spending money. The project expands upon the Visa CLI command line tool that the company first released in March. Users can now connect their agents to marketplaces like Taskmarket to perform paid work. These agents earn payments in the form of OUSD, which is a dollar stablecoin.

The pilot program is currently invite only and limited to personal Visa card holders residing in the United States. Eligible users must hold cards from US banks, as corporate and prepaid cards are not permitted. Each single account is allowed to run up to 25 agents, and every agent has its own spending limit and signing key. To verify ownership, a user provides card details and a one time code to register the agent in the Trusted Agent Protocol directory. Payouts are handled through the Bridge firm, which issues the OUSD stablecoin backed by cash and US Treasuries.

Cuy Sheffield stated that Visa Crypto Labs believes ordinary people should be able to earn income from the AI economy. Visa clarified that the card verification process is not a sanctions screening or a formal know your customer procedure. The company uses Turnkey for non custodial storage to ensure that the human owner maintains control over all funds and approvals. During an October contest on Taskmarket, ten winners earned 1 OUSD each, with the final settlement occurring in 76 minutes. This specific test involved creative tasks such as the production of 15 second video advertisements.

The system integrates several different layers, including the identity directory from Visa and the stablecoin infrastructure from a Stripe company. This setup allows agents to perform tasks like market research, gaming projects, and surveys on the Taskmarket platform. Taskmarket typically covers the network transaction costs for users and does not charge a platform fee on Tempo. Visa has not yet announced if this pilot will expand to other countries or different types of cards. The company has not provided details regarding who is liable if an agent submits plagiarized work or breaks marketplace rules.

stories.Headline: Viola Fintech's Noam Inbar says distribution is now the real moat in enterprise AI, vertical AI and fintech
stories.Summary:
Noam Inbar, General Partner at Viola Fintech, made the statement in an interview with CTech for its 2027 VC Survey, published on 23.11.26 at 10:17. The interview was conducted by Elihay Vidal and Zachy Hennessey. Inbar said Israel has always won on deep technical moats, but in enterprise AI, vertical AI and fintech the real moat is now distribution. Inbar said Israel has never excelled at distribution. Inbar said developing that commercial muscle is the big challenge and opportunity for the next generation of Israeli companies.

Viola Fintech has $210 million in total assets under management. Its partners and managers are Daniel Tsiddon and Noam Inbar. Its notable portfolio companies are Planck, Rewire, Quinn, Advance, Insurify, Cowbell and True Accord. Its notable exits are Planck and Rewire. Inbar said the fund's strategy is to go earlier than it used to and look for defensible niches, markets that are not purely winner-takes-all.

Inbar said AI has lowered the barrier to building a convincing story or an impressive early product, which forces the fund to be much sharper in its underwriting. Inbar said technical execution is becoming more commoditized, so the fund cares far less about what specific tech unit someone came out of in the army and much more about raw leadership, grit, stamina, risk appetite and integrity. Inbar said heavy capital concentration has made things trickier for a smaller fund like Viola Fintech. Inbar said the fund is not built to compete in hyper-rounds at inflated valuations and does not want to back underfunded copycats or tiny companies destined for a quick acqui-hire. Inbar said cyber is not Inbar's focus and left it to others, though Inbar believes the ecosystem needs to diversify its core strengths.

Inbar said defense tech is too exposed to shifting geopolitics and global attitudes toward Israel to be a pillar to bet everything on. Inbar said foreign appetite is split, with Tier-1 global funds still very active in Israel while mid-tier funds that used to be important syndicate partners are largely sitting out due to inflated valuations and mega-rounds. Inbar said depending solely on a handful of top-tier funds is a fragile position. Inbar said domestic political instability and growing global alienation are real risks to the ability to scale companies from Israel. Inbar said the concentration in startup funding reflects concentration among VCs themselves, with a small handful of massive funds holding a huge share of the capital and funneling it into a small number of companies.

Inbar said those mega-funds have become true market makers, which makes it tough for smaller funds to compete on traditional terms. Inbar said the market is moving way too fast for 12-year fund cycles to make sense anymore. Inbar said locking up capital for over a decade with little to no liquidity is not worth the uncertain upside. Inbar said startups can build and scale with far less capital today, so outside the mega-rounds a growing number of good companies are choosing to bypass VC altogether. Inbar said in the mid-market there will likely be some convergence between VC and private equity, with faster paths to liquidity, different ownership structures and more flexible capital.

Inbar said the exact blueprint is not yet clear because the industry is still figuring out what the next step should look like. Inbar named Quinn, Livez and Advance as startups worth watching this year. Inbar said Quinn lets financial institutions give customers an agentic experience built on each customer's unique financial DNA and a judgement layer. Inbar said Quinn is the only company in its space that is SEC certified, giving it a significant edge, and that it already works with top brands with larger ones underway. Inbar said Livez lets employers and insurers turn every mobile phone into an AI-powered screening tool that spots risk early and acts on it automatically, booking care and navigating benefits for each person.

Inbar said Advance is the financial platform built for how insurance moves money, automating collection, reconciliation and payments and giving agencies and brokers real-time visibility. Inbar said Advance turns premium money from a passive liability into an asset that works for agencies and brokers. Inbar said the US healthcare system is built to treat illness, not to prevent it. Inbar said that when prevention finally happens at scale, employees, employers and insurers all win. Inbar said insurance runs on money that never stops moving, with premiums coming in, carriers getting paid and commissions being split, yet most of the industry still handles that money with spreadsheets, disconnected systems and generic bank accounts where errors stay hidden and balances sit idle.

stories.Headline: Researchers find general purpose AI models provide inconsistent dental treatment recommendations
stories.Summary:
Researchers Santosh R. Patil and Mohmed Isaqali Karobari found that general purpose AI models provide inconsistent dental recommendations. They published these findings in the Digital Dentistry Journal. The study evaluated how four leading AI systems handled repeated clinical prompts. The researchers conducted this benchmarking evaluation to test the repeatability of clinical management. The results showed substantial disparities in how the models responded to standardized dental scenarios.

The study tested GPT-5.2 by OpenAI, Claude Opus 4.1 by Anthropic, Gemini 3.1 Pro by Google, and DeepSeek V4. It used 96 expert-validated scenarios across eight dental disciplines in Chennai, India, at Saveetha Dental College and Hospitals. The researchers collected responses between August 3 and August 10, 2026, using standard consumer web interfaces. GPT-5.2 achieved complete consistency in 86.5 percent of cases, while DeepSeek V4 reached only 27.1 percent. The testing followed TRIPOD-LLM reporting guidelines and received approval from the Scientific Review Board.

The researchers stated that a model's ability to identify expert-approved pathways does not guarantee stability. They noted that individual generations frequently drifted into suboptimal or contraindicated treatment choices. The authors found that identical diagnostic descriptions yielded different therapeutic recommendations across eight independent repetitions. They observed that model architecture and scenario complexity were strong independent predictors of instability. The investigators used a six-item complexity rubric to categorize cases as low, moderate, or high.

The study affected the evaluation of autonomous clinical reasoning tools used for dental decision support. Two blinded clinical evaluators categorized outputs into four tiers from expert-preferred care to potentially unsafe recommendations. They found that DeepSeek V4 had the highest rate of decision drift at 41.7 percent. GPT-5.2 had the lowest decision drift at 5.2 percent of cases. The evaluators also found that some models generated potentially unsafe outputs in several scenario sets.

Sixteen dental specialists authored 124 candidate scenarios to create a representative assessment library. The final 96 scenarios included 32 low, 40 moderate, and 24 high complexity cases. These cases covered domains like endodontics, periodontology, oral surgery, and pediatric dentistry. The specialists used consensus guidelines from bodies like the American Dental Association to set reference standards. The researchers excluded patient-identifiable material and images to ensure each model received identical input parameters.

The study shows that high scenario complexity markedly amplifies the odds of incomplete consistency. All four systems reached the same modal recommendation in 60.4 percent of the evaluated scenarios. The researchers used a multivariable regression model to identify predictors of recommendation instability. The articles do not state how these findings will change current AI deployment in dentistry. They leave open whether future model updates will resolve these stability and safety issues.

Articles.Title: Dental AI Recommendations Vary Widely Across Repeated Clinical Prompts

stories.Headline: Croissant launches Remy AI shopping assistant to recommend luxury brands and plans browser extension rollout
stories.Summary:
Croissant launched Remy, an AI shopping assistant, on Nov. 18, PYMNTS reported, and CEO John Howard told PYMNTS CEO Karen Webster that Croissant plans to add Remy to its browser extension within a couple of weeks. Remy uses what shoppers have bought and whose taste they trust to recommend pieces that fit their wardrobe. Shoppers get a way to discover unfamiliar labels, and brands get a way to reach people who have not searched for them. Croissant is a luxury shopping and resale platform, and Howard co-founded it and serves as CEO. Howard spoke with Webster in a Monday Conversation.

Croissant launched in 2023 with a service that gave shoppers a price for eligible items they were ready to sell. Howard put Croissant's shopper base at 200,000 at the time of the interview. Croissant started with financing, paying brands upfront against future orders, because it had few shoppers of its own at the outset. Howard offered the example of Johanna Ortiz, which plans to open a store in the Hamptons, to explain how Croissant finances merchants. The brand gets cash upfront and fulfills orders on its own site as shoppers check out through Croissant's integration, and Howard said the merchant owes no principal or interest payments.

Howard said the same two requests kept coming from fashion and beauty brands: new customers at a cost of acquisition that makes more sense than ads on the Meta platform or AdWords, and capital to grow their business. Howard calls Croissant "the wallet for luxury," holding resale proceeds, brand offers and purchase rewards of 10% for standard members or 15% for premium members. He said Croissant was testing a version of Remy that could flag similar pieces a shopper already owns while she is looking at a retailer's product page. Howard said he sees more value in helping shoppers decide what to buy and is considering putting Remy directly on partner sites. Howard told Webster that at its core Croissant's mission is more intentional commerce.

Webster, who consigns designer purchases through The RealReal, said she may get her credit right away but is limited as to where she can go shopping. A November 2025 Shorr Packaging survey of 2,013 U.S. consumers found that 75% preferred a full refund over store credit. In its 2026 U.S. fashion retail benchmark, parcelLab found that 14.3% of retailers reviewed offered bonus store credit, such as an extra 10%, when shoppers returned merchandise. Howard said shoppers split roughly evenly between cash and credit worth about 20% more before Croissant switched to credit-only payouts. Shoppers can earn Croissant credit at retailers that do not accept it, then spend with participating brands.

Howard spent eight years as a FinTech investor at KKR, where he watched installment plans, card innovations and same-day shipping make it easier to buy on impulse. During setup, Remy asks shoppers to review the pieces and brands it picked out from their receipts. Shoppers can remove items, add favorites by hand and name the stylists or creators they follow on Instagram, LTK and other platforms. Howard said Remy can suggest labels favored by people who shop similar brands and follow the same creators. Shoppers can refine future recommendations by rating individual picks or editing preferences, such as a rule against prominent logos.

Howard said some users get as far as generating a drop-off code and never send in the item, and those who connected Gmail to get their quotes have already imported receipts Remy can use. Croissant is also paying for ads and creator content, while retail partners are telling their customers they can turn past purchases into credit to spend with them again. Croissant has discussed letting Remy complete purchases. The app also shows a cost-to-own estimate that factors in rewards, available wallet credit and an estimated future buyback value. Croissant's merchant documentation describes either payment after a sale, less its commission, or an upfront purchase of the brand's store credit.

stories.Headline: Anthropic accuses a company of model distillation
stories.Summary:
A user posting as weli said on Hacker News on 24 November 2026 that Anthropic is accusing them and their company of using Anthropic's API for distillation, and that they are not doing so. The poster said their company does not train its own models. The poster said their only usage that could get them flagged is automated regression benchmarks run whenever they change some AI settings. The poster said this is not against Anthropic's policy. The poster said they now have 24 hours to prove they did not distill.

The post was submitted 3 hours before it was read and had 150 points and 93 comments. The poster asked how to prove they are not distilling Anthropic models without breaking their users' privacy. One commenter suggested submitting the same evidence to Claude and asking it whether it is sufficient to make distilling seem unlikely. Another commenter suggested vetting the evidence with a second, adversarial Claude session. A commenter said they skip straight to a second Claude session to review their code. A commenter warned that Anthropic will read their logs and determine the evidence is an attempt to distill.

Commenters said Anthropic will use a Claude agent to review the submission anyway. One commenter suggested migrating to Bedrock via AWS, saying a serious bill brings a dedicated account rep who is an actual human being. A commenter said Bedrock is not zero data retention, linking a Claude support article. A commenter said zero data retention does not necessarily help, because a single prompt can still flag an account. A commenter said AWS still runs automated checks on input and output even when Bedrock is zero data retention.

A commenter said they would not be surprised if Anthropic builds a cumulative risk score that predicts distillation without retaining data. A commenter said a carve-out permits retention of data that fails a risk score for breaking laws or attempting to violate safety. A commenter said dropping whole accounts for bad prompts would become a new attack vector. A commenter asked what the point is of continuing to give money to a company that treats you this way. A commenter said switching providers cannot be done overnight.

A commenter said switching is not as easy as changing an API key, because you must find everything you tested with one model and make sure it still works. A commenter said they set up evals early and are saving 50% or more by routing tasks properly. A commenter said that if quality matters you must re-tweak settings and prompts for whichever model you switch to. A commenter said models do not all work the same or in the same order for all tasks. A commenter asked whether the poster had lost their API keys, suggesting someone stole them and is running distillation.

A commenter said a stolen key would have produced a surprise bill. A commenter said a distillation attack might be hidden in a lot of usage, spread across many keys to avoid discovery. A commenter doubted that most big corporations, let alone startups, audit bills against internal metrics. A commenter said they were doing innocuous work on IRS forms and had a subagent flagged for "reasoning extraction". A commenter said asking the model to look at past session transcripts, export earlier chats as HTML pages or look at tool calls from previous sessions seems to trigger an overeager classifier.

A commenter said competition is needed because being locked out by a single leading AI provider is a death sentence. A commenter disagreed, saying you can get Claude through Bedrock, Vertex or Foundry, or use GPT, Grok, Gemini, GLM, Kimi, Mistral or open weight models. A commenter said proving a negative is hard and suggested telling Anthropic what you have been doing and asking what part is an issue. A commenter said Big Tech refuses to do this, calling the risk department judge, jury and executioner. A commenter said they started building their company after a similar message, realizing they could not depend on one provider.

A commenter said distillation attacks are spread throughout numerous accounts and the poster has likely triggered some detection. A commenter said the best approach is to show the work is part of a real project and to explain any outliers. A commenter said they do not use Anthropic for serious work because normal work has been flagged for cyber security exploits many times. A commenter said they cannot imagine how to prove a negative and does not know if the poster is innocent. A commenter said the situation shows how crazy things would be if the AI provider landscape settled into a monopoly or duopoly.

A commenter said most people will be economically handicapped as a side effect of progress and that controlling the weights and means of inference will accumulate most of that value. A commenter said they were thinking shorter term, when AI still needs human babysitters for most knowledge work. A commenter said on a longer timeline everyone is in trouble without massive upheavals in socioeconomic systems. The articles do not say what evidence the poster submitted or whether Anthropic responded. The articles do not say what happens to the account after the 24 hours. The articles do not give the company's name or Anthropic's statement on the case.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Agentic Commerce Accountability: Who Pays When an AI Agent Buys Wrong
stories.Summary:
Pine Labs launched a research series called The Agentic Fine Print at the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026, and its first edition found that no major payment market in India or Southeast Asia has rules that clearly settle who absorbs the loss when an AI agent spends a customer's money outside its instructions. The research was authored by Ben Charoenwong, an associate professor of finance at INSEAD, and it maps how payment rules across India and five Southeast Asian markets assign responsibility as of 8 September 2026. It examines three failure modes: stolen or compromised credentials, purchases that exceed the customer's instructions, and payment execution errors. According to the research, existing rules across all six markets handle third-party fraud reasonably well but say little about an agent's own mistakes.

The gap falls between contract law, agency rules and payment regulation, none of which was drafted with autonomous software buyers in mind, and Charoenwong proposes a single test for any agentic payment design: whether the customer can prevent, pause and reverse an agent's purchase. He singles out India as the only market in the study where a payment rail explicitly names AI Profiles, yet he concludes that writing AI into a regulation does not automatically settle how it should behave. The National Payments Corporation of India is reported to be developing a Unified Agent Protocol that would let AI agents make small payments on the Unified Payments Interface under pre-set rules, and NPCI chief Dilip Asbe has publicly called for a regulatory framework for agentic payments and said the system needs to trace the instructions and consent a user gave an agent when something goes wrong. A Reserve Bank of India committee has separately recommended a 26-point framework for AI in the financial sector, and UPI processed 24.51 billion transactions worth 29.82 trillion rupees in August 2026 alone.

Andrew Harte, a fintech analyst at BTIG, has argued that the growth of agentic payments depends less on the models and more on industry progress around trust, governance and interoperability, alongside finding cases where buyers are genuinely willing to delegate. Pine Labs is not a neutral observer, since it has its own agentic products in market, including a core-infrastructure partnership with OpenAI announced in February 2026 and the Pine Labs Payment Protocol launched in June 2026, and a clear liability regime would directly benefit their adoption. The company listed on India's NSE and BSE on 14 November 2025 in an offering of about 3,900 crore rupees and reported a loss of roughly 1.45 billion rupees for the 2025 financial year. The company notes that Singapore's IMDA and MAS, and India's DSCI, are each publishing guidance that touches parts of the same questions, and further editions on discoverability, verifiability, payments and interoperability are to follow.

stories.Headline: JPMorgan's Mac Gorain says AI borrowing binge keeps sovereign bond yields elevated
stories.Summary:
Seamus Mac Gorain of JPMorgan Asset Management stated on November 23, 2026, that sovereign bond yields are unlikely to drop significantly. He believes that a massive borrowing binge related to artificial intelligence is currently holding back a potential bond rally. This trend is creating a supply and demand imbalance that keeps yields elevated across global markets. Mac Gorain suggests that the market is currently experiencing one of its worst periods regarding the impact of artificial intelligence.

The current situation requires a fade in AI debt issuance and a retreat in energy prices to ease inflation. Mac Gorain expects the 10-year Treasury yield to remain between 4.5% and 5.25% until these dynamics shift. He notes that the 10-year Treasury yield recently hit 5% for only the second time since 2007. Furthermore, an OECD report predicted that sovereign bond issuance would reach a record 18 trillion dollars in 2026. These factors, combined with central banks reducing their portfolios, continue to cap any significant rally in bonds.

Mac Gorain explained that hyperscalers and other firms are competing for cash to fund the artificial intelligence buildout. He mentioned that this spending exerts upward pressure on inflation and supports the case for higher interest rates. The portfolio manager noted that while governments are spending freely, the bond market is signaling that France must tighten its fiscal policy. He added that the European Central Bank might eventually slow its quantitative tightening due to a change in leadership. He believes that issuance from AI firms may finally start to fall after 2027.

The broader context involves a global selloff where central banks like the Federal Reserve and Bank of England are shrinking balance sheets. This process forces private markets to absorb a larger volume of government and corporate bonds. Mac Gorain is currently avoiding French debt in favor of Italian debt following a surge in the French-German spread. He suggests that the market will remain volatile until productivity gains from artificial intelligence are more widely felt. Future movements depend on whether governments can rein in borrowing or if central bank policies shift.

stories.Headline: Researchers link honorary authorship and hidden AI writing to misrepresented credit in science
stories.Summary:
Researchers linked honorary authorship and hidden artificial intelligence writing to misrepresented credit in science, according to an analysis published in the Hellenic Journal of Cardiology. The authors Panos Macheras and Panos E. Vardas wrote the analysis. The analysis was published on 23 November 2026, according to bioengineer.org. The article says both practices misrepresent genuine scholarly input and undermine accountability across research disciplines. The article says the two practices emerged from different technological eras but both obscure who actually performed the intellectual work.

The analysis says authorship serves as a record of intellectual contribution and a foundation for recognition, career advancement and responsibility for published findings. It says honorary or cosmetic authorship rose widely in the late twentieth century in multi-investigator biomedical papers as teams expanded and academic competition accelerated. It says Moulopoulos and colleagues argued in 1983 that journals must define individual roles, including the initial idea, study design, data collection, analysis and manuscript drafting. It says the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors set criteria requiring substantial contributions to conception or design, participation in writing or critical revision, approval of the final manuscript and formal accountability. It says many leading journals require contributorship statements but the requirement is not universal and can be inaccurate or misleading.

The authors said honorary authorship and undisclosed artificial intelligence writing both misrepresent genuine scholarly input. They said both practices are tied to academic pressures, with career advancement and research funding tied to publication metrics that reward volume over genuine scholarly effort. They said addressing the challenges requires institutions and publishers to mandate detailed contributorship statements, enforce full transparency about artificial intelligence assistance and reform evaluation criteria to reward intellectual quality and authentic participation. They disclosed in their own paper that their graphical abstract was generated with the assistance of the ChatGPT large language model. They said automated algorithms cannot accept legal or ethical responsibility for scientific findings.

The article says John Ioannidis documented that improper authorship practices persist among highly productive investigators in fields such as cardiology. It says the academic community collectively created the fictitious scientist Camille Noûs to highlight unresolved concerns over credit and responsibility. It says editorial organizations and publishers have established consensus rules barring artificial intelligence systems from being listed as authors. It says publishers increasingly mandate explicit disclosure whenever artificial intelligence assists in preparing a manuscript. It says junior researchers often feel compelled to add superiors to protect their institutional standing, while department heads, senior researchers and peripheral colleagues are added to acknowledge hierarchy, enhance prestige or repay professional favors.

The article says the growth of collaborative research, driven by complex laboratory experiments, interdisciplinary methodologies and extensive datasets requiring multi-institutional cooperation, created systemic opportunities for authorship inflation. It says honorary authorship dilutes the value of authorship as a marker of intellectual engagement and makes it difficult to identify who actually conducted the study. It says researchers credited without meaningful involvement may be unable or unwilling to assume responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of published work. It says large language models can help non-native English speakers improve clarity and grammar and help investigators organize concepts, evaluate phrasing and summarize background literature. It says unchecked language generation risks introducing inaccurate assertions, fabricated references and misleading interpretations, and ease of producing prose may reduce scrutiny during manuscript preparation.

The article says formal contributorship requirements can be undermined by inaccurate declarations where implemented. It says the scientific community might have mitigated such distortions by implementing verifiable systems to evaluate contributions. It says the expanding sophistication of generative tools raises critical questions about intellectual ownership and attribution. It says the article's account of artificial intelligence ends where the true authorship of text generated in substantial portions becomes unclear. More to follow.

stories.Headline: OpenAI removes the Sora 2 API and leaves developers to rebuild integrations without a replacement model
stories.Summary:
OpenAI shut down the Sora 2 API on September 24, 2026, which caused every product and plugin built on the model to return errors. This event followed a two stage wind down that began on March 24, 2026, when the company announced the discontinuation of Sora and sent deprecation notices to developers. The consumer website and application for the tool closed on April 26, while the API remained active for five more months. On the final date in September, OpenAI removed the Videos API along with every version of the Sora 2 and Sora 2 Pro models.

The shutdown requires teams that relied on these tools to choose new providers and rebuild their integrations from scratch. This change affects how brands and agencies handle concepting, localisation, and social cut downs, as they no longer have access to the Sora 2 pipeline. Because OpenAI named no replacement model and provided no upgrade path, users face significant dependency and consistency risks. These teams must now rewrite their integrations and retest outputs to ensure they meet broadcast specifications and regional advertising rules.

The team at Cape.io expressed concern over what happens to marketing campaigns when the underlying tools simply disappear from the market. They stated that the Sora 2 shutdown serves as a wake up call for those who wired AI video into their production workflows. The group argued that a model agnostic validation layer is necessary to check outputs regardless of which tool produced them. They suggested that keeping a quality bar outside of any single generative tool makes swapping technology a manageable change rather than a crisis.

The current AI landscape is shifting rapidly, and the authors claim that tools will continue to arrive and leave faster than campaign cycles. Creative and media teams are encouraged to map their dependencies and avoid single points of failure for critical production tasks. They should archive source files and prompts so that assets can be recreated on different models if another shutdown occurs. The goal is to build workflows that do not depend on any single model to maintain brand consistency and delivery schedules.

stories.Headline: Nio CEO says AI boom drives memory chip prices up fivefold
stories.Summary:
Nio Founder and Chief Executive Officer William Li spoke at a user event in Changzhou on Saturday. He stated that the artificial intelligence boom has pushed memory chip prices up fivefold. This cost shock occurred between the first and second quarters of the current year. Li compared this sudden price spike to the lithium price surge of 2022. He noted that nobody saw this coming at the end of last year.

The cost increase is about 14,000 yuan per car, which is roughly 2,100 dollars. Li said costs would rise another 2,000 to 3,000 yuan in the second half of the year. This takes the total increase to between 16,000 and 17,000 yuan, or 2,400 to 2,500 dollars. Memory accounted for about 10,000 yuan of that total cost increase. He noted that 1.5 billion yuan is gone every quarter.

William Li said AI data centers are taking all the demand and all the supply. He claimed that carmakers cannot outbid these data centers for memory chips. Li stated that the industry has taken several blows from the AI boom. He said that if suppliers provide chips at all, they are doing a favor. He noted that some buyers pay five to eight times the price for circuit boards.

The cost shock falls hardest on the most intelligent cars because they use the most memory. Li said that cars using little memory are hit less by these price increases. He claimed that the auto industry is the biggest application industry for artificial intelligence. He stated that AI value creation in autos is 1.2 trillion dollars. He noted that the global auto industry is 7 trillion to 9 trillion dollars.

Li said the squeeze extends to copper, aluminum, circuit boards, and some basic chips. He noted that capital markets chased AI concepts in the first half of the year. This shift caused other industries, including autos, to lose out on finite liquidity. He also cited a war for talent involving embodied AI startups and large model companies. He compared the current situation to the 2022 lithium carbonate price surge in China.

Li said the impact on the auto industry will last about two more years. He believes memory and bulk material prices should fall somewhat by 2028. Nio will report third quarter results on December 1 to cover the second half. The company plans to unveil NWM 3.0 at a technology day on November 25. The articles leave open how Nio will manage these costs to protect margins.

stories.Headline: Zurich and St Gallen study finds AI risks could exceed private insurance capacity
stories.Summary:
A joint study by Zurich Insurance Group and the University of St. Gallen, developed as part of the Zurich AI Lab and published on 23 November 2026, concludes that artificial intelligence can create new risks and significantly amplify existing dangers, and that in the extreme case losses could exceed the capacity of the private insurance market. The report, titled "The AI Resilience Challenge," is based on interviews with 50 experts, including 36 Zurich executives and specialists and 14 external experts, conducted between July and September 2026. The authors see a key challenge in the growing concentration among a few technology providers, since companies using different AI applications can still depend on the same underlying models, cloud infrastructures or data sources. As an example of the consequences of technological dependencies, the study points to the global IT outage in 2024, when a faulty software update from a cybersecurity provider disabled around 8.5 million devices and affected banks, airlines and hospitals, although the incident was not directly related to AI.

The study distinguishes four categories of AI risk, ranging from limited and understandable losses that existing insurance products can in principle cover, through risks with identifiable causes that can hit numerous companies at once, to difficult-to-understand errors where liability or decision pathways remain unclear, and finally systemic risks whose scale and causes can hardly be determined in advance. It notes that matters become especially critical when AI systems independently conclude contracts, purchase services or execute transactions, because there is still insufficient experience regarding the frequency and extent of possible losses in such autonomous applications. Insurance works especially well when risks are measurable, losses are limited and individual events are largely independent of one another, and AI can undermine these conditions at the same time, so that risks can no longer be spread as effectively across a large portfolio when many policyholders depend on the same technologies or similar errors occur. As possible early warning signs the study cites rising premiums, lower coverage limits, additional exclusions and higher requirements for risk documentation, which it describes as possible developments rather than already proven general changes in insurance terms.

Zurich CEO Mario Greco and HSG professor Karolin Frankenberger emphasize in the foreword that AI risks cannot be completely ruled out, and that what matters is to identify errors in time, limit their spread and keep the consequences manageable. The study recommends that companies more closely track their AI applications and technological dependencies, clearly define responsibilities, and create ways to shut down critical systems in the event of malfunctions or switch to alternatives. Insurers, for their part, should increasingly examine how companies actually use AI and what shared risks are building up in their portfolios as a result. In the case of especially large systemic losses, the authors believe public-private solutions may be required, citing existing models for covering natural catastrophes and terrorism risks as general examples.

stories.Headline: ILO reports on AI use and governance risks in China's social security administration
stories.Summary:
The International Labour Organization published a report on November 19, 2026, regarding the use of artificial intelligence within China's social security administration. This study, titled From digital to intelligent social security administration, was created in collaboration with the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security. The research documents how AI is being used to improve risk management, administrative efficiency, and the delivery of services. It examines 45 specific cases across 15 provincial-level regions to highlight both the benefits and the governance risks.

The report finds that 47 percent of these cases focus on service delivery, while 33 percent support operations and 20 percent involve decision support. These applications include automated review systems, virtual assistants, and AI-powered chatbots to handle public needs. In Beijing's Haidian District, automated systems processed over 70,000 transactions in 2024, which reportedly improved efficiency by more than 80 percent. By July 2025, AI-assisted systems in Guangdong Province processed over seven million cases across 34 services, reducing manual workloads by more than 640,000 staff hours.

The International Labour Organization identified risks regarding algorithmic bias, accountability, personal data protection, and the accuracy of knowledge systems. The organization recommends implementing stronger data governance, workforce training, and safeguards to ensure that AI supports rather than replaces human decisions. They specifically mentioned the need for oversight in work injury assessments and benefit eligibility. The group also called for the maintenance of offline services to prevent the exclusion of persons with disabilities, older people, and others facing digital barriers.

stories.Headline: Review authors find retinal AI models for systemic disease lack clinical validation
stories.Summary:
A critical review by A. Pavithra and V. Bhanumathi, published in Discover Imaging on November 23, 2026, evaluated artificial intelligence models trained to predict systemic diseases from retinal images. The review examined machine learning, deep learning and multimodal algorithms that use the eye's microvascular window to detect chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular disease and diabetes mellitus. Published studies consistently showed positive discriminatory performance when identifying systemic disorders from non-invasive ocular scans. However, reported performance indicators varied dramatically across individual works. Discrepancies in diagnostic metrics, including the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, sensitivity and specificity, stemmed from widespread heterogeneity in study cohorts.

The review warned that current predictive figures cannot be legitimately pooled or used to establish a definitive methodological hierarchy. It highlighted that substantial translational hurdles must be resolved before retinal artificial intelligence can transition into clinical practice. The authors cautioned that observed retinal abnormalities, including altered arteriolar and venular caliber, microaneurysms and localized retinopathy, should be interpreted as surrogate phenotypic traits associated with systemic vascular strain. They stressed a vital distinction between automated diabetic retinopathy grading and true de novo diabetes prediction. The review also emphasized that apparent performance gains in multimodal models cannot be credited entirely to retinal imaging.

The authors said multimodal models, which fuse retinal image representations with structured clinical variables such as patient age, blood pressure, lipid profiles and laboratory chemistry, consistently report superior predictive accuracy compared to models relying solely on fundus photographs. They said clinical variables such as chronological age, glycemic control or baseline blood pressure already carry immense prognostic power for chronic vascular and metabolic conditions. Without directly benchmarking a multimodal architecture against an identical baseline model trained exclusively on structured clinical data, the authors said, researchers cannot determine whether retinal imaging adds meaningful, independent prognostic value. They said demonstrating true clinical utility requires rigorous comparative testing to isolate incremental diagnostic contributions directly attributable to ocular biomarkers. The authors also identified widespread methodological vulnerabilities across published literature, including dataset bias, data leakage and uncontrolled confounding.

Research by Charumathi Sabanayagam and colleagues showed that integrating retinal features with routine clinical risk factors improves chronic kidney disease detection over ocular scans alone. Deep learning systems trained by Kang Zhang and colleagues across multi-center cohorts confirmed automated models reliably identify renal impairment across diverse populations. Explorations by Eugene Yu-Chuan Kang and colleagues indicated that microvascular alterations signal early functional renal impairment before overt pathology manifests. Youngmin Bhak and colleagues established that combining fundus photographs with urine dipsticks improves diagnostic precision, while Songyang An and colleagues underscored that algorithmic accuracy fluctuates heavily depending on how glomerular filtration rate thresholds are operationalized. Karma M. Fathalla led comparative investigations demonstrating that automated retinal vessel analysis could estimate cardiovascular risk with discriminatory capability comparable to established clinical calculators like the Framingham Risk Score and QRISK.

The review outlined how conditions like hypertension, metabolic syndrome and vascular deterioration trigger shared pathophysiological cascades, including endothelial dysfunction, chronic low-grade inflammation, oxidative stress and impaired vascular autoregulation. Within both the ocular fundus and the renal parenchyma, these injurious processes induce microvascular remodeling, basement membrane thickening, luminal narrowing and compromised perfusion. The fundamental rationale supporting image-based systemic disease prediction lies in shared anatomical and physiological characteristics linking retinal microvasculature to distant organ systems, particularly the kidneys and heart. Because the small vessels of the retina can be directly visualized through fundus photography and optical coherence tomography, they provide a measurable reflection of systemic vascular integrity without surgical intervention. Cohorts such as the UK Biobank, the Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Diseases, the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study and the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis supply vital biochemistry data, including serum creatinine, glycated hemoglobin, lipid panels, blood pressure measurements and longitudinal diagnostic codes.

The review stated that widely utilized public benchmarking archives such as EyePACS, APTOS 2019 and Messidor were curated exclusively for diabetic retinopathy detection and entirely lack linked cardiovascular or renal health indicators. It noted that foundational image segmentation datasets like DRIVE and STARE are restricted to vessel tracing tasks. The authors emphasized that ophthalmic sets cannot substitute for clinically characterized population cohorts when evaluating systemic disease risk. Most evaluated models were constructed using retrospective, single-center or ethnically homogeneous cohorts. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Retinal Artificial Intelligence Predicts Systemic Disease Risk but Lacks Clinical Validation

stories.Headline: Dentsu reports 82 per cent of CMOs plan to raise analogue spending as brands turn to puppets and craft
stories.Summary:
Dentsu's annual CMO Report found that 82 per cent of CMOs plan to increase their analogue investments, creative.salon reported on 23 November 2026. The report was covered in an article by Cerys Holliday. Dentsu's 2026 trends report found that over half of respondents across all ages agreed with the statement, "I'm tired of the algorithm recommending more and more of the same". The article reported that Google searches for "analogue hobbies" increased by 160 per cent this year alone. The article said 45 per cent of Gen Z are interested in using devices like brick phones and MP3 players.

The article said nearly three in four Gen Z punish brands that use AI. Pats McDonald, global chief strategy officer at Dentsu Creative, said customers are very drawn to analogue and craft at the moment. McDonald said people really want things that are handwritten and handcrafted. McDonald said it almost feels like the ultimate luxury is something someone has made and touched with their hands. Dan Watts, CCO at Pablo, said AI is another tool to use.

Watts said that if you use AI with no idea, it is really shit. Watts said that if you use it as a tool, it can be potentially useful and interesting. Watts said he is seeing a real backlash, particularly with younger people. Watts said his kids kick off whenever he uses AI, Claude, anything like that. Watts said you look at comments on anything AI-based and it is people going, "Why are you using AI?"

Ruairi Curran, executive strategy director at Gravity Road, said he is slightly sceptical of the idea that there is an analogue resurgence. Curran said we have been talking about analogue as a reaction to digital, and authenticity as a cultural value, for at least 15 years. Curran said what AI has changed is the scale and economics of the alternative. Curran said that now that AI transparency and disclosure are becoming real issues, we are inevitably becoming even more conscious of how things are made.

Louise Wardle, global CMO at Subway, said AI gives you infinite versions of creativity, whereas with out of home you need to be confident to put stuff out there. The article cited Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, which it said dominated the water cooler moment this summer. The article said Nolan committed to filmmaking without CGI. The article said the stop-motion film Wildwood took 16 years to make entirely, and 231 puppets were created for the film.

The article said the puppets include details such as silicone to emulate muscle movement. The article cited the furore around Dior's "hand drawn" Christmas campaign and its possible use of AI. The article cited TWIX's Two Is More Than One instalment with two ventriloquist puppets singing to Nelly and Kelly Rowland's Dilemma, by adam&eve\TBWA. The article said Columbia Sportswear asked customers to use a fax machine to reach out for a free fleece and received over 4,000 faxes in under 36 hours.

The article cited Confused.com's puppets by Leo UK, made by Andy Biddle and Adeena Grubb. The article cited LNER's mascot Eleanor with McCann and Morrison's Festive Spirit Christmas ad, which used animatronics for the bears. The article said Ace of Hearts brought Lebara's capybara mascot to life in November with director Jeff Low using hand-made stop-motion animation. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Copper prices drop below 12,000 dollars as AI demand uncertainty grows
stories.Summary:
Copper prices fell below 12,000 dollars per tonne on the London Metal Exchange on Monday, November 23, 2026. This price drop happened for the first time since March amid uncertainty over demand in the artificial intelligence sector. The metal briefly dipped below that mark before it rebounded to 12,160 dollars per tonne at 9.18am UAE time. This decline followed a nine per cent tumble last week, which was the third biggest weekly drop in a decade. The price movement occurred during a broader sell-off of stocks related to artificial intelligence.

The metal is used widely in energy infrastructure and the construction of data centres. Copper hit a record high of 14,694 dollars per tonne in September, beating a January record of 14,527.50 dollars. A stronger US dollar is making the metal more expensive for buyers who use currencies other than the greenback. Higher interest rate expectations and possible Federal Reserve rate increases next month are driving the stronger US dollar. Democratic victories in US midterm elections have also raised expectations of tighter AI regulations and more data-centre scrutiny.

Ole Hansen, the head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank, said the Democratic sweep raised concerns about future investment. He stated that public resistance to costs, environmental impact, and electricity requirements for data centres has increased market uncertainty. Tony Sage, chief executive of Critical Metals, said investors are unwinding bullish positions that linked copper to data-centre growth. Sage noted that rising expectations for Federal Reserve rate increases have added pressure by raising the cost of holding metal. He also mentioned that these factors are weighing on broader risk sentiment.

Investors cast doubts regarding the sustainability of AI spending, which caused major US indexes to end the week lower. These indexes included the Nasdaq Composite, the Dow Jones Industrial Average, and the S&P 500. Anthropic saw its stock tumble 8.5 per cent to 88.19 dollars on Friday despite a record 81.3 billion dollar IPO. This initial public offering was claimed to be the largest in history. Buyers using currencies other than the US dollar are affected by the rising cost of the greenback-priced metal.

Copper is regarded as an essential component for electrification, grid expansion, electric vehicles, and building artificial intelligence. The US Geological Survey added the metal to its critical minerals list last year. China is the largest consumer of refined copper and accounts for well over half of all global use. The International Monetary Fund trimmed its economic growth projection for China this year by 0.1 percentage point to 4.5 per cent. China faces challenges in traditional copper-consuming sectors, specifically in construction and property.

Near-term prices are likely to remain sensitive to Federal Reserve policy signals, the US dollar, and AI investment sentiment. Tony Sage believes the underlying supply-demand balance should reassert itself once current positioning and macro pressures ease. He suggests this balance will support a firmer tone for the metal over the medium term. The articles do not state when the Federal Reserve will announce its next interest rate decision. They also leave open the specific nature of the expected tighter AI regulations.
