stories.Headline: Cloud-native survey finds virtual machines host 53 per cent of production applications
stories.Summary:
New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and Linux Foundation Research finds that virtual machines host an average of 53 per cent of production applications in cloud-native environments. The survey was conducted in September 2026 and included 492 cloud-native practitioners and technology leaders. The findings challenge previous assumptions that containers would replace virtual machines. The research shows that organisations are increasingly combining virtual machines and containers to meet different application and security requirements.

Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 47 per cent cited security and isolation as a contributing factor, and 34 per cent identified AI and agentic workloads. MicroVM sandboxing adoption is expected to grow from 20 per cent current use to 30 per cent planned use, while confidential computing is expected to rise from 12 per cent to 26 per cent. Some 61 per cent of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated. Among respondents using VMs, 8 per cent reported using KubeVirt, a CNCF project that allows virtual machines to be managed through Kubernetes resources and APIs.

The research indicates that Kubernetes and containers remain important but are not the sole execution model for every workload. Virtual machines offer a stronger isolation boundary than conventional containers, which share the host operating system kernel. This isolation is described as crucial as AI agents increasingly generate and execute code that interacts with tools and external systems. Managing different workload types is increasingly becoming a shared platform engineering responsibility.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches Pando backend to scale Git for concurrent coding agents
stories.Summary:
OpenAI introduced Pando, a new backend designed to scale Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads, according to the company, and it now powers all development in OpenAI's monorepo. The system achieves nearly 80 per cent lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches. Pando went into production in April 2026 and serves nearly a petabyte of Git data daily in that monorepo. OpenAI attributes the increased load to Codex-driven development, where each push can trigger multiple CI jobs that all fetch the same history.

Rather than replacing Git's client and protocol, OpenAI changed how the backend coordinates reference updates and stores and transfers objects. On a push, Pando validates the incoming packfile as it streams to immutable blob storage without unpacking it, and a metadata transaction records the reference version and atomically updates the reference pointer. Updates to unrelated references can proceed independently, while updates to the same reference still require coordination, which OpenAI calls causal consistency with serialisable updates to individual references and read-your-own-write consistency. Fetching multiple branches will not provide a repository-wide snapshot, and clients may see different branch versions during concurrent updates, a trade-off that removes a shared coordination point for unrelated pushes. By default, when a client pushes a new feature branch, the server advertises only a designated trunk branch as its base, and repeated or stacked branch pushes can resend objects outside trunk, trading some bandwidth for reusable packs.

For fetches, Pando maps client commits to reference versions and selects appropriate stored packs, and Git's packfile-uri capability lets the server return download links instead of generating a bespoke pack. Express, a regional pack-delivery cache, serves these downloads, and OpenAI reports cache-hit rates exceeding 99 per cent, while clone and fetch operations saturated 10 Gbps network links in tests. Background compaction groups packs into larger, geometrically sized covers resembling compaction in a log-structured merge-tree, and Pando keeps packs at every level so clients with different histories can still be served. The design contrasts with Anthropic's Scion, which replaces Git's underlying model with changesets and moves repository operations server-side, with clients retrieving missing immutable trees and blobs instead of negotiating Git packfiles. Both systems use immutable data and regional caches to reduce repeated computation, but Pando preserves Git's object model and client-side workflows while Scion assumes an online client and moves repository operations to a dedicated service.

Git compatibility did not eliminate migration work for OpenAI, which deployed Pando as a read- and write-through proxy, moved clients in phases, and migrated hundreds of integrations. OpenAI also distributed its own Git build, which supports parallel downloading and indexing of independent packs, and some client improvements are already upstream, with others available in its public repository. OpenAI reports on push latency, while Anthropic reports checkout speedups and infrastructure reductions for its own system.

stories.Headline: Meta AI and Gemini give more complete cosmetic dental guidance than ChatGPT
stories.Summary:
Researchers found that Meta AI and Google's Gemini produced significantly more complete, actionable and safely framed responses than OpenAI's ChatGPT when answering patient questions about minimally invasive cosmetic dental treatments. The comparative observational study was published in The Saudi Dental Journal. The investigation assessed 126 conversational responses generated across the three platforms to forty-two authentic questions. The questions covered tooth whitening, resin infiltration, composite bonding and porcelain veneers. The authors emphasized that direct professional dental supervision remains indispensable.

The study evaluated the free consumer web interfaces of ChatGPT, Gemini and Meta AI between May 12 and May 15, 2026. Newly created user accounts operated under default platform settings, with personalization, historical memory tracking and customized behavioral preferences disabled. Each of the forty-two standardized questions was submitted within a completely isolated browser session. The benchmark questions were harvested from six publicly accessible online repositories, including Reddit's r/askdentists community, Google People Also Ask, Quora, YouTube, Instagram and dental clinic frequently asked questions pages. The initial retrieval yielded 426 inquiries, which were refined into forty-two standardized questions.

The authors said that because no platform consistently satisfied all benchmarks for comprehensive, safe and accessible guidance, direct professional dental supervision remains indispensable. They stressed that an empathetic tone cannot substitute for comprehensive clinical judgment. They said direct professional consultation remains indispensable to prevent misinformed, irreversible aesthetic dental decisions. The authors noted that modest initial concordance underscored the subjective complexity of qualitative clinical evaluations. They reported findings based on the public consumer endpoints accessible during the standardized testing window rather than inferred backend model versions.

The Modified DISCERN instrument produced mean total scores of 6.26 for ChatGPT, 7.63 for Gemini and 8.19 for Meta AI. All three platforms maintained high baseline accuracy scores, and patient-centeredness scores clustered between 4.50 and 4.70 out of five. None of the evaluated platforms satisfied established health literacy thresholds, with every system exceeding recommended reading grade levels. None met the recommended Grade 8 reading threshold established for patient health literature. The study was confined to four elective procedures evaluated in English, without direct assessment by lay consumers or patients.

The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into everyday life has reshaped how the public seeks healthcare information. In aesthetic dentistry, this transition coincides with surging public interest in elective cosmetic procedures. Platforms such as ChatGPT, which accumulated over 700 million users by late 2025, alongside Gemini and Meta AI, now routinely serve as preliminary diagnostic sounding boards for prospective patients. Prior investigations examined chatbot performance in implantology, periodontology and dental traumatology. The comparative performance of Meta AI remained largely unexplored in aesthetic dentistry.

The research did not assess longitudinal stability across repeated identical queries. It did not investigate whether specialized prompt engineering or fine-tuned clinical parameters could improve performance. Because consumer training datasets remain proprietary, potential exposure of the models to public online sources from which benchmark questions were derived could not be verified. Raw query transcripts were not archived prior to question consolidation. The findings capture a temporal snapshot based on unguided, single-iteration queries conducted in May 2026.

stories.Headline: Google cuts 2027 Broadcom TPU shipments by about 1M units and plans more MediaTek chips, Kuo says
stories.Summary:
Google has reduced its planned 2027 shipments of Broadcom-designed AI chips while preparing to increase shipments of a MediaTek-designed alternative, according to technology supply-chain analyst Ming-Chi Kuo. The report was published on November 20, 2026, based on Kuo's latest industry survey rather than an official Google announcement. Kuo said Google had cut planned 2027 shipments of its Broadcom-designed TPU 8i series by approximately 1 million units. That reduction represents roughly 20 percent of the series' previously expected shipment volume, implying a drop from about 5 million chips to 4 million. Most of the cuts affect the higher-priced 8i Max, also known as Whalefish, according to Kuo.

The reported changes concern 2027 shipments, and Kuo's post did not provide pricing, contract terms, or an estimate of the financial effect on Broadcom. Kuo also reported that Google plans to increase 2027 shipments of the MediaTek-designed TPU 8t series, though the details remain unsettled. The post did not specify the size of that increase, leaving it unclear whether additional 8t shipments would fully offset the reduction in the 8i family. Broadcom shares were down 8.9 percent on the day amid broad-based selling across the semiconductor sector. The decline should not be attributed solely to the reported shipment changes, according to the article.

Kuo, an analyst at TF International Securities best known for his technology supply-chain research, linked the change to Google's prioritization of frontier model development. According to his post, Google has repeatedly emphasized in recent months that frontier development receives first call on available computing resources. He characterized the changing TPU shipment mix as an adjustment to that priority amid tight supply chains and data-center power constraints. Kuo's post did not provide enough technical or economic detail to establish exactly why Google would favor additional 8t shipments over the affected 8i models. The reported changes suggest Google is adjusting the mix of its custom AI processors, not necessarily pulling back on its broader AI ambitions.

For investors, the report is directionally unfavorable for expectations surrounding Broadcom's Google TPU business and potentially favorable for MediaTek's role in Google's chip plans. It does not, however, establish the eventual revenue impact for either company. The report adds uncertainty around Broadcom's future Google-related revenue as investors reassess expectations for AI-chip suppliers. Kuo's findings point to a potential reshuffling within Google's AI-chip supply chain, not clear evidence of a retreat from AI investment. The distinction matters because a reduction in one chip family does not automatically mean Google expects less overall demand for AI computing.

TPUs, or Tensor Processing Units, are Google's custom processors for AI workloads. The reported changes could instead reflect a decision to allocate scarce manufacturing capacity, infrastructure, and electricity differently. Kuo based the report on an industry survey rather than an official Google announcement. With the shipment changes concerning 2027, the outlook remains subject to revisions. The concentration of cuts on the higher-priced 8i Max could make the potential revenue impact more significant than the unit reduction alone suggests.

The key questions are how much Google ultimately increases its MediaTek-designed chip orders, whether those gains offset the Broadcom-designed reductions, and what the final mix means for supplier revenue. Kuo's post did not provide enough technical or economic detail to establish the eventual revenue impact for either company. The report leaves open whether additional 8t shipments would fully offset the reduction in the 8i family. The outlook remains subject to revisions because the shipment changes concern 2027. For now, the report adds uncertainty around Broadcom's future Google-related revenue.

stories.Headline: Virginia lawyers discuss how AI affects hourly billing
stories.Summary:
The Supreme Court of Virginia approved Legal Ethics Opinion 1901 on Nov. 24, 2025, addressing reasonable fees when generative artificial intelligence is used, according to an article by Jason Boleman published Nov. 23, 2026. The opinion responds to concerns over how generative AI could impact traditional billing practices in Virginia. LEO 1901 reiterates that a lawyer shall charge reasonable fees under Rule 1.5 of the Virginia Rules of Professional Conduct. The opinion offers guidance for attorneys looking to shift from the traditional time-based billing structure. It states that time-based billing can only be based on the actual time spent on a task.

LEO 1901 states that Rule 1.5 does not equate reduced time with proportionally reduced fees when a lawyer uses generative AI or other productivity-enhancing tools. The opinion says such an approach would fail to account for the investment lawyers make in developing AI expertise and the continuing value of their professional judgment. It states that the skill requisite to perform the legal service properly might actually increase, as effective AI use could require specialized knowledge to prompt, verify, supplement and integrate AI outputs. LEO 1901 departs from guidance from other states and the American Bar Association, which stated in a formal opinion in 2024 that a flat fee may be unreasonable if a generative AI tool allowed the attorney to complete the task quicker. The Virginia opinion concluded that it is not automatically unreasonable for the same non-hourly fee to be charged if AI is used to assist an output.

Tricia Dunlap, founder and managing partner of Dunlap Law in Richmond, is a longtime proponent of alternative billing structures and said AI has transformed her firm for the better. Dunlap said that for decades small businesses went without preventive legal counsel because hourly billing made it unaffordable, and that AI and flat fees changed that. She has pivoted her firm from time-based billing to value-based billing, setting flat fees for work while ensuring rates are reasonable and ethical. Dunlap said her firm has become more profitable and has increased its services, and that it helped a small business uncover significant legal risks through a flat-fee engagement that traditional billing would have priced beyond its reach. Dunlap Law uses a proprietary AI-powered platform called DLOS that she said has helped increase collections by 25% and cut costs by 34%.

Richmond attorney Tim Bechen, a principal at Woods Rogers, said in his experience he has seen an increase in billable hours rather than time saved. Bechen credited that to an uptick in AI use by clients, saying clients now ask more complex questions and that AI does not have a lot of discernment. He estimated that sometimes his work will double in cost due to time spent addressing additional concerns brought forward by a client consulting generative AI platforms, and said he has had conversations explaining that a normally $10,000 project had become a $20,000 project. Bechen, who serves on Woods Rogers' AI committee, said he has noted an uptick in litigation in pro se third parties using AI and demand letters that are clearly AI-generated. He said traditional time-based billing remains the industry standard and that fears of the death of the billable hour have been greatly overexaggerated, going back to when he started practicing in 2000.

Bechen said the reason the billable hour exists is that it is a great way for the client and the attorney to know they are both getting a fair deal. He added that in flat-fee billing, concerns could arise around clients believing they are not getting a fair and equitable rate due to time saved by AI usage. Bechen said use of AI tools allows attorneys to focus on the more important issues versus the mundane stuff, starting from second base because AI gives them the concept. He cautioned that attorneys spend the same amount of time on tasks to fact-check AI outputs and engage in deeper analysis. Bechen said the idea of AI taking over the legal profession is completely blown out of proportion, and that AI is always going to be an unpaid assistant, not a new first-year associate but an unlicensed paralegal that can give a first draft.

Dunlap is described as a frequent speaker on AI and legal ethics, and Bechen uses hourly billing in his practice at Woods Rogers. LEO 1901 states that the opinions it cites fail to appreciate the value of advancing technology and the reaction of the legal markets to that technology. The opinion states that while over time the market rate might drop based on dramatic improvements in efficiency, Rule 1.5 should not require the lawyer to surrender any benefit from the efficiency gains if clients continue to receive value from the lawyer's output. The article reports that one year after the opinion, attorneys report varying degrees of implementing alternative fee structures. The article leaves open how widely alternative fee structures will spread among Virginia attorneys.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Wells Fargo warns customers they use AI agents at their own risk as US banks tighten agent controls
stories.Summary:
Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers about AI agents starting on Tuesday, according to WIRED. The bank's new terms warn that any use of an AI Agent is at the user's own risk, the article said. The article reported that multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings as the end of the year approaches. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with customer credentials, and that same day Bank of America warned its customers not to share login information with agents, the article said.

Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents, according to the article. The article said AI agents automate online tasks and click on a user's behalf, and that the technology remains nascent even as a growing subset of power users latched onto personal bots this year. It said some early adopters publicly embarrassed themselves when agents made major mistakes, such as posting bank details for everyone at work to see. The article said the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, but US-based banking institutions are already tired of third-party AI agents.

It also said Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent from making purchases on its platform, and United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on a customer's behalf. Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University, told the article that consumers authorize goals rather than every click, and said she does not expect the policy moves by financial institutions to scare off early adopters already using the tools daily. Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst, said all of the data shows most people do not even know what agents are, much less use them, and said banks are fundamentally risk-averse, so proactive measures make sense even if most agentic issues remain edge cases. Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia, said people are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper, and described banks as locking the door to outside agents while building their own.

The article said American Express announced that some agentic mistakes may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if a customer cannot get money back from the original retailer. The article said banks are all-in on first-party tools, noting that users have interacted with Wells Fargo's generative AI question tool over a billion times, that Bank of America revamped its EricaAssist agent this year to help employees, and that Citigroup launched an internal development platform centered on agents. Kodali said buying on Amazon or Walmart is not difficult and that most of those transactions do not need an agent. The article did not say what happens next beyond the terms taking effect.

stories.Headline: Clinicians must critically assess AI outputs at each decision stage to ensure safe care
stories.Summary:
A perspective published in Discover Artificial Intelligence on the safe clinical use of artificial intelligence argues that safety may depend less on how well a model performs and more on whether clinicians can evaluate what it produces. The authors are Ryan W. Hunton, Tama The and Jonathan Ilgen, and the article is titled The arc of uncertainty across clinicians' interactions with AI, published in volume 6, issue 1, as Article 1936, with DOI 10.1007/s44163-026-02851-3. The piece was reported by Blake Davidson on November 21, 2026, through Scienmag, and carried by bioengineer.org the same day. The authors describe large language models as increasingly used across clinical settings to support clinical reasoning and decision-making.

The analysis holds that AI-assisted reasoning should be examined as an unfolding sequence of decisions rather than a single isolated moment, beginning with the choice of whether to consult AI for a given clinical question. The process then moves through deciding how to engage with the tool, how to interpret its output, and finally whether to act on the guidance in a clinical case. Each stage, the authors say, introduces distinct points of vulnerability and potential failure, including inappropriate tool selection, incomplete or biased inputs, overconfidence in fluent responses, and failure to recognize underlying errors or appreciate clinical nuance. They add that these vulnerabilities are shaped by the same clinician factors that govern clinical reasoning more broadly, such as medical experience, clinical workload and how providers handle uncertainty. Early studies suggest strong performance on medical knowledge and reasoning tasks with the potential to reduce medical errors, but emerging evidence also highlights safety concerns, since outputs can contain clinically significant management errors that are not readily apparent to users.

The authors conclude that safe clinical implementation depends not merely on advancing model quality but on cultivating the clinician's ability to critically assess model responses. They say preparing clinicians to identify when algorithmic outputs must be questioned, verified or entirely set aside will be crucial as automated reasoning tools become more deeply embedded in routine patient care. Recognizing that AI-clinician collaboration is a continuous process, they argue, reveals key opportunities for targeted medical training. The article leaves open the central question of how to integrate these tools into practice to consistently improve patient outcomes.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike schedules virtual event on AI threats and agentic SOC shift
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced a virtual event titled The Next Era of Cyber Defense: Fighting AI-Powered Threats with AI, scheduled for December 9 in the Americas, December 10 in JAPAC and December 10 in Europe. The company said AI is changing the speed and scale of cyberattacks and that defenders need to keep pace. CrowdStrike leaders will give a special update on the latest AI threats, frontier AI readiness and the shift to the agentic SOC. Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike Senior Vice President of Counter Adversary Operations, will give a special AI threat briefing on the latest AI-enabled adversary activity. The briefing will include real-world examples of attackers putting agentic AI to work.

The event covers AI threats, frontier AI readiness and the shift to the agentic SOC, according to CrowdStrike. CrowdStrike describes its Next-Gen SIEM as the world's only AI-native SOC platform, a claim the company makes. CrowdStrike calls its threat intelligence offering the leader in cyber threat intelligence, backed by world-class research and elite threat hunting. CrowdStrike describes its endpoint security offering as the leader in EPP and EDR, built to secure the agentic endpoint. CrowdStrike lists Project QuiltWorks as an industry coalition mobilizing to close the frontier AI vulnerability gap at scale.

CrowdStrike says AI is changing the speed and scale of cyberattacks and defenders need to keep pace. The company says its event will give an update on the latest AI threats, frontier AI readiness and the shift to the agentic SOC. CrowdStrike says Meyers will brief on the latest AI-enabled adversary activity. The company says the briefing will show real-world examples of attackers putting agentic AI to work. CrowdStrike says its Falcon Complete service stops breaches across the entire attack surface with elite 24/7 managed detection and response.

CrowdStrike says its AI Security Services secure AI systems and operationalize AI in the SOC. The company says its Frontier AI Readiness and Resilience Service reduces frontier AI-driven risk as the time between patch and exploit continues to collapse. CrowdStrike says its Shadow AI Visibility Service discovers hidden AI tools, activity and agents across endpoint, cloud and SaaS. The company says its Automated AI Security Testing tests every AI model, application and agent for security weaknesses before deployment.

CrowdStrike says its Agentic Adversary Emulation red teams an environment to simulate real-world attacks and validate defenses. CrowdStrike says its AI Detection & Response detects, investigates and stops threats to AI systems with unified, runtime security. The company says its Agent Security secures AI agents across the agentic lifecycle, from development to adoption to runtime. CrowdStrike says its Supply Chain Security stops supply chain threats as coding agents introduce third-party packages at scale.

The company says its AI Observability evaluates agents pre-deployment and then observes their behavior and enforces accountability in production. CrowdStrike says its Seraphic Enterprise Browser secures the modern workforce by protecting users, data and AI in the browser. CrowdStrike says registration is open for the event. The company says the event is a virtual event.

CrowdStrike says the event features CrowdStrike leaders. The company says the event includes a special AI threat briefing from Meyers. The articles do not say what else the event will cover. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Spartanburg Water CEO says AI posts mislead as utility reviews outage cause
stories.Summary:
Guy Boyle, the CEO of Spartanburg Water, spoke at Monday's city council meeting to explain a water outage that lasted several days and affected residents across much of Spartanburg County, according to WSPA. He said the exact cause of the power blip that turned into the water outage is still unknown, but he noted that blips or loss of power, while very infrequent, are not uncommon. He said Spartanburg Water, alongside Duke Energy and their external electrical contractors, are in the preliminary stage of investigations into what happened. Teams reviewing the water timelines have determined that the outage was due to damage to the main 42-inch and secondary 24-inch lines rather than a lack of water. Boyle said the utility is looking at any design weaknesses, valve analysis, surge relief systems and additional levels of protection to mitigate against future events.

Boyle also addressed several topics that circulated on social media and among residents in the hours and days after the water went out, including AI-generated posts, the utility's relationship with Duke Energy, data centers and why residents did not receive direct notice. He called AI-generated photos depicting fake conversations between Duke Energy and Spartanburg Water, with each company blaming the other, incomplete, and said comments online indicating Duke caused the damage are both inaccurate and were not communicated by Spartanburg Water. He said the company considers Duke Energy a partner and that a post-mortem review of what led up to and caused the damage is underway. He said initial indicators show the power outage at the main plant may have lasted less than 10 seconds, but data is still being analyzed. He also said comments suggesting the lack of water had to do with data centers under construction or in development are fictional and irresponsible, noting that the meter that will serve NorthMark has not been ordered, installed or connected, and that other water service providers in the county meant some industry, including businesses in the Tiger River Industrial Park, was unaffected.

On communication, Boyle said comments on social media about a slow notification have merit and the utility recognizes that, explaining that its previous system does not distribute messages to all 276,000 customers simultaneously, so it relied on social media and traditional media. He said the situation had been corrected by Sunday when the advisory was canceled via the Spartanburg Emergency Management Division, and that the utility is already working on its notification system so it is better positioned to issue systemwide notifications in the future. He said ice machines in Lyman and Woodruff that were photographed working are serviced by the SJWD and WRWD water districts and were purposely left on so customers who needed ice would have access because those districts were unaffected. The systemwide boil water advisory was lifted Sunday, and Spartanburg Water asked anyone still experiencing cloudy water or air in their lines to call. Boyle said that while preliminary internal data supports a power outage, the plant has had power loss in the past without missing a beat, citing Hurricane Helene as an example when some infrastructure ran for nearly two weeks without grid power.

stories.Headline: Thinking Machines Lab releases Inkling 2 Mini local AI model
stories.Summary:
Thinking Machines Lab released the Inkling 2 Mini local AI model last Friday. This new open-weight model was created by the startup founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati. The release follows the earlier launch of the Inkling 2 Small model on November 5. This local AI is designed to match the performance of state-of-the-art models from eighteen months ago. It specifically targets tasks involving agentic coding, tool use, and document work.

The model weighs 26.4 billion parameters and runs on a MacBook with 32 GB of RAM. It also works on a powerful graphics card with 24 GB of VRAM or one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The weights are available on Hugging Face and the company platform called Tinker under Apache 2.0. It uses 24 layers in four blocks, where the middle two blocks run three times each. This looping technique allows 48 passes per token while only storing 24 physical layers.

Mira Murati founded Thinking Machines in February 2025 with about thirty researchers mostly from OpenAI. She promised that the first product from the company would include an open-source component. The company claims Inkling 2 Mini outperforms all open models under 100 billion parameters in agentic coding. It reportedly scored 79.2 percent on the SWE-bench Verified and 79.0 percent on the BrowseComp benchmark. These figures are self-reported by Thinking Machines and should be taken with a grain of salt.

The model is a local option for developers who need agentic coding and multimodal capabilities. It accepts text and images as input but only returns text to the user. Users may find it weaker in knowledge recall and following instructions in multi-turn conversations. In those specific areas, the model must yield to the Qwen3.8-27B model. The model is compared to Claude Opus 4.1, which scored 74.5 percent on the SWE-bench Verified.

Thinking Machines raised 2 billion dollars in July 2025 at a valuation of 12 billion dollars. The model uses a Mixture-of-Experts technique with 3.4 billion active parameters on a per-token basis. Training the looped model required 7.5 percent more compute than a model without these loops. However, an unlooped model needed 140 percent more inference compute to reach the same performance level. The team pruned experts during training and used a 1T-token distillation run to heal the model.

The model supports a context window of up to one million tokens for various tasks. It uses NVFP4 for expert layers and MXFP8 for the last four layers to remove loss. Future research variants may train with between one and five passes to test different results. The articles leave open whether other AI models will adopt this layer reuse technique. They also leave open how the model will perform in independent tests outside company reports.

Articles.Title: Inkling 2 Mini: 2026’s local AI outperforms last year’s Claude
Meet Thinking Machines Inkling 2 Mini: 26B Looped MoE Runs on a 32GB Mac
